whyItTastes: Beer adds a grain bitterness that water does not, and the simmer keeps the casing from splitting before the grill browns it. Pork and spice in the brat stay the main flavor. The Lake Michigan picnic habit is a long afternoon of this two-step, not a smokehouse cure.
authenticTouch: Discard the beer after simmering. It has touched raw sausage and is not a broth to serve.
method: Simmer fresh brats in beer and onions, then grill them to a safe center temperature.
served: On a hard roll with mustard and onion if you want them. The roll and the beer both contain wheat. Mustard would add a mustard allergen.
funFacts: Sheboygan brats are simmered in beer and then grilled, which is the local two-step.
Ordinary beer contains gluten, so this recipe is not gluten-free.
variations: A gluten-free beer would change the allergen claim only if the brat label is also free of wheat. This written recipe uses regular beer.
ingredients: 8 plain fresh pork bratwursts, no cheese
steps: Put the brats, beer, and onion in a pot and simmer about 15 minutes. Do not boil so hard that the casings split. The beer contains wheat.
Discard the beer and onion. Heat a grill to medium.
Grill the brats, turning, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C) and the casing is browned.
Serve on rolls, which also contain wheat. This plate is not gluten-free.

name: Door County Fish Boil
culture: Scandinavian American cooks on the Door Peninsula
flavor: Whitefish and potatoes boiled over a fire, salty, with butter at the table.
history: The Door County fish boil is a Scandinavian American kettle cook over an open fire: potatoes and whitefish in heavily salted water, often finished with a dramatic boil-over that throws off fish oils. It is not a grill. Immigrant fishing communities on the peninsula made the boil a public supper. This recipe keeps the kettle and skips any claim about a single first restaurant.
background: An open-fire fish boil, not a grilled fillet. Whitefish and potatoes are the core. Butter is served at the table.
whyItTastes: A hard salted boil seasons the potato skins and keeps the whitefish moist in a way a dry grill does not. The boil-over, when cooks throw fuel or fat on the fire so the pot erupts, carries off some of the fish oil. Butter at the end is the supper habit, dairy and all.
authenticTouch: This is a kettle over fire, not a grate. Do not call it a grilled fish. Stand back if you force a boil-over.
method: Boil potatoes, then whitefish, in salted water over an open fire until the fish flakes.
served: On plates with the potatoes, melted butter, and lemon. Cherry pie is a local supper ending and is not part of this pot.
funFacts: Door County fish boils are cooked in a kettle over open fire, not on a grill grate.
The custom is tied to Scandinavian American fishing communities on the Door Peninsula.
variations: Lake trout is sometimes boiled the same way when whitefish is scarce. Cook it to the same temperature.
steps: Set a heavy kettle over a steady open fire, or over a burner if you are indoors. This is a boil, not a grill.
Boil the potatoes in the salted water until they are nearly tender.
Add the whitefish and cook until the thickest steak reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes. A vigorous boil-over is a traditional way to throw off oil; stand back if you do it.
Lift out fish and potatoes. Serve with melted butter and lemon.

name: Minnesota Grilled Walleye
culture: Minnesota lake-country cooks grilling walleye
flavor: Mild, sweet walleye with butter, salt, and a light char.
history: Walleye is the state fish of Minnesota, and grilled fillets are a standard lake-country plate in summer. The fish is lean and mild, so the cook is short and the seasoning is light. This is a fillet on a grate, not a Door County boil and not a smoked whitefish.
background: Grilled walleye fillets with butter. A Minnesota lake plate. Keep the fish cold until it goes on the fire.
whyItTastes: Walleye is lean, so butter and a hot grate add the richness the fillet does not have on its own. Overcooking makes it cottony, which is why the plate is a quick grill rather than a smoke. Northern lakes are the reason the fish is on the table at all.
authenticTouch: Oil the grate and turn the fillet only once. Walleye sticks and then breaks if you fuss with it.
method: Grill walleye fillets over a hot fire until they flake.
served: Whole fillets with lemon. Potatoes or a green salad sit beside them. Butter is in the recipe.
funFacts: Walleye is the state fish of Minnesota.
The fillet is lean, so a short grill and a little butter keep it from drying.
variations: A broiler can finish the same fillets if a grill is impossible. Use the same temperature.
steps: Pat the fillets dry. Brush with butter and season with salt and pepper.
Heat a grill hot and oil the grate.
Grill, turning once, until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the fish is opaque and flakes.
Serve with lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Michigan Smoked Whitefish
culture: Great Lakes home cooks, in a fishery also worked by Anishinaabe communities and by commercial smokehouses
flavor: Hot-smoked whitefish, salty at the surface and moist inside.
history: Anishinaabe communities and later commercial smokehouses both have relationships with Great Lakes whitefish, and those practices are not the same. This recipe is a home hot-smoke to 145°F. It is not a treaty fishery, not a commercial license, and not a traditional preparation claimed for any nation. Leland's fish shacks are one place a traveler sees the commercial smoke.
background: A home hot-smoked whitefish. It does not stand in for Anishinaabe fishing practice or for a shop's cold-smoke formula.
whyItTastes: Whitefish is rich enough to take smoke without a heavy glaze. Salt on the surface and a moderate pit set the flake. A hot smoke cooks the fish; a cold smoke would be a preserving method this page does not teach.
authenticTouch: Buy the fish from a legal seller. Smoking it at home does not make the cook part of a treaty harvest.
method: Salt whitefish and hot-smoke it until it flakes and reaches a safe temperature.
served: Warm or slightly cooled, with potatoes or lemon. Bread would add wheat and is not in this recipe. Eat it within a few days from the refrigerator.
funFacts: Great Lakes whitefish is both an Anishinaabe food and a later commercial smokehouse fish, and those practices differ.
This page is a home hot-smoke to 145°F, not a treaty fishery and not a curing manual.
variations: Fillets smoke faster than a dressed whole fish. Measure the thickest part either way.
ingredients: Hardwood chunks for a hot smoke
steps: Salt and pepper the fillets. Refrigerate them while the smoker comes to about 250°F (121°C). This is a hot smoke, not a cure.
Smoke over indirect heat, with a clean fire rather than wet, smoldering chips.
Cook until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the fish is opaque and flakes.
Serve warm with lemon. This cook is not a commercial or treaty fishery.

name: Cleveland Grilled Kielbasa
culture: Polish American cooks in Cleveland grilling sausage with mustard and kraut
flavor: Grilled kielbasa with sharp mustard and sour sauerkraut.
history: Cleveland's Polish American tables grill kielbasa and eat it with mustard and sauerkraut. This plate does not require a beer simmer, which is how it differs from Sheboygan brats and from the Pennsylvania coal-region simmer. Sausage labels vary. Use a kielbasa whose label lists no wheat if you need the plate to stay gluten-free, and still read every line of the package.
background: Grilled sausage with mustard and kraut, no beer in the recipe. A Cleveland Polish American plate, not a Pennsylvania water simmer.
whyItTastes: Mustard and fermented cabbage are the sharp side of a salty smoked sausage, a pairing carried by Polish American groceries and church festivals. The grill only browns the casing. Without beer, nothing in the written method adds wheat besides what the sausage package might already contain.
authenticTouch: Heat a cooked kielbasa through. Do not assume every brand is fresh, gluten-free, or free of milk. The label decides.
method: Grill kielbasa and serve it with mustard and warmed sauerkraut. No beer is used.
served: Sliced, with kraut and mustard. A rye bun would add wheat; this recipe does not include the bun.
funFacts: This Cleveland plate is grilled sausage with mustard and sauerkraut, and the recipe uses no beer.
It is a different cook from Pennsylvania's simmered kielbasa and from Sheboygan's beer brats.
variations: If the only kielbasa you can buy lists wheat, drop the gluten-free claim and follow the label.
ingredients: 2 pounds smoked kielbasa whose label lists no wheat and no cheese
steps: Read the sausage label. This recipe is gluten-free only when the package lists no wheat. Brands differ. No beer is used.
Warm the sauerkraut in a small pot. Heat a grill to medium.
Grill the kielbasa until it browns. If it is fully cooked smoked sausage, heat the center to 165°F (74°C). If it is fresh and raw, cook it to 160°F (71°C).
Serve with mustard and kraut. Mustard is an allergen.

name: Indiana Fair Pork Chop
culture: Indiana fair and backyard cooks grilling a thick pork chop
flavor: A thick bone-in pork chop with a salty, peppery crust and a juicy center.
history: Thick bone-in pork chops, salted and peppered, are a standard plate at Indiana fairs and backyard grills. This one has no glaze. It is not the Iowa chop with mustard and apple, and it does not borrow a festival story beyond the fairground habit of cooking a plain chop over heat.
background: Salt and pepper on a thick chop. An Indiana fair and backyard plate, deliberately plain.
whyItTastes: A thick chop can take a hard sear and still stay moist at the bone, which is why fair cooks cut them heavy. Salt and pepper are the whole seasoning so the pork itself is the taste. Direct heat, not smoke and sauce, defines it against a pit shoulder.
authenticTouch: Buy chops at least an inch thick. A thin chop will be past temperature before the crust exists.
method: Grill thick bone-in pork chops with only salt and pepper.
served: Whole, on a plate. No glaze. Corn or a salad can sit beside them.
funFacts: The Indiana plate here is a thick bone-in chop with salt and pepper, without a sweet glaze.
It is written to stay distinct from the Iowa chop, which carries mustard and apple.
variations: A cooler side of the grill finishes a very thick chop if the outside browns too fast.
ingredients: 4 bone-in pork chops, about 1 to 1 1/4 inches thick
steps: Oil the chops lightly and season both sides with salt and pepper. Do not add a glaze.
Heat a grill for direct cooking, with a cooler zone.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes before serving.

name: Iowa Mustard-Glazed Pork Chop
culture: Iowa cooks glazing pork chops with mustard and apple
flavor: A thick pork chop with a sharp mustard and apple glaze.
history: Iowa raises a great deal of pork, and a glazed chop is a common supper. This one uses mustard and apple, which makes it a different plate from the salt-and-pepper Indiana fair chop. Mustard is an allergen here. The glaze is a home seasoning, not a state-fair prize recipe with a documented inventor.
background: Grilled pork chops with mustard and apple. Distinct from the plain Indiana chop. Contains mustard.
whyItTastes: Mustard cuts chop fat, and apple softens that sharpness into a glaze. Putting it on late keeps the sugars from burning, the same rule as any sweet finish on a hot grill. The pork stays the center, which fits a state where the chop is an ordinary cut rather than a specialty.
authenticTouch: Glaze in the last two minutes. Mustard and apple will bitter if they sit over direct flame the whole time.
method: Grill thick pork chops and finish them with a mustard and applesauce glaze.
served: Whole chops with the glaze spooned over. Potatoes fit beside them.
funFacts: This Iowa chop carries a mustard and apple glaze, so it is not the salt-and-pepper Indiana chop.
Mustard in the glaze is an allergen.
variations: Apple butter instead of applesauce makes a thicker glaze. Keep the mustard.
ingredients: 4 bone-in pork chops, about 1 inch thick
steps: Salt and pepper the chops. Stir mustard, applesauce, and vinegar into a glaze.
Heat a grill for direct cooking.
Grill the chops until the center reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes, brushing the glaze on at the end over lower heat so it does not burn.

name: Plains Grilled Bison Steak
culture: Modern grill cooks of bison, on plains where Lakota and other nations cooked bison long before ranches
flavor: Lean bison with a salted crust and a pink center.
history: Plains nations, including the Lakota, dried and fire-cooked bison long before ranches and rail shipments. This steak is a modern whole-muscle grill from ranch or market bison. It is not a ceremonial recipe, and it is not a dried-meat method. The temperature here is 145°F with a rest, because bison is lean and dries out if it is cooked like a well-done roast.
background: A ranch or market bison steak on a hot grill. It does not claim to be a Lakota ceremonial dish or a historical drying recipe.
whyItTastes: Bison is leaner than most beef, so the flavor is beefy without a thick fat cap, and a short hot grill is what keeps it tender. Salt is enough. The Plains relationship to this animal is older than the steakhouse cut, which is why the history and the recipe are not the same thing.
authenticTouch: Pull the steak at 145°F and rest it. Cooking bison to brisket temperatures will turn a steak dry and chalky.
method: Grill bison steaks quickly over a hot fire and rest them.
served: Sliced, with the juices. It does not need a sweet sauce.
funFacts: Lakota and other Plains nations dried and fire-cooked bison long before ranch steaks existed.
This is a modern whole-muscle grill, not a ceremonial recipe.
variations: A ribeye or strip from bison uses the same temperature. Do not treat it as brisket.
steps: Oil the steaks and season them with salt and pepper. Let the grill get hot.
Grill, turning once. Bison is lean, so do not walk away.
Cook until the center reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes. This is a market steak, not a ceremonial cook and not a drying recipe.

name: Dearborn Lamb Skewers
culture: Lebanese American cooks grilling lamb over charcoal in Dearborn
flavor: Charcoal lamb with garlic, salt, and a little allspice.
history: Dearborn is home to a large Lebanese American community, and charcoal lamb skewers are part of that home and restaurant table. No one restaurant invented the practice. The seasoning here is a simple garlic and allspice marinade a home cook can mix, not a secret house blend. The meat is lamb, cooked to a whole-muscle temperature and rested.
background: Lebanese American charcoal lamb in Dearborn. A skewer cook, not a claim that one shop owns the recipe.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat browns over charcoal, and garlic and allspice are seasonings Lebanese American cooks use without needing a sweet barbecue sauce. Cutting the meat into cubes shortens the cook so the inside stays juicy. Migration from Lebanon to industrial Detroit is why this fire sits in Dearborn rather than only on a Mediterranean coast.
authenticTouch: Keep the marinade refrigerated and grill the same day. Do not leave garlic in oil on the counter.
method: Marinate lamb cubes briefly and grill them on skewers over charcoal.
served: Off the skewers, with rice or a salad. A pita would add wheat and is not in this ingredient list.
funFacts: Dearborn's Lebanese American community has made charcoal lamb a local table, not the invention of one restaurant.
The marinade is used the same day and kept cold, because garlic in oil should not sit at room temperature.
variations: Beef cubes can be grilled the same way. This written recipe is lamb.
ingredients: 2 pounds lamb shoulder, cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes
steps: Toss the lamb with oil, garlic, salt, pepper, and allspice. Refrigerate it and grill it the same day. Do not store the garlic oil at room temperature.
Thread the cubes on metal skewers. Heat charcoal until it is hot.
Grill, turning, until the center of a cube reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes. Serve with rice or salad. Pita is not part of this recipe.

name: Upper Peninsula Venison Steak
culture: Upper Peninsula cooks grilling venison steaks
flavor: Lean venison with salt, pepper, and a hot-grill crust.
history: Deer is a major food in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, and a steak on a hot grill is a common way to cook a hindquarter. Wild venison can carry parasites, so some cooks take it to 160°F even though a whole-muscle steak is otherwise guided to 145°F and a rest. This page gives both. It is not a sausage cure and not a claim about a particular tribal hunt.
background: Grilled venison steak. Give wild meat the extra temperature caution. Farmed venison from a inspected seller is a different risk from a deer you shot.
whyItTastes: Venison is lean, with a flavor stronger than beef, so salt, pepper, and a short sear are the whole cook. A long stay on the grill dries it. Northern woods and a cold season are why the meat is on Upper Peninsula tables in the fall.
authenticTouch: If the venison is wild, consider 160°F. If it is inspected farmed meat and you accept the 145°F rest, say which one you cooked.
method: Grill venison steaks quickly and choose 145°F with a rest, or 160°F for wild meat.
served: Sliced against the grain. A sharp jelly is common and is not in this ingredient list.
funFacts: Wild venison can carry parasites, which is why some cooks take it to 160°F.
A whole-muscle steak is otherwise guided to 145°F and a 3-minute rest.
variations: Backstrap medallions use the same choice of temperatures and cook even faster.
safety: Cook whole-muscle venison to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes. Wild venison can carry parasites, so some cooks take it to 160°F (71°C).
steps: Oil, salt, and pepper the steaks. Heat the grill hot.
Grill, turning once. Venison dries out if it stays over the fire too long.
For inspected farmed steaks, cook to 145°F (63°C) and rest at least 3 minutes. For wild venison, some cooks continue to 160°F (71°C) because of parasite risk.
Slice against the grain and serve.

name: Santa Maria Tri-Tip
culture: Santa Maria Valley cooks grilling beef over red oak, in a ranch and vaquero beef culture
flavor: Beefy tri-tip with salt, pepper, garlic, and red-oak smoke.
history: Santa Maria tri-tip belongs to the California central coast and its ranch and vaquero beef culture. The local fire is red oak, and the cut is the triangular bottom sirloin. Pinquito beans, a small pink local bean, are often served beside the meat as a pairing, not as a step in this roast. The cook is an open grill, not a Southern offset pit.
background: Tri-tip over red oak on the central California coast. Western US fire. Beans and salsa can sit beside it and are separate recipes.
whyItTastes: Red oak gives a lighter smoke than mesquite, which suits a roast that is sliced at steak temperature rather than cooked to shreds. Salt, pepper, and garlic are the rub. The dry coast and an open grate brown the fat cap without a long stall.
authenticTouch: Slice across the grain. Tri-tip grain changes direction, so turn the knife when the slices start to look stringy.
method: Grill a salted tri-tip over red oak coals and rest it before slicing.
served: Sliced, with salsa. Pinquito or another small pink bean can be on the table and is not cooked inside this roast.
funFacts: Red oak is the wood Santa Maria names for tri-tip.
Pinquito beans are a small pink bean associated with the valley, served beside the meat rather than inside this recipe.
variations: Another oak is the workable substitute if coastal red oak is unavailable. Say you used it.
ingredients: Red oak for the fire, or another oak
steps: Mix salt, pepper, and garlic powder and rub the tri-tip. Rest it in the refrigerator if you season ahead.
Burn red oak, or another oak, down to coals in an open grill.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C). Local plates are often pink; this is the safety line used here.
Rest at least 3 minutes and slice across the grain.

name: Huli Huli Chicken
culture: Hawaiian cooks turning chickens in the style Ernest Morgado popularized
flavor: Sweet-salty grilled chicken with soy, pineapple, and ginger.
history: Ernest Morgado is the person Hawaii credits with huli huli chicken in the 1950s, chickens turned over a fire and brushed with a teriyaki-like sauce. Huli means turn. The sauce uses soy sauce, so this plate contains soy and wheat and is not vegan. It is a twentieth-century Hawaiian grill, not a kalua pig and not an imu.
background: Rotisserie or grill chicken with a soy and pineapple baste. A Hawaiian plate tied to Morgado's 1950s chicken, separate from kalua pork.
whyItTastes: Soy, pineapple, and ginger make a salty-sweet glaze that caramelizes when the bird turns over charcoal. Turning, which the name names, keeps one side from burning while the sugar browns. Kiawe charcoal is a common Hawaiian grill fuel if you can get it; ordinary charcoal still cooks the chicken.
authenticTouch: Turn the chicken often and move it off the highest flame once the glaze goes on. The sugar in soy and pineapple will scorch.
method: Baste chicken with a soy, pineapple, and ginger sauce and cook it on a rotisserie or a covered grill, turning it.
served: Jointed, with rice. Rice is the usual starch. The soy sauce already makes the dish not gluten-free.
funFacts: Huli means turn, which is what the cook does to the chickens.
Ernest Morgado is credited in Hawaii with this chicken in the 1950s.
variations: Halves on a grill, turned often, are the home stand-in for a long rotisserie.
steps: Stir soy sauce, pineapple juice, brown sugar, ketchup, ginger, garlic, and vinegar. Soy sauce brings soy and wheat. Reserve some sauce that has not touched raw chicken for a final brush.
Salt is already in the soy. Put the chicken on a rotisserie or over indirect grill heat. Turn it often.
Baste with the portion that touched the raw chicken only while the bird is still cooking. Cook until the thigh, away from bone, reaches 165°F (74°C).
Brush with the clean reserved sauce in the last minutes, rest, and serve. Do not serve the chicken rare.

name: Kalua Pig
culture: Native Hawaiian imu cooking, with a labeled home-pot version
yieldText: about 10 servings from a home pot
flavor: Very salty, tender shredded pork.
history: Kalua pig is pork cooked in an imu, a Native Hawaiian earth oven of heated stones, traditionally seasoned with salt. An imu is a specific oven and a specific practice. This recipe is a covered pot or oven roast, labeled as not an imu. It is a respectful home stand-in for the salt and the tenderness, and it does not claim that a Dutch oven is the ceremony.
background: A covered-pot home version of kalua pig. It is not an imu. Native Hawaiian earth-oven cooking is the source tradition.
whyItTastes: Salt and a long enclosed cook turn shoulder collagen soft and leave the pork tasting of pork, not of a sweet glaze. A real imu also tastes of the wood, the leaves, and the steam in the ground, which a pot does not reproduce. Saying so is more useful than pretending liquid smoke is a pit.
authenticTouch: Call the pot a pot. If you are invited to a real imu, that is someone else's oven and someone else's lead.
method: Salt a pork shoulder and cook it covered, with a little water, until it shreds. This is not an imu.
served: Shredded, with its juices, beside rice or cabbage. It is salty on purpose.
funFacts: An imu is a Hawaiian earth oven of heated stones. A covered pot is not an imu.
Kalua pig is seasoned with salt. This home version does not add a sweet glaze.
variations: Banana or ti leaves are used in a real imu. They are not required for this covered pot, and the pot is still not an imu if you add them.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon Hawaiian salt or kosher salt for the fat side
1 tablespoon Hawaiian salt or kosher salt for the meat side
steps: Score the fat lightly and rub the salt over the shoulder. This covered pot is the home version. It is not an imu.
Put the shoulder in a heavy pot or a roasting pan with the water. Cover tightly.

Cook at 325°F (163°C) until the center reaches about 195–205°F (90–96°C) and the pork shreds. Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest; kalua-style shoulder is taken higher for tenderness.
Rest, shred, and moisten with the pot juices. Tell the table this was an oven, not an earth oven.

name: Northwest Cedar-Plank Salmon
culture: Home grill cooks on the Northwest Coast, where salmon practices differ by nation
flavor: Salmon with a light cedar smell, salt, and a moist flake.
history: Northwest Coast practices differ by nation, including Coast Salish, Nuu-chah-nulth, Tlingit, Haida, and others. Salmon is central to many of those foodways, and the methods are not one recipe. This is a home plank grill, not a potlatch dish. The country of the recipe as written is the United States, and salmon cookery of this coast is also Canadian.
background: A home cedar-plank salmon. It is not a potlatch dish and not a single nation's recipe. Soak an untreated plank.
whyItTastes: The wet plank steams the salmon a little while the cedar perfumes the surface, and a hot grill underneath finishes it. Salt is enough because the fish is already rich. The plank is a backyard technique, which is why it should not be described as a ceremonial cook.
authenticTouch: Use an untreated cedar plank and soak it. A varnished board is not a cooking tool.
method: Grill a salted salmon fillet on a soaked cedar plank until it flakes.
served: Lifted off the plank in portions, with lemon. Do not eat the plank.
funFacts: Coast Salish, Nuu-chah-nulth, Tlingit, Haida, and other Northwest Coast nations do not share one salmon recipe.
A plank on a home grill is not a potlatch dish.
variations: A covered grill helps the top of a thick fillet cook before the plank scorches.
ingredients: 1 untreated cedar plank, soaked in water for at least 1 hour
steps: Soak the untreated plank. Do not use a finished or painted board. This is a home grill, not a potlatch.
Salt and pepper the salmon. Heat a grill to medium-high and set the soaked plank on it until it begins to smell aromatic, not until it is in flames.
Lay the salmon on the plank, cover the grill if you can, and cook until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the fish flakes and looks opaque.
Serve off the plank with lemon. Discard the plank if it has charred through.

name: New Mexico Green Chile Pork
culture: New Mexico cooks stewing pork with roasted green chile
flavor: Pork simmered with roasted Hatch or other New Mexico green chile, savory and hot to the degree the chiles are.
history: Pork with roasted green chile is a New Mexico plate, tied to the Hatch Valley and to other New Mexico chile fields. It is not Texas barbecue, and it does not use a brisket rub. Heat varies with the field and the year. This version roasts the chiles, then cooks pork shoulder in them until it is tender.
background: New Mexico green chile pork. A chile stew, not a Lockhart smoke and not a sweet glaze. The chile's heat is part of the ingredient, not a fixed number.
whyItTastes: Roasting green chile brings out a grassy, slightly bitter sweetness that canned jalapeño does not copy. Pork shoulder fat stands up to that chile. High-desert cultivation and a late-summer harvest are why the dish belongs to New Mexico rather than to a generic pepper sauce.
authenticTouch: Taste the chile before you add all of it. Hatch and other New Mexico chiles can be mild or very hot in the same bushel.
method: Roast New Mexico green chiles, then simmer pork shoulder in them until the meat is tender.
served: In a bowl, with tortillas or rice. Flour tortillas would add wheat; corn tortillas keep this batch gluten-free.
funFacts: Hatch, New Mexico, is a center of the green-chile harvest, and this pork is not a Texas barbecue.
The heat of New Mexico green chile changes with the crop, so taste before you commit the whole batch.
variations: Frozen roasted New Mexico green chile is a workable stand-in when fresh Hatch is out of season.
ingredients: 3 pounds pork shoulder, cut into chunks
1 1/2 pounds Hatch or other New Mexico green chiles
steps: Roast the chiles on a hot grill or under a broiler until blistered. Steam them in a covered bowl, peel them, and chop them. Taste one before you add them all.
Salt the pork and brown it in a heavy pot. Add onion, garlic, cumin, chiles, and water.
Cover and simmer until the pork reaches about 195–205°F (90–96°C) and is easy to shred. Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest; this stew goes further so the shoulder softens.
Taste for salt. Serve with corn tortillas, not as a Texas brisket plate.

name: Nevada Basque Lamb Chops
culture: Basque American sheepherder families and their restaurants in northern Nevada
flavor: Lamb chops with garlic, salt, and a hot-grill crust.
history: Basque immigrants worked as sheepherders in Nevada through the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and lamb stayed on the table in towns such as Elko. These chops are a simple grill: salt, pepper, and garlic. This page does not invent a festival and does not claim a single boarding house wrote the recipe.
background: Grilled lamb chops in the Basque American sheep-camp and boarding-house orbit of northern Nevada. A home grill, not a invented fair.
whyItTastes: Lamb from that sheep economy is the ingredient, and garlic and salt are enough because the fat browns on a hot fire. The Great Basin's sheep camps are why Basque cooking is part of rural Nevada rather than only an imported restaurant theme. A short grill keeps the chop pink at the safety line used here.
authenticTouch: Pull chops at 145°F and rest them. Lamb fat flares, so keep a cooler side of the grill.
method: Rub lamb chops with garlic, salt, and pepper and grill them over a hot fire.
served: Whole chops, with beans or a salad. No special sauce is required.
funFacts: Basque sheepherders worked flocks in Nevada in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
Elko is one of the northern Nevada towns where that lamb table is still part of local cooking.
variations: A small roast uses the same seasoning and must still reach 145°F with a 3-minute rest, with a longer cook.
steps: Rub the chops with garlic, oil, salt, and pepper. Keep them cold until the grill is hot, and cook them the same day.
Heat the grill hot and leave a cooler zone for flare-ups.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes. Serve without a sweet glaze.

name: Colorado Ranch Lamb Chops
culture: Ranch-country cooks in Colorado grilling lamb chops
flavor: Plain grilled lamb, salty and peppery, with a browned fat edge.
history: Colorado ranch country raises lamb, especially on the western slope and in the northwest of the state. These chops are salt and pepper on a hot grill. They are not the garlic-heavy Nevada Basque chop, and this page does not invent a festival to explain them. The distinction is the plain seasoning and the ranch supply of lamb.
background: Salt-and-pepper lamb chops from Colorado ranch country. No fabricated fair. Not the Basque garlic marinade used in the Nevada entry.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat and a hot grate make the crust, and salt and pepper stay out of the way. High, dry air and a quick grill brown the surface before the lean meat dries. The plate tastes like the animal because nothing sweet is added.
authenticTouch: Do not borrow the Basque garlic rub if you want this plate to stay the Colorado one. Salt and pepper are the recipe.
method: Grill lamb chops with salt and pepper only.
served: Whole chops. Beans or potatoes can sit beside them.
funFacts: Colorado ranch country raises lamb, and this chop is only salt and pepper on a hot grill.
It is written as a different plate from Nevada Basque lamb, which uses garlic.
variations: Shoulder chops need a slightly longer cook than loin chops. Use the thermometer, not the minute count.
steps: Oil the chops and season them with salt and pepper only.
Heat a grill hot, with a cooler zone.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest at least 3 minutes. Do not add a garlic marinade if you are cooking this Colorado plate.

name: Owensboro Burgoo
culture: Western Kentucky barbecue crowds cooking a community meat-and-vegetable kettle
flavor: A thick stew of chicken, beef, corn, and lima beans, peppery and long-cooked.
history: Burgoo is a community kettle associated with western Kentucky barbecues, including the mutton picnics around Owensboro. It is not a single nineteenth-century recipe this page can verify, so none is claimed. This pot uses chicken and beef with vegetables. Cooks have used other meats, including mutton, when that was what the picnic had.
background: A Kentucky barbecue stew, not a settled antique formula. Chicken and beef are both cooked through. It often sits beside mutton rather than replacing it.
whyItTastes: Long simmering turns several meats and a sack of vegetables into one spoonable pot, which is how a picnic feeds a line. Black pepper and tomato keep it savory instead of sweet. The same western Kentucky fires that cook mutton are why burgoo belongs on that table.
authenticTouch: Simmer until the vegetables collapse and the stew thickens. A thin soup is not yet burgoo.
method: Simmer chicken and beef with vegetables until the meats are safe to eat and the stew is thick.
served: In bowls, beside mutton or on its own, with bread if you want it. Bread would add wheat.
funFacts: Burgoo is a community kettle associated with western Kentucky barbecues, not a single verified nineteenth-century recipe.
Owensboro picnic tables have served it beside mutton.
variations: Lamb can replace the beef if you are cooking it next to a mutton barbecue. Give it the same long simmer.
steps: Put chicken, beef, onion, potato, tomato, salt, pepper, and water in a large pot.
Simmer until the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part and the beef is at least 145°F (63°C) and tender. Keep simmering so the meats soften in the stew.
Add lima beans and corn and cook until the vegetables are tender and the stew is thick. Frozen limas still need to be heated through in the pot.
Remove chicken bones, shred the meat back in, and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Hickory-Smoked Turkey
culture: Appalachian and Southern holiday cooks smoking turkey over hickory
flavor: Turkey with a mild hickory smoke, salt, and pepper.
history: A hickory-smoked turkey, breast or whole bird, is a holiday roast in the southern Appalachians and across the inland South. Hickory is the local hardwood. This recipe uses a bone-in breast so a home smoker can finish it in an afternoon. It is not a cured turkey and not a pork shoulder.
background: Holiday turkey smoked over hickory. Poultry must reach 165°F. The mountain and Southern wood is the point, not a sweet glaze.
whyItTastes: Turkey is lean, so hickory smoke does the seasoning that a fatty pork shoulder would get from its own drippings. Salt and pepper in the rub keep the skin savory. A moderate pit, not a raging grill, cooks the breast before the smoke turns harsh.
authenticTouch: Take the temperature in the thickest breast, not touching bone. A pop-up timer is a worse guide than a thermometer.
method: Salt a turkey breast and smoke it over hickory until the meat is at a safe poultry temperature.
served: Sliced, warm or cold, as a holiday meat. Gravy is optional and not in this ingredient list.
funFacts: Hickory is the smoke wood for this holiday turkey in the southern mountains and the inland South.
A breast is the practical home cut; a whole bird uses the same final temperature in the thickest part.
variations: A whole turkey takes longer. Measure the breast and the thigh, and do not stop until both are at temperature.
steps: Dry the turkey breast and rub it with salt, pepper, and paprika. Refrigerate it while the smoker heats.
Smoke over indirect hickory heat at about 275°F (135°C).
Cook until the thickest part of the breast, not touching bone, reaches 165°F (74°C).
Rest at least 10 minutes before slicing. Do not serve turkey rare. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Eastern North Carolina Vinegar Sauce
culture: Eastern North Carolina pit cooks seasoning chopped hog
flavor: Sharp vinegar with red pepper, black pepper, and salt, and no tomato.
history: Eastern North Carolina sauce is vinegar, pepper, and salt. Tomato is not part of it, which is how a cook tells it from Lexington dip. It dresses chopped whole hog, or the home shoulder-and-belly version of that plate. No single inventor owns the formula.
background: A vinegar-pepper sauce with no tomato. It is the seasoning for eastern Carolina pork, not a sweet glaze and not a ketchup dip.
whyItTastes: Vinegar cuts hog fat, and cayenne and black pepper supply the heat that a tomato sauce would sweeten away. In a humid climate the sharpness stays bright instead of cloying. The sauce is the barbecue, as much as the smoke is.
authenticTouch: Do not add ketchup. If the sauce turns red from tomato, you have left eastern Carolina.
method: Stir vinegar, water, salt, and pepper. Warm it only enough to dissolve the salt.
served: On chopped pork, and in a bottle on the table so people can add more.
funFacts: Eastern North Carolina sauce has vinegar and pepper and no tomato.
Lexington dip is the neighbor that adds a little ketchup. This one does not.
variations: More crushed red pepper makes it hotter. The base stays vinegar.
steps: Stir vinegar, water, salt, red pepper, and black pepper in a saucepan. There is no tomato in this sauce.
Warm over low heat about 5 minutes, just until the salt dissolves. It does not need to boil.
Cool it. This is a sauce, not a meat cook and not a canning recipe. Keep it refrigerated and use it within a week.
Spoon it over chopped pork that has already been cooked to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). The sauce itself has no meat temperature.

name: Lexington Dip
culture: Piedmont North Carolina cooks reddening a vinegar dip with a little tomato
flavor: Vinegar dip blushed with ketchup, still thin and peppery.
history: Lexington dip is the Piedmont sauce: vinegar with a little ketchup or tomato, plus pepper and salt. It is different from eastern North Carolina sauce, which has no tomato. The dip seasons pork shoulder and also dresses red slaw. This page does not name an inventor.
background: A thin vinegar-and-ketchup dip for Lexington shoulder. It is not the tomato-free eastern sauce and not a thick city glaze.
whyItTastes: Most of the flavor is still vinegar, so the pork stays sharp, and a small amount of ketchup adds color and a little sweetness. Pepper keeps it from tasting like a mild tomato soup. The dip is thin because it is meant to soak chopped shoulder, not to coat it like paint.
authenticTouch: Stop at about one part ketchup to three parts vinegar. More ketchup and you have left the dip.
method: Stir vinegar, ketchup, water, salt, and pepper. Do not boil it down into a thick sauce.
served: On chopped pork shoulder and in red slaw. Put a bottle on the table.
funFacts: Lexington dip contains a little ketchup or tomato. Eastern vinegar sauce does not.
The same dip is used to dress Lexington red slaw.
variations: Tomato paste instead of ketchup keeps the dip a shade less sweet. Use less of it.
steps: Stir vinegar, ketchup, water, salt, and both peppers until the ketchup is dissolved and the dip is thin.
Do not cook it into a paste. Taste it. Vinegar should lead and tomato should follow.
Refrigerate it and use it within a week. This is not a canning recipe.
Serve it on pork shoulder that has been cooked to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). The dip itself is not a meat cook.

name: South Carolina Mustard Barbecue Sauce
culture: Midlands South Carolina cooks, in a mustard style widely linked to German settlement
flavor: Yellow mustard, vinegar, and a little sugar, tangy rather than sweet.
history: The mustard sauce of the South Carolina Midlands is widely linked to German settlement there. That is an association, not a proven single origin, and this recipe does not crown an inventor. It is the yellow sauce for pork shoulder, different from vinegar-only eastern Carolina and from Lexington's ketchup dip. Mustard is an allergen.
background: A Midlands mustard sauce. Yellow mustard is the body of it. It is not a tomato barbecue sauce.
whyItTastes: Mustard brings acid and a sharp aroma that cuts pork fat, and vinegar keeps the sauce pourable. A little sugar rounds the raw edge of the mustard without turning the bowl into molasses. The yellow color is how the Midlands plate is recognized.
authenticTouch: Warm it only until the sugar dissolves. A long boil dulls the mustard.
method: Stir yellow mustard with vinegar and sugar and warm it briefly.
served: On chopped pork and in a bowl beside the meat. It also seasons some pots of hash.
funFacts: Midlands mustard sauce is widely linked to German settlement, which is not a documented single inventor.
Yellow mustard is an allergen in this sauce.
variations: A pinch of cayenne makes it hotter. This written sauce has no chile.
steps: Stir mustard, vinegar, brown sugar, salt, and pepper in a saucepan.
Warm over low heat about 10 minutes, until the sugar dissolves. Do not boil it hard.
Cool and refrigerate. Use within a week. This is not a canning recipe. Mustard is an allergen.
Serve with pork cooked to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). The sauce itself contains no meat.

name: Alabama White Sauce
culture: Decatur barbecue cooks following the Big Bob Gibson mayonnaise sauce
flavor: Cool, peppery mayonnaise loosened with vinegar.
history: Alabama white sauce comes from Big Bob Gibson's barbecue in Decatur in the 1920s, a mayonnaise and vinegar sauce for smoked chicken. It is a documented restaurant sauce, not an ancient folk recipe. Mayonnaise means egg. The sauce is not vegan, and it should not be boiled.
background: A cold mayonnaise sauce for smoked chicken. Egg is in it. It is not a tomato sauce and not a vinegar-only mop.
whyItTastes: Mayonnaise carries black pepper and cayenne onto smoked chicken skin, and vinegar keeps the fat from tasting flat. Sugar, just a little, takes the edge off the acid. Because the base is already an emulsion, heat would break it, so the sauce stays cold against hot chicken.
authenticTouch: Whisk it and refrigerate it. Do not simmer mayonnaise. Use a mayonnaise made from egg and oil, and keep it out of the sun.
method: Whisk mayonnaise, vinegar, pepper, and a little sugar. Serve it cold.
served: On or beside smoked chicken. It is also used on turkey by some cooks. This batch is the sauce alone.
funFacts: Big Bob Gibson in Decatur put this mayonnaise sauce on smoked chicken in the 1920s.
The egg in the mayonnaise means the sauce is not vegan.
variations: A spoon of prepared horseradish makes it sharper. Leave it out if you want the Decatur baseline.
ingredients: 1 cup mayonnaise made from egg, oil, and vinegar
steps: Whisk mayonnaise, vinegar, pepper, cayenne, salt, and sugar until smooth.
Do not heat the sauce. Boiling will break the mayonnaise.
Refrigerate it immediately and use it within a few days. Do not leave it at room temperature more than 2 hours.
Serve it with chicken that has been cooked to 165°F (74°C). The sauce itself is egg and vinegar, not a meat cook.

name: Kansas City Barbecue Sauce
culture: Kansas City restaurants building a thick sweet sauce for ribs and burnt ends
flavor: Thick, sweet, and smoky-tasting tomato sauce with molasses.
history: Kansas City's table sauce is thick, tomato-sweet, and darkened with molasses, the glaze associated with the city's ribs and burnt ends. Henry Perry is the early barbecue seller local history credits; the thick sauce is the later restaurant style, and this page does not claim he bottled this exact formula. Molasses is not honey. Ordinary Worcestershire in the pot contains anchovy and usually wheat.
background: A thick molasses-tomato sauce. Not gluten-free, because of Worcestershire, and not vegetarian, because of the anchovy in that ingredient.
whyItTastes: Molasses adds a bitter-sweet depth that plain sugar does not, and tomato and vinegar keep it from being only sweet. A simmer thickens it so it clings to ribs at the end of a smoke. Kansas City's railroad stockyards and later restaurants made this heavy sauce the city's signal, against the thinner dips of the Carolinas.
authenticTouch: Simmer until it coats a spoon, then stop. Cooked too long, the sugar turns harsh. Put it on meat late in the cook.
method: Simmer ketchup, molasses, vinegar, and Worcestershire into a thick sauce.
served: On ribs, burnt ends, or in a cup beside sliced meat. It is a finishing sauce, not a mop for the whole smoke.
funFacts: This Kansas City sauce uses molasses, not honey.
Ordinary Worcestershire sauce contains anchovy and usually wheat, so the sauce is not gluten-free.
variations: A gluten-free Worcestershire, if the label truly has no wheat, would change only that allergen. This recipe uses the ordinary kind.
steps: Stir ketchup, molasses, brown sugar, vinegar, Worcestershire, paprika, and pepper in a saucepan. Molasses is not honey. Ordinary Worcestershire contains fish and usually wheat.
Simmer about 20 minutes, stirring, until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon.
Cool and refrigerate. Use within a week. This is not a canning recipe.
Brush it on ribs only near the end of cooking, after the meat is approaching about 195°F (90°C), so the sugar does not burn for hours.

name: Memphis Dry Rub
culture: Memphis pit cooks seasoning pork before a dry smoke
flavor: Paprika, salt, black pepper, and a little brown sugar.
history: A Memphis dry rub is the seasoning on ribs that are served without sauce on the meat. Paprika, salt, pepper, and sugar are the core, and the sugar helps the bark color. It is not the wet Memphis sauce, and it is not a salt-and-pepper-only Texas rub. The sugar here is ordinary brown sugar, not honey.
background: A dry spice mix for Memphis ribs. No sauce is part of this rub. It is a pantry mix, not a cooked condiment.
whyItTastes: Paprika and a little sugar brown in hickory smoke and make the crust people expect on a dry rib. Salt seasons the pork underneath. Leaving out tomato and molasses is the decision that keeps a dry rib dry.
authenticTouch: Rub the meat and then leave it alone. Do not oil it so heavily that the spices steam instead of crusting.
method: Stir paprika, salt, pepper, sugar, and garlic powder. Store the mix dry.
served: Pressed onto pork ribs or shoulder before a smoke. Sauce, if any, stays off the dry-rib plate.
funFacts: A Memphis dry rub uses paprika, salt, pepper, and sugar, and the rib under it is served without sauce.
The sugar in this rub is brown sugar, not honey.
variations: A little cayenne makes the rub hotter. The base stays paprika and pepper.
steps: Stir paprika, salt, pepper, brown sugar, garlic powder, and onion powder in a bowl.
Store the rub in a dry jar. It is not cooked, and it is not a canning recipe.
Press it onto pork before smoking. Do not add sauce to a dry rib.
Cook those ribs to about 195–203°F (90–95°C) for tenderness. Pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) after a 3-minute rest. The rub itself has no internal temperature.

name: Texas Dalmatian Rub
culture: Central Texas meat-market cooks seasoning beef with salt and coarse pepper
flavor: Only salt and coarse black pepper.
history: The Central Texas rub called Dalmatian is salt and coarse black pepper, nothing else, and the speckled look suggested the name. It is the seasoning on Lockhart-style brisket and on beef plate ribs. Sugar, paprika, and garlic are left out on purpose. The mix is gluten-free, dairy-free, and nut-free because those ingredients are not in it.
background: Salt and coarse pepper only. Not a Memphis paprika rub and not a sweet Kansas City sauce. A dry mix for beef.
whyItTastes: Coarse pepper toasts in post-oak smoke and makes the bark, while salt seasons the beef all the way through a long cook. Extra spices would cover the meat, which is the opposite of the meat-market idea. The wood, not the rub, supplies the smoke.
authenticTouch: Use coarse pepper, not fine dust. Fine pepper disappears into the salt and does not speckle the crust.
method: Stir equal parts kosher salt and coarse black pepper. Stop there.
served: Rubbed onto brisket, beef ribs, or other Central Texas beef before the smoke.
funFacts: A Dalmatian rub is only salt and coarse black pepper.
Central Texas brisket uses this rub and treats sauce as optional.
variations: Some cooks shift the ratio toward more pepper. They still add nothing else.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons kosher salt for the fat side
2 tablespoons coarse black pepper for the fat side
1 tablespoon kosher salt for the meat side
1 tablespoon coarse black pepper for the meat side
steps: Stir the salt and the coarse pepper together. Do not add sugar, paprika, or garlic.
Keep the mix dry in a jar. It is not cooked.
Coat beef on every side before a low smoke over post oak or other oak.
For brisket, cook to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). Whole beef is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a rest. The rub itself is only salt and pepper.

name: Texas Beef Mop
culture: Central Texas pit cooks basting beef during a long smoke
flavor: A thin, savory basting liquid of beef stock, vinegar, and Worcestershire.
history: A Texas beef mop is a thin liquid brushed on brisket or beef ribs during a long cook, not a thick table sauce. Beef stock, vinegar, and Worcestershire keep the surface moist without becoming the point of the meat. Salt and pepper remain the rub. Ordinary Worcestershire contains anchovy and usually wheat, so this mop is not gluten-free and not vegetarian.
background: A thin basting mop, not a Kansas City glaze and not a finishing sauce. It uses cooked beef stock. Do not mop with raw meat juices that have not been boiled.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and a little Worcestershire refresh the bark during a cook that would otherwise dry the surface, while beef stock echoes the meat instead of sweetening it. Because the mop is thin, it does not hide the post-oak smoke. It is a tool during the cook, which is why it should not be confused with sauce on the side.
authenticTouch: Mop lightly. A soaking-wet brisket steams and softens the bark you waited for.
method: Simmer beef stock, vinegar, and Worcestershire into a thin mop and brush it on sparingly.
served: Used on beef during the smoke. It is not usually poured over the sliced meat.
funFacts: A mop is a thin baste used during the cook, not the same thing as a thick table sauce.
Worcestershire in this mop brings fish and, in ordinary brands, wheat.
variations: Some pits use only beef stock and a splash of vinegar. This one includes Worcestershire.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups cooked beef stock, not raw drippings
steps: Combine cooked beef stock, vinegar, Worcestershire, and pepper. Ordinary Worcestershire contains anchovy and usually wheat.
Simmer 10 minutes. If you started from anything that touched raw meat, boil it fully before it goes back on cooked food.
Cool what you will not use immediately and refrigerate it. This is not a canning recipe.
Brush a little on beef during a smoke. Finish the brisket at about 195–205°F (90–96°C). Do not soak the bark.

name: Kentucky Black Dip
culture: Owensboro cooks dressing mutton with a Worcestershire dip
flavor: Dark, peppery, and sharp from Worcestershire and vinegar.
history: Black dip is the dark sauce Owensboro serves with mutton barbecue. Worcestershire and black pepper dominate it, which is why it looks nearly black beside a tomato sauce. It belongs to the parish-picnic mutton table, not to a pork shoulder with Carolina vinegar. Ordinary Worcestershire contains anchovy and usually wheat.
background: A Worcestershire-heavy dip for mutton or lamb. Not a sweet glaze. Not vegetarian, because of the anchovy in Worcestershire.
whyItTastes: Mutton is stronger than young lamb or pork, and a peppery, salty dip cuts that flavor instead of covering it with sugar. Vinegar thins the Worcestershire so it works as a dip rather than as a glaze. Western Kentucky picnic pits made this the companion to sheep, which is why the sauce is not a generic steak sauce.
authenticTouch: Keep it thin enough to spoon, not boil it into a syrup. The darkness should come from Worcestershire, not from burnt sugar.
method: Stir Worcestershire, vinegar, water, and black pepper and warm the dip briefly.
served: Beside chopped or sliced mutton, and on the meat if people want it.
funFacts: Black dip is the Worcestershire sauce Owensboro serves with mutton.
Ordinary Worcestershire contains anchovy and usually wheat, so this dip is not gluten-free.
variations: A pinch of allspice is used by some picnic cooks. This written dip relies on pepper.
steps: Stir Worcestershire, water, vinegar, pepper, and allspice. Ordinary Worcestershire contains fish and usually wheat.
Warm the dip 5 minutes. Do not reduce it to a glaze.
Cool and refrigerate. Use within a week. This is not a canning recipe.
Serve with lamb or mutton that has reached at least 145°F (63°C) and rested, or about 195°F (90°C) if you are chopping a shoulder.

name: Santa Maria Salsa
culture: Santa Maria Valley cooks chopping fresh tomato salsa for tri-tip
flavor: Fresh tomato, onion, chile, and cilantro, chunky and bright.
history: Santa Maria tri-tip is served with a fresh tomato salsa, not with a sweet barbecue sauce. The salsa is chopped tomato, onion, chile, and cilantro, and it belongs to the central-coast beef plate. It is not a cooked Texas mop and not a molasses glaze. This version is gluten-free, dairy-free, and nut-free.
background: A fresh salsa for tri-tip. Uncooked. Not a bottle of sweet barbecue sauce. Western US table habit beside red-oak beef.
whyItTastes: Cold raw tomato and onion cut the richness of grilled beef the way a pickle does in other regions, and cilantro and green chile add a fresh top note. Because the salsa is not cooked, it stays bright against smoke. The dry central coast grows the beef and the tomatoes that end up on the same plate.
authenticTouch: Salt it and let it sit 15 minutes so the tomato makes a little juice. Do not cook it.
method: Chop tomatoes, onion, jalapeño, and cilantro and season them with salt and lime.
served: Cold, beside sliced tri-tip. It can also go on beans. It is not brushed on the roast while it cooks.
funFacts: Santa Maria salsa is a fresh tomato relish for tri-tip, not a sweet cooked barbecue sauce.
This batch is uncooked and contains no gluten, dairy, or nuts.
variations: Leave the jalapeño seeds in if you want more heat. Taste the chile first.
steps: Chop the tomatoes, onion, jalapeño, and cilantro. Stir in salt and lime juice.
Let the salsa sit 15 minutes in the refrigerator so it juices. Do not cook it.
Taste for salt and heat. This is not a canning recipe. Keep it cold, below 40°F (4°C) if you are holding it, and use it within a few days.
Serve it beside tri-tip that has been cooked to 145°F (63°C) and rested. Do not paint it on the meat over the fire.

name: Eastern North Carolina Vinegar Slaw
culture: Eastern North Carolina cooks dressing cabbage with vinegar, not mayonnaise
flavor: Crisp cabbage in a sweet-sharp vinegar dressing, with no mayonnaise.
history: Eastern North Carolina coleslaw is dressed with vinegar, sugar, and pepper, in the same spirit as the hog sauce, and it does not use mayonnaise. It sits beside chopped pork. It is not Lexington red slaw, which is tinted with dip, and it is not a creamy picnic slaw.
background: A vinegar slaw with no egg and no dairy. A side for eastern Carolina barbecue. The cabbage stays crisp.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and a little sugar match the sharp pork sauce so the plate tastes like one idea. Cabbage adds crunch that chopped meat does not have. Leaving out mayonnaise keeps the slaw from going dull in a warm picnic yard as fast as a creamy slaw would, though it still needs the refrigerator if it sits.
authenticTouch: Salt the cabbage, wait, and squeeze out a little water before you dress it. Wet cabbage makes a watery slaw.
method: Dress shredded cabbage with vinegar, sugar, salt, and pepper. No mayonnaise.
served: Cold, beside chopped hog. It can go on a sandwich if the sandwich can take the vinegar.
funFacts: Eastern North Carolina slaw in this style uses vinegar, not mayonnaise.
It is a different slaw from Lexington red slaw, which is dressed with tomato dip.
variations: A spoon of the eastern pepper sauce can replace part of the vinegar if you want it hotter.
steps: Toss the cabbage with the salt and let it stand 15 minutes, then squeeze out some of the water.
Stir vinegar, sugar, black pepper, and red pepper. There is no mayonnaise.
Dress the cabbage and refrigerate it. Hold it cold, below 40°F (4°C). This is not a canning recipe.
Serve beside pork that has already been cooked to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). The slaw itself is raw cabbage.

name: Lexington Red Slaw
culture: Lexington cooks dressing cabbage with the same dip used on the pork
flavor: Cabbage in a red vinegar-ketchup dressing, tangy and a little sweet.
history: Lexington red slaw, sometimes called barbecue slaw, is cabbage dressed with the same style of dip used on Piedmont pork shoulder: vinegar with a little ketchup. It is not a mayonnaise slaw and not the paler vinegar slaw of eastern Carolina. The red color is the dip, not food dye.
background: Cabbage dressed with Lexington-style dip. No mayonnaise. A side for pork shoulder, and often a sandwich topping.
whyItTastes: The dip's vinegar and ketchup soak the cabbage so the slaw tastes like the pork sauce beside it. A little sugar softens the acid. Because there is no egg or cream, the texture stays crunchy rather than coated.
authenticTouch: Use a thin dip. If you stir in enough ketchup to make a paste, the slaw stops being red slaw and becomes a tomato salad.
method: Dress shredded cabbage with vinegar, a little ketchup, sugar, and pepper.
served: Cold, on or beside chopped Lexington shoulder.
funFacts: Lexington red slaw is dressed with the dip, which is why it is red, and it does not use mayonnaise.
It is a different slaw from the tomato-free vinegar slaw of eastern North Carolina.
variations: Finely chopped cabbage, rather than long shreds, is how many Lexington trays make it.
steps: Chop the cabbage fine and toss it with the salt. Let it stand 10 minutes and drain off excess water.
Stir vinegar, ketchup, sugar, and pepper into a thin red dip. No mayonnaise.
Mix the dip into the cabbage and refrigerate it below 40°F (4°C). This is not a canning recipe.
Serve with pork shoulder cooked to about 195–205°F (90–96°C). The slaw is a vegetable side.

name: Central Texas Pinto Beans
culture: Central Texas pit kitchens simmering a pot of pinto beans
flavor: Soft pinto beans with onion, garlic, and salt.
history: Pinto beans are the usual pot beside Central Texas barbecue. Many pits season them with salt pork or a piece of bacon, and this version does not. It is a meatless pot of beans, onion, garlic, and salt, so it can sit next to any plate. Salt pork is a common addition you are not using here.
background: A vegetarian pot of pinto beans. No salt pork in this batch. The beans must be boiled until they are completely tender. This is a side, not the brisket.
whyItTastes: Long boiling turns dried pintos creamy, and onion and garlic are enough seasoning when the meat on the board is already salty and smoky. Leaving out salt pork keeps the bean flavor cleaner and makes the pot usable for a vegetarian at the table. Central Texas markets served beans because they were the inexpensive pot next to expensive beef.
authenticTouch: Boil the beans hard until they are fully soft before you decide they need more salt. Acid too early keeps them gritty.
method: Boil dried pinto beans with onion and garlic until they are completely tender. No meat.
served: In a cup beside brisket or beef ribs, with some of the bean broth.
funFacts: Salt pork is a common addition to Texas pinto beans. This pot leaves it out.
The beans are boiled until they are completely tender, which is the doneness that matters.
variations: A jalapeño in the pot adds heat. It is not required for the meat-market bean.
ingredients: 1 pound dried pinto beans, picked over and rinsed
steps: Rinse the beans and cover them with the water in a heavy pot. Add onion and garlic. Do not add salt pork or bacon.
Bring them to a full boil, 212°F (100°C), and boil for several minutes, then simmer.
Cook until the beans are completely tender, which often takes 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours from dried beans. Add water if they go dry. Do not hold raw dried beans warm without a real boil.
Salt them near the end, once they are soft. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Southern Collard Greens
culture: Black Southern cooks simmering collards with a smoked turkey wing
flavor: Soft, savory collards in a smoky pot liquor.
history: Collard greens simmered until soft, with the broth saved, are a foundation of Black Southern cooking. A smoked turkey wing is a seasoning meat in many of those pots. The liquid left in the pot is pot liquor, and it is meant to be eaten, not thrown out. This is a greens pot, not a myth about who invented barbecue.
background: Collards cooked fully, with a smoked turkey wing and the pot liquor kept. The turkey means the pot is not vegetarian. The greens, not a barbecue legend, are the subject.
whyItTastes: Long cooking softens collard leaves that are too tough for a quick saute, and the turkey wing seasons the broth with smoke. Vinegar at the end brightens the richness. Pot liquor carries that flavor, which is why it is served with the greens rather than drained off like a blanching water.
authenticTouch: Save the pot liquor. A ladle of it over the greens, or with cornbread for dipping, is the point of the pot.
method: Simmer cleaned collards with onion and a smoked turkey wing until the leaves are fully tender and the wing is heated through.
served: With a cup of pot liquor. Cornbread is a usual companion and is a separate recipe.
funFacts: Pot liquor is the broth in the collard pot, and it is meant to be eaten.
A smoked turkey wing is a common seasoning meat in Black Southern collard pots.
variations: A piece of smoked pork can season the pot instead of turkey. It would still be a meat dish, cooked through.
ingredients: 2 large bunches collard greens, stems stripped, leaves chopped and washed
steps: Wash the collards in several changes of water so the grit is gone. Put them in a pot with the turkey wing, onion, garlic, salt, pepper, and water.
Simmer, covered, until the leaves are completely tender, not chewy, usually about 1 to 1 1/2 hours.
Heat the smoked turkey wing through in the simmer to 165°F (74°C). It is already a cooked product; the long pot finishes the greens and heats the wing.
Stir in the vinegar. Serve the greens with pot liquor. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a story about the origin of barbecue.

name: Pit-Side Baked Macaroni and Cheese
culture: Southern pit kitchens baking macaroni and cheese as a side
flavor: Baked macaroni in a cheese custard, browned on top.
history: Baked macaroni and cheese is a standard side at Southern barbecue pits, scooped next to pork or brisket. This version is baked in an oven, not smoked, and it contains no bacon, so it is vegetarian. The pasta is wheat, the sauce is milk and cheese, and an egg sets the custard.
background: An oven-baked pit side. Vegetarian because there is no bacon. Not vegan, not gluten-free, and not dairy-free. It is not a smoker recipe.
whyItTastes: Cheese and milk make a rich custard that bakes onto the pasta, and a hot oven browns the top so the dish has a crust. Beside salty smoked meat, that richness is the contrast pits are after. It earned a place on the tray as a Southern supper dish long before it was a restaurant extra.
authenticTouch: Bake it until the center is hot and the egg is set. A pale, loose pan is not finished, and a dry one has gone too long.
method: Boil macaroni, fold it into a cheese and egg custard, and bake it.
served: Warm, in squares or scoops, beside barbecue. No bacon is added.
funFacts: This macaroni and cheese is baked in an oven. It is not put in the smoker.
There is no bacon in the dish, so the written recipe is vegetarian.
variations: A different sharp cheese changes the flavor. Keep the milk, butter, and egg if you want this custard.
steps: Heat the oven to 350°F (177°C). Boil the macaroni in salted water until just tender, then drain it.

Heat milk and butter until the butter melts. Take the pan off the heat. Beat the eggs and stir in a little hot milk to warm them, then stir the eggs back into the milk with the cheese, salt, and pepper.
Fold in the macaroni, pour it into a buttered baking dish, and bake until the center reaches 165°F (74°C) and the top is browned. That temperature sets the egg.
Rest 10 minutes before serving. There is no bacon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Brunswick Stew
culture: Georgia and Virginia cooks arguing over a chicken-and-vegetable barbecue stew
flavor: A thick chicken stew with corn, lima beans, and tomato.
history: Brunswick, Georgia, and Brunswick County, Virginia, both claim Brunswick stew. This page does not settle the argument. The pot here is a chicken-and-vegetable kettle of the kind served beside barbecue, not a reconstruction of a first pot. Chicken is cooked to a poultry temperature, and the vegetables are cooked until soft.
background: A chicken and vegetable stew claimed by both Georgia and Virginia. This version does not pick a winner. It is a side kettle, not a whole-hog plate.
whyItTastes: Long cooking breaks chicken and vegetables into one thick spoonful, with tomato acid against sweet corn and lima beans. That thickness is what picnic lines expect from the stew beside chopped pork. The two Brunswicks can keep their dispute; the pot still tastes like a Southern barbecue side.
authenticTouch: Cook it until the spoon stands up a little. A thin chicken soup is not yet the stew people mean.
method: Simmer chicken with onion, tomato, potatoes, corn, and lima beans until the chicken is safe to eat and the stew is thick.
served: In bowls, beside chopped pork or on its own.
funFacts: Brunswick, Georgia, and Brunswick County, Virginia, both claim this stew.
This pot is a chicken-and-vegetable kettle, not a settlement of that argument.
variations: Some older descriptions use other meats. This written kettle is chicken and vegetables.
steps: Put chicken, onion, potatoes, tomato, salt, pepper, and water in a heavy pot.
Simmer until the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, away from bone, and is easy to shred. Do not serve the chicken rare.
Remove the bones, return the meat, and add corn and lima beans. Cook until the vegetables are tender and the stew has thickened.
Taste for salt. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Both Georgia and Virginia claim the name; this pot does not decide it.

name: Hush Puppies
culture: Southern fish-fry and pit cooks frying cornmeal dough
flavor: Crisp fried cornmeal, salty, with a little onion.
history: Hush puppies are fried cornmeal dough served at fish fries and at some barbecue pits. They are fried, not smoked. This batter uses cornmeal and a spoon of wheat flour, plus an egg, and it is fried in oil that is not peanut oil. The name has folk explanations this page does not treat as documented history.
background: A fried side, not a pit smoke. Wheat and egg are in the batter. There is no dairy and no peanut oil, so the written recipe is dairy-free and nut-free, and not gluten-free.
whyItTastes: Cornmeal fries into a crust while the center stays soft, which is the contrast people want next to smoky fish or pork. Onion in the batter is the savory note. Frying in a skillet is a different craft from a smoker, which is why these belong beside the pit and not in it.
authenticTouch: Fry in small spoonfuls and do not crowd the pan. A crowded pot of oil drops in temperature and greases the dough instead of crusting it.
method: Mix a cornmeal batter and fry spoonfuls in hot oil until the centers are cooked.
served: Hot, beside fried fish or barbecue. They are a bread, not a meat.
funFacts: Hush puppies are fried cornmeal dough, which is why they show up at fish fries.
They are fried in a skillet of oil, not smoked over the pit.
variations: A batter of cornmeal only, with no wheat flour, could be gluten-free if every other ingredient agrees. This one uses a spoon of wheat flour.
ingredients: Neutral oil for frying, such as corn or canola, not peanut oil
steps: Stir cornmeal, wheat flour, egg, water, salt, and onion into a thick batter. The flour is wheat, so this is not gluten-free.
Heat 2 inches of oil to 350°F (177°C) in a deep skillet. Do not use peanut oil.
Fry spoonfuls, turning once, until they are deep golden and the center is cooked and hot, about 2 to 3 minutes. Do not crowd the pan.
Drain them. They are fried, not smoked. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Skillet Cornbread
culture: Appalachian and Southern home cooks baking cornbread in a hot skillet
flavor: Crusty cornbread, savory from buttermilk and salt, not cakey-sweet.
history: Skillet cornbread is an everyday bread in the southern Appalachians and across the South, baked in a preheated pan so the edge fries a little in fat. This one uses cornmeal, egg, buttermilk, and butter, and a baking powder labeled gluten-free, with no wheat flour and no sugar. It is a bread for beans and greens, not a dessert.
background: A savory skillet bread. Dairy and egg are in it. No wheat flour is added, and the baking powder is the gluten-free kind, so the written recipe is gluten-free. It is not hush puppies and not a sweet cake.
whyItTastes: A hot greased skillet browns the batter at the edge, which is the crust mountain tables expect. Buttermilk and egg moisten the cornmeal. Corn, not wheat, is the grain, which fits a region that grew corn for bread. Beside salty soup beans, the bread is the mild contrast.
authenticTouch: Heat the skillet with the butter in it until the butter is hot before the batter goes in. A cold pan makes a pale, steamy round.
method: Pour cornmeal batter into a hot buttered skillet and bake it until the center is set.
served: Warm, with soup beans, greens, or a barbecue plate. It is not sweetened.
funFacts: This skillet cornbread has no wheat flour and no sugar.
A preheated skillet is what browns the crust before the center sets.
variations: A spoon of sugar is a sweeter Southern habit. This mountain-leaning pan leaves it out.
steps: Heat the oven to 425°F (218°C). Put the butter in a 9-inch cast-iron skillet and set the skillet in the oven until the butter melts and the pan is hot.
Stir cornmeal, baking powder, and salt. Beat in the egg and buttermilk. There is no wheat flour.
Pour the batter into the hot skillet and bake until the center is set and the top is browned, about 20 to 25 minutes.
Cool a few minutes before cutting. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mustard Potato Salad
culture: Southern pit and picnic cooks dressing potatoes with mustard and egg
flavor: Potatoes in a sharp mustard dressing with egg.
history: Mustard potato salad is a Southern picnic and pit side, sharper than a sweet mayonnaise-only salad. This one uses boiled potatoes, hard-cooked eggs, mayonnaise, and yellow mustard. Egg and mustard are both in it. It is a cold side, not a smoke.
background: A cold potato salad with egg and mustard. Vegetarian, and dairy-free if the mayonnaise is the egg-and-oil kind. Not vegan.
whyItTastes: Mustard and vinegar cut boiled potato starch, and egg yolk from the mayonnaise and the chopped eggs makes the dressing rich without cream. Beside fatty barbecue, the sharpness is the reason it lasts on the plate. It is picnic food, held cold, not a hot grill dish.
authenticTouch: Dress the potatoes while they are still slightly warm so they take the seasoning, then chill the bowl.
method: Boil potatoes and eggs, then fold them into mayonnaise and mustard.
served: Cold, beside pork, chicken, or ribs.
funFacts: This potato salad uses both mustard and egg, so those allergens are part of the side.
It is dressed and chilled. It is not smoked.
variations: Celery and a little onion add crunch. They do not replace the mustard.
ingredients: 1/2 cup mayonnaise made from egg, oil, and vinegar
steps: Cover the potatoes with water, bring the pot to a boil at 212°F (100°C), and cook until the potatoes are tender. In a second pot, boil the eggs until the yolks are firm, about 10 minutes, then cool them.
Drain the potatoes. Chop the eggs.
Fold in mayonnaise, mustard, celery, salt, and vinegar while the potatoes are still slightly warm. Mustard and egg are allergens.
Refrigerate until cold, below 40°F (4°C), and serve the same day or the next. Do not leave it out in the sun.

name: Pit Baked Beans
culture: Southern pit cooks baking beans in molasses and mustard
flavor: Soft navy beans in a sweet-tangy molasses and mustard sauce.
history: Baked beans sweetened with molasses and sharpened with mustard are a common side at Southern pits. This pot uses no bacon, so it is vegetarian and vegan. Molasses is not honey. The beans are dried navy beans, boiled until tender before the sweet sauce goes in, because sugar and acid keep beans from softening.
background: A meatless baked-bean side. No bacon. Mustard is an allergen. The beans are fully boiled, then baked. This is not a canning recipe.
whyItTastes: Molasses sweetens and darkens the pot, and mustard keeps it from tasting like dessert. Navy beans take on that sauce once they are already tender. Pits adopted the dish because a bean pot feeds a line next to more expensive meat, and a meatless version still does that job.
authenticTouch: Boil the dried beans until they are soft before you add molasses, ketchup, or vinegar. Sweetness added too early leaves them chalky.
method: Boil dried navy beans until tender, then bake them with molasses and mustard. No bacon.
served: Warm, beside ribs or brisket. Tell people there is no bacon in this batch.
funFacts: This bean pot has no bacon, so the written recipe is vegetarian and vegan.
Molasses, not honey, is the dark sweetener, and mustard is in the sauce.
variations: A piece of bacon is a common pit addition. It would add meat and remove the vegetarian claim. It is not used here.
ingredients: 1 pound dried navy beans, picked over and rinsed
steps: Cover the beans with water, bring them to a full boil at 212°F (100°C), and boil for several minutes. Then simmer until they are completely tender. Add water if needed. Do not add the sweet sauce yet.
Drain most of the liquid, leaving about a cup. Stir in onion, molasses, mustard, ketchup, brown sugar, vinegar, and salt. There is no bacon and no honey.
Bake covered at 325°F (163°C) until the sauce is thick and the beans are still tender, about 1 hour.
Serve warm. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Mustard is an allergen. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Grilled Peaches
culture: Southern grill cooks marking ripe peaches over a hot fire
flavor: Warm, juicy peaches with a little char and no glaze.
history: Ripe peaches on a hot grill are a short Southern side or dessert when the fruit is in season, especially in peach-growing parts of Georgia. This version uses fruit, a pinch of salt, and a little oil. There is no honey and no butter, so it stays vegan and dairy-free. The cook is only long enough to mark the cut side.
background: Grilled ripe peaches with no honey and no butter. A hot-grill fruit side. Vegetarian and vegan as written.
whyItTastes: Heat concentrates the juice and browns the cut face, which makes a ripe peach taste fuller without a sauce. Georgia's summer crop is the reason the fruit is on a pit table at all. A pinch of salt keeps it from tasting only sweet. Butter or honey would be a different dish.
authenticTouch: Use peaches that are ripe but still firm. A mushy peach falls through the grate, and a hard one never juices.
method: Halve ripe peaches and grill them cut side down until marked and hot.
served: Warm, as a side or a plain dessert. No ice cream is in this recipe.
funFacts: These peaches are grilled with oil and salt only. There is no honey and no butter.
The cook is a few minutes. The fruit is not smoked for hours.
variations: A pat of butter on the hot fruit adds dairy and removes the vegan and dairy-free claims.
ingredients: 4 ripe but firm peaches, halved and pitted
steps: Brush the cut faces with oil and salt them lightly. Do not add honey or butter.
Heat a grill hot and oil the grate.

Grill cut side down until marked and the center of the fruit is hot, a few minutes, around 160°F (71°C) if you measure it. Fruit has no meat safety line. Turn them briefly if you want the skin side warm.
Serve warm. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Banana Pudding
culture: Southern cooks layering banana pudding for gatherings, including some barbecue tables
flavor: Vanilla custard, banana, and soft vanilla wafers.
history: Banana pudding is a Southern bowl dessert of vanilla wafers, sliced bananas, and custard, served at gatherings that sometimes include a barbecue plate. It is not fire cooking. It does not go on a grill or in a pit. Vanilla wafers bring wheat, the custard brings milk and egg, and the bananas are the fruit.
background: A chilled dessert side. Not smoked, not grilled, and not a pit technique. It contains dairy, egg, and wheat. It is vegetarian and not vegan.
whyItTastes: Custard softens the wafers and coats the banana, so the dessert eats as one spoonful rather than as three ingredients. Vanilla is the flavor that runs through it. It landed on barbecue tables because Southern suppers already knew the bowl, not because smoke improves a custard.
authenticTouch: Cook the custard until it thickens and the egg is heated through, then chill the dish. A raw egg mixture poured over bananas and left warm is not this pudding.
method: Cook a vanilla custard, layer it with bananas and vanilla wafers, and chill it. Do not put it near the fire.
served: Cold, in bowls, after the barbecue or beside it on a crowded table. It is plainly not a fire dish.
funFacts: Banana pudding is a bowl dessert. It does not go on the pit or the grill.
Vanilla wafers are the usual cookie, and they contain wheat.
variations: A meringue top is another Southern finish. This version stops at custard, bananas, and wafers.
steps: Whisk sugar, cornstarch, salt, and egg yolks in a saucepan. This dessert is not cooked on a fire.
Stir in milk and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the custard thickens and reaches 175°F (79°C), so the egg yolks are cooked.
Take it off the heat, stir in vanilla, and cool it 10 minutes. Layer wafers, bananas, and custard in a dish.
Cover and refrigerate until cold, below 40°F (4°C). Serve cold. Do not set the dish on a grill.

name: Appalachian Chow-Chow
culture: Appalachian home cooks making a refrigerator vegetable relish
flavor: Tangy chopped cabbage, green tomato, and onion in a mustard-seed brine.
history: Chow-chow is a chopped vegetable relish kept in mountain and Southern refrigerators and spooned beside beans and greens. This recipe is a refrigerator relish, not a shelf-stable canning recipe, and it gives no processing time for jars. Mustard seed is in the brine, so mustard is an allergen. Use it within a week.
background: A cold chopped relish for the Appalachian table. Not canned. Not a fermented crock left at room temperature. Cabbage, green tomato, and onion are the body.
