whyItTastes: Vinegar, sugar, and mustard seed pickle the vegetables just enough to stay crisp, which gives a sharp spoonful against rich soup beans or pork. End-of-summer gardens in the mountains are why the relish mixes green tomato with cabbage instead of being a single-vegetable pickle. The refrigerator, not a canner, is what makes this batch safe to describe.
authenticTouch: Cool the relish and refrigerate it the same day. Do not seal it in jars for a shelf. This page is not a canning manual.
method: Salt chopped vegetables, rinse them, cover them with a hot vinegar brine, cool them, and refrigerate.
served: Cold, by the spoon, beside soup beans, cornbread, or pork. It is a condiment.
funFacts: This chow-chow is a refrigerator relish, not a shelf-stable canning recipe.
Mustard seed in the brine means the relish contains mustard.
variations: A hotter chile can be chopped in. It does not change the refrigerator rule.
steps: Toss the vegetables with the salt and let them stand 30 minutes. Rinse and drain them well.
Simmer vinegar, sugar, mustard seed, and celery seed until the sugar dissolves and the brine is hot, at a simmer around 212°F (100°C).
Pour the hot brine over the vegetables. Cool the bowl. This is not a canning recipe. Do not process jars for shelf storage, and do not give these vegetables a canning time.
Refrigerate and use within a week, holding it below 40°F (4°C). Mustard seed is an allergen.

name: Appalachian Soup Beans
culture: Appalachian home cooks simmering a pot of pinto beans
flavor: Creamy pinto beans in a simple broth with onion.
history: Soup beans are pinto beans simmered into a brothy pot, an everyday Appalachian meal with cornbread. A ham hock is a common seasoning, and this version does not use one. It is a vegetarian pot of beans, onion, garlic, and salt. The beans are boiled until they are completely tender.
background: A meatless pot of Appalachian soup beans. No ham hock. Serve them with their broth. They are a meal as often as they are a side.
whyItTastes: Pintos break down just enough to thicken their own broth, which is the soup in soup beans. Onion cooked the whole time is the savor that a ham hock would otherwise dominate. Cornbread beside the bowl is the mountain habit, because the beans were the daily protein and the bread was the daily grain.
authenticTouch: Leave them brothy. Soup beans are not refried and not drained dry. Spoon off broth with the beans.
method: Boil dried pinto beans with onion until they are completely tender and still soupy. No pork.
served: In bowls, with cornbread and often chow-chow. The cornbread is a separate recipe.
funFacts: A ham hock is common in soup beans. This pot does not use one.
The beans are served in their broth, which is why they are called soup beans.
variations: A dried red pepper in the pot adds heat without adding meat.
ingredients: 1 pound dried pinto beans, picked over and rinsed
steps: Rinse the beans and put them in a pot with onion, garlic, and water. Do not add a ham hock.
Bring them to a full boil at 212°F (100°C), boil for several minutes, then simmer.
Cook until the beans are completely tender and the pot is still brothy, usually 1 1/2 to 2 1/2 hours. Add water if they get dry. Do not hold dried beans warm from raw without boiling them.
Salt them once they are soft. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Syracuse Salt Potatoes
culture: Syracuse cooks boiling new potatoes in very salty water
flavor: Small potatoes with a salty crust on the skin, served with butter.
history: Syracuse salt potatoes are small potatoes boiled in water salty enough to leave a white crust on the skins. The city was built on salt works, and the potatoes are associated with that history. They are the usual companion to Cornell chicken, and they are boiled, not grilled. Butter at the table makes this a dairy dish.
background: A boiled potato side for Cornell chicken. Not a grill recipe. The salt is in the water, and the butter is dairy. They are vegetarian and not vegan.
whyItTastes: Very salty water seasons the potato through the skin and dries to a light crust, so each bite is saltier than a normally boiled potato. Butter melts into that crust. They share a plate with Cornell's vinegar chicken because upstate cookouts put the sharp bird next to the salty potato, not because the potatoes ever saw the coals.
authenticTouch: Use small potatoes and enough salt that the water tastes like brine. A pinch of salt makes ordinary boiled potatoes, not salt potatoes.
method: Boil small potatoes in very salty water until tender, then serve them with butter.
served: Hot, skins on, with melted butter, beside Cornell chicken. They are not grilled.
funFacts: Syracuse salt potatoes are boiled in water salty enough to leave a crust on the skins.
They are the companion to Cornell chicken, and they are not a grill dish.
variations: Without the butter they would be dairy-free. This recipe serves them with butter.
ingredients: 2 pounds small potatoes, skins on and scrubbed
steps: Put the potatoes, salt, and water in a pot. The water should taste strongly salty. This is a boil, not a grill, and it is the companion to Cornell chicken.
Bring the pot to a boil at 212°F (100°C).
Cook until the potatoes are tender all the way through when pierced. Drain them. A salty film on the skins is expected.
Serve hot with melted butter. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Yucatán Cochinita Pibil
culture: Maya cooks in Yucatán, and the families who kept the pib after new ingredients arrived
flavor: Sour orange, achiote, and slow pork, dyed red and soft enough to shred.
history: The pib is a Maya pit: a hole of heated stones used to cook food in the ground. Pork and sour orange arrived in Yucatán after Spanish contact. Achiote, the seed of Bixa orellana, is native to the tropical Americas and is what turns the pork red. A covered pan in a home oven can borrow the seasoning, and it should be labeled as not a pib.
background: Cochinita pibil is young pig, or a pork shoulder in a home kitchen, wrapped and cooked until it shreds. It is Yucatecan fiesta food and also a weekday taco filling. The oven version is a substitute for the pit, not the pit itself.
whyItTastes: Achiote is earthy and slightly peppery, and sour orange cuts the fat of the shoulder. In a pib the meat steams against hot stone and banana leaf instead of searing. That covered heat is why the pork tastes dyed and tangy rather than like a grilled chop. The home oven can echo the steam, without the wood and the ground.
authenticTouch: Grind the achiote with the garlic and juice so the paste stains the meat, and do not skip the rest after it leaves the heat.
method: Marinate a pork shoulder in achiote and sour orange, wrap it, and cook it covered until it shreds. A home oven is not a pib.
served: Shred it and eat it with warm corn tortillas, pickled red onion, and a habanero salsa on the side if you want more heat.
funFacts: Achiote comes from Bixa orellana, a plant native to the tropical Americas.
Sour orange and pork reached Yucatán after Spanish contact; the pib is older than those ingredients.
variations: Some cooks add a little habanero to the recado; this version keeps the chile in a side salsa.
Banana leaves are the usual wrapper when they are sold. Parchment works in a home oven and is not a leaf.
ingredients: 1/2 cup sour orange juice, or 1/4 cup orange juice plus 1/4 cup lime juice
2 large banana leaves, passed over a flame until flexible, or parchment if you have no leaves
steps: Blend the achiote, sour orange juice, garlic, oregano, salt, and pepper into a paste. Coat the pork. The meat is still raw and is not ready to eat. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

Wrap the coated pork in banana leaf or parchment and set it in a heavy pot with a tight lid. Refrigerate it if it sits more than 2 hours. Do not leave the paste at room temperature. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Heat a home oven to 325°F (165°C). This oven is not a pib. Cook the wrapped pork until the center is at least 145°F (63°C). For cochinita that shreds, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

Rest the pork 3 minutes, then shred it. The center should already have reached the temperature in the cooking step. Serve warm, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Poc Chuc
culture: Yucatecan home cooks who grill pork in sour orange
flavor: Grilled pork with a sharp sour-orange marinade and a little char.
history: Poc chuc is Yucatán grilled pork, sliced and turned over a hot fire after a sour-orange marinade. Sour orange is a citrus that reached the peninsula after Spanish contact. The cook stays on the grill, in pieces, which is why it is not cochinita from a pib. Pickled onion is the usual bright relish beside it.
background: This is everyday Yucatecan pork, not a buried pit roast and not Mexico City al pastor. A shoulder steak or a thin whole-muscle slice is the home cut. It is grilled, rested, and sliced.
whyItTastes: Sour orange seasons the surface and keeps the pork from tasting flat. A hot grill browns the marinade instead of steaming it. Wood or charcoal adds a light smoke that a covered pib would hide. The result is tangy and charred, in slices rather than shreds.
authenticTouch: Grill it hot and do not let the sour-orange sugar burn black. A clean grate and a short cook keep the citrus taste.
method: Marinate thin pork in sour orange, garlic, and oregano, then grill it over a hot fire to a whole-muscle temperature.
served: Serve the slices with corn tortillas, pickled red onion, and a simple tomato salsa.
funFacts: Poc chuc is grilled, so the pork stays in slices rather than becoming cochinita shreds.
Pickled red onion is the relish most often set beside Yucatecan grilled pork.
variations: A thin pork loin chop works if shoulder steaks are not sold, and it still needs 145°F (63°C).
Some tables add a whole grilled onion beside the meat.
ingredients: 1/2 cup sour orange juice, or 1/4 cup orange juice plus 1/4 cup lime juice
1 small red onion, sliced, for a quick pickle with 1/2 cup vinegar and 1/2 teaspoon salt
steps: Mix the juice, garlic, oregano, salt, and oil. Coat the pork and refrigerate it for 30 minutes. The pork is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Stir the sliced onion with vinegar and salt. That relish is not a canned preserve. Keep it cold and use it within a few days. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the pork over a hot fire until the thickest steak reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested pork. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Eat it the same day, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mexico City Al Pastor
culture: Taqueros in Mexico City working a trompo that grew from Levantine shawarma
flavor: Chile-stained pork with pineapple, crisp at the edge and juicy where the slice is thin.
history: In the twentieth century, Lebanese shawarma in central Mexico became the vertical trompo of al pastor. Taquerías in Mexico City stacked pork, stained with achiote or guajillo, and set pineapple on the spit. The home cook who grills thin slices on a grate or a sheet is not running a vertical spit unless a spit is actually in the kitchen. The seasoning can still be the same.
background: Al pastor is a Mexico City taco of marinated pork and pineapple. It is not Yucatecan cochinita, and it is not Lebanese shawarma served as lamb. The written steps are the home grill, labeled as such.
whyItTastes: Guajillo and achiote give the pork a dried-chile color and a mild heat, and pineapple adds acid and sugar at the edge of the slice. The trompo bastes the meat in its own fat as it turns. A home grill still browns thin pork quickly, which is the part of the taste you can reach without the spit.
authenticTouch: Slice the pork thin before it cooks. Thick chunks will not taste like pastor even if the chile paste is right.
method: Marinate thin pork in guajillo and achiote, then roast it on a vertical spit if you have one. Otherwise grill or sheet-cook the slices and call that a home version, not a trompo.
served: Chop the cooked pork with a little grilled pineapple and eat it in small corn tortillas with onion and cilantro.
funFacts: The vertical trompo is a Levantine shawarma spit adapted in central Mexico in the twentieth century.
Pineapple on the pastor spit is a Mexican addition to that spit method.
variations: Achiote alone, without guajillo, is a common paste. This recipe uses both.
If you own a vertical spit, stack the slices and cook them there. That is the only version that is a trompo.
ingredients: 3 pounds boneless pork shoulder, sliced about 1/4 inch thick
4 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
steps: Toast the guajillos in a dry pan until fragrant, cover them with hot water for 15 minutes, and blend them with achiote, pineapple juice, garlic, cumin, and salt. Coat the raw pork. It is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

If you have a vertical spit, stack the pork, oil the outside, and roast it, shaving slices as the face browns. If you do not, this is not a vertical spit: grill the slices or lay them on a hot sheet. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook every slice until the thickest piece reads 145°F (63°C). Grill the pineapple until it browns. Rest the pork 3 minutes.
Chop the rested pork. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Eat it in tortillas the same day, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Sonoran Carne Asada
culture: Grill cooks in Sonora and across the border in southern Arizona
flavor: Beef grilled over mesquite, salted, with a flour tortilla as the wrap rather than a dough in the meat.
history: Carne asada in Sonora is a northern Mexican grill: beef over mesquite, eaten in flour tortillas. Wheat tortillas belong to the north as a pairing. They are not mixed into the steak. The same table is part of life in southern Arizona, which is why this stop also carries the United States. It is not the Salvadoran plate of the same Spanish name.
background: Sonoran carne asada is a ranch and backyard steak, often thin, often mesquite. The meat itself is beef and salt. Beans, salsa, and grilled onions sit beside it. This page does not put wheat in the rub.
whyItTastes: Mesquite coals are hot and a little sweet, and they mark beef faster than a mild hardwood. Northern Sonora is cattle and desert country, so the meal is steak and a wheat tortilla rather than a long chile stew. The lime and salt on the meat stay sharp because the cook is short.
authenticTouch: Burn mesquite down to coals before the steak goes on. Flames from fresh logs will taste like soot, not like Sonoran mesquite.
method: Salt a thin steak and grill it hot over mesquite coals to a whole-muscle temperature, then rest it.
served: Slice it and eat it with flour tortillas, grilled spring onions, and a fresh salsa. The tortilla is a pairing.
funFacts: Mesquite is the usual grilling wood of Sonora.
Flour tortillas are the northern wrap; the steak in this recipe has no wheat in it.
variations: A gas grill with a mesquite chunk on the coals is a home stand-in, and it is not a mesquite fire.
Ranchera, flank, or skirt all appear on this grill. Cook each one as a whole cut.
ingredients: 2 pounds thin beef steak, such as ranchera or skirt
Mesquite wood or charcoal, burned to coals
steps: Oil the steak lightly and season it with salt and pepper. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. There is no flour in this step. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Burn mesquite or charcoal to a bed of coals. A flaming log is not the grilling stage. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice across the grain. The steak should have reached 145°F (63°C) and rested. Squeeze lime at the table. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Monterrey Cabrito
culture: Asadores in Monterrey who roast kid goat over wood or on a spit
flavor: Young goat, salted, with a browned skin and a mild, meaty center.
history: Cabrito in Monterrey is kid goat, cooked on a spit or opened over an open fire. Nuevo León made the dish a restaurant and family standard in the twentieth century, in a city already tied to northern ranching. The animal is young, which is what the word means. A full-grown goat is a different cook.
background: This is Monterrey goat, not a lamb barbacoa and not a pork pibil. Restaurants often open the kid flat beside glowing coals. A home cook with a leg or a small shoulder should say that the cut is not a whole kid.
whyItTastes: Kid goat is leaner than a pork shoulder, so the taste is mild and a little sweet if the fire is gentle. Mesquite or oak coals in this dry northern city brown the skin without a sweet glaze. Salt is the seasoning that lets the meat stay the point of the plate.
authenticTouch: Keep the fire beside the meat or under a steady bed of coals. A roaring flame dries a lean kid before the center is done.
method: Salt a kid, or a home-size leg labeled as not the whole animal, and roast it on a spit or beside coals to a whole-muscle temperature.
served: Cut it into pieces and eat it with flour or corn tortillas, salsa, and beans. The tortillas are pairings.
funFacts: Cabrito means a young goat, not a full-grown animal.
In Monterrey it is cooked on a spit or opened flat beside the fire.
variations: A bone-in leg is the workable home cut. Call it a leg, not a whole cabrito.
Some asadores use only salt. A little garlic is a home addition and should stay light.
ingredients: 1 bone-in kid goat leg, about 4 pounds, labeled as a home cut and not a whole kid
Wood or charcoal for a spit or an open grill
steps: Rub the leg with oil, salt, pepper, and garlic. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it until the fire is ready. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Spit the leg or set it beside a bed of coals, not in open flame. This is the Monterrey fire, scaled to one leg. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the thickest part, away from bone, reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Carve the rested leg. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Norteño Discada
culture: Norteño camp and backyard cooks who fry a mixed grill on a plow disc
flavor: A mixed pan of beef, pork, bacon, chile, and onion, browned on a wide steel disc.
history: Discada is a norteño mixed grill cooked on a discarded plow disc, the disco. It belongs to ranch and camping cooks across Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango, and neighboring northern states, and it spread as a backyard party pan in the twentieth century. Beef, pork, and often bacon share the disc. A large skillet is the home stand-in, and it is not a plow disc.
background: This is one pan with more than one kind of meat, so the temperatures are not all the same. Whole strips of beef and pork are one target. Fresh sausage or ground meat in the same disc is another. The cook is northern Mexico, not an asado from the southern cone.
whyItTastes: The disc is thin steel over a hot fire, so meat browns in its own fat the way a plancha does. Bacon fat carries onion and green chile across the beef and pork. The flavor is a camp fry, wide and savory, from a tool that started as farm equipment rather than from a sauce.
authenticTouch: Cook the ground meat or sausage to its own temperature before you lean on the look of the steak strips. They finish at different points.
method: Brown bacon, sausage, and strips of beef and pork with onion and chile on a plow disc, or in a heavy skillet labeled as not a disco.
served: Eat it from the disc with tortillas, salsa, and beans. Keep the pan hot and the cooked meat above the raw scraps.
funFacts: The pan is an agricultural plow disc, which is why the cook is called discada.
It is a norteño camp dish shared across several northern states, not a single city recipe.
variations: A wok or a large skillet replaces the disc at home. Say that it is not a disco.
Some cooks add hot dog pieces. If you do, heat them until they are steaming, and still hold the fresh sausage to 160°F (71°C).
safety: Cook ground meat and fresh sausage to 160°F (71°C). Cook whole strips of beef and pork to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest them 3 minutes. Cook bacon until it is crisp and hot.
ingredients: 1/2 pound fresh raw chorizo, casings split, or 1/2 pound ground beef
A plow disc set over a fire, or a large heavy skillet if you have no disc
steps: Set the disc or skillet over a hot fire. If this is a skillet, it is not a plow disc. Start the bacon until it is crisp and steaming hot, at least 145°F (63°C). The other meat is still raw.
Add the fresh chorizo or ground beef and cook it, breaking it up, until it reaches 160°F (71°C). Do not stop at a browned outside.
Add the beef strips, pork strips, onion, jalapeño, garlic, and salt. Cook until the whole cuts read 145°F (63°C). Rest those strips 3 minutes. Keep the ground meat at or above 160°F (71°C).

Taste a vegetable, not a raw piece. The beef and pork strips should have reached 145°F (63°C) and rested, and the sausage or ground meat should have reached 160°F (71°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Oaxacan Tasajo
culture: Market grill cooks in the Central Valleys of Oaxaca
flavor: Thin salted beef, grilled quickly, chewy at the edge and beefy in the middle.
history: Tasajo is thin salted beef sold in Oaxaca markets and grilled to order. Salting and drying were how butchers kept beef before refrigeration, and the grilled slice became a market breakfast and a fonda plate. This home recipe does not ask you to cure meat in the sun. Buy market tasajo if you can, or salt a thin steak briefly in the refrigerator.
background: Oaxacan tasajo is beef, not pork cecina from the same market stall, though the two are often grilled side by side. It is a hot, fast grill. It is not a long smoke.
whyItTastes: Salt concentrates the beef, and the thin cut takes a hard sear before the inside dries out. The Central Valleys grill is charcoal, close to the meat, so the surface browns while the slice stays small. Onion and salsa are the fresh contrast buyers expect at the stand.
authenticTouch: Keep the slice thin. A thick steak salted for an hour is only a seasoned steak, not market tasajo.
method: Grill thin salted beef hot and fast to a whole-muscle temperature. Do not sun-dry meat at home.
served: Eat it with corn tortillas, grilled spring onion, salsa, and a radish. Cecina and chorizo on the same grill are separate meats.
funFacts: Tasajo is beef that Oaxaca markets sell already salted and thin for the grill.
This recipe does not include home curing or sun-drying.
variations: If you buy prepared tasajo, rinse the surface salt if it looks heavy, then grill it.
A skirt steak sliced thin is the home stand-in, and it should be named as a stand-in.
ingredients: 1 1/2 pounds beef skirt or flank, sliced 1/4 inch thick
2 teaspoons salt, for a short refrigerator seasoning, or 1 pound purchased tasajo
steps: If you are not using market tasajo, salt the thin beef and refrigerate it for 1 hour, then pat it dry. That is seasoning, not a cure. Do not dry it in the sun. The meat is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Oil the slices lightly. Grill the spring onions beside them. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the beef until the thickest slice reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
The rested slices should have reached 145°F (63°C). Eat them hot with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Yucatán Tikin Xic
culture: Coastal and town cooks in Yucatán who grill fish in achiote
flavor: Fish stained with achiote and sour orange, gently charred, sometimes steamed a little by a leaf.
history: Tikin xic is a Yucatecan fish cook: achiote and sour orange on a fillet or a split fish, sometimes wrapped in banana leaf and grilled. Achiote is a native American seed. Sour orange arrived after Spanish contact. The leaf is a wrapper cooks use when they have it. This page does not turn the grill into a ceremony.
background: The dish is fish, in the same seasoning family as Yucatecan pork, with a different animal and a shorter cook. A home kitchen without banana leaves can use parchment and should say so.
whyItTastes: Achiote colors the fish and adds a peppery earth taste, and sour orange keeps it bright. If a banana leaf is on the grill, the fish steams a little as well as browns. Without the leaf, the same paste tastes more directly of the fire. Either way the fish, not the wrapper, is the center.
authenticTouch: Oil the leaf or the parchment so the paste does not stick and tear the cooked fish.
method: Coat fish with achiote and sour orange and grill it, in a leaf if you have one, until it flakes.
served: Eat it with corn tortillas, pickled onion, and a tomato salsa.
funFacts: Achiote and sour orange are the Yucatecan seasoning pair used here on fish.
A banana leaf wraps the fish when cooks have one; it is not itself the seasoning.
variations: Grouper, snapper, or another firm white fish all work. Cook each to the fish temperature.
No banana leaf: use parchment, and say the packet is not the leaf.
ingredients: 2 pounds firm white fish fillets, such as snapper or grouper
1/4 cup sour orange juice, or 2 tablespoons orange juice plus 2 tablespoons lime juice
steps: Mix achiote, juice, garlic, oregano, salt, and oil. Coat the fish. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.

Wrap the fish in a banana leaf, or in parchment if you have no leaf. Parchment is not a banana leaf. Refrigerate it if it waits more than 2 hours. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Grill the packet over a medium-hot fire, turning once, until the center of the thickest fillet reads 145°F (63°C) and the fish is opaque and flakes.
Open the packet carefully. The fish should already be at 145°F (63°C). Eat it the same day, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mixiote in Maguey or Parchment
culture: Cooks in Hidalgo and the central highlands who wrap meat for a pit or a steam
flavor: Lamb steamed in a chile paste, soft, with a concentrated guajillo taste.
history: Mixiote is meat wrapped for a pit or a steamer in the central highlands, especially Hidalgo, the State of Mexico, Puebla, and Tlaxcala. The older wrapper is the thin cuticle of a maguey leaf. Maguey leaves are often hard to buy, and cutting them can harm the plant, so many home cooks use parchment. Parchment is a substitute and it is not the same as maguey. A home packet is also not a pit.
background: The usual meat is lamb or mutton, though chicken and rabbit appear in the same kind of packet. This page is lamb. The chile paste is the flavor you can keep even when the wrapper changes. Say which wrapper you used.
whyItTastes: Guajillo and a covered packet concentrate chile and lamb juices instead of grilling them off. Maguey has a light vegetal smell that parchment does not have. The highland pit adds wood and stone. A home oven still tastes of chile and lamb, and it should not be described as the maguey pit.
authenticTouch: Tie the packet so the juices stay in. Mixiote that boils dry in an open pan is a different, harder dish.
method: Wrap chile-rubbed lamb in maguey if you have it, or in parchment labeled as a substitute, and cook it covered until the lamb is at a safe whole-muscle temperature.
served: Open the packet at the table and eat the lamb with corn tortillas, salsa, and nopales or beans.
funFacts: The traditional wrapper is the cuticle of a maguey leaf, used in the central highlands.
Parchment keeps steam in, and it is not maguey.
variations: Chicken in the same paste must reach 165°F (74°C). This written recipe is lamb.
Avocado leaves scent some highland packets. Leave them out if you cannot tell culinary leaves from ornamental ones.
ingredients: 3 pounds boneless lamb shoulder, in large pieces
4 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
Parchment paper and kitchen string, unless you have food-safe maguey wrappers
steps: Toast and soak the guajillos, then blend them with garlic, cumin, oregano, salt, and vinegar. Coat the lamb. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Wrap the lamb in parchment and tie the packet. If you do not have maguey, say so: parchment is a substitute and it is not the same. A home oven is not a pit. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Set the packet in a covered pot with a cup of water, or cover it tightly. Cook at 325°F (165°C) until the thickest piece reads at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes. For pullable shoulder, continue toward 195°F (90°C).
Open the rested packet. The lamb should have reached at least 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Arrachera a la Parrilla
culture: Home and ranch cooks across Mexico who grill skirt steak
flavor: Skirt steak, garlicky and lime-sharp, sliced across a loose grain.
history: Arrachera is the skirt, a diaphragm muscle, and grilling it is a widespread Mexican practice rather than one town's patent. On a ranch grill it is often only salt, garlic, and lime over a hot fire. This page is that straightforward parrilla steak. It is not Sonoran carne asada with its mesquite and flour-tortilla table, and it is not a trompo.
background: The name on this page is Arrachera a la Parrilla. The cut is whole muscle. Slice it across the grain after it rests, or the texture stays stringy even when the temperature is right.
whyItTastes: Skirt is loose and beefy, so a very hot grate browns it before the inside overcooks. Lime and garlic sit on the surface because the cook is short. The flavor is the steak and the fire, not a long marinade of dried chiles.
authenticTouch: Find the direction of the grain before you grill, then slice the other way after the rest.
method: Grill skirt steak hot with salt, garlic, and lime, then rest and slice it across the grain.
served: Serve the slices with corn tortillas, a tomato and onion salsa, and lime.
funFacts: Arrachera is skirt steak, a diaphragm muscle, and it is sliced across the grain.
It is a hot grill, not a long smoke and not a vertical spit.
variations: Flank can stand in if skirt is not sold. Say which cut is on the plate, and cook it as a whole steak.
A hotter salsa can be served beside it without changing the mild seasoning on the meat.
steps: Rub the skirt with oil, garlic, salt, and pepper. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill until it is very hot and the grate is clean. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the skirt until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice across the grain. The steak should have reached 145°F (63°C) and rested. Add lime at the table. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Guatemalan Churrasco with Chirmol
culture: Guatemalan grill cooks who serve steak with chirmol
flavor: Grilled beef with a roasted tomato and onion chirmol.
history: In Guatemala, churrasco is a grilled steak, and chirmol is the roasted tomato, onion, and cilantro relish that comes with it. The Spanish word also names the Argentine mixed grill, which is a different meal in a different country. This page stays with the Guatemalan plate. Corn tortillas and a simple salad are the usual company.
background: Chirmol is chopped or lightly roasted, fresh, and seasoned with lime. It is not Argentine chimichurri and not Honduran chimol, though both are herb and onion relishes. The steak is a whole cut of beef.
whyItTastes: A hot grill gives the beef a browned crust, and the chirmol stays raw-tasting and sharp from lime and cilantro. Roasting the tomatoes first makes them sweeter than a fully raw salsa. The contrast is the point: charred meat, bright relish, warm tortillas.
authenticTouch: Char the tomatoes and onion before you chop them. A fully raw sauce is closer to another country's chimol than to this chirmol.
method: Grill a steak to a whole-muscle temperature and serve it with a roasted tomato chirmol.
served: Eat the steak with chirmol, corn tortillas, and a little cabbage or lettuce.
funFacts: Chirmol is a fresh roasted tomato and onion relish, not a bottled steak sauce.
Guatemalan churrasco is a Central American plate, not the Argentine mixed grill that shares the Spanish word.
variations: Some cooks leave the chirmol fully chopped and raw. This one roasts the tomato and onion first.
A thin ranch steak or a thicker sirloin both work if the center reaches the same temperature.
ingredients: 1 1/2 pounds beef steak, about 1 inch thick
steps: Salt and oil the steak. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Char the tomatoes and onion on the grill, then chop them with cilantro, jalapeño, lime juice, and a pinch of salt. Keep this chirmol cold until you eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested steak. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Spoon on the chirmol. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Salvadoran Carne Asada
culture: Salvadoran home cooks who grill meat and set curtido beside it
flavor: Grilled beef with a tangy cabbage curtido.
history: Salvadoran carne asada is grilled beef eaten with curtido, the cabbage relish also served with pupusas. The name matches Sonoran carne asada in Spanish and not in the plate: there is no mesquite rule here, and the relish is curtido rather than a flour-tortilla steak house spread. This curtido is a quick refrigerator mix, not a canned preserve.
background: The steak is the cook. Curtido is included because it is how many Salvadoran tables finish the plate. It is cabbage, carrot, onion, oregano, and vinegar, used cold.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and oregano in the cabbage cut the richness of grilled beef. The steak itself is simply salted, so the char stays clear. Curtido is crunchy and sour, which is a different contrast from the tomato chirmol of Guatemala or the chimol of Honduras.
authenticTouch: Salt the curtido and let it sit while the grill heats, so the cabbage softens slightly without becoming a jam.
method: Grill beef to a whole-muscle temperature and serve a quick curtido beside it.
served: Eat the steak with curtido, corn tortillas or rice, and fried plantains if you have them.
funFacts: Curtido is the cabbage relish Salvadoran cooks also use beside pupusas.
This carne asada is not the mesquite steak of Sonora, even though the Spanish name matches.
variations: A longer curtido, fermented a day or two in the refrigerator, is traditional in some kitchens. This one is the quick version.
Thin sliced pork shoulder is sometimes grilled the same day. Pork still needs 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest. This recipe is beef.
steps: Toss the cabbage, carrot, onion, jalapeño, oregano, vinegar, and 1 teaspoon salt. This is a quick curtido, not a canned preserve. Refrigerate it and use it within five days. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Oil and salt the steak. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested steak. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve it with the cold curtido. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Honduran Carne Asada with Chimol
culture: Honduran cooks who grill beef and chop a fresh chimol
flavor: Grilled beef with a raw, bright chop of tomato, onion, and cilantro.
history: Honduran carne asada is grilled beef with chimol, a finely chopped mix of tomato, onion, and cilantro. Chimol is fresh, not roasted like Guatemalan chirmol and not the parsley sauce of an Argentine parrilla. The plate often includes fried plantains, beans, and tortillas. It is its own Central American grill.
background: The chimol is a relish, chopped small, with lime and salt. The steak is a whole cut. Neither one is a bottled sauce.
whyItTastes: Raw onion and cilantro stay sharp against beef that has taken a direct char. Because the chimol is not cooked, it tastes like a salad spooned over a hot steak. Lime juice is the acid, so the plate is fresher and wetter than a dry salted grill.
authenticTouch: Chop the chimol fine and salt it just before serving so the tomato does not weep into a puddle.
method: Grill a steak to a whole-muscle temperature and spoon raw chimol over the slices.
served: Serve with tortillas, beans, and fried plantains.
funFacts: Chimol is the Honduran chopped relish of tomato, onion, and cilantro.
It is a different relish from Guatemalan chirmol and from Argentine chimichurri.
variations: A little minced green chile makes the chimol hotter. This amount stays mild.
Chicken on the same grill would need 165°F (74°C). This recipe is beef.
steps: Oil and salt the steak. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Mix tomato, onion, bell pepper, cilantro, lime juice, and a pinch of salt. This chimol stays raw. Keep it cold. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested steak. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Spoon on the chimol. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Nicaraguan Churrasco
culture: Nicaraguan home cooks who grill beef and serve it with gallo pinto
flavor: Grilled beef with a simple garlic sauce, beside rice and beans.
history: Nicaraguan churrasco is a grilled beef steak, often a thin cut, eaten with gallo pinto and a simple garlic sauce. Gallo pinto, rice and beans cooked together, is the everyday plate of Nicaragua. The garlic sauce is a Nicaraguan table sauce of garlic, onion, and acid. It is not the parsley chimichurri of an Argentine asado, and this page does not copy that sauce.
background: The beef is the grill. The sauce is garlic and sour orange or lime, used the day it is mixed. Gallo pinto is a pairing, not a second recipe buried inside the steak.
whyItTastes: Garlic and acid cut a simply grilled steak, and the beans and rice beside it make the meal filling in a way a sauce alone does not. The grill taste stays light because the meat is not buried in herbs. What you remember is beef, garlic, and gallo pinto.
authenticTouch: Mix the garlic sauce the day you eat it. Do not store garlic in oil at room temperature.
method: Grill beef to a whole-muscle temperature and serve it with a fresh garlic sauce and gallo pinto.
served: Serve with gallo pinto, fried plantains, and a cabbage salad. A crumb of queso fresco is a common extra at the table.
funFacts: Gallo pinto, rice and beans cooked together, is the usual plate beside this steak.
The garlic sauce on this page is a Nicaraguan table sauce, written separately from Argentine chimichurri.
variations: Sour orange is the acid when it is sold. Lime juice is the home substitute.
A thinner steak cooks faster and still needs the same center temperature.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons sour orange juice or lime juice
2 tablespoons neutral oil, for the sauce
steps: Salt and oil the steak. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Stir garlic, onion, juice, cilantro, oil, and a pinch of salt. Refrigerate the sauce and use it the same day. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested steak. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Spoon on the garlic sauce and eat it with gallo pinto. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Costa Rican Carne Asada
culture: Costa Rican home cooks grilling beef for a weekend plate
flavor: Grilled beef with a homemade onion and lime sauce.
history: Costa Rican carne asada is grilled beef, often cooked for a family lunch and eaten with rice, beans, and a simple relish. A commercial bottled sauce is common on Costa Rican tables, and this recipe does not reproduce it. The onion sauce here is homemade, it contains no tamarind, and it is not Salsa Lizano.
background: The written sauce is onion, sweet pepper, cilantro, and lime. It is a fresh relish for the steak. The beef is a whole cut, salted and grilled.
whyItTastes: Onion and lime stay raw and sharp, so they brighten beef that has picked up a light char. Without a bottled sauce, the plate tastes of the grill and the fresh chop, not of a sweet vegetable concentrate. Rice and beans make it a full Costa Rican lunch.
authenticTouch: Rinse the chopped onion in cold water if you want it milder, then dry it before it meets the lime.
method: Grill beef to a whole-muscle temperature and serve an onion and lime sauce that is not a commercial condiment.
served: Serve with rice and beans, fried plantains, and a small salad.
funFacts: The onion sauce in this recipe is homemade, contains no tamarind, and is not Salsa Lizano.
Costa Rican carne asada is a weekend grill, usually beside rice and beans.
variations: A few slices of tomato can go into the onion sauce. They do not turn it into a bottled product.
Chicken would be a different dish and would need 165°F (74°C).
steps: Salt and oil the steak. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Mix the onion, sweet pepper, cilantro, lime juice, and a pinch of salt. This sauce contains no tamarind and it is not Salsa Lizano. Keep it cold. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the steak until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested steak. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Spoon on the onion sauce. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Belizean Grilled Snapper
culture: Creole and Garifuna cooks on the Belizean coast
flavor: Whole snapper grilled with lime, garlic, and thyme.
history: On the Belizean coast, snapper is a boat fish, and grilling it is ordinary cooking in Creole and Garifuna towns. Garifuna communities carry African and Island Carib histories and have lived on this coast since the late eighteenth century. The seasoning here is lime, garlic, thyme, and a little hot pepper. The page is that grill and nothing invented beyond it.
background: A whole snapper cooks evenly if the cavity is open and the fire is medium. The flesh is fish, and it is done when it flakes. Plantains or rice and beans are the usual starch beside it.
whyItTastes: Coastal thyme and lime are bright against the sweet, lean flesh of snapper. A whole fish over coals picks up a little smoke in the skin and stays moist behind it. The hot pepper is there for the people who want it, not to hide the fish.
authenticTouch: Score the sides of the fish so the heat reaches the backbone, and check the temperature there, not only in the thin tail.
method: Stuff a whole snapper with garlic, thyme, and lime and grill it until the flesh flakes.
served: Eat it with rice and beans, fried plantain, and extra lime.
funFacts: Snapper is a routine reef fish on the Belizean coast, which is why it is a grill and not a special import.
Creole and Garifuna kitchens both cook coastal fish, and they do not use one identical seasoning.
variations: Fillets work if a whole fish is not available. Cook them to the same fish temperature and say they are fillets.
Leave the pepper out for a milder plate. The lime and thyme still carry the dish.
ingredients: 1 whole snapper, about 3 pounds, gutted and scaled
1 lime, sliced, plus 1 lime for the table
steps: Pat the fish dry, oil it, and salt the cavity and the skin. Tuck in garlic, thyme, lime, and the pepper if you are using it. The fish is raw and is not ready to eat. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Heat a grill to medium and oil the grate so the skin can release. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Grill the fish, turning once, until the thickest part at the backbone reads 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes.
The fish should already be at 145°F (63°C). Serve it with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Jamaican Jerk Chicken
culture: Jamaican cooks, in a line of seasoning tied to Maroon communities
flavor: Chicken with allspice, thyme, and Scotch bonnet, smoky if the fire has pimento wood.
history: Jerk is tied to Maroon communities in Jamaica, people of African descent who escaped slavery and cooked seasoned meat over pimento wood in the hills. Allspice is the berry of that pimento tree, native to the Caribbean region, and Scotch bonnet is a New World chile. Chicken is the piece most cooks grill now. The older pork shoulder is a separate, longer cook.
background: The paste is scallion, thyme, allspice, garlic, ginger, and Scotch bonnet. Pimento wood is the traditional smoke. A charcoal grill without that wood is a home fire, and it is not the same smoke. The chicken still has to reach a poultry temperature.
whyItTastes: Pimento wood is the allspice tree, so the smoke repeats the spice ground into the paste. Thyme and scallion are green and sharp, and Scotch bonnet brings a high, fruity heat. Chicken fat carries those flavors across a shorter cook than a pork shoulder can stand.
authenticTouch: Burn pimento wood down to coals if you can get it. If you cannot, say the grill is not a pimento fire, and keep the allspice in the paste.
method: Rub chicken with a jerk paste and grill it over coals until the thickest meat reaches a poultry temperature.
served: Eat it with festival dumplings or bread, roasted breadfruit, and a cold drink. The heat is in the pepper.
funFacts: Scotch bonnet is a Caribbean chile, Capsicum chinense.
Pimento is the Jamaican name for the allspice tree, and its wood is the traditional jerk smoke.
variations: Seed the Scotch bonnet for a hot paste. Leaving the seeds in pushes it hotter.
A covered charcoal grill is the home tool. It is not a pimento-wood pit unless that wood is on the fire.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 pounds, cut into 8 pieces
steps: Blend scallions, thyme, allspice, Scotch bonnet, garlic, ginger, salt, oil, and lime juice into a paste. Wear gloves with the pepper. Coat the chicken. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Refrigerate the coated chicken if it sits. Do not leave the garlic paste at room temperature. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Grill over coals, ideally with pimento wood if you have it, turning often, until the thickest piece reads 165°F (74°C) away from the bone. Juices should run clear.
Rest the chicken a few minutes. Every piece should have reached 165°F (74°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Jamaican Jerk Pork Shoulder
culture: Jamaican pit cooks who still jerk pork shoulder, the older cut
flavor: Pork shoulder with a heavy allspice and Scotch bonnet paste, cooked until you can slice or chop it.
history: Pork is the older jerk meat. Maroon cooks in the Jamaican hills used pimento wood and a hot, aromatic paste on pig, long before chicken became the more common restaurant order. A shoulder needs hours, not the short grill of chicken pieces, which is why this is a separate recipe. Scotch bonnet is a New World chile, and allspice is a Caribbean tree.
background: This shoulder is seasoned more heavily than the chicken, and it stays on a covered fire until the center is safe and, if you want it tender enough to chop, much hotter than the sliceable minimum. It is not the chicken recipe with a different label.
whyItTastes: Shoulder fat melts slowly and carries allspice, thyme, and Scotch bonnet into the meat. A long fire, especially one with pimento wood, dries the surface into a bark while the inside stays moist. Chicken cannot sit that long without going dry, so the pork tastes deeper and more perfumed.
authenticTouch: Use a full measure of allspice. The berry should be obvious in the pork, not a faint dusting.
method: Coat a pork shoulder in a thick jerk paste and cook it covered for several hours, to a pork temperature that matches how you will serve it.
served: Chop or slice it and eat it with breadfruit, festival, or rice and peas.
funFacts: Jerk was a pork cook before chicken became the more common restaurant order.
A shoulder needs a longer fire than chicken pieces, which is why the two recipes are separate.
variations: For sliced pork, stop at the whole-muscle temperature and a rest. For chopped jerk, keep going until the shoulder softens.
No pimento wood: cook it on a covered charcoal grill and say the smoke is not pimento.
steps: Blend scallions, allspice, thyme, Scotch bonnets, garlic, ginger, brown sugar, salt, vinegar, and oil into a thick paste. Coat the pork. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not leave the paste out. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Set up a covered grill or oven for a long, moderate cook, about 300°F (150°C). This is hours, not the chicken grill.
Cook until the center of the shoulder is at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes if you will slice it. If you want it choppable, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C), then rest it.

Slice or chop the rested pork. It should already have reached the temperature you chose in the cooking step. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Cuban Lechón Asado
culture: Cuban feast cooks, including the criollo line of Spanish and African Cuban kitchens
flavor: Skin-on pork with garlic and sour orange, roasted until the skin crackles.
history: Pigs came to Cuba with Spanish colonization, and enslaved and free Africans cooked a large share of the island's pork, which is the criollo background of lechón asado. A whole pig is the feast; a skin-on shoulder is the home lechón and should be labeled as that. The English word barbecue passed through Spanish barbacoa, from a Taíno word for a framework of sticks, a Caribbean path into English rather than a single recipe. Cuban lechón is not that Taíno framework, and it is not Haitian boukannen.
background: This page is the spit or the covered roast of a whole pig, scaled at home to a skin-on shoulder. The seasoning is Cuban mojo. The oven shoulder that follows on its own page is a different, wetter cook.
whyItTastes: Sour orange and a large amount of garlic season the fat, and a long fire dries the skin until it blisters. The meat underneath stays porky and sour rather than sweet. Trade brought the citrus and the pig; the island's cooks, including African Cuban cooks, set the amounts. A home shoulder can taste of that mojo even when it is not a whole animal.
authenticTouch: Dry the skin and salt it. Wet skin will not crackle, no matter how strong the mojo is.
method: Season a skin-on pork shoulder, the home lechón, with mojo and roast it on a spit or uncovered until the center is safe and the skin is crisp.
served: Chop the meat and crackling together and eat it with white rice, black beans, and yuca.
funFacts: A whole pig is the feast lechón; a skin-on shoulder is the home size and should be called that.
The word barbecue reached English through Spanish barbacoa, from a Taíno word for a stick framework.
variations: A covered grill can stand in for a spit. Say so if you are not actually turning the meat.
Sour orange is the acid. Orange juice plus lime is the substitute when sour oranges are not sold.
ingredients: 6 pounds skin-on pork shoulder, the home lechón, not a whole pig
1 cup sour orange juice, or 1/2 cup orange juice plus 1/2 cup lime juice
steps: Mix the juice, garlic, oregano, cumin, salt, pepper, and oil. Rub it under the skin and over the meat. The pork is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not store this garlic mojo at room temperature. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

Dry the skin. Spit the shoulder or set it uncovered on a rack. This is the home lechón, not a whole pig. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

Roast it, starting moderate and finishing hotter if you want the skin to blister, until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes. For pullable meat, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C) before the rest.

Chop the rested pork, skin included if it crackled. The center should already have reached the temperature you cooked to. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Cuban Mojo Pork Shoulder
culture: Home cooks in Cuba who roast a pork shoulder in mojo
flavor: A covered pork shoulder soaked with garlic, cumin, and sour orange.
history: Mojo is the Cuban marinade of sour orange, garlic, oregano, and cumin. At home it is often poured over a pork shoulder and roasted in a covered pan, which is a different meal from the spit-roasted whole pig. The pig and the citrus both belong to the island's history after Spanish colonization, and African Cuban cooks shaped how those flavors were used. This page is the home shoulder only.
background: Do not use this recipe as a stand-in for the whole-pig lechón. The pan is covered for part of the cook, the skin is not the point, and the sauce stays spoonable. It is still Cuban, and it is still pork.
whyItTastes: A covered pan keeps the sour orange and garlic against the shoulder instead of drying them off on a spit. Cumin and oregano, pantry spices of the Spanish and Canary trade into the Caribbean, round the acid. The pork tastes braised and bright, not like crackling.
authenticTouch: Mash the garlic with salt to a paste before it meets the juice. Floating garlic bits will not season a five-pound shoulder.
method: Roast a pork shoulder in mojo in a covered home pan until it reaches a pork-shoulder temperature.
served: Slice or shred it and spoon the pan juices over rice and beans. This is not the chopped crackling of a lechón feast.
funFacts: This is an oven shoulder for a home kitchen, not the spit-roasted whole pig.
Sour orange is the acid; orange juice plus lime is the stand-in when sour oranges are not sold.
variations: Uncover the pan at the end if you want a little browning. It will still not be a crackling lechón.
A picnic shoulder with the bone in needs the same center temperature, checked away from the bone.
ingredients: 3/4 cup sour orange juice, or 6 tablespoons orange juice plus 6 tablespoons lime juice
8 garlic cloves, mashed with 2 teaspoons salt
steps: Stir juice, garlic, oregano, cumin, pepper, and oil. Pour it over the pork and onion in a covered pot. The pork is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not leave the mojo at room temperature. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Heat an oven to 325°F (165°C). This is a covered home roast, not a spit and not a whole pig.
Cook, covered, until the center is at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes to slice. For shredded pork, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C), then rest.

Slice or shred the rested pork and spoon on the juices. The center should already have reached the temperature you chose. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Puerto Rican Lechón Asado
culture: Puerto Rican lechoneros, especially along the road above Cayey
flavor: Roast pork seasoned with garlic, oregano, and achiote, with a salted skin.
history: Puerto Rican lechón asado is a whole pig on a spit, sold at lechoneras and cooked for holidays. The seasoning is adobo, garlic, salt, pepper, and oregano, and many cooks also paint the skin with achiote. That is not the Cuban mojo page: cumin and sour orange are not the center here. Guavate, in the hills of Cayey, became famous for a road of these pits. A home shoulder is the workable size and should be labeled as a shoulder.
background: Adobo on this page is a garlic and oregano rub you mix yourself, not a packet with unnamed additives. Achiote oil colors the skin. The cook is a spit or a stand-in roast, and the meat is pork.
whyItTastes: Garlic, black pepper, and oregano sit in the fat, and achiote stains it a deep orange without tasting like a chile. A long spit dries the skin in the open air of the hills. The flavor is savory and porky, closer to a salted roast than to a sour Cuban mojo.
authenticTouch: Warm the annatto seeds in oil and strain them. Use that colored oil the same day. Do not store it on the counter.
method: Rub a skin-on pork shoulder with Puerto Rican adobo and achiote oil, then spit-roast or oven-roast it to a pork-shoulder temperature.
served: Chop meat and skin together and eat it with arroz con gandules or plain rice and a salad.
funFacts: Guavate, above Cayey, is known for a road of lechoneras.
Achiote colors this pork. The seasoning is not Cuban mojo.
variations: Some cooks skip achiote and use only adobo. The pork is still this dish.
A home oven, uncovered, replaces a spit. Say that it is not a roadside pit.
ingredients: 6 pounds skin-on pork shoulder, a home lechón
steps: Warm the annatto seeds in the oil until the oil is red, then strain them out. Mix that oil with garlic, oregano, salt, pepper, and vinegar. Use it the same day. Do not leave it at room temperature. The pork is still raw. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

Rub the mixture under and over the skin. Refrigerate it if it waits. This is a shoulder, not a whole pig, unless you are actually cooking a whole pig. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Spit-roast it, or roast it uncovered on a rack, until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes. For meat you can pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C) before the rest.

Chop the rested pork. The center should already have reached the temperature you cooked to. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Puerto Rican Pinchos
culture: Street grill cooks at kiosks and roadside stands in Puerto Rico
flavor: Grilled pork cubes with garlic, oregano, and a light sweet-sharp glaze.
history: Pinchos are pork skewers sold from small grills along Puerto Rican roads and beaches. They use the island's adobo tastes, garlic and oregano, and often a light glaze. They are a street portion, not the whole pig of a lechonera. The cubes are whole muscle, so they are cooked as pork pieces rather than as ground meat.
background: This is a skewer for a hot grill. The glaze is brown sugar, garlic, and vinegar, mixed at home. It is not a bottled barbecue sauce, and it is not the long roast of lechón.
whyItTastes: Small cubes brown on all sides, so you get more crust than a roast shoulder. Garlic and oregano match the rest of the island's pork, and a little sugar in the glaze darkens on the coal without turning the meat into candy. Sea air and a quick grill are the street setting, and the seasoning still works in a backyard.
authenticTouch: Cut the cubes the same size so they finish together. A thick end next to a thin one will mislead a single thermometer reading.
method: Skewer garlic-seasoned pork cubes and grill them, brushing on a small glaze near the end.
served: Eat the skewers on a piece of bread if you want the street sandwich, or without bread. Bread is a pairing and adds wheat.
funFacts: Pinchos are street skewers, sold from grills along roads and beaches.
They are pork cubes, not the whole animal of a lechonera.
variations: A spoon of guava paste in the glaze is a common street version. This recipe uses brown sugar instead.
Chicken pinchos would need 165°F (74°C). These are pork.
ingredients: 2 pounds pork shoulder, in 1 1/2 inch cubes
steps: Toss the pork with garlic, oregano, salt, and oil. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Thread it onto skewers. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Stir brown sugar, vinegar, and tomato paste into a small glaze. Keep it cold until the grill is ready. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the skewers, turning, until the center of the thickest cube reads 145°F (63°C). Brush on the glaze in the last few minutes. Rest the skewers 3 minutes.
The cubes should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Eat them hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Dominican Wasakaka Chicken
culture: Dominican cooks who grill or roast chicken and dress it with wasakaka
flavor: Roasted or grilled chicken with a fresh garlic and herb sauce.
history: Wasakaka is a Dominican sauce of garlic, herbs, and lime or sour orange, spooned over grilled or roasted chicken. It belongs to the Dominican table, including the pollo a la brasa and pollo al carbón that families buy and cook. The sauce is not Argentine chimichurri and not Cuban mojo, even though garlic and acid appear in all three. The bird is poultry and is cooked through.
background: The chicken can be grilled or roasted. The wasakaka is mixed the day you eat it and kept cold. Oregano and cilantro, or parsley, are the herbs. This page uses cilantro.
whyItTastes: Chicken skin browns over direct heat, and the raw garlic sauce stays sharp because it never goes on the fire for long. Lime or sour orange is the Caribbean acid, and oregano is the dried herb of the Spanish-speaking islands. Together they make the plate taste fresh rather than glazed.
authenticTouch: Salt the sauce enough to season the chicken. A pale, unsalted wasakaka will taste like wet garlic.
method: Grill or roast chicken to a poultry temperature and dress it with wasakaka mixed the same day.
served: Serve with tostones, white rice, and beans. The sauce is spooned at the table.
funFacts: Wasakaka is a Dominican garlic and herb sauce for grilled or roasted chicken.
It is a Dominican sauce, not chimichurri and not Cuban mojo.
variations: Sour orange replaces lime when you can buy it.
An oven roast reaches the same poultry temperature if you do not have a grill.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 pounds, cut into pieces
3 tablespoons neutral oil, for the sauce
steps: Oil and salt the chicken. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).

Stir garlic, cilantro, oregano, lime juice, oil, and salt into wasakaka. Refrigerate it and use it the same day. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Grill or roast the chicken until the thickest piece reads 165°F (74°C) away from the bone.
Rest it briefly. Every piece should have reached 165°F (74°C). Spoon on the wasakaka. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Haitian Boukannen
culture: Haitian cooks who grill and smoke pork with epis
flavor: Grilled pork with garlic, thyme, and a hot pepper, edged with smoke.
history: Boukannen is Haitian grilled or smoked pork, usually built on epis, the garlic, thyme, and pepper seasoning of the kitchen. The French word boucan and the Spanish word barbacoa are related Caribbean words for a wooden frame used over fire, and both passed into later languages from that region. Related words are not the same dish: a boucan is not a Cuban lechón, and it is not a Mexican barbacoa. This page is the Haitian pork cook.
background: Epis is blended and used the day you cook, then kept cold. The pork here is a whole-muscle steak or thick slice, grilled, not a fried griot. Smoke is welcome. A long cure is not part of the recipe.
whyItTastes: Thyme, garlic, and Scotch bonnet are the taste of epis, and an open fire dries the surface of the pork. The related words boucan and barbacoa point at a Caribbean way of setting meat over a frame, but the flavor on the plate is Haitian seasoning, not a generic smoke. The pepper is hot, and the thyme stays visible.
authenticTouch: Cook epis pork soon after you season it, or refrigerate it. Garlic and oil should not sit out while the fire burns down.
method: Season pork with epis and grill or lightly smoke it to a whole-muscle temperature.
served: Slice it and eat it with plantains, pikliz if you already have a jar, and rice.
funFacts: French boucan and Spanish barbacoa are related Caribbean words, and they are not the same dish.
Haitian boukannen is grilled or smoked pork, seasoned in a Haitian kitchen.
variations: A covered grill with a little wood gives more smoke. An open grate is still boukannen.
Griot is pork that is fried after a marinade. It is a different cook and not this page.
ingredients: 1/4 cup sour orange juice or lime juice
steps: Blend scallions, garlic, thyme, Scotch bonnet, juice, salt, and oil into epis. Coat the pork. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not leave the paste at room temperature. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Burn wood or charcoal to coals. The pork can sit beside a little smoke or directly over the grate. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the thickest steak reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested pork. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Trinidadian Grilled Kingfish
culture: Trinidadian cooks who marinade fish with chadon beni
flavor: Grilled kingfish or mahi with culantro, garlic, and a hot pepper.
history: In Trinidad and Tobago, kingfish is a common grill, and the marinade is built on chadon beni, the local name for culantro, with garlic and thyme. Chadon beni is Eryngium foetidum, a different herb from cilantro, with a stronger leaf. The fish may be kingfish or mahi when that is what the market has. Both are cooked as fish, to the same temperature.
background: Green seasoning is an everyday Trinidadian blend, not a single bottled brand. This one is culantro, garlic, thyme, pepper, and lime. The fish is the meal. It is not a meat dish with a fish name.
whyItTastes: Culantro is more pungent than cilantro, so a short marinade still tastes green and garlicky after the grill. Lime keeps the oil from feeling heavy. A hot grate marks the steaks, and the pepper, a Caribbean chile, sits in the fat of the fish rather than in a separate sauce.
authenticTouch: If you only have cilantro, use more of it and say it is not chadon beni. The two herbs are related and not interchangeable in strength.
method: Marinate kingfish or mahi in culantro and garlic, then grill it until it flakes.
served: Eat it with pepper sauce, a slice of avocado, and coconut-scented rice if that is on the table.
funFacts: Chadon beni is culantro, Eryngium foetidum, which Trinidadian cooks use by the bunch.
It is a different herb from cilantro, though the two are related.
variations: Mahi-mahi replaces kingfish when kingfish is not sold. Name the fish you actually cooked.
Leave the seeds out of the pepper if you want the plate less hot.
ingredients: 2 pounds kingfish steaks, or mahi-mahi if kingfish is not sold
1 cup chopped chadon beni (culantro), or a larger handful of cilantro labeled as a substitute
steps: Blend culantro, garlic, thyme, pepper, lime juice, salt, and oil. Coat the fish. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. If you used cilantro, tell people it is not chadon beni. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Refrigerate the fish if it sits more than a few minutes. Do not leave the garlic marinade out. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Grill over a hot fire until the thickest steak reads 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes.
The fish should already be at 145°F (63°C). Serve it hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Barbadian Grilled Flying Fish
culture: Barbadian fish cooks, including the Friday grills at Oistins
flavor: A light, herb-seasoned fish with lime, whether it is flying fish or a named substitute.
history: Flying fish is the fish most associated with Barbadian cooking, often fried or steamed with cou-cou and also grilled at seaside stalls. Oistins is one of the places people go for that fish. When flying fish is not sold where you live, a mild white fish such as tilapia is a substitute and has to be named as one. Do not call the substitute flying fish.
background: The seasoning is thyme, garlic, onion, lime, and a mild pepper. The fish is small and quick on a hot grill. Cou-cou, a cornmeal side, is a pairing and is not cooked in this recipe.
whyItTastes: Flying fish is mild and a little sweet, so thyme and lime do the seasoning instead of a heavy sauce. A short grill keeps it from drying. A substitute white fish can take the same herbs, and it will taste like that fish, which is why the name on the plate has to stay honest.
authenticTouch: Dry the fillets well. Small fish stick and tear if they go onto a wet grate.
method: Season flying fish, or a stated mild white fish, and grill it until it flakes.
served: Eat it with lime, a little pepper sauce, and cou-cou or rice if you have it.
funFacts: Flying fish is the fish most associated with Barbadian cooking.
When it is not sold where you live, a mild white fish is a substitute and should be named as one.
variations: Whole small flying fish and fillets both work. Check the thickest part either way.
Cou-cou is the classic side and is not required to call the fish grilled.
ingredients: 2 pounds flying fish fillets, or 2 pounds mild white fish such as tilapia if flying fish is unavailable
steps: If you are not using flying fish, label the substitute out loud and on any note you serve with it. Pat the fish dry and rub it with salt, garlic, onion, thyme, lime juice, and oil. It is raw and is not ready to eat. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Oil a hot, clean grate. The fish is not ready to eat until it reaches 145°F (63°C) and turns opaque.
Grill the fillets until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C) and the fish is opaque and flakes. Small fillets may be done in only a few minutes.
The fish should already be at 145°F (63°C). Serve with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Bahamian Grilled Spiny Lobster
culture: Bahamian cooks who split spiny lobster for the grill
flavor: Spiny lobster grilled with lime, garlic, and a little pepper.
history: The lobster of the Bahamas is spiny lobster, a warm-water animal without the big claws of a cold-water lobster. Grilling a split tail is a common cook on the islands. This version is lime, garlic, and a little goat pepper or other mild heat. It is not the Antiguan grill, which is built on butter and thyme.
background: Spiny lobster tails are shellfish. They are done when the flesh is opaque and pearly and has reached the shellfish temperature. A clawed lobster is a different animal and not what this page describes.
whyItTastes: Lime and garlic stay bright on a lean, sweet shellfish, and a short grill over coals adds a little browning without a dairy sauce. The Bahamian pepper is floral and hot, used in a small amount so the lobster remains the taste. Butter and thyme would push the plate toward the Antiguan version, so they are left off here.
authenticTouch: Split the tail and grill it shell side down first so the meat cooks in the shell instead of drying on the open grate.
method: Grill split spiny lobster tails with lime and garlic until the flesh is opaque.
served: Eat it with lime, peas and rice, and a simple slaw.
funFacts: Bahamian lobster is spiny lobster, which does not have the big claws of a cold-water lobster.
This lime and garlic grill is a different plate from the Antiguan butter and thyme lobster.
variations: Leave the pepper out if you want the lobster only lime and garlic.
A clawed lobster tail can be cooked to the same temperature, and it should not be called Bahamian spiny lobster.
ingredients: 4 spiny lobster tails, about 8 ounces each, split lengthwise
1/2 mild hot pepper such as a Bahamian goat pepper, seeded and minced
steps: Loosen the meat from the shell but leave it in place. Rub it with oil, garlic, salt, lime juice, and pepper. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. The shellfish is not ready to eat until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Heat a grill to medium-high. The shellfish is not ready to eat until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Grill shell side down, then turn, until the flesh is opaque and pearly and the center reads 145°F (63°C).
The lobster should already be opaque and at 145°F (63°C). Serve with more lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Saint Lucian Coal Pot Chicken
culture: Saint Lucian home cooks who grill chicken on a clay coal pot
flavor: Charcoal chicken with garlic, thyme, and a local pepper, cooked over a small clay stove.
history: A coal pot is a small clay charcoal stove used in Saint Lucia and across the eastern Caribbean. Chicken cooked on one is a home grill: seasoned, set over the coals in the pot's crown, and turned until it is done. This page is that Saint Lucian chicken. It is not a smokehouse bird and not a jerk pit, even though thyme and hot pepper appear in all of them.
background: The seasoning is garlic, thyme, chive, lime, and a minced hot pepper. The coal pot is the fire. A small charcoal grill is the home substitute if you do not own a clay pot, and it should be described as a substitute.
whyItTastes: A coal pot burns a short bed of charcoal close to the meat, so the skin browns and the thyme and garlic stay on the surface. Lime keeps the seasoning sharp. The taste is a backyard charcoal chicken, smaller and more direct than a long smoke.
authenticTouch: Wait until the charcoal in the coal pot is covered in ash. Cooking over smoking, unlit coals tastes like fuel.
method: Season chicken and grill it over a coal pot, or a clearly labeled substitute grill, to a poultry temperature.
served: Eat it with boiled green fig and saltfish if that is the day's starch, or with rice and a green salad.
funFacts: A coal pot is a small clay charcoal stove, not a smoking barrel.
Coal pots are used across the eastern Caribbean; this page is the Saint Lucian chicken.
variations: A kettle grill replaces a clay coal pot. Say that it is not a coal pot.
Green seasoning can include culantro where it is sold. This recipe uses thyme and chive.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 pounds, cut into pieces
1 small hot pepper, seeded and minced
steps: Rub the chicken with garlic, thyme, chives, salt, lime juice, pepper, and oil. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Light charcoal in a coal pot and wait until it is ashed over. If you use another grill, say it is not a coal pot. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Grill the chicken, turning, until the thickest piece reads 165°F (74°C) away from the bone.
Rest it briefly. Every piece should have reached 165°F (74°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Poulet Boucané
culture: Creole cooks in Martinique and Guadeloupe who smoke chicken
flavor: Smoked chicken with garlic, thyme, and a West Indian pepper.
history: Poulet boucané is smoked chicken in the Creole cooking of Martinique and Guadeloupe. Boucané means smoked, and the word sits in the same Caribbean family as French boucan, a frame for drying and smoking meat. The chicken itself is a later Creole plate, seasoned with garlic, thyme, and piment. This page pins the map on Martinique and counts Guadeloupe as the other island where the same name is used.
background: This is a smokehouse or covered-smoker bird, not the open coal-pot grill of Saint Lucia and not Jamaican jerk. The smoke is part of the name. A home kettle with a small wood chunk is a substitute and should be called a home smoker, not a boucan.
whyItTastes: Smoke settles on seasoned skin, and thyme and garlic stay recognizable underneath it. The pepper is a Caribbean chile, used in a measured amount so the thyme still shows. Because the bird cooks longer than a quick grill, the flavor is rounder and less sharp than coal-pot chicken.
authenticTouch: Keep the smoke thin and the temperature moderate. Bitter, heavy smoke will cover the thyme.
method: Season a chicken and smoke it until the thickest meat reaches a poultry temperature.
served: Serve it with rice, red beans, and a little pickled chile.
funFacts: On a Martinique or Guadeloupe menu, boucané means the meat has been smoked.
The same name is used on both islands. This pin is Martinique, and Guadeloupe is the other country listed.
variations: A cut-up chicken smokes faster than a whole bird. Check every piece.
No smoker: a covered grill with a small wood chunk is a home substitute. Say so.
ingredients: 1 West Indian hot pepper, seeded and minced
Wood chunks for a smoker, such as a mild fruit wood
