steps: Rub the chicken with garlic, thyme, salt, oil, pepper, and onion. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not leave the paste out. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Heat a smoker or a covered grill set up for indirect heat to about 300°F (150°C), with a thin stream of smoke. A home kettle is not a traditional boucan.
Cook until the thickest part of the thigh and the breast each read 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest the chicken briefly. It should have reached 165°F (74°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Antiguan Grilled Lobster
culture: Antiguan cooks who grill lobster with butter, thyme, and local pepper
flavor: Lobster grilled with butter, thyme, and a local hot pepper.
history: Grilled lobster in Antigua and Barbuda is a butter, thyme, and hot-pepper cook, different from the lime and garlic spiny lobster of the Bahamas. The animal is usually a warm-water lobster tail. Butter carries the thyme and the pepper onto the meat as it browns. This page keeps those three seasonings and does not copy the Bahamian plate.
background: The written recipe uses butter, so it is not dairy-free. The pepper is minced into the butter rather than served only as a side sauce. The flesh is shellfish and is cooked until opaque.
whyItTastes: Butter browns at the edge of the shell and holds thyme against the sweet meat. A local hot pepper, the kind grown in the eastern Caribbean, adds heat without the citrus-first taste of the Bahamian grill. The result is richer and more herbal.
authenticTouch: Melt the butter with the thyme before it goes on the lobster so the herb actually flavors the fat.
method: Grill lobster tails with thyme butter and a minced hot pepper until the flesh is opaque.
served: Serve with more thyme butter, bread if you want it, and a green salad. Bread adds wheat and is a pairing, not part of the lobster.
funFacts: Antiguan grilled lobster is seasoned with butter, thyme, and a local hot pepper.
It is a different seasoning from the Bahamian lime and garlic lobster.
variations: A split tail and a whole tail both work if the center of the meat is checked.
Clarified butter resists burning. Ordinary butter is what this recipe uses, watched closely.
ingredients: 4 lobster tails, about 8 ounces each, split
1 small Antiguan or other hot pepper, seeded and minced
steps: Melt the butter with thyme, pepper, garlic, and salt. Keep it warm and use it the same day. Do not leave garlic butter at room temperature for later. The lobster is raw and is not ready to eat. The shellfish is not ready to eat until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Brush the cut meat with some of the butter. The shellfish is not ready to eat until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Grill, shell side down first, until the flesh is opaque and pearly and the center reads 145°F (63°C). Brush once more near the end.
The lobster should already be opaque and at 145°F (63°C). Serve with the remaining warm butter. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Jamaican Roast Breadfruit
culture: Jamaican cooks who roast breadfruit on coals
flavor: Soft, roasted breadfruit with a browned skin and a mild, starchy center.
history: Breadfruit is a tree fruit from the Pacific. It was brought to the Caribbean in the late eighteenth century, including on the British voyage that stocked Jamaican gardens, as food for enslaved people on plantations. Jamaican cooks made the fruit their own. Roasting it on coals is one ordinary way to cook it. This is a cook of the fruit, not a meat dish.
background: There is no meat, fish, or shellfish in the recipe. The fruit is set on coals until the stem end loosens and the center is soft. It is a side beside jerk or a plate by itself with salt and lime.
whyItTastes: The coals dry and char the skin while the starchy interior steams. That contrast is the flavor: a little smoke, a soft crumb, and almost no seasoning. The fruit traveled from the Pacific into Caribbean yards, and the roast tastes of that adopted staple rather than of a sauce.
authenticTouch: Turn the fruit a few times so one side does not carbonize before the center softens. The stem pulls when it is ready.
method: Roast a whole breadfruit on coals until the center is soft. This cooks the fruit and nothing else.
served: Split it, scoop out the center core, and eat the flesh with salt and lime. It can sit beside jerk, and it is still not meat.
funFacts: Breadfruit was carried from the Pacific to the Caribbean in the late eighteenth century.
Roasting it on coals cooks the fruit. There is no meat in the dish.
variations: A peeled wedge in a pan over the fire is easier to turn. It is the same fruit.
Butter at the table is common and would add dairy. This written recipe has none.
ingredients: 1 ripe but firm breadfruit, about 3 pounds
Coals from a wood or charcoal fire
steps: Leave the breadfruit whole. There is no meat to season. Cut a small cross at the stem so steam can leave.
Set it directly on ashed-over coals, not in an open flame.
Turn it until the skin is well browned all over and a skewer into the center meets soft flesh, about an hour. The stem end should pull.
Cool it until you can handle it, peel it, and cut away the central core. Season with salt and lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This remains a fruit, not a meat dish.

name: Argentine Asado
culture: Argentine parrilla cooks on the pampas and in the cities
flavor: Salted beef cooked over wood coals, with chimichurri as a table sauce.
history: An Argentine asado is a mixed grill on a parrilla, wood burned down to coals, with salt as the seasoning. Cattle ranching on the pampas made beef the center of the meal. Vacío, a flank cut, and tira de asado, cross-cut beef short ribs, are two cuts the fire is built to hold, and each has its own page here. Chimichurri is the green sauce beside the meat, not a glaze cooked onto it. Indigenous nations of the plains had their own fires; this parrilla is the later criollo cattle cook.
background: This page is the mixed fire, not a single steak and not a Uruguayan cross. The meat is whole beef. Chimichurri is a pairing, with its own recipe in this file, so it is not repeated as an ingredient here.
whyItTastes: Hard woods of the region burn to a steady coal, and the beef cooks in dry heat with little more than salt. Fat bastes the cut as it sits. The flavor is beef and wood, and the sharp parsley sauce is there to cut it afterward. A rushed gas grill without coals will brown the meat and miss the wood.
authenticTouch: Salt early, then leave the meat alone. Moving it every minute tears the crust the coals are trying to make.
method: Grill vacío and tira de asado over wood coals with coarse salt, to a whole-beef temperature, and serve chimichurri beside them.
served: Eat the cuts as they are ready, with chimichurri, bread, and a simple salad. Bread is a pairing and adds wheat.
funFacts: Vacío and tira de asado are two cuts a parrilla is built to cook, and each has its own page.
Chimichurri is a table sauce. The meat on this fire is salted, not buried in the sauce.
variations: Some parrillas serve beef pinker than this guidance. This recipe uses 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest.
A kettle grill with wood chunks is a home fire. Say so if it is not a parrilla grate over coals.
ingredients: 2 pounds tira de asado, beef short ribs cut across the bone
Wood such as a hard regional firewood, burned to coals
steps: Salt both cuts. They are still raw and are not ready to eat. Let the salt sit while the wood burns to coals. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Spread the coals under a grill grate. This is a parrilla fire, not a closed smoker. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the thickest part of each cut reads 145°F (63°C). Rest the meat 3 minutes. The rib may stay on longer if you want it looser, which will be past 145°F (63°C).
Slice the rested beef. Both cuts should have reached at least 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve chimichurri on the side. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Argentine Vacío
culture: Parrilla cooks in Buenos Aires and on the pampas
flavor: Flank grilled over coals, salted, sliced thin across the grain.
history: Vacío is a flank cut on the Argentine parrilla, thinner than a roast and quicker than a rack of ribs. It is its own page because the cut cooks differently from tira de asado and from a mixed grill. The seasoning is coarse salt. Chimichurri stays on the side. Mataderos in Buenos Aires is one neighborhood where Sunday fires still draw a crowd.
background: This is flank, whole muscle, not short ribs and not a sausage. Slice it across the grain after the rest. It is still an asado cut, cooked on the same kind of wood fire.
whyItTastes: Flank is beefy and a little loose, so it picks up coal smoke quickly and stays interesting when sliced thin. Salt is enough because the cut has its own flavor. A long sauce cook would hide the thing the parrilla is trying to show.
authenticTouch: Grill it in one piece and slice after the rest. Precut strips dry out before the center is done.
method: Salt a flank and grill it over coals to a whole-beef temperature, then slice it across the grain.
served: Serve the slices with chimichurri and bread. The bread is a pairing.
funFacts: Vacío is a flank cut, thin enough to grill more quickly than a thick rib.
It is not short ribs and not a ground sausage.
variations: A labeled flank steak from another butcher chart is the right home cut if vacío is not the name in the case.
Some cooks like it pinker than 145°F (63°C). This recipe holds the safety line and the rest.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef flank, in one piece
Wood or charcoal burned to coals
steps: Salt the flank. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill it over coals, turning when the first side is browned. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested flank across the grain. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Argentine Tira de Asado
culture: Argentine grill cooks who cut short ribs across the bone
flavor: Cross-cut beef short ribs, salted and grilled on the bone.
history: Tira de asado is beef short rib cut across the bones into a strip, a standard cut on an Argentine parrilla. The bones stay in. It is not vacío and not a boneless steak. Salt and coals are the method. Cooks who want the meat looser leave the strips on past the safety temperature. This page is only the ribs.
background: Ask a butcher for beef short ribs cut across the bone, about an inch thick. Pork ribs are a different animal and a different temperature conversation. These are whole beef.
whyItTastes: The bone and the fat between the ribs baste the meat while the coals brown the outside. Because the strip is thin, you taste char and beef in the same bite. Salt is the only seasoning, so the wood and the fat are what you notice.
authenticTouch: Keep the strips in one layer. Stacked ribs steam, and steamed tira is not the grill cut.
method: Salt cross-cut beef short ribs and grill them over coals to at least a whole-beef temperature.
served: Serve the strips with chimichurri and a tomato and onion relish.
funFacts: Tira de asado is beef short rib cut across the bones into strips.
The bones stay in. This is not a boneless steak.
variations: Leaving the ribs on longer, past 145°F (63°C), makes the meat looser. The safety line is still 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest.
A thicker strip needs more time. Check the meat, not the clock.
ingredients: 3 pounds beef short ribs, cut across the bone into strips
Wood or charcoal burned to coals
steps: Salt the strips. They are still raw and are not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill them over coals in one layer, turning as the fat browns. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the thickest meat reads 145°F (63°C). Rest 3 minutes. If you want them looser, continue past 145°F (63°C) after that line is met.
Serve the rested ribs. They should have reached at least 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Choripán
culture: Street and parrilla cooks in Argentina and the Río de la Plata
flavor: Grilled fresh chorizo in bread, with a sharp green sauce.
history: Choripán is a grilled fresh chorizo split into bread, a street sandwich of the Río de la Plata asado. The sausage is ground pork, so it has to be cooked through the way other ground meat is. The bread is wheat. Chimichurri or salsa criolla goes on the crumb. It is not a dried Spanish chorizo eaten cold.
background: Buy a fresh, raw chorizo meant for the grill, often called chorizo parrillero. A fully cooked smoked sausage is a different product. The roll is part of the dish, which is why this page includes wheat.
whyItTastes: Pork fat, paprika, and garlic inside the sausage drip onto the coals and flavor the crust. The bread catches that fat. A vinegar sauce cuts it. The sandwich tastes of a quick street grill, not of a long cured sausage.
authenticTouch: Split the sausage lengthwise once the outside is set, so the center can brown and so you can check the temperature in the middle.
method: Grill fresh chorizo to a ground-meat temperature and serve it in bread.
served: Put the split sausage in a roll with chimichurri. Eat it as a sandwich.
funFacts: The sausage is a fresh chorizo, so it is cooked through like other ground meat.
The bread is part of the dish, which is why this one is a sandwich.
variations: A Uruguayan choripán is the same idea. This page is written from the Argentine street grill.
Salsa criolla instead of chimichurri is a common choice on the same sausage.
ingredients: 6 fresh raw pork chorizos, about 4 ounces each
1/2 cup chimichurri, from the chimichurri recipe or a parsley, garlic, vinegar, and oil sauce
steps: Prick the sausages once if the casings are very tight. They are raw ground pork and are not ready to eat. Ground meat is not ready to eat until it reaches 160°F (71°C).
Grill them over coals or a hot grate, turning, until the center of each sausage reads 160°F (71°C). Split them to check the middle if you need to.
Toast the cut rolls on the grill for a minute. The bread is wheat. Ground meat is not ready to eat until it reaches 160°F (71°C).
Every sausage should have reached 160°F (71°C) before it goes in the bread. Add chimichurri. Refrigerate leftover meat within 2 hours.

name: Argentine Grilled Mollejas
culture: Parrilla cooks who grill sweetbreads beside the other cuts
flavor: Grilled sweetbreads with a browned crust and a mild, rich center.
history: Mollejas on an Argentine menu are sweetbreads, usually the thymus, grilled on the parrilla. They are offal, cooked through and served with lemon. They are a standard cut beside the steaks, not a novelty. This page treats them as food and gives a clear temperature.
background: Buy fresh sweetbreads from a butcher you trust. Soak and trim them, then grill them. They are beef offal and need at least 145°F (63°C) and a rest. They are not a sausage and not a steak.
whyItTastes: Sweetbreads are mild and fatty, so a hard grill gives them a crust that the inside does not have on its own. Lemon and a little salt are the usual finish. Wood coals add the same dry heat the rest of the asado uses, which keeps the plate in one fire rather than in a separate fryer.
authenticTouch: Peel the membrane after a short simmer, or the grilled outside will be papery. Dry the pieces well before they hit the grate.
method: Simmer, trim, and grill beef sweetbreads until they reach an offal temperature.
served: Salt them and eat them with lemon. Chimichurri is optional and is a pairing.
funFacts: Mollejas on an Argentine menu are sweetbreads, usually the thymus.
They are offal, and they are cooked to at least 145°F (63°C).
variations: A piece of grilled lemon is enough. A heavy spice rub is not the parrilla habit.
If you buy them already cleaned, you still dry them and you still take a temperature.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon neutral oil or a brush of beef fat
Water and a teaspoon of salt, for the short simmer
steps: Soak the sweetbreads in cold water in the refrigerator for an hour, then simmer them in salted water for 10 minutes. They are not yet grilled and are not ready to eat. Drain, cool enough to handle, and peel the membrane. This offal is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes.
Dry the pieces, oil them, and salt them. This offal is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes.
Grill over coals until the center of the thickest piece reads at least 145°F (63°C). Rest 3 minutes.
The rested sweetbreads should have reached at least 145°F (63°C). Serve with lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Provoleta
culture: Parrilla cooks who melt a thick slice of provolone on the fire
flavor: Grilled provolone, browned at the edge, with oregano and a little chile.
history: Provoleta is a thick round of provolone grilled in a small metal dish on the Argentine parrilla, usually before the larger cuts are eaten. It is a side of the asado, and it is cheese, so it is vegetarian and it is not vegan. Oregano and dried chile are the usual scatter on top.
background: There is no meat in the dish. Butter is not required if the cheese has enough fat to brown. The provolone is dairy. People who avoid dairy should skip this page.
whyItTastes: Provolone browns where it meets the hot dish and stays soft in the center, so you get a toasted edge and a mild, salty middle. Oregano and chile are dry and sharp against the fat of the cheese. It tastes of the same fire as the beef, without being beef.
authenticTouch: Use a thick slice, at least an inch. A thin deli slice melts through the grate and disappears.
method: Grill a thick piece of provolone in a small pan until it softens and the top browns.
served: Eat it hot with bread. The bread is a pairing and adds wheat. The cheese itself is the side.
funFacts: Provoleta is a thick slice of provolone grilled on the same fire as the meat.
It is vegetarian, and it is not vegan, because the ingredient is cheese.
variations: A drizzle of olive oil on top is common. It does not replace the cheese.
A home oven broiler can brown the top. It is not a parrilla, and it still melts the cheese.
ingredients: 1 pound provolone, in a single thick slice about 1 inch deep
steps: Set the provolone in a small cast-iron skillet or provoletera. There is no meat in this dish.
Drizzle the oil and scatter the oregano and chile.
Grill over coals or broil until the cheese is soft throughout and the top is spotted brown. Do not walk away. It goes from melted to scorched quickly.
Eat it hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. It is cheese, so it is not a vegan plate.

name: Uruguayan Asado al Espeto
culture: Uruguayan cooks who set meat on a cross beside a wood fire
flavor: Beef roasted slowly beside wood, on a cross rather than a quick grate.
history: Uruguayan asado al espeto is often a cross of iron or wood set beside a wood fire, and the pace is slower than a steak on a grate. The Argentine meal people picture first is often a parrilla, a grill over coals, though Argentina also uses a cross, especially for lamb in Patagonia. This page does not claim that only Uruguay cooks on an espeto. It describes the Uruguayan cross.
background: A whole side of beef is the countryside version. A large roast or a rack is the home version and should be named as a smaller cut. The seasoning is salt. The fire sits beside the meat so the cook can watch the pace.
whyItTastes: A side fire browns the beef more slowly than a grate directly over coals, so the outside dries a little and the inside stays even. Wood smoke is light if the flames are not licking the meat. Salt and time are the flavor, which is why this cross tastes different from a fast city steak even when the animal is the same.
authenticTouch: Keep flames from touching the meat. The espeto is beside the fire, and the cook turns the cross when one side has had enough.
method: Salt a large beef roast and cook it on a spit or a cross beside wood until it reaches a whole-beef temperature.
served: Slice it and eat it with chimichurri or a simple salad. The sauce is a pairing.
funFacts: Asado al espeto is often a cross beside the fire, at a slower pace than a grate over the coals.
Uruguay and Argentina share asado, and both countries use more than one kind of fire.
variations: A home rotisserie is closer to an espeto than a frying pan is. Say if you are not using a cross.
Lamb on a cross is a Patagonian page in this file, not this beef cook.
ingredients: 4 pounds boneless beef roast, a home stand-in for a larger cut on the cross
Wood for a fire beside a spit or a sturdy rotisserie
steps: Salt the roast. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Tie it if the shape is uneven. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Set it on a spit or a cross beside a wood fire, not in the flames. A home rotisserie should be described as a rotisserie if you have no cross. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook, turning, until the center reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Brazilian Picanha
culture: Churrasco cooks in southern Brazil, and the restaurants that adopted the cut
flavor: Rump cap grilled with its fat cap on, seasoned only with coarse salt.
history: Picanha is the rump cap of the beef, grilled with the fat cap left on and with coarse salt as the seasoning. It is a defining cut of Brazilian churrasco, strongly associated with the south and now cooked across the country. It is not carne de sol, the salted beef of the Northeast. Some restaurants serve it pinker than the temperature on this page. The guidance here is 145°F (63°C) and a rest.
background: The fat cap is not trimmed off. It bastes the meat. A long spice paste is not what makes the cut picanha. Steaks or a C-shaped skewer are both used. This page uses a skewer and allows a hot grill.
whyItTastes: The fat cap melts over the lean cap of the rump, so each slice tastes richer than a lean steak from the same animal. Coarse salt stays on the surface and crackles. Southern Brazilian churrasco is a wood or charcoal fire, and that dry heat browns the fat instead of steaming it.
authenticTouch: Score the fat cap in a crosshatch, without cutting into the meat, so the salt has somewhere to sit and the fat can render.
method: Salt the fat-on rump cap and grill it on a skewer, fat toward the heat, to a whole-beef temperature.
served: Slice it against the grain and eat it with farofa, a vinaigrette relish, and rice. Those sides have their own pages.
funFacts: The cut is the rump cap, and the fat cap stays on.
Coarse salt is the seasoning. A long spice paste is not what makes it picanha.
variations: Thick steaks on a hot grill, fat cap down first, are a home version of the skewer. Say if you are not using a skewer.
Carne de sol is a different Brazilian beef and not a stand-in for this cut.
ingredients: 2 1/2 pounds beef picanha, rump cap, fat cap left on
Long metal skewers, or a hot grill if you name it as the home version
steps: Score the fat cap and salt the meat. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Fold the piece onto skewers with the fat outward, or lay steaks fat side down on a hot grill and say that is the home version. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested meat across the grain. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Brazilian Grilled Linguiça
culture: Brazilian grill cooks who put fresh linguiça over the coals
flavor: Garlicky pork sausage with a browned casing and a cooked-through center.
history: Linguiça is a Brazilian pork sausage, usually garlic and paprika, grilled beside the other cuts at a churrasco. The sausage on this page is fresh and uncooked, so it is ground meat and needs 160°F (71°C). It is not Argentine chorizo in a roll, and it is not a dried sausage eaten cold. Southern Brazil grills it often. The same sausage also shows up far from the pampas.
background: Read the label. This recipe assumes pork, salt, garlic, and paprika, with no wheat filler. If your package lists wheat, do not call the plate gluten-free. A fully cooked smoked linguiça only needs to be heated, and it is a different product from the raw one written here.
whyItTastes: Garlic and paprika stain the pork fat, and the grill dries the casing until it snaps. The center stays juicy only if you pull it when it is cooked through, not when it is merely brown. Charcoal is the usual fire, and it adds a little bitterness that the sweet fat can stand.
authenticTouch: Turn the links often. A sausage that splits and dumps its fat onto the coals will dry out before the center is hot enough.
method: Grill fresh pork linguiça until the center reaches a ground-meat temperature.
served: Eat it with rice, farofa, and a vinaigrette relish. A roll is optional and would add wheat.
funFacts: Linguiça is a Brazilian pork sausage, seasoned with garlic and often paprika.
Fresh linguiça is ground meat and needs 160°F (71°C) even when the outside looks browned.
variations: If you only have a fully cooked smoked linguiça, heat it until it is steaming hot, at least 145°F (63°C), and do not treat it as the raw sausage in this recipe.
Chicken linguiça would need 165°F (74°C). This one is pork.
ingredients: 1 1/2 pounds fresh uncooked pork linguiça, labeled pork, salt, garlic, and paprika, with no wheat
1 teaspoon coarse salt, only if the links are not already very salty
A hot grill of charcoal or wood coals
steps: Check the label for wheat. The sausages are raw ground pork and are not ready to eat. Ground meat is not ready to eat until it reaches 160°F (71°C).
Grill them over medium coals, turning often. Ground meat is not ready to eat until it reaches 160°F (71°C).
Cook until the center of each link reads 160°F (71°C). A brown casing is not enough.
Every link should have reached 160°F (71°C) before it is served. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Brazilian Chicken Heart Skewers
culture: Churrascaria cooks who grill chicken hearts as coração
flavor: Salted chicken hearts with a browned outside and a fully cooked center.
history: Chicken hearts, coração, are a standard skewer at Brazilian churrascarias. They are poultry offal, salted and grilled as everyday food. Because they are poultry, this page cooks them to 165°F (74°C), the ground-poultry temperature used here for hearts. They are everyday protein on the fire, often one of the first skewers to come off.
background: Trim the veins and any hard bits, salt the hearts, and thread them so they cook evenly. They are not beef heart, which is the Peruvian anticucho on another page, and they are not a chicken sausage.
whyItTastes: Hearts are lean and mineral, and coarse salt plus a hot skewer give them a crust before they dry out. Charcoal is the usual fire. They taste direct and savory, which is why they sit on the same rod as the larger cuts without a sweet glaze.
authenticTouch: Thread the hearts close together so they stay juicy, and spread the skewers so the heat still reaches the centers.
method: Salt chicken hearts and grill them on skewers to 165°F (74°C).
served: Eat them from the skewer with a vinaigrette relish and farofa.
funFacts: Chicken hearts are a standard skewer at Brazilian churrascarias and are called coração.
They are poultry, and this recipe cooks them to 165°F (74°C).
variations: A squeeze of lime at the table is enough. A heavy marinade is optional and not required.
Beef heart is a different skewer, with a different temperature, on the Peruvian page.
steps: Trim the hearts, dry them, and toss them with oil and salt. They are raw poultry and are not ready to eat. Thread them on skewers. These are poultry and are not ready to eat until they reach 165°F (74°C).
Heat a grill until it is hot. These are poultry and are not ready to eat until they reach 165°F (74°C).
Grill, turning, until the center of a heart in the middle of the skewer reads 165°F (74°C).
Every heart you serve should have reached 165°F (74°C). Rest them a minute and eat them hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Brazilian Costela
culture: Gaucho cooks in Rio Grande do Sul who leave beef ribs beside a wood fire
flavor: Beef ribs cooked a long time beside wood, salty and deeply browned.
history: Costela is beef rib cooked for hours beside a wood fire in southern Brazil. Gaucho cooks often take it until the meat is tender, which is past 145°F (63°C). That longer cook is a choice of texture. The ribs do not need to reach a brisket temperature to be costela. The safety line for the whole cut is still 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest.
background: This is beef rib, whole muscle, not pork rib and not picanha. Salt is the seasoning. The fire is open, watched, and slower than a steak. A home oven can finish the same cut and should be called an oven if that is what you used.
whyItTastes: A long stay beside wood dries the surface and softens the collagen without a sweet sauce. The fat cap and the bones baste the meat. Southern camps use whatever hard wood is at hand, and the flavor is beef and light smoke rather than a spice crust.
authenticTouch: Start with the bone side toward the gentler heat. A roaring flame will char the outside long before the inside eases.
method: Salt a rack of beef ribs and cook it beside an open wood fire, or in a moderate oven, past the whole-muscle safety line if you want it tender.
served: Slice between the bones and eat it with farofa, vinaigrette, and rice.
funFacts: Costela is beef rib, cooked long beside a wood fire in southern Brazil.
Many gauchos cook it past 145°F until it is tender. A brisket temperature is not required.
variations: Stop at 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest if you want the rib sliceable like a steak.
An oven at 300°F (150°C) is a home finish. It is not a camp fire.
ingredients: 5 pounds beef ribs, in a rack
Wood for an open fire, or an oven if you are cooking at home
steps: Salt the ribs. They are still raw and are not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Set them beside a wood fire, not in the flames, or on a rack in a 300°F (150°C) oven. Say which fire you used.

Cook until the thickest meat reads at least 145°F (63°C), then rest 3 minutes. Many gauchos continue until the ribs are tender, past 145°F (63°C). They do not have to reach 195°F (90°C) to count as costela.
Slice the rested ribs. They should have reached at least 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Northeastern Carne de Sol
culture: Cooks in the Brazilian Northeast who grill salted beef
flavor: Salty grilled beef from the Northeast, served with cassava and a fresh relish.
history: Carne de sol is beef salted in the Northeast of Brazil, traditionally dried in the sun and then cooked. The name means meat of the sun. It is a sertão food, not the fat-capped picanha of southern churrasco, and it does not belong to the southern asado set. This home recipe does not ask you to cure or sun-dry meat. Buy prepared carne de sol, or salt a steak briefly in the refrigerator and grill it.
background: The written cook is a hot grill of whole-muscle beef. A short refrigerator salting is seasoning, not a cure. Sun-drying in the yard is not a step. Cassava and a tomato relish are the usual company.
whyItTastes: Salt concentrates the beef, and a hot grill browns it before the slice dries out. The Northeast is hotter and drier than the southern grasslands, which is why salting, rather than a long wood roast of a fat cap, became the keeping method. The plate tastes salty and direct, with lime or a fresh relish to balance it.
authenticTouch: If the market meat is very salty, soak it in cold water in the refrigerator and change the water once before you grill.
method: Grill prepared or briefly salted beef to a whole-muscle temperature. Do not cure it at home.
served: Serve it with boiled cassava, rice, and a tomato relish. Butter on the cassava would add dairy and is not in this recipe.
funFacts: The name means meat of the sun and belongs to the Northeast, where salt was a way to keep beef.
It is not picanha, and this recipe does not include home curing.
variations: Purchased carne de sol may only need a rinse and a grill. Follow the salt you taste, and still take a temperature.
A thin steak salted for one hour in the refrigerator is the stand-in, and it should be called a stand-in.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef steak, or purchased carne de sol
2 teaspoons salt, only if you are not using already salted meat
Cold water, if the purchased meat needs a rinse
steps: If the beef is already salted, rinse it and refrigerate it in cold water for 30 minutes, then pat it dry. If it is fresh steak, salt it and refrigerate it for 1 hour. Do not sun-dry it and do not cure it. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Oil the meat lightly and heat a grill. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Chilean Asado
culture: Chilean backyard cooks who grill beef over wood or coals
flavor: Salted beef from a Chilean grill, with a little merkén and a fresh relish beside it.
history: A Chilean asado is beef grilled in a backyard quincho, over wood or charcoal, salted and eaten with pebre more often than with Argentine chimichurri. Merkén, a smoked chile and coriander condiment from Mapuche cooking, is one seasoning Chilean cooks reach for. The asado itself is a criollo grill, not a claim that the whole fire is a Mapuche ceremony. This page is that Chilean grill.
background: Pebre, a chopped onion, tomato, and cilantro relish, is the usual table sauce and is listed as a pairing rather than cooked onto the meat. The beef is a whole cut. If you cannot buy merkén, say that smoked paprika is not merkén.
whyItTastes: Coals brown the beef, and salt keeps the flavor on the meat. Merkén adds smoke and a mild chile heat that a plain Argentine salt crust does not have. The fresh pebre at the table is sharp and raw, so the plate tastes of grill plus a salad, not of a cooked sauce.
authenticTouch: Use merkén as a finish or a light rub, not a thick paste. The beef should still taste like beef.
method: Salt a steak, dust it with merkén, and grill it over coals to a whole-beef temperature.
served: Rest it, slice it, and eat it with pebre, bread, and a tomato salad. Bread is a pairing and adds wheat.
funFacts: A Chilean asado is its own grill, often served with pebre rather than Argentine chimichurri.
Merkén is a Mapuche smoked-chile and coriander condiment.
variations: No merkén: grill the steak with salt only, and do not rename smoked paprika.
A thicker roast on the same fire still needs 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef steak or a small roast
1 teaspoon merkén, or 1 teaspoon smoked paprika labeled as not merkén
Wood or charcoal burned to coals
steps: Oil the beef and season it with salt and merkén. It is still raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Burn the fuel to coals and set a grate over them. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve pebre on the side. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Chilote Curanto
culture: Chilote cooks on Chiloé, in a practice with a long Indigenous history
flavor: Mussels, pork, chicken, and potatoes cooked together, smoky in a pit and softer in a pot.
history: Curanto is a Chilote earth oven with a long Indigenous history on the archipelago. Chono and Huilliche practice is part of that older root, and later Chilote families kept the pit as a feast of shellfish, meat, and potatoes. Curanto en olla, the home pot on this page, is a pot and is not the earth oven. The foods overlap. The fire does not.
background: The pot holds pork, chicken, and mussels, so the temperatures are not the same. Pork is a whole cut, chicken is poultry, and mussels are shellfish. Discard any mussel that stays shut. This is a Chilote meal, written for a kitchen pot.
whyItTastes: In the ground, hot stones and leaves steam shellfish liquor into the meat and the potatoes. A pot keeps those juices and loses the stone and the leaf. The taste is still sea and pork and potato, which is why the pot is worth cooking, and why it should not be described as the pit.
authenticTouch: Layer potatoes under the meat so they take the drippings, and do not stir once the mussels go in.
method: Cook pork, chicken, potatoes, and mussels in a covered pot, each to its own temperature. Call it curanto en olla, not a pit.
served: Bring the pot to the table with a green salad. The broth at the bottom is part of the meal.
funFacts: Curanto is a Chilote earth oven with a long Indigenous history on the Chiloé archipelago.
Curanto en olla is a home pot and is not that earth oven.
variations: Clams can join the mussels. They are shellfish and are done when open and opaque, at 145°F (63°C).
A real pit is a different project. This recipe does not pretend to be one.
safety: Cook pork to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes. Cook chicken to 165°F (74°C). Cook mussels until the shells open and the flesh is opaque, about 145°F (63°C), and discard any that stay closed.
ingredients: 1 1/2 pounds pork shoulder, in large chunks
steps: Put potatoes, onion, garlic, salt, and water in a heavy pot. Add the pork and chicken. The meats are raw and are not ready to eat. This pot is curanto en olla, not an earth oven. Pork needs at least 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest, chicken needs 165°F (74°C), and mussels need to open with opaque flesh at 145°F (63°C).
Cover and simmer until the pork reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and the chicken reaches 165°F (74°C) away from the bone. Rest the pork 3 minutes if you remove it. Keep the chicken at 165°F (74°C).
Add the mussels, cover again, and cook until they open and the flesh is opaque and pearly, 145°F (63°C). Discard any mussel that stays closed.
Check the pork again at 145°F (63°C) or hotter and the chicken at 165°F (74°C) before serving. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Peruvian Anticuchos
culture: Afro-Peruvian street cooks in Lima and other coastal cities
flavor: Beef heart skewers with vinegar, garlic, and a dried red chile.
history: Anticuchos are beef-heart skewers. Enslaved Africans in coastal Peru, and the Afro-Peruvian cooks who followed them, turned this offal into a skilled street food, and Lima still grills it at night. Aji panca, a dried Peruvian red chile, is the usual pepper. Another dried red chile can be used if you say it is a substitute and not aji panca. The heart is whole muscle and is cooked to at least 145°F (63°C).
background: This is offal, treated as a regular cook. Vinegar, garlic, cumin, and the dried chile are the marinade. The skewers are street food, eaten with potato and aji.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and aji panca taste sharp and dried-chile sweet, which is how Afro-Peruvian cooks seasoned beef heart for the grill. Charcoal browns the outside while the heart stays a whole muscle. The flavor is that marinade and that fire, tied to a history of labor, not to a garnish.
authenticTouch: Cut the heart across the grain into even cubes so the skewers finish together and stay tender enough to chew.
method: Marinate beef heart in aji panca, vinegar, and garlic, then grill it on skewers to an offal temperature.
served: Eat the skewers with boiled potato and a spoon of the same chile sauce.
funFacts: Anticuchos are beef-heart skewers associated with Afro-Peruvian cooking.
Aji panca is a dried Peruvian red chile. Another dried red chile is a substitute and not the same pepper.
variations: If aji panca is not sold, use 2 tablespoons of another ground dried red chile and name it.
A hotter aji can be served on the side. The skewer in this recipe stays mild.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef heart, trimmed and cubed
3 tablespoons aji panca paste, or 2 tablespoons ground dried red chile named as a substitute
steps: Mix the chile, vinegar, garlic, cumin, salt, and oil. Coat the heart. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. This offal is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes.
Thread the cubes onto skewers, leaving a little space between them. This offal is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes.
Grill over hot coals, turning, until the center of a cube reads at least 145°F (63°C). Rest the skewers 3 minutes.
The heart should have reached at least 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve it hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Peruvian Pollo a la Brasa
culture: Lima restaurant cooks who made rotisserie chicken an everyday meal
flavor: Rotisserie chicken with garlic, cumin, and a mild dried red chile.
history: Rotisserie chicken became a Lima restaurant food in the mid-twentieth century, and pollo a la brasa is now an ordinary meal across the city. This page does not treat a single founder story as settled fact. The bird is seasoned with garlic, cumin, and aji panca and cooked as poultry to 165°F (74°C). A home oven bird is not a rotisserie unless it actually turns on a spit.
background: The written marinade has no soy sauce and no beer, so the recipe stays free of those allergens. Restaurant blends vary. The temperature does not. Serve it with fries and a green sauce if you like, as pairings.
whyItTastes: Turning the bird in dry heat crisps the skin while cumin and garlic stay in the fat. Aji panca is mild and fruity rather than sharp. Lima's version became popular because it was a whole chicken, seasoned and ready, not because of one secret ingredient. The taste is that spice and that browned skin.
authenticTouch: Truss the bird so the heat is even, and check both breast and thigh. One reading is not the whole chicken.
method: Marinate a chicken and roast it on a spit, or in an oven labeled as not a rotisserie, to a poultry temperature.
served: Cut it into pieces and eat it with salad, potatoes, and aji verde if you have it.
funFacts: Rotisserie chicken became a Lima restaurant food in the mid-twentieth century.
This page does not name a single founder as settled fact.
variations: An oven rack is the home stand-in. Say that it is not a spit.
A hotter aji on the table does not change the mild rub on the bird.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons aji panca paste, or 1 tablespoon ground dried red chile named as a substitute
steps: Mix garlic, chile, cumin, salt, pepper, vinegar, and oil. Rub the chicken under and over the skin. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. The poultry is not ready to eat until the thickest part reaches 165°F (74°C).
Spit-roast it if you have a rotisserie. If you do not, roast it on a rack in a 400°F (200°C) oven and say it is not a rotisserie.
Cook until the thickest part of the breast and the thigh each read 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest the chicken briefly. Both readings should have reached 165°F (74°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Andean Pachamanca
culture: Quechua and other Andean cooks who use an earth oven
flavor: Pork and chicken steamed with herbs, potato, and corn, concentrated and soft.
history: Pachamanca is an Andean earth oven. The name is Quechua. Quechua communities and other Andean communities cook it, and the meats, herbs, and hot stones vary by valley. A covered pan in a home oven is not a pachamanca. This page says so, and it still gives a workable packet with temperatures for pork and for chicken.
background: Huacatay and chincho are herbs some valleys use. Mint is a home stand-in and is not those herbs. The pork and the chicken have different safe temperatures. Potatoes and corn cook in the same pot and do not change those numbers.
whyItTastes: An earth oven steams meat against hot stones and herbs, so the flavor is juicy and herbal rather than charred. Valley by valley, the herb changes. A home pot keeps garlic, cumin, and mint against the meat and misses the stone. That is a real difference, and it is the reason to name the method honestly.
authenticTouch: Keep the lid on. Every time you check early, you lose the steam that makes the packet taste like anything but a roast.
method: Cook pork and chicken with potatoes in a covered home pot until each meat is at its own temperature. Do not call the pot a pachamanca.
served: Open the pot at the table and eat the meats with the potatoes and corn.
funFacts: Pachamanca is an Andean earth oven, and the name is Quechua.
Practices vary by community. A home oven packet is not a pachamanca.
variations: Lamb in the same pot would be a whole cut at 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest. This written recipe is pork and chicken.
Huacatay, if you know the herb, can replace the mint. Say which leaf you used.
safety: Cook pork to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes. Cook chicken to 165°F (74°C). A home pot is not a pachamanca.
ingredients: 2 pounds pork shoulder, in large chunks
2 ears of corn, cut into rounds
1/4 cup chopped mint, or huacatay if you know that herb
steps: Toss the pork and chicken with garlic, cumin, salt, and mint. They are raw and are not ready to eat. This covered pot is not a pachamanca. The pork is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes, and the chicken is not ready until it reaches 165°F (74°C).

Layer potatoes and corn in a heavy pot, add the meat and the water, and cover tightly. The pork is not ready to eat until it reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes, and the chicken is not ready until it reaches 165°F (74°C).
Cook at a steady simmer or in a 325°F (165°C) oven until the pork reads at least 145°F (63°C) and the chicken reads 165°F (74°C) away from the bone. Rest the pork 3 minutes.
Both temperatures should already be met before you serve. For pork you want softer, continue past 145°F (63°C). Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Bolivian Pacumutu
culture: Grill cooks in Santa Cruz and the Bolivian Chaco
flavor: Salted beef skewers with a browned edge, eaten with yuca.
history: Pacumutu is a grilled meat skewer served in Santa Cruz and the Bolivian Chaco. The meat is usually beef, cut in large pieces and cooked over a hot fire, with yuca beside it. This page keeps the dish regional and does not invent a single origin story for the name. It is a plains and lowland grill, not the Andean earth oven and not an Argentine parrilla.
background: The written recipe is beef on skewers, salted, cooked as a whole cut. Yuca is a pairing you boil separately. A hot sauce at the table is optional and is not mixed into the meat.
whyItTastes: Large cubes take a crust on the outside and stay juicy if you stop at the whole-muscle temperature. Salt is the seasoning, so the taste is beef and charcoal. Yuca, mild and starchy, is the contrast people in Santa Cruz expect, rather than a wheat tortilla.
authenticTouch: Cut the cubes large and even. Tiny pieces will dry before they taste like this skewer.
method: Salt beef cubes, skewer them, and grill them to a whole-beef temperature.
served: Eat the skewers with boiled yuca, rice, and a simple onion salsa.
funFacts: Pacumutu is a grilled meat skewer of Santa Cruz and the Bolivian Chaco.
Yuca, not a wheat tortilla, is the usual starch beside it.
variations: Pork on the same skewer would need 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest. This recipe is beef.
A thicker piece cooked beside the fire, rather than over it, is still this dish if the temperature is met.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef steak, in 1 1/2 inch cubes
steps: Toss the beef with oil, salt, and pepper. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Thread it onto skewers. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill until the coals are hot. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest cube reads 145°F (63°C). Rest the skewers 3 minutes.
The beef should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve it with yuca. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Colombian Carne a la Llanera
culture: Cooks on the Colombian llanos who grill beef over wood
flavor: Beef grilled over wood, salted, with a charred edge and a juicy center.
history: Carne a la llanera is beef from the Colombian llanos, the cattle plains east of the Andes, grilled over wood. Villavicencio is a gateway to that country. The cook is an open fire, often a large cut on a frame or a grate. It shares a landscape with Venezuelan carne en vara and it is not the same recipe. Salt is the seasoning.
background: A home-size roast stands in for the very large cuts of a llanero fire. Say so. The meat is whole beef. Yuca, plantain, and aji are the usual sides, listed here as pairings.
whyItTastes: Wood on the open plains burns hot and clean, and the beef tastes of that dry heat and of salt. There is no long spice paste. The flavor is the animal and the fire, which is the point of calling it a la llanera rather than a city steak with a sauce.
authenticTouch: Burn the wood to coals before a thick roast goes on. Flames will crust the outside while the center is still raw.
method: Salt a beef roast and grill it over wood coals to a whole-beef temperature.
served: Slice it and eat it with yuca, plantain, and a fresh aji salsa.
funFacts: The llanos are the cattle plains of eastern Colombia.
The beef is cooked over wood, which is why it is called a la llanera.
variations: A thin steak on the same coals cooks faster and still needs 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest.
A gas grill is a home substitute. It is not a wood fire on the llanos.
steps: Oil the roast and salt it. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Spread wood coals under a grate. Keep a flame from touching the meat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Colombian Chuzos
culture: Colombian street cooks who grill pork skewers
flavor: Pork skewers with cumin, garlic, and a little tomato.
history: Chuzos are Colombian street skewers, usually pork or chicken, grilled and often served with potato and a sauce. They are not Peruvian anticuchos, which are beef heart, and they are not the large beef of the llanos. This recipe is pork, a whole muscle, cooked to 145°F (63°C). Chicken on the same stick would be a different temperature.
background: The marinade is garlic, cumin, oil, and a little tomato paste. It is a street seasoning, not a long cure. Arepa or potato can sit beside the skewer. Arepa is a pairing and, if made with wheat, would add gluten. Corn arepas do not. They are not in the ingredient list.
whyItTastes: Small cubes brown on every side, so the cumin and garlic crust is a large part of each bite. Charcoal is the street fire. The pork stays mild and a little sweet if you do not push the chile, which lets the potato beside it matter.
authenticTouch: Cut the pork evenly. A skewer with one thick cube and several thin ones will not finish at one temperature.
method: Marinate pork cubes, skewer them, and grill them to a whole-pork temperature.
served: Eat them with boiled potato and a simple aji or tomato sauce.
funFacts: Chuzos are Colombian street skewers, usually pork or chicken, not beef heart.
They are a different skewer from Peruvian anticuchos.
variations: Chicken chuzos use the same seasoning and must reach 165°F (74°C). This written recipe is pork.
A piece of sausage on the stick is ground meat and would need 160°F (71°C). It is not in this recipe.
ingredients: 2 pounds pork shoulder, in 1 1/2 inch cubes
steps: Mix garlic, cumin, salt, tomato paste, oil, and vinegar. Coat the pork. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Thread it onto skewers. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill to medium-high. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest cube reads 145°F (63°C). Rest the skewers 3 minutes.
The pork should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Serve it hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Venezuelan Carne en Vara
culture: Cooks on the Venezuelan llanos who roast beef on sticks beside wood
flavor: Beef cooked on sticks beside a wood fire, salted and smoky at the edge.
history: Carne en vara is beef cooked on sticks beside a wood fire in the Venezuelan llanos. The sticks hold large pieces next to the heat rather than directly in a flame. It shares the plains with Colombian carne a la llanera and it is written here as its own dish, with its own salt and its own pace. Yuca and a mashed avocado sauce are common at the table.
background: A home roast on skewers or on a spit beside coals is the workable size. A whole side of beef is the countryside version and is not what this ingredient list buys. The meat is whole beef.
whyItTastes: Cooking beside the fire, instead of over it, dries the surface slowly and keeps a beef taste without a heavy crust of spices. Wood smoke is light. Salt is the seasoning. The llanos are cattle country, and the plate tastes like that plain fire.
authenticTouch: Plant the sticks so you can turn them. A piece that faces the fire the whole time will burn before the far side is cooked.
method: Salt large pieces of beef and cook them on sticks beside a wood fire to a whole-beef temperature.
served: Slice the beef and eat it with yuca. Guasacaca, an avocado sauce, is a pairing and is not required for the meat to be done.
funFacts: In the Venezuelan llanos the meat is cooked on sticks beside a wood fire.
It is a plains beef cook, related in landscape to Colombian carne a la llanera and written as its own dish.
variations: A rotisserie beside a fire is a fair home tool. Say if you are using one.
A thinner steak over the coals is closer to a grill than to carne en vara. Keep the pieces large.
ingredients: 3 pounds beef, in large thick pieces
Strong sticks, long skewers, or a spit
steps: Oil the beef and salt it. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Fix it on sticks or a spit. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Build a wood fire and cook the meat beside the coals, not in the flames. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Turn the sticks until the center of the thickest piece reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Paraguayan Asado
culture: Paraguayan grill cooks who serve beef with yuca
flavor: Beef grilled over wood or coals, salted, with yuca on the plate.
history: A Paraguayan asado is beef on a grill, eaten with yuca and often with sopa paraguaya or chipa at the same table. It belongs to Paraguay's own Sunday fire, in a country that also speaks Guaraní and Spanish. It is not a renamed Argentine parrilla, even though the word asado is shared. The meat is salted and cooked over coals.
background: The recipe is the beef. Yuca is the pairing that makes the plate Paraguayan in this file. Chipa and sopa paraguaya are corn and cheese breads and are not cooked here, so this meat recipe has no wheat and no dairy.
whyItTastes: Coals and salt give the beef a clear grilled taste. Boiled or roasted yuca beside it is mild and filling, which changes the meal from a steak-and-chimichurri plate. The fire is the same family of southern South American grills, and the starch beside it is the local difference.
authenticTouch: Let the beef rest before you slice it. The juices matter because the plate is not covered in sauce.
method: Salt beef and grill it over coals to a whole-beef temperature, then serve it with yuca.
served: Slice the beef and eat it with boiled yuca and a simple onion and tomato salad.
funFacts: A Paraguayan asado is commonly eaten with yuca.
It is a grill in Paraguay, not a renamed Argentine parrilla.
variations: A rack of beef ribs uses the same salt and the same 145°F (63°C) line.
Chipa at the table is a cheese bread and would add dairy and, depending on the recipe, wheat. It is not in this meat.
ingredients: 2 pounds beef steak or a small roast
Charcoal or wood burned to coals
steps: Oil and salt the beef. It is raw and is not ready to eat. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill it over coals. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the thickest part reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Slice the rested beef. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Eat it with yuca. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Patagonian Cordero al Asador
culture: Estancia cooks in Argentine Patagonia who roast lamb on a cross
flavor: Lamb roasted beside a wood fire, salted, with a browned outside.
history: Cordero al asador is lamb opened on an iron cross beside a wood fire in Argentine Patagonia. A whole lamb is the estancia version. A leg is the home version on this page and is not a whole lamb. Mapuche and Tehuelche histories are part of Patagonia, and this cross is an estancia fire rather than a claim to be their only cook. The seasoning is salt.
background: The fire sits beside the cross, and the cook turns the lamb. Uruguay's asado al espeto in this file is a beef cross. This one is Patagonian lamb. Both can be true without becoming the same page.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat bastes the meat as it faces the wood, and the pace is slow because the fire is to the side. Wind and dry wood in Patagonia make a hot, clean coal. Salt is enough. The taste is lamb and light smoke, not a marinade.
authenticTouch: Keep the flames off the leg. The cross works because the heat is steady and near, not because the meat is on fire.
method: Salt a leg of lamb, the home stand-in, and roast it on a spit beside wood to a whole-lamb temperature.
served: Slice it and eat it with a simple salad and bread. Bread is a pairing and adds wheat.
funFacts: Cordero al asador is lamb on a cross beside a Patagonian wood fire.
A single leg is the home version and is not a whole lamb.
variations: A home rotisserie counts if you say it is not an iron cross on an estancia.
Some cooks rub a little garlic. Salt alone is the version written here, plus oil so the salt sticks.
ingredients: 1 bone-in leg of lamb, about 5 pounds, a home cut and not a whole lamb
Wood and a spit, a cross, or a rotisserie you will name honestly
steps: Oil the leg and salt it. It is raw and is not ready to eat. This is a leg, not a whole lamb on a cross. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Set it on a spit beside a wood fire, or on a rotisserie, and say which tool you used. Whole cuts are not ready to eat until they reach at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the thickest part, away from the bone, reads 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes.
Carve the rested lamb. It should have reached 145°F (63°C) before the rest. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ecuadorian Hornado
culture: Highland cooks in Ecuador who roast pork in a wood-fired oven
flavor: Roast pork with garlic, cumin, and achiote, sliced, with a browned outside.
history: Traditional hornado is a long roast in a wood-fired oven, often a whole pig, in the Ecuadorian highlands. Ambato is one city known for it, and the cook is wider than one town. A home oven shoulder is the workable version and is not that long wood-oven pig. Garlic, cumin, and achiote are the seasoning. This recipe uses vinegar instead of beer so the written shoulder has no wheat.
background: The shoulder is pork, cooked until it is safe to slice, and longer if you want it to pull. The skin can crisp if it stays uncovered and dry. Call the pan a home oven roast.
whyItTastes: A long oven visit gives the garlic and cumin time to season the fat, and achiote colors it without a chile burn. Highland wood ovens add a gentle roast flavor that a covered braise does not. The home oven keeps the spice and loses some of the wood. The pork still tastes of those spices.
authenticTouch: Salt the skin and leave it uncovered if you want it crisp. A tight lid will steam it soft.
method: Rub a pork shoulder with garlic, cumin, and achiote and roast it in a home oven to a pork-shoulder temperature.
served: Slice it and eat it with llapingachos or potatoes, and a simple onion relish. Those sides are pairings.
funFacts: Traditional hornado is a long wood-oven roast, often a whole pig, in the Ecuadorian highlands.
A home oven shoulder is the workable version and should be called that.
variations: For sliced pork, stop at 145°F (63°C) and a 3-minute rest. For meat you can pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Beer appears in some marinades. This one uses vinegar so the written recipe has no wheat.
ingredients: 4 pounds skin-on pork shoulder, a home hornado
steps: Mix garlic, achiote, cumin, salt, pepper, vinegar, and oil. Rub it over the pork and under the skin if you can. The pork is raw and is not ready to eat. Refrigerate it if it waits. Do not leave the paste at room temperature. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Heat a home oven to 325°F (165°C). This is not a wood-fired highland oven and not a whole pig.
Roast uncovered until the center is at least 145°F (63°C). Rest it 3 minutes to slice. For pullable pork, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C), then rest.

Slice or pull the rested pork. The center should already have reached the temperature you chose. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The pork is not ready to eat until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and rests 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

name: Argentine Chimichurri
culture: Cooks who set a bowl of green sauce on an asado table
flavor: Parsley, oregano, garlic, vinegar, oil, and chile, chopped and sharp.
history: Chimichurri is the green sauce of the Argentine asado: parsley, oregano, garlic, vinegar, oil, and chile. Stories about the name are disputed, so this page does not pick one. It is a table sauce, stirred and rested, not a cooked glaze. It belongs beside grilled beef, and it is not the Dominican wasakaka or the Nicaraguan garlic spoon.
background: There is no meat, egg, dairy, or wheat in the bowl. It is vegetarian and vegan. Garlic in oil should be refrigerated and used within a few days. Do not leave it at room temperature.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and raw garlic cut the fat of grilled beef, and parsley and oregano keep the sauce green and herbal. Dried chile adds a small heat without making a pepper paste. On a Río de la Plata table the sauce is the contrast to salted meat and wood coals.
authenticTouch: Chop the parsley by hand if you can. A blender makes a bitter, uniform puree that is a different sauce.
method: Chop parsley, oregano, garlic, and chile, then stir them with vinegar, oil, and salt.
served: Spoon it over sliced grilled beef, or serve it in a bowl so people take what they want.
funFacts: The sauce is parsley, oregano, garlic, vinegar, oil, and chile.
Stories about the name are disputed, so this page does not choose one.
variations: A red chimichurri adds tomato and more chile. This one stays green.
Red wine vinegar and white vinegar are both used. This recipe uses red wine vinegar.
steps: Chop the parsley and mince the garlic. There is no meat in this sauce.
Stir in oregano, vinegar, oil, chile flakes, and salt.
Taste for salt. Let it sit 15 minutes in the refrigerator so the garlic softens into the vinegar.
Serve cold or cool. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Argentine Salsa Criolla
culture: Asado cooks who chop a fresh onion relish
flavor: Raw onion, tomato, and pepper in vinegar and oil.
history: Argentine salsa criolla is an onion, tomato, and pepper relish for the asado, dressed with vinegar and oil. It is not Peruvian salsa criolla, which is built more on onion and lime, and it is not chimichurri, which is a herb sauce. The vegetables stay raw. It is a salad-sauce, eaten the day it is made.
background: There is no meat and no dairy. It is vegetarian and vegan. Salt the onion and let it sit so it softens slightly. Keep it cold. It is not a preserve.
whyItTastes: Raw onion and vinegar cut grilled fat the way a pickle does, and tomato and pepper add water and sweetness. On a Córdoba or Buenos Aires table it sits next to chimichurri so people can choose herbal or fresh. The flavor depends on the onion being fine and the salt being enough.
authenticTouch: Slice the onion very thin and rinse it if you want less bite, then dry it before it meets the oil.
method: Chop onion, tomato, and pepper and dress them with vinegar, oil, and salt.
served: Spoon it over grilled meat or eat it as a small salad beside the fire.
funFacts: Argentine salsa criolla is an onion, tomato, and pepper relish.
It is not Peruvian salsa criolla, which is built differently.
variations: A little parsley is common. This version leaves the herbs to the chimichurri.
Red or green bell pepper both work. Keep the pieces small.
ingredients: 1 large white onion, sliced very thin
steps: Toss the onion with the salt and let it stand 10 minutes. There is no meat in this relish.
Add the tomato, bell pepper, vinegar, and oil.
Stir and taste. Add salt only if the onion needs it.
Serve the same day, cold. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. This is not a canned preserve.

name: Molho à Campanha
culture: Brazilian churrasco cooks who chop a vinaigrette relish
flavor: A fresh chop of tomato, onion, and pepper in vinegar and oil.
history: Molho à campanha is the vinaigrette relish of a Brazilian churrasco, named for the southern grasslands, the campanha. It is chopped tomato, onion, and pepper with vinegar and oil. It is not chimichurri. The herbs, when they appear, are a handful, and the body of the sauce is the vegetables. It is eaten the day it is made.
background: There is no meat in the bowl. It is vegetarian and vegan. The campanha name points at Rio Grande do Sul, and the same relish is now on plates far from that border. Keep it cold.
whyItTastes: Vinegar and raw onion brighten fatty grilled beef, and the tomato makes the sauce wetter than a herb paste. On a southern Brazilian table it sits next to farofa, so you get something fresh and something toasted. The taste is the chop, not a cooked tomato sauce.
authenticTouch: Cut the pieces small and even. Large chunks of onion fall off the meat and never season it.
method: Chop tomato, onion, and pepper and dress them with vinegar, oil, and salt.
served: Spoon it over picanha, linguiça, or rice. Use it the same day.
funFacts: Molho à campanha is the fresh vinaigrette relish of a Brazilian churrasco.
It is not chimichurri. The body is chopped tomato, onion, and pepper.
variations: Cilantro or parsley can be added. This bowl uses cilantro.
A minced hot pepper makes it hotter. The written amount has none.
steps: Chop the vegetables small. There is no meat in this relish.
Stir in cilantro, vinegar, oil, and salt.
Let it stand 10 minutes in the refrigerator, then taste for salt.
Serve cold the same day. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. This is not a canned preserve.

name: Farofa
culture: Brazilian cooks who toast cassava flour in fat
flavor: Toasted cassava flour, buttery and crumbly, with a little onion.
history: Farofa is cassava flour toasted in fat until it becomes a savory crumb for meat, beans, and rice. This recipe uses commercial toasted manioc flour, the kind sold as farinha de mandioca torrada. It does not start from raw cassava, and it does not process bitter cassava at home. Raw bitter cassava is not part of this recipe. Bacon is a common addition. This version uses butter so the written side stays vegetarian.
background: Read the package and use flour that is already safe to cook. Do not grate or soak raw cassava for this page. Butter makes it dairy. It is not vegan. There is no wheat if the flour is only manioc.
whyItTastes: Toasted manioc flour turns nutty in hot butter, and onion softens into the crumb. Beside grilled beef it soaks up juice without becoming a porridge. Cassava is an American root that Brazilian cooks made into this everyday side, and the flavor here is the toasting, not a meat stock.
authenticTouch: Stir constantly once the flour goes in. It burns in spots if it sits, and burned farofa tastes bitter.
method: Cook onion in butter, then toast commercial manioc flour until it smells nutty and looks dry.
served: Sprinkle it over rice, beans, or grilled meat. It is a side, not a dough.
funFacts: This recipe starts with commercial toasted manioc flour and does not process raw cassava.
Farofa is a toasted crumb. Raw bitter cassava is not an ingredient.
variations: Chopped cooked egg is a common add-in and would add egg. It is not in this version.
Oil instead of butter would make it dairy-free. This one uses butter.
ingredients: 2 cups commercial toasted manioc flour (farinha de mandioca torrada), not raw cassava
steps: Read the package. Use commercial toasted manioc flour only. Do not start from raw or bitter cassava.
Melt the butter in a skillet and cook the onion until it is soft. There is no meat in this pan.
Add the flour and salt. Stir over medium heat until the crumb smells toasted and looks dry, about 8 minutes.
Taste for salt. Serve warm. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. The butter means this version is not vegan.

name: Pão de Alho
culture: Churrascaria cooks who toast garlic bread for the grill
flavor: Toasted wheat bread with garlic butter and parsley.
history: Pão de alho is garlic bread cooked for a Brazilian grill, often wrapped and warmed at the edge of a churrascaria fire. The bread is wheat, and the spread is butter and garlic, so the side is vegetarian and not vegan. It is a bread, not a meat, and it is not farofa. Make the butter the day you eat it.
background: There is no meat in the recipe. Butter is dairy. The loaf is wheat, so the dish is not gluten-free. Do not leave garlic butter at room temperature.
whyItTastes: Butter carries raw garlic into toasted crumb, and a minute on the grill dries the edge of the bread. Parsley keeps it from tasting only of garlic. Next to a salty picanha it is rich and soft, which is why the churrascaria bothers to toast it.
authenticTouch: Spread the butter to the crust, then wrap the bread so the garlic steams into the crumb before the outside browns.
method: Spread garlic butter on a split loaf and heat it until the bread is hot and the edges toast.
served: Cut it in strips and eat it with the grilled meat. It is a side.
funFacts: Pão de alho is garlic bread cooked for the Brazilian grill.
The bread is wheat, and the butter makes it a dairy side.
variations: A little grated cheese on top is common and is still dairy. This version has no extra cheese.
An oven heats it as well as a grill. Say which one you used.
ingredients: 1 wheat baguette or small loaf, split
steps: Mash the butter with garlic, parsley, and salt. There is no meat in this spread. Use it the same day. Do not leave garlic butter at room temperature.
Spread it on the cut bread. The loaf is wheat.
Wrap it in foil and heat it on a grill or in a 375°F (190°C) oven until the bread is hot and the edges are toasted, about 10 minutes.
Open the foil for a minute if you want more color. Serve warm. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Santa Maria Pinquito Beans
culture: Ranch and backyard cooks of the Santa Maria Valley in California
flavor: Small pink beans, soft and savory, with onion, garlic, and chile.
history: Pinquito beans are the small pink beans grown around Santa Maria, California, and they are the pot that sits beside the valley's grilled beef. The Santa Maria grill is a central-coast ranch table. Some pots add cured pork. This written recipe has no meat, so it stays vegetarian. The beans are boiled until they are completely tender.
background: Use dried pinquito beans, or small pink beans if the local name is not on the bag. Soak them, then boil them. Do not hold raw dried beans warm. There is no bacon, no lard, and no dairy in the pot.
whyItTastes: Small pink beans take on onion, garlic, and a dried chile and stay a little brothy. Next to beef grilled over red oak, the traditional local wood, they are the mild, filling side. This pot leaves the meat on a different plate, so the bean flavor stays vegetal and clean.
authenticTouch: Boil the beans hard for at least ten minutes before you drop to a simmer. Tender means no chalky center, not just a soft skin.
method: Soak dried pinquito beans, boil them until they are completely tender, and season them with onion, garlic, and chile.
served: Eat them beside grilled beef, salsa, and bread. The beef and the bread are pairings and are not in this pot.
funFacts: Pinquito beans are the small pink bean associated with the Santa Maria Valley in California.
This pot has no meat, so the written recipe stays vegetarian.
variations: Small pink beans are the stand-in if a bag does not say pinquito. Say which bean you cooked.
A cured-pork version exists on some ranch tables. It is not this recipe.
ingredients: 1 pound dried pinquito beans or small pink beans, picked over
1 dried mild chile such as guajillo, stemmed
steps: Rinse the beans and soak them overnight in plenty of water in the refrigerator. Drain them. There is no meat in this pot.
Cover the soaked beans with the 8 cups of water. Bring them to a hard boil for at least 10 minutes. Do not cook raw dried beans only at a warm temperature.
Add the onion, garlic, chile, and oil. Simmer until the beans are completely tender, about 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Add water if they go dry.
Stir in the salt near the end. The beans should be fully soft, with no chalky center. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mexican Elote
culture: Street cooks in Mexico who grill ears of corn
flavor: Grilled corn with chile, lime, and salt.
history: Elote is ear corn grilled over coals in Mexico and dressed at the cart. Many street servings add mayonnaise and cotija cheese. Mayonnaise would bring egg, and cheese or crema would bring dairy. This recipe is the chile-and-lime version only, so the written ear is vegan. The corn is the dish.
background: There is no meat, egg, or dairy in the ingredients. A guajillo chile keeps the heat mild. People who want the creamy street version should know it is a different set of allergens and not this page.
whyItTastes: Grilling dries the kernels and sweetens them, and lime and salt make that sweetness sharper. Mild chile adds color and a little warmth without a sauce. Char from the coals is the smoke. The ear tastes of corn first, which is the point of leaving the creamy dressings off.
authenticTouch: Grill the ears in the husk for a few minutes if you want them juicier, then husk them and char the kernels directly.
method: Grill corn and dress it with lime, salt, and mild chile. Do not add mayonnaise or cheese.
served: Eat the ears hot, with extra lime. It is a side or a street snack.
funFacts: Elote is corn grilled over coals and dressed at the cart.
This version is chile and lime. It does not include mayonnaise or cheese.
variations: A creamy street elote with mayonnaise and cotija is common, and it would add egg and dairy. It is not this recipe.
Chile de árbol instead of guajillo makes the same corn hotter.
ingredients: 4 ears of corn, husks pulled back or removed
1 teaspoon ground guajillo or other mild chile powder
steps: Oil the ears and salt them lightly. There is no meat, mayonnaise, or cheese in this recipe.
Grill the corn over hot coals, turning, until the kernels are browned in spots.
Squeeze on lime and dust the ears with chile and salt.
Eat them hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This version stays vegan because the creamy street dressings are not on it.

name: English Hog Roast
culture: English cooks feeding a crowd from a spit at a fair, a wedding, or a home fire
flavor: Salted pork, crackling, and wood smoke, with enough fat to baste the meat.
history: Turning a pig over a fire is an old English way to feed a gathering. The everyday Sunday roast is usually an oven joint, and the spit is the older fire method. A whole animal needs a long spit, a steady cook, and more meat than most kitchens can hold, so this home version uses a pork shoulder. Salt, time, and a dry skin do the work that a sweet glaze would only cover.
background: This is crowd food for English celebrations, not a weekly supper. The shoulder stands in for a whole hog when the spit and the animal are out of reach. It is still a roast, carved, not a pulled-pork sandwich recipe.
whyItTastes: Pork shoulder carries fat and collagen, and a wood fire browns the skin while the interior stays moist. English cooks have long used that contrast: a crisp outside and a sliceable or shreddable inside. The oven Sunday joint tastes of the kitchen; the spit tastes of the fire that came before it.
authenticTouch: Score the skin and salt it ahead of the fire so the crackling dries. Keep the flames under the fat, not licking the skin into soot.
method: Salt a pork shoulder and turn it on a spit over hardwood coals, or roast it on a rack over a pan if the spit is small. Carve when the temperature and the skin are both ready.
served: Carved onto plates with apple sauce and a sharp salad. Leftover meat is good cold.
funFacts: A home Sunday roast in England is usually cooked in an oven, while the spit is the older open-fire method.
A whole hog is still a fair and wedding roast; a shoulder is the practical home cut.
variations: A whole small pig on a proper spit, for a crew that can tend it all day.
The same salted shoulder in a hot oven when there is no spit.
ingredients: 1 pork shoulder, about 6 lb, skin on
Hardwood chunks or charcoal for the fire
