The horizontal spit bastes the stack with its own drippings. A grate can brown the meat, but it will not copy that slow turning stack, which is why the label matters.
authenticTouch: Slice the lamb evenly and grill it in a single layer. Say that this is a home grill, not the horizontal spit, when you serve it.
method: Season sliced lamb and grill it on a hot grate. This home version is not a horizontal spit.
served: With onion, herbs, and grilled tomato. Eat it hot, as slices.
funFacts: Cağ kebab in Erzurum is cooked on a horizontal spit of stacked lamb slices.
The home recipe is layered sliced lamb on a grill and is not that spit.
variations: A real horizontal spit if you have one and know how to stack the meat safely.
Lamb shoulder slices if leg is not available, still a whole-muscle cut.
ingredients: 2 lb boneless lamb leg, sliced 1/3 inch thick
steps: Toss the lamb slices with salt, pepper, and oil. This home version is grilled slices, not a horizontal spit.
Heat a grill until it is hot. Lay the slices in one layer.
Grill, turning once, until the thickest slice reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Give the meat a 3-minute rest.
Serve with onion. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Lebanese Shish Taouk
culture: Lebanese grill cooks marinating chicken in yogurt and grilling it on skewers
flavor: Chicken with yogurt, garlic, lemon, and a light char.
history: Shish taouk is chicken on skewers, a standard of Lebanese grills. A yogurt marinade is common, which means the dish contains dairy and is not vegan. Garlic and lemon sharpen it. The pieces are small so they cook quickly over charcoal. It is poultry, and it has to be cooked through. This is not lamb kafta and not a garlic sauce by itself.
background: Lebanese restaurants and home cooks grill taouk for a weeknight or a spread. The yogurt makes it dairy. Toum, the garlic sauce, is a separate emulsion and is not in this recipe.
whyItTastes: Yogurt clings to chicken and browns in spots, while lemon and garlic stay bright if you do not burn them. Charcoal adds smoke the oven misses. The dairy is part of the flavor, not a garnish, which is why a dairy-free claim would be false for this version. Small cubes cook evenly, which suits breast or thigh if the temperature is checked.
authenticTouch: Use thigh meat if you can, and wipe off thick yogurt before the grill so it does not carbonize. Check the center of a cube, not the skewer.
method: Marinate chicken in yogurt, garlic, and lemon, then grill on skewers until the poultry is cooked through.
served: With salad, pickles, and rice. A garlic sauce on the side is optional and, if it contains egg, is a separate allergen.
funFacts: Lebanese shish taouk is chicken on skewers, often in a yogurt marinade.
Yogurt means the dish is dairy and not vegan.
variations: Breast meat, watched closely so it does not dry after it reaches temperature.
A dairy-free oil marinade, which would be a different recipe and is not this one.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless chicken thigh, cut in cubes
steps: Mix the yogurt, garlic, lemon juice, salt, and oil. Add the chicken and refrigerate 30 minutes.
Thread onto skewers, letting extra yogurt drip off. Heat the grill to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the thickest cube reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone if any bone remains.
Rest a few minutes. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Lebanese Kafta
culture: Lebanese cooks pressing minced lamb, parsley, and onion onto skewers
flavor: Minced lamb with parsley, onion, and a grilled crust.
history: Lebanese kafta is minced lamb with parsley and onion, pressed on skewers and grilled. The herbs are mixed into the meat, which makes it different from a plain koobideh and from Adana's hot pepper kebab. It is everyday grill food from the coast inland. The meat is ground and cooked through. Allspice is a frequent addition and is included here in a small amount.
background: Home cooks and grill restaurants across Lebanon make kafta. It is not chicken taouk and not a raw kibbeh. Parsley and onion are part of the mince, not only a salad on the side.
whyItTastes: Parsley and onion lighten lamb fat, and the grill dries the surface so the herbs do not taste steamed. A little allspice is a Levantine pantry note. Charcoal smoke ties it to the other skewers on a mixed grill without making it the same as those skewers. The green flecks are how you know the mix.
authenticTouch: Squeeze the onion dry so the mince does not fall off the skewer. Keep the parsley fine, or it will char in strands.
method: Mix minced lamb with parsley and onion, mold it onto skewers, and grill until the center is cooked.
served: With salad, pickles, and rice. Hummus on the side would add chickpeas and often tahini, which is sesame, so it is not in this recipe.
funFacts: Lebanese kafta mixes parsley and onion into minced lamb before it is grilled.
It is a different mince from Iranian koobideh and from Adana kebab.
variations: A mix of beef and lamb, still ground.
Patties grilled without skewers, cooked to the same temperature.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry
steps: Mix the lamb, onion, parsley, salt, and allspice until the meat holds together.
Mold onto skewers in a long shape. Heat the grill to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C).
Serve with salad. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Baghdad Masgouf
culture: Baghdad cooks grilling carp beside an open fire
flavor: Carp with salt, tamarind, olive oil, and the smoke of a fire beside the fish.
history: Masgouf is a Tigris fish cook: carp, split open and staked or set beside an open fire in Baghdad, then finished with a brush of sauce. Riverside restaurants made it famous, and families cook it when they can get the fish. If carp is hard to buy, a firm white fish may be eaten as a substitute, and that substitute is not masgouf. This recipe is written for carp.
background: Baghdad cooks along the Tigris are the reference. The dish is carp and fire, not a fried fish and not a stew. A different species does not inherit the name.
whyItTastes: Carp is rich, and standing it beside the fire, rather than over a hard flame, renders some of that fat slowly and smokes the skin. Tamarind and salt cut the oil. Olive oil at the end shines it. The river fish and the slow side-fire are the taste, which is why a random white fillet in a pan is a different dinner.
authenticTouch: Keep the carp beside the fire, skin toward the heat, and do not rush it. If you must use another fish, say so and do not call the plate masgouf.
method: Split a carp open, salt it, and cook it beside an open fire until it flakes, then brush it with tamarind and oil.
served: With onion and tomato. The fish is the plate.
funFacts: Masgouf is Baghdad's grilled carp, a Tigris fish cook set beside the fire.
A firm white fish can be a substitute, and that substitute is not masgouf.
variations: A covered grill with the fish on a rack away from direct flame, still using carp.
A little turmeric in the brush, which some cooks add.
ingredients: 1 whole carp, about 3 lb, split open and scaled
steps: Pat the carp dry and salt it. Mix tamarind, olive oil, and turmeric into a brush.
Build an open fire. Set the carp skin-side toward the heat, beside the flames rather than in them, on a rack or stakes.
Cook until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes. Brush with the tamarind mixture near the end.
Serve with onion. This recipe is for carp. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Iranian Koobideh
culture: Iranian grill cooks working minced lamb onto wide skewers
flavor: Minced lamb and onion, salted, with a smoky grilled crust.
history: Koobideh is an Iranian minced-lamb kebab pressed on a wide skewer. The name is widely linked to the verb for pounding, because the mince is worked until it stays on the metal. Onion and salt are the core seasoning. It is restaurant and home food in Tehran and across Iran. It is not the saffron chicken kebab, and it is not Lebanese kafta with a handful of parsley. The meat is ground and cooked through.
background: Iranian kebab houses grill koobideh next to barg and joojeh. This page is only the mince. It does not use a chile-heavy Adana mix.
whyItTastes: Grated onion kept in the mince makes the kebab moist and slightly sweet, and charcoal dries the outside so it does not taste boiled. Salt is enough because the lamb is the flavor. Working the meat changes the texture: it holds, and it bites smoothly. That texture is as important as any spice.
authenticTouch: Grate the onion and squeeze out a little liquid so the kebab is moist but not soggy. Press it onto a wide skewer with wet hands.
method: Knead minced lamb with onion and salt, form it on wide skewers, and grill until the center is cooked.
served: With rice, grilled tomato, and raw onion. Sumac is a common sprinkle.
funFacts: Koobideh is minced lamb worked until it holds on a wide skewer.
The name is widely linked to pounding, which describes how the meat is prepared.
variations: A blend of beef and lamb, still ground.
A pinch of turmeric, which some home cooks add.
steps: Mix the lamb, onion, salt, pepper, and baking soda until the paste is sticky. Chill 20 minutes.
Press onto wide skewers. Heat charcoal until it is hot.
Grill, turning often, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C).
Serve with rice and tomato. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Iranian Joojeh Kabab
culture: Iranian cooks marinating chicken with saffron for the grill
flavor: Saffron chicken with lemon and onion, charred at the edges.
history: Joojeh kabab is saffron chicken on skewers, a standard Iranian grill beside the minced lamb. Saffron is the point, bloomed and rubbed into the meat, not a thread scattered on the plate after cooking. Lemon and onion are the usual partners. The dish is poultry and is cooked through. This version stays dairy-free. A dairy marinade would be a different recipe.
background: Iranian kebab cooks grill joojeh for people who want chicken rather than lamb. Without saffron it is just grilled chicken, so the spice is not optional on this page.
whyItTastes: Saffron's floral, slightly bitter note clings to chicken fat and smells stronger once the surface browns. Lemon keeps it sharp. Onion sweetens the marinade. Charcoal adds smoke that a pan cannot. The color is a side effect of the flavor, not the reason to buy the spice.
authenticTouch: Grind the saffron with a pinch of salt and bloom it in warm lemon juice before it touches the chicken. Do not toast it until it tastes like hay.
method: Marinate chicken in bloomed saffron, lemon, and onion, then grill on skewers until the poultry is cooked.
served: With rice and grilled tomato.
funFacts: Joojeh kabab is Iranian saffron chicken on skewers.
Saffron is the point of the marinade, not a last-minute garnish.
variations: Thighs instead of breast, which stay moister after they reach temperature.
A dairy marinade, which would be a different recipe from this dairy-free one.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless chicken thigh, cut in cubes
steps: Grind the saffron with a pinch of the salt and stir it into the lemon juice. Mix with onion, the rest of the salt, and oil. Add the chicken and refrigerate 30 minutes.
Thread onto skewers. Heat the grill to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the thickest cube reaches 165°F (74°C).
Rest a few minutes and serve with rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Omani Shuwa
culture: Omani families cooking spiced lamb for Eid, with a home oven standing in for the earth oven
flavor: Lamb with cumin, coriander, and chili, slow-cooked until the fat softens.
history: Shuwa is lamb cooked for Eid in an earth oven in Oman. The meat is rubbed with spice, wrapped, and buried with fire until it is very tender. A home oven is not a pit. This page uses a covered pot in an oven and says so. The Omani mix is often cumin, coriander, chili, and sometimes a shop blend. There is no single secret formula. The rub below is a simple published-style mix of those spices.
background: Omani households prepare shuwa for Eid al-Adha and other gatherings. The earth oven is the traditional pot. The home cook here is not digging a pit. It is not a quick grill.
whyItTastes: A long, enclosed cook turns lamb fat and spice into one smell: cumin and coriander stay earthy, and chili warms rather than chars. The pit does this by trapping steam and smoke. A covered oven pot keeps the moisture and loses the buried-fire smoke, which is an honest trade. Shop blends vary, so the taste at two houses will not match, and that is normal.
authenticTouch: Wrap the lamb so the spice stays on the meat, and do not uncover the pot for the first half of the cook. Call it a home oven, not a pit.
method: Rub a lamb shoulder with a simple cumin, coriander, and chili mix, wrap it, and cook it covered in a home oven until it is safe and tender.
served: With rice. It is Eid food for the families who make it, pulled or sliced.
funFacts: Omani shuwa is Eid lamb cooked in an earth oven, and a home oven is not that pit.
Cumin, coriander, and chili are a common mix, and shop blends vary. There is no single secret formula.
variations: A shop spice blend from an Omani grocer, used in place of the simple mix and named on the jar.
Goat shoulder with the same method, still a whole-muscle roast.
steps: Mix cumin, coriander, chili, salt, garlic, and oil. Rub the shoulder. This is a simple spice mix, not a secret formula. Wrap the meat in parchment and then foil.
Set it in a covered pot. Heat a home oven to 325°F (165°C). This is a home oven, not an earth pit.
Cook until the thickest part reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest. For a shoulder you want to pull, continue toward 195°F (90°C).
Rest, then slice or pull. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Yemeni Chicken Mandi
culture: Yemeni cooks making meat and rice in the mandi manner, with a covered pot at home
flavor: Chicken and rice with a hawaij-style spice of cumin, coriander, turmeric, and pepper.
history: Mandi is a Yemeni dish of meat and rice cooked in a pit or a taboon, now also made in homes and restaurants far beyond Yemen. The pit is traditional, and a covered oven pot is the home version. This page uses chicken and a simple hawaij-style spice. It does not assign the dish to one community as an owner. Lamb is the other common meat. Chicken, as poultry, is cooked to 165°F.
background: Yemeni families and the cooks who learned the dish from them make mandi for gatherings. The home pot is labeled. It is not a quick grill and not a single household's secret.
whyItTastes: Rice cooked under the meat takes the drippings and the spice, which is why mandi is a pot and not only a roasted bird. Cumin, coriander, turmeric, and black pepper make a straightforward hawaij-style mix; real blends vary by shop and house. A pit adds smoke a home oven only suggests. The chicken stays the protein, and the rice is the rest of the plate.
authenticTouch: Brown the chicken first so the rice has some roasted drippings. Keep the pot covered. Do not claim a pit you did not dig.
method: Rub chicken with a simple spice mix, brown it, and cook it with rice in a covered oven pot until the poultry is done.
served: Chicken over the rice, with a salad. It feeds a group from one pot.
funFacts: The pit or taboon is the traditional mandi cook, and a covered oven pot is the home version.
This page does not assign mandi to one community.
variations: Lamb shoulder instead of chicken, cooked as a whole muscle to at least 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, and longer if you want it tender.
A shop hawaij, checked for its own allergens, in place of the simple mix.
steps: Mix cumin, coriander, turmeric, pepper, and salt. Rub half on the chicken. This is a simple hawaij-style mix, not a claim of one correct blend.

Brown the chicken in oil in an oven-safe pot. Add onion, rice, the rest of the spice, and water. Set the chicken on the rice and cover the pot. A covered oven pot is the home version; the pit is traditional.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the thickest thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone, and the rice is tender.
Rest 10 minutes covered. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Moroccan Mechoui
culture: Moroccan families roasting a celebration lamb in a pit or on a spit
flavor: Lamb with cumin, salt, and the fat of a long roast.
history: Mechoui is a Moroccan celebration lamb, cooked in a pit or on a spit for Eid al-Adha and other gatherings. Amazigh (Berber) communities and other Moroccan families both cook it. It is not one village's secret. A whole lamb is the feast; a shoulder is the home piece on this page, still seasoned with salt and cumin and roasted slowly. The name refers to roasting. It is a celebration, not a weeknight chop.
background: Moroccan hosts, in the Atlas and in cities, cook mechoui when the occasion calls for a whole animal or a large cut. The home shoulder is a scale change, not a different cuisine. It is not a tagine and not a minced brochette.
whyItTastes: Slow heat renders lamb fat over salt and cumin until the spice smells toasted rather than raw. A pit or a spit smokes the outside; an oven roast is milder and still tastes of the same seasoning. Cumin is the spice people expect on the meat once it is pulled apart. The celebration setting, especially Eid, is why the animal is large and shared.
authenticTouch: Salt the lamb more than you would a chop, and rub the cumin in with oil. If you are roasting a shoulder at home, say it is a shoulder, not a whole pit lamb.
method: Rub a lamb shoulder with salt and cumin and roast it slowly on a spit or in a covered grill. A pit or a whole lamb is the celebration method when you have both.
served: Pulled or carved, with bread and cumin on the side for dipping. People eat it with their hands at a celebration table.
funFacts: Mechoui is a Moroccan celebration lamb, pit or spit, cooked for Eid and other gatherings.
Amazigh communities and other Moroccan families cook it. It is not one village's secret.
variations: A whole lamb in a pit or on a spit for a real gathering, with the same salt and cumin.
A home oven shoulder, labeled as a home oven, if there is no spit.
steps: Mix salt, cumin, pepper, garlic, and oil. Rub the shoulder thoroughly.
Spit-roast over coals or roast on a rack in a covered grill at a moderate heat. A whole lamb in a pit is the celebration version if you have the animal and the pit.
Cook whole lamb to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest. For a shoulder you want to pull, continue toward 195°F (90°C).
Rest, then carve or pull. Offer more cumin and salt. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Egyptian Kofta
culture: Egyptian grill cooks shaping minced beef or lamb with parsley and onion
flavor: Minced beef and lamb with parsley, onion, and a grilled crust.
history: Egyptian kofta is grilled minced beef or lamb, mixed with parsley, onion, and spices, and cooked over charcoal in Cairo and elsewhere. It is a different plate from Moroccan kefta brochettes, which have their own spice and skewer habit. The Egyptian mix here leans on parsley, cumin, and coriander. The meat is ground and cooked through. It is street and home food, not a festival invention.
background: Egyptian households and grill shops cook kofta as ordinary meat. North Africa is the region for this page. It is not raw kibbeh and not a meatball in tomato sauce.
whyItTastes: Parsley and onion cut the fat of a beef-and-lamb mince, and cumin and coriander toast on the grill. Charcoal gives a bitter-brown edge that pan frying only approximates. The blend is familiar across Egyptian grills and still not the same as a Moroccan brochette heavy on paprika. Ground meat needs a cooked center, which sets the texture.
authenticTouch: Grate and squeeze the onion. If the mix is wet, the kofta will slump through the grate.
method: Mix minced beef and lamb with herbs and spices, form sausages or patties, and grill them until the center is cooked.
served: With salad, tahini sauce if you eat sesame, and rice. Tahini is not in this recipe, so sesame is not an allergen here.
funFacts: Egyptian kofta is grilled minced beef or lamb with parsley and onion.
It is a different plate from Moroccan kefta brochettes.
variations: All beef or all lamb, still ground.
On skewers, which is a shape change, not a different spice mix.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry
steps: Mix the beef, lamb, onion, parsley, cumin, coriander, and salt until the meat holds together.
Form eight short sausages. Heat a grill to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C).
Serve with salad. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Nigerian Suya
culture: Hausa grill cooks and the city stands that sell their beef skewers
flavor: Beef with a hot peanut spice, smoke, and a salty crust.
history: Suya is a Hausa beef skewer from northern Nigeria, now sold at night stands in cities across the country. Yaji, the spice sprinkled on the meat, commonly includes ground peanut, ginger, and hot pepper. The beef is sliced thin from whole muscle, not minced. Kano is one of the northern centers. The peanut is an allergen, and this recipe is not nut-free.
background: Hausa mallams and the suya stands that grew from that grill are the cooks. It is a street skewer. It is not kilishi, the dried meat, and it is not Ghanaian kyinkyinga, which is related and separate.
whyItTastes: Thin beef browns fast over charcoal, and the peanut-pepper dust sticks to the oil on the surface. Ginger and chili heat the fat. Groundnut, long grown in the region, is what makes yaji taste like itself rather than like a plain pepper rub. Smoke from the roadside coals is the other half.
authenticTouch: Slice the beef thin, grill it hot, and dust it with more yaji as it comes off. Tell guests about the peanut before they eat.
method: Coat thin beef in a peanut-pepper spice and grill it on skewers until the whole muscle is safe, then rest it.
served: With more yaji, sliced onion, and tomato. Eat it off the stick while it is hot.
funFacts: Suya is a Hausa beef skewer, widely sold at Nigerian street grills.
Yaji commonly includes ground peanut, which is an allergen, so this dish is not nut-free.
variations: Chicken pieces only if they reach 165°F (74°C), which is a different protein.
A milder dust for people who want less chili, still with peanut.
steps: Mix the peanuts, ginger, paprika, cayenne, and salt. Toss the beef with oil and half the spice. Thread onto skewers.
Heat a grill until it is hot.
Grill, turning, until the thickest slice reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Give the beef a 3-minute rest. This is whole muscle, not ground meat.
Dust with the remaining spice and serve. The peanut allergen is in the spice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Nigerian Asun
culture: Yoruba cooks grilling and peppering goat for parties
flavor: Chopped grilled goat with ginger, garlic, and a heavy pepper heat.
history: Asun is spicy grilled goat associated with Yoruba parties in southwestern Nigeria. The meat is grilled, chopped, and tossed with pepper, onion, and ginger so the spice coats every piece. Ibadan and Lagos parties both claim it as a tray that disappears fast. It is party food, not a quiet weekday soup. The goat is a whole-muscle cut cooked to a safe temperature before it is chopped.
background: Yoruba hosts and the cooks they hire for celebrations make asun. It is goat, not beef suya, though both can show up at a large party. The pepper is the point.
whyItTastes: Goat fat carries ginger and chili better than a lean chop does. Grilling first gives a browned edge, and chopping lets the raw-heat of fresh pepper sit on the hot meat without a long stew. That two-step is why asun tastes both smoky and freshly hot. It belongs to a crowded table.
authenticTouch: Grill the goat far enough that the center is safe, then chop it and toss it with pepper off the fire so the fresh chili stays bright.
method: Season goat, grill it, rest it, chop it, and toss it with onion, ginger, and chili.
served: In a pile, with more onion, at a party. Plantain is a common side and is not fried in this recipe.
funFacts: Asun is spicy grilled goat associated with Yoruba parties in southwestern Nigeria.
The meat is grilled and then chopped and peppered, which is why it is party food rather than a single chop on a plate.
variations: A milder pepper level, still goat.
Bone-in pieces served whole if you would rather not chop them.
ingredients: 3 lb bone-in goat shoulder or leg, in large pieces
steps: Rub the goat with ginger, garlic, salt, and oil. Heat a grill for medium-high cooking.
Grill, turning, until the meat is browned.
Cook whole goat to at least 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part, away from bone, and give it a 3-minute rest.
Chop the meat, toss it with onion and fresh chile, and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ghanaian Kyinkyinga
culture: Ghanaian street cooks grilling meat skewers kin to Hausa suya
flavor: Beef skewers with ginger, chili, and ground peanut, charred at the edges.
history: Kyinkyinga, also called chichinga, is a Ghanaian meat skewer sold on the street in Accra and in other cities. The kinship with Hausa suya is real: both are spiced beef on sticks with a peppery groundnut dust. They are not identical. This mix is ginger-forward, with lime, and it is cooked and sold as Ghanaian street food. The beef is whole muscle. Peanut is in the spice, so the dish is not nut-free.
background: Ghanaian street vendors grill these to order. The page does not treat them as a renamed Nigerian suya. Northern Ghanaian Hausa grilling is part of the kinship, and the Accra stick is its own sale.
whyItTastes: Peanut, ginger, and chili cling to thin beef and toast over charcoal. Lime at the end brightens a spice that would otherwise taste only of fat and pepper. The kinship with suya is in that groundnut heat. The difference is in the balance and in the Ghanaian street where you buy it, not in a claim that one copied the other word for word.
authenticTouch: Grill the meat hot and dust it again after cooking. Name the peanut when you serve it.
method: Spice thin beef with a ginger and peanut mix, grill it on skewers, and finish with lime.
served: Off the stick with onion. It is street food.
funFacts: Kyinkyinga is a Ghanaian meat skewer, also called chichinga.
It is kin to Hausa suya and it is not the same dish.
variations: Goat instead of beef, still a whole-muscle cut.
Less cayenne, with the peanut and ginger kept.
steps: Mix peanuts, ginger, cayenne, and salt. Toss the beef with oil and most of the spice. Thread onto skewers.
Grill over a hot fire, turning once or twice.
Cook the beef to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Dust with the rest of the spice and add lime. Peanut is in the dust. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ghanaian Grilled Tilapia
culture: Ghanaian grill cooks charring whole tilapia
flavor: Charred tilapia with ginger, garlic, and chili.
history: Grilled tilapia is a common fish plate in Ghana, often eaten with banku and shito. Banku is a fermented corn and cassava dough, and shito is a hot sauce whose recipes vary. This page grills the fish and names those pairings without copying a full shito or banku recipe, because the sauces and the dough are their own crafts. The fish is seasoned with ginger and chili and cooked until it flakes.
background: Ghanaian chop-bar and street grill cooks make this. The recipe is the fish. Shito is mentioned, not reproduced. It is not a fried fillet in batter.
whyItTastes: Tilapia is a mild freshwater fish, so ginger, garlic, and chili do the seasoning that an oily sea fish would not need. A hot grill dries the skin into a crust. Banku on the side is sour from fermentation, and shito is hot, which is why the plate is a contrast even though only the fish is written out here. The lake and pond fisheries are why tilapia is the fish on the grate.
authenticTouch: Score the fish so the ginger paste reaches the flesh. Oil the skin or it will stick and tear.
method: Rub whole tilapia with ginger, garlic, and chili, and grill until the flesh flakes.
served: With banku and shito as pairings. Shito recipes differ and are not copied in full here. Read a bought sauce for fish and other allergens.
funFacts: Grilled tilapia in Ghana is commonly paired with banku and shito.
This page does not copy a full shito recipe, because those sauces vary.
variations: A whole fish from another freshwater species, named as what it is.
Less chili in the rub, with the heat left to the sauce on the side.
steps: Cut slashes in the fish. Mix ginger, garlic, chile, salt, and oil and rub it inside and out.
Heat a grill and oil the grate.
Grill, turning once, until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes.
Serve with the pairings you have. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Senegalese Dibi
culture: Wolof street grillers cooking lamb over charcoal
flavor: Grilled lamb with onion and a sharp mustard relish.
history: Dibi is grilled lamb at Wolof street grills in Dakar and in other Senegalese cities. The meat is often lamb chops or a larger piece carved after the fire, served with raw onion and mustard. It is street food you eat at the grill, not a restaurant tasting menu. This recipe uses chops and a simple onion-mustard relish. The lamb is a whole-muscle cut.
background: Wolof dibiterie cooks tend these fires. The dish is lamb and charcoal. It is not yassa, the onion stew, though onion is on the plate.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat over charcoal is the base, and raw onion and mustard cut it the way a heavy sauce would not. The street grill is close to the coals, so the outside browns before the inside overcooks. Mustard is sharp and familiar at these stands. The combination is simple because the fire is doing the work.
authenticTouch: Serve the onion raw and the mustard cold against the hot meat. Do not cook the relish into a jam.
method: Season lamb chops, grill them, rest them, and serve with an onion and mustard relish.
served: Chopped or on the bone, with the relish, at the grill or at home.
funFacts: Dibi is grilled lamb associated with Wolof street grills in Senegal.
Onion and mustard are a common accompaniment at the stand.
variations: A larger leg, roasted and then sliced, still checked with a thermometer.
Less mustard in the relish if you want the onion to lead.
steps: Salt and oil the chops. Stir the onion with mustard and pepper for the relish.
Grill the chops over hot coals, turning once.
Cook whole lamb to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve with the onion-mustard relish. Mustard is an allergen in the relish. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Senegalese Poisson Braise
culture: Senegalese cooks grilling whole fish over charcoal
flavor: Grilled fish with chili, lime, garlic, and a charred skin.
history: Poisson braisé is grilled fish in Senegal, cooked at street fires and at home along the coast, including in Saint-Louis. The catch changes, and the method does not: a whole fish, scored, rubbed with garlic, chili, and lime, and set over charcoal. It is a different plate from dibi, which is lamb. The fish is done when it flakes.
background: Coastal Senegalese grill cooks make this from the day's fish. It is not a fried fritter and not a fish yassa stewed in onion, though those are also Senegalese.
whyItTastes: A hot grate blisters the skin and keeps the flesh moist if the fish is not left over dying coals. Lime and chili cut the oil of a sea fish. Garlic cooks on the surface. Saint-Louis and the Atlantic coast supply the habit of cooking the whole animal rather than a boneless fillet.
authenticTouch: Leave the fish whole and turn it once with a wide spatula. Stuffing the cavity with too much wet marinade will steam it.
method: Rub a whole fish with garlic, chili, and lime, and grill it until it flakes.
served: With lime, onion, and rice or boiled millet. Eat it hot.
funFacts: Poisson braisé is grilled fish in Senegal, at street fires and at home.
The species follows the catch, and the method is a whole fish over charcoal.
variations: Sea bream or another firm fish, named as the fish you bought.
A milder chile if the one you have is very hot.
ingredients: 4 whole firm fish, about 1 lb each, gutted and scaled
steps: Score the fish. Mix garlic, chile, lime juice, salt, and oil and rub the fish inside and out.
Heat a charcoal grill and oil the grate.
Grill, turning once, until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh flakes.
Serve with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ivorian Poulet Braise
culture: Ivorian street grillers cooking chicken over charcoal
flavor: Charcoal chicken with garlic, onion, and chili, served beside fried plantain.
history: Poulet braisé is grilled chicken in Côte d'Ivoire, a street and maquis staple in Abidjan. The bird is seasoned with garlic, onion, and chili and cooked over charcoal. Alloco, fried ripe plantain, is the usual pairing and is named here rather than turned into a second full recipe. The chicken is poultry and is cooked through. It is everyday grill food.
background: Ivorian grill cooks at open-air restaurants make this to order. It is not a groundnut stew and not a festival ceremony. Alloco sits beside it.
whyItTastes: Chicken skin over charcoal picks up smoke and chili, and garlic browns in the fat. The heat is present without being the only note. Sweet fried plantain, if you make it separately, balances the char. The street fire is close and a little uneven, which is why the skin blisters in spots.
authenticTouch: Spatchcock or cut the chicken so the thighs are not still raw when the breast is done. Check the thigh, not the wing.
method: Rub chicken with garlic, onion, and chili, and grill it over charcoal until the thick meat is cooked.
served: With alloco, the fried plantain pairing, and sliced onion. The plantain is a side, fried in its own pan.
funFacts: Poulet braisé is grilled chicken sold widely in Côte d'Ivoire.
Alloco, fried ripe plantain, is a usual pairing.
variations: Thighs and drumsticks only, which are simpler to cook evenly.
A hotter chili paste if that is how the stand you know does it.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 lb, cut into pieces
steps: Mix onion, garlic, chile, salt, and oil. Rub the chicken and rest it 20 minutes in the refrigerator.
Heat a charcoal grill for medium heat.
Grill, turning, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest 5 minutes. Serve with alloco if you have fried it separately. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Cameroonian Soya
culture: Cameroonian street cooks grilling beef skewers related to suya
flavor: Beef skewers with a heavy local chili heat and ginger, and no groundnut.
history: Soya in Cameroon is a beef skewer related to Nigerian suya, sold on streets in Douala and other cities. This mix is not a copy of yaji. It uses more chili and no groundnut, so it is a different spice and it is nut-free. The kinship is the thin beef, the stick, and the pepper culture of the region. The meat is whole muscle and is cooked to a safe temperature.
background: Cameroonian street grillers cook soya as snack food. The page keeps it distinct from suya by the spice. It is not a groundnut sauce.
whyItTastes: Chili and ginger on thin beef toast quickly over charcoal and taste hotter because there is no groundnut to round them. That sharpness is the choice of this recipe. Smoke still binds it to the wider family of West and Central African street skewers. Leaving the groundnut out changes the dish on purpose.
authenticTouch: Use a fresh chili you know the heat of, and salt the meat before the spice so the crust is not only burn.
method: Rub thin beef with chili and ginger, without groundnut, and grill it on skewers.
served: With onion and tomato. It is a hot skewer, not a mild one.
funFacts: Cameroonian soya is a beef skewer related to suya.
This spice uses more chili and no groundnut, so it is not a copy of Nigerian yaji.
variations: A groundnut dust would make it closer to suya and would remove the nut-free label. This recipe does not do that.
Goat, still whole muscle, with the same chili rub.
steps: Mix the chiles, ginger, paprika, salt, and oil. Toss with the beef. There is no groundnut in this mix. Thread onto skewers.
Grill over a hot fire, turning as needed.
Cook the beef to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve with onion. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: South African Boerewors
culture: South African braai cooks grilling a coil of fresh sausage
flavor: Beef and pork sausage with toasted coriander, vinegar, and a grilled casing.
history: Boerewors means farmer's sausage in Afrikaans, and grilling a coil of it is a defining braai habit in South Africa. Coriander is the spice people expect. Commercial wors often contains a grain filler; this home mix does not. The sausage is fresh and ground, and it is cooked through. It is backyard and holiday food.
background: South African households cook boerewors on a braai. This page is a fresh coil without a grain filler. It is not a smoked frank and not a lamb chop.
whyItTastes: Toasted coriander and a splash of vinegar cut a fatty beef-and-pork grind. Charcoal browns the casing and renders the surface. Leaving out a grain filler changes the texture toward a looser sausage, which is an honest home choice. The braai smoke is shared with the rest of the South African fires in this set.
authenticTouch: Toast the coriander in a dry pan before you grind or mix it. Grill the coil over moderate coals so it does not split and dump its fat.
method: Mix a fresh beef and pork sausage with coriander and vinegar, form a coil or logs, and grill until the center is cooked.
served: Sliced, with pap or a salad. Mustard on the side is optional and is not in the sausage.
funFacts: Boerewors means farmer's sausage, and it is a standard sausage on a South African braai.
This home mix leaves out the grain filler many shop sausages contain.
variations: In natural casings if you have them, still cooked to the same temperature.
A higher share of beef, which is traditional in many recipes, as long as there is enough fat.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons coriander seeds, toasted and ground
steps: Mix the meats, coriander, vinegar, salt, pepper, and cloves. Form a long coil or six fat logs. Chill 20 minutes. There is no grain filler in this mix.
Heat a braai or charcoal grill to medium.
Grill, turning often, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C). Fresh sausage is ground meat.
Rest a few minutes and slice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: South African Lamb Tjops
culture: South African braai cooks grilling lamb chops
flavor: Lamb chops with salt, a browned fat edge, and braai smoke.
history: Tjops are lamb chops on a South African braai. The word is the Afrikaans pronunciation of chops. Karoo and other ranching districts built a reputation on lamb, and the chop is the quick piece: salted and grilled, not marinated for days. Beaufort West stands in for that dry interior. The meat is a whole cut and is rested after it reaches temperature.
background: South African braai cooks put tjops on the grid next to sausage and salad. It is lamb, plainly seasoned. It is not sosaties and not a mutton stew.
whyItTastes: A hot grid crisps the fat cap and leaves the eye of the chop juicy if you do not cook it to shreds. Salt and wood or charcoal smoke are the seasoning. Karoo and similar grazing have a reputation for a clean lamb flavor, which a thick sauce would cover. The braai is social, and the chops are one of the faster items on it.
authenticTouch: Salt the chops and leave them. Turn once. A flare-up from the fat should be moved, not pressed out.
method: Salt lamb chops and grill them over a hot braai, then rest them.
served: With a green salad or pap. Lemon is optional.
funFacts: Tjops is the braai name for lamb chops in South Africa.
The word comes from the Afrikaans pronunciation of chops.
variations: A light sprinkle of coriander, which some braai cooks borrow from the sausage tin.
Shoulder chops, which need a little more time than a thin loin chop.
steps: Oil the chops and season them with salt and pepper.
Grill over a hot braai, turning once, until the fat browns.
Cook whole lamb to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve at once. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Cape Malay Sosaties
culture: Cape Malay families in Cape Town grilling curry-and-apricot lamb skewers
flavor: Lamb skewers with apricot, cumin, coriander, and a little chili.
history: Sosaties are Cape Town lamb skewers marinated with apricot and warm spice. Cape Malay cooking was built by enslaved and exiled people from the Indian Ocean world who were brought to the Cape under the Dutch East India Company, including people from Southeast Asia and South Asia, and by their descendants. They were not one people with one recipe, and this skewer should not be told as a single stereotype. The name is widely connected to sate. The meat here is lamb, a whole-muscle cut.
background: Cape Town families who keep Cape Malay foodways grill sosaties for gatherings and for the table at home. The history is forced movement and skill under the Dutch East India Company, not a costume. It is not a generic curry and not Nigerian suya.
whyItTastes: Apricot jam sweetens the edge of the lamb, and cumin, coriander, and chili toast on the grill. That sweet-spice balance is a Cape kitchen pattern built through Indian Ocean trade and through the cooking of people who were enslaved and exiled at the Cape. Charcoal browns the cubes. The fruit and the spice are doing different jobs, which is why the skewer is not just hot and not just sweet.
authenticTouch: Thread onion between the lamb cubes. Wipe off thick marinade so the apricot does not burn black before the meat is done.
method: Marinate lamb in apricot and spice, skewer it with onion, and grill until the cubes are safe, then rest.
served: With rice and a salad. Yellow rice is a common Cape side and is not required for the meat to be finished.
funFacts: Sosaties are a Cape Town skewer, and the name is widely connected to sate.
Cape Malay cooking comes from enslaved and exiled people of the Indian Ocean world at the Cape, including people from Southeast Asia and South Asia, not from one stereotype.
variations: A firmer apricot jam or a few soaked dried apricots chopped into the marinade.
Beef cubes with the same marinade, still a whole-muscle cut.
ingredients: 2 lb boneless lamb, cut in 1 1/2 inch cubes
steps: Mix the jam, cumin, coriander, chili, vinegar, and salt. Toss with the lamb and one chopped onion. Refrigerate for a few hours if you can.
Thread lamb and onion chunks on skewers. Heat a braai to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the thickest cube reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Give the meat a 3-minute rest.
Serve with rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Shisa Nyama
culture: Black South African township cooks sharing a social braai
flavor: Beef and pork chops with salt, char, and the smoke of a shared fire.
history: Shisa nyama is a township braai. The Zulu name means burn the meat. In practice it is a social fire in Black South African townships, including places such as Soweto, where people buy meat, grill it, and eat together. It is not a costume and not a theme party. This recipe uses beef steaks and pork chops, both whole cuts, each cooked to temperature. Pap and chakalaka often share the table and have their own pages.
background: The cooks are township butchers, grillers, and the people who come to eat. The fire is social. It should be described as food and company, not as dress-up.
whyItTastes: Meat over an open coal fire tastes of fat, salt, and smoke, and the point of shisa nyama is that taste in company. Beef and pork on the same grid give two fats and two textures. The name's plainness, burn the meat, matches the method: a hot fire, not a sweet glaze. The setting is the township braai, which is a real social institution.
authenticTouch: Salt the meat and tend your own grid. Do not turn the meal into a costume. Check beef and pork separately.
method: Grill beef steaks and pork chops over coals, and pull each when it reaches a safe temperature and has rested.
served: With pap, chakalaka, or a simple salad, eaten at the fire with other people.
funFacts: Shisa nyama is Zulu for burn the meat.
It is a social fire in Black South African townships, not a costume.
variations: Lamb chops on the same fire, still a whole cut at the same temperature.
Sausage added only if the ground meat reaches 160°F (71°C).
ingredients: 2 lb beef steaks, about 1 inch thick
steps: Oil the steaks and chops and season them with salt and pepper.
Grill over a hot open coal fire, turning as needed. Keep beef and pork identifiable so you can temp them.
Cook the beef and the pork chops, both whole cuts, to at least 145°F (63°C) and give them a 3-minute rest.
Slice and serve at the fire. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Chicken Potjiekos
culture: South African camp and farm cooks simmering a cast-iron pot over coals
flavor: Chicken and vegetables simmered in a covered pot over coals, lightly spiced.
history: Potjiekos is food cooked in a three-legged cast-iron pot set over coals. The pot style came with European settlers and became a South African camp, farm, and backyard dish. It is not a grill. The lid stays on, and the pot simmers. This version is a chicken and vegetable pot. The chicken still has to reach a poultry temperature. You do not stir it like a stew on the stove.
background: South African camp cooks and households make potjie when there is time to leave a pot alone. It is a covered coal cook, not a chop on a grid. The chicken and vegetables are layered.
whyItTastes: Steam trapped in iron softens onions, potatoes, and chicken together, and a little smoke leaks in from the coals under the pot. Paprika and garlic season the juice. Because you do not grill the meat in the open, the flavor is rounded and soupy rather than charred. That is the point of using a pot instead of a grid.
authenticTouch: Layer the ingredients and do not stir. Check the chicken temperature without turning the pot into a boil.
method: Brown chicken, layer it with vegetables in a cast-iron pot, and simmer over coals with the lid on. This is not a grill.
served: From the pot, with rice or pap. The juices are the sauce.
funFacts: Potjiekos is cooked in a cast-iron pot over coals, and it is not a grill.
The lid stays on so the pot simmers instead of roasting in the open.
variations: Lamb neck in place of chicken, cooked as a whole muscle to at least 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, and longer if you want it tender.
A Dutch oven on a grate if you do not own a three-legged potjie.
steps: Brown the chicken in oil in the pot. Take it out. Soften the onion in the same pot. This cook is a pot over coals, not a grill.
Layer potatoes, carrots, garlic, tomatoes, paprika, salt, and the chicken. Add the water. Cover.
Set the pot over a small bed of coals and cook gently until the thickest thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone, and the vegetables are tender.
Rest 10 minutes. Do not stir it into mush. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Cape Snoek Braai
culture: Cape west-coast cooks braaing snoek
flavor: Oily snoek with apricot jam, a little chili, and braai char.
history: Snoek is an oily fish braaied on the Cape west coast, often split open and painted with a little apricot and chili near the end. Lambert's Bay is one of the harbors tied to the catch. If snoek is unavailable, a firm oily fish is a different dish. This recipe is written for snoek. The fish is cooked until it flakes. Apricot on snoek is a Cape habit, not a dessert glaze.
background: West-coast and Cape Town braai cooks grill snoek when the boats land it. A mackerel cooked the same way should be called mackerel. It is not the fish this page is naming.
whyItTastes: Snoek is rich and firm, so a hot grid chars the skin while the flesh stays moist. A thin apricot and chili brush sweetens the oil without burying it. Sea fish and a beach or harbor fire are the setting. Substituting another species changes the fat and the flake, which is why the name should change with the fish.
authenticTouch: Grill snoek skin-side carefully and add the apricot late so the sugar does not blacken. If you cannot buy snoek, cook a different oily fish and do not call it snoek.
method: Season split snoek, grill it, and brush it lightly with apricot and chili at the end.
served: With a salad. Sweet potato is a common Cape side.
funFacts: Snoek is an oily fish braaied on the Cape coast, often with a little apricot.
If snoek is unavailable, a firm oily fish is a different dish.
variations: Mackerel, labeled as mackerel, if snoek cannot be bought. That plate is not snoek.
Salt and pepper only, without the apricot brush.
steps: Pat the snoek dry. Oil and salt it. Mix jam, chili, and vinegar for a late brush. This recipe is for snoek.
Grill skin-side down over a medium-hot braai, then turn.
Cook until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh flakes. Brush with the apricot mix in the last minute.
Serve hot. A different oily fish would be a different dish. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Kenyan Nyama Choma
culture: Kenyan grill cooks roasting goat over charcoal
flavor: Goat with salt, a charred edge, and a squeeze of lime or chili salt.
history: Nyama choma is Swahili for grilled meat. In Kenya it is often goat, and beef is also served, at roadside stops and in Nairobi restaurants built around the fire. The meat is salted, roasted, and often chopped. It is social food. This recipe uses goat pieces as whole muscle. A kachumbari salad of tomato and onion is the usual fresh side.
background: Kenyan butchers and nyama choma houses cook this to order. It is grilled goat, not a sauced stew and not a minced kebab. People wait while it roasts.
whyItTastes: Goat over charcoal tastes of its own fat once the surface dries and browns. Salt is enough because the fire is the seasoning. Tomato and onion on the side add water and acid that the meat does not have. The social wait is part of the dish: the meat comes in batches, hot, and is eaten with the hands or with a knife at a shared table.
authenticTouch: Roast larger pieces than thin steaks so the goat stays juicy, then chop them after the rest. Do not hide the meat under a sweet sauce.
method: Salt goat pieces and grill them over charcoal until they reach a safe temperature, rest them, and chop if you want the usual plate.
served: With tomato-onion salad and ugali or potatoes. Ugali is a maize side related to other East African porridges.
funFacts: Nyama choma is Swahili for grilled meat.
In Kenya the meat is often goat, and beef is also served.
variations: Beef steaks on the same fire, still a whole cut at the same temperature.
A chili-salt sprinkle at the table.
ingredients: 3 lb bone-in goat, in large pieces
steps: Rub the goat with oil, salt, and pepper. Heat a charcoal grill to medium-high.
Grill, turning, until the meat is browned on the outside.
Cook whole goat to at least 145°F (63°C), away from bone, and give it a 3-minute rest.
Chop if you like, and serve with tomato, onion, and lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Tanzanian Mishkaki
culture: Tanzanian street cooks grilling beef skewers
flavor: Beef cubes with ginger, garlic, and a light chili char.
history: Mishkaki are beef skewers grilled on the street in Dar es Salaam and in other Tanzanian towns. Mshikaki is the related name along the Swahili coast, including Zanzibar. They are cousins, coastal and inland skewers, not copies of one recipe. This page uses a ginger and garlic beef cube and does not claim to be the Zanzibar stick. The meat is whole muscle.
background: Tanzanian street vendors thread and grill mishkaki to order. The kinship with mshikaki is stated without pretending the spice lists match. It is not nyama choma chopped on a board, though both are grilled meat.
whyItTastes: Cubes of beef take a fast char, and ginger and garlic cling to the oil. A little chili warms the surface. Coastal and inland cooks share the skewer and change the marinade, which is why calling them copies would be wrong. Charcoal smoke is the common note. Lime at the end is optional and bright.
authenticTouch: Do not pack the cubes. A tight skewer steams. Say mishkaki or mshikaki according to the place you are actually cooking from.
method: Marinate beef briefly with ginger and garlic, skewer it, and grill it, then rest.
served: With lime, onion, and chips or rice. Eat it from the stick.
funFacts: Mishkaki and mshikaki are related Swahili-coast and inland skewers.
They are cousins, not copies of a single recipe.
variations: A coastal mshikaki marinade if you are following a Zanzibar cook you trust, named as that version.
Goat cubes with the same ginger rub.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb beef sirloin, cut in 1 inch cubes
steps: Toss the beef with ginger, garlic, chili, salt, and oil. Thread onto skewers with space between cubes.
Grill over hot coals, turning so the faces brown.
Cook whole beef to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve with lime and onion. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ugandan Muchomo
culture: Ugandan roadside cooks roasting goat over an open fire
flavor: Roasted goat with salt, a little chili, and smoke from an open fire.
history: Muchomo is the usual word in Uganda for meat roasted over an open fire, sold at roadsides into Kampala and eaten at gatherings. Goat is a common choice, and beef is also roasted. The seasoning is often salt and a chili salt rather than a long marinade. It is a fire you stand next to. This recipe uses goat and keeps the method plain.
background: Ugandan roadside roasters and hosts at weekend fires cook muchomo. It is roasted meat, not a groundnut stew. The goat is a whole-muscle cut.
whyItTastes: An open fire dries the surface of goat and smokes the fat. Salt and chili are added so each piece is seasoned after or before the roast, not buried in a sauce. The roadside setting means the meat is eaten hot, often with banana or cassava that has been cooked separately. The fire is the flavor.
authenticTouch: Turn the pieces often over the coals. A still roast burns one side and leaves the other raw.
method: Salt goat and roast it over an open fire until it is safe, then rest and slice it.
served: Sliced, with chili salt, tomato, and onion. Matooke or another starch can sit beside it if you cook that starch on its own.
funFacts: Muchomo is the usual word in Uganda for meat roasted over an open fire.
Goat is a common choice at roadside fires.
variations: Beef on the same fire, still a whole cut.
A hotter chili salt mixed at the table.
steps: Rub the goat with oil, salt, and half the chili. Build an open coal fire.
Roast over the coals, turning often, until the outside is browned.
Cook whole goat to at least 145°F (63°C), away from bone, and give it a 3-minute rest.
Slice and serve with onion and the rest of the chili. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Ethiopian Grilled Tibs
culture: Ethiopian cooks grilling beef with berbere
flavor: Beef with berbere, onion, and a hot grilled edge.
history: Tibs is Ethiopian beef cooked with berbere and onion. It is often a hot pan and sometimes a grill. This recipe is the grilled version. It is not kitfo, and it is not served raw. Berbere blends differ by house and shop; the rub here is a simple chili, paprika, ginger, and garlic mix, not a claim that one tin is the only berbere. The beef is a whole-muscle cut cooked to temperature.
background: Ethiopian restaurants and home cooks in Addis Ababa make tibs as a cooked meat dish. Kitfo is a different food and is raw or lightly warmed. This page does not serve raw beef.
whyItTastes: Berbere's chili and warm spices bloom on beef fat as the surface browns. A grill adds char that a covered pan softens. Onion, grilled beside the meat or served raw, sweetens the heat. The difference from kitfo is total: tibs is cooked. A shop berbere may be more complex than this simple mix, and that is fine to use if you know what is in the tin.
authenticTouch: Cut the beef in strips so the spice coats it, and do not serve it raw. If your berbere tin lists other allergens, follow the tin.
method: Rub beef with a simple berbere-style spice and grill it until it reaches a safe temperature, then rest it.
served: With cooked vegetables. Injera may be eaten beside it and is not in this recipe. The beef is fully cooked.
funFacts: Tibs is often cooked in a hot pan or on a grill, and this recipe is the grilled version.
It is not kitfo, and it is not served raw.
variations: A spoon of a shop berbere you have read the label on, in place of the simple spice.
A pan tibs at home, still cooked through, if you have no grill.
steps: Mix paprika, chili, ginger, garlic, salt, and oil. Toss with the beef. This is a simple berbere-style rub, not a single official blend.
Grill the beef and the onion over a hot fire. This is the grilled version of tibs, not a raw dish.
Cook whole beef to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest. Do not serve it raw.
Serve hot with the onion. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mozambican Peri-Peri Chicken
culture: Mozambican grill cooks basting chicken with peri-peri chile
flavor: Charcoal chicken with garlic, lemon, and a very hot peri-peri chile.
history: Peri-peri chicken in Mozambique is a charcoal bird seasoned with the small hot chile that reached Africa from the Americas through Portuguese trade. On this side of that route the dish is Mozambican grill food, not a chain-restaurant recipe and not a British invention. Maputo grills and home fires both cook it. The bird is poultry and is cooked through. The Portuguese charcoal chicken is a related plate with its own page.
background: Mozambican cooks baste chicken with chile, garlic, and lemon over coals. The history of the chile is a trade history. The page does not hand the dish to a restaurant brand.
whyItTastes: The small chile is sharply hot, and chicken fat carries it better than a lean sauce does. Lemon and garlic keep the baste from tasting only of burn. Charcoal smoke is the other flavor. Telling the story from Mozambique matters: the chile's African life is not a footnote to a European menu or a chain.
authenticTouch: Baste late so the sugar and chile do not carbonize. Check the thigh. Wash your hands after handling the chiles.
method: Marinate a flattened chicken in peri-peri, garlic, and lemon, and grill it until the thigh is cooked.
served: Cut up, with rice and a salad. The sauce is hot.
funFacts: The peri-peri chile reached Africa from the Americas through Portuguese trade, and Mozambican grills made it a charcoal-chicken seasoning.
This plate is Mozambican grill food, not a chain-restaurant recipe.
variations: Thighs only, easier to cook evenly.
A milder chile, named as milder, if the bird's-eye heat is too much.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 lb, backbone removed and flattened
steps: Blend or finely chop the chiles with garlic, lemon juice, oil, and salt. Rub the chicken, including under the skin. Refrigerate 30 minutes.
Heat a charcoal grill for indirect heat.
Grill, turning, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest 5 minutes and cut. Boil any leftover marinade before using it as a sauce. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Angolan Mufete
culture: Angolan cooks grilling fish and serving it with beans and plantain
flavor: Grilled fish with palm oil, onion, beans, and sweet plantain.
history: Mufete is an Angolan plate of grilled fish with beans and plantain, strongly associated with Luanda weekends. The fish is whole, the beans are cooked through, and ripe plantain is boiled or grilled until soft. Palm oil is a common finish. This page does not use raw bitter cassava. The fish is the center, and the beans and plantain are part of the plate rather than optional garnish.
background: Luanda households cook mufete when there is fish and time. It is a grilled fish plate, not a stew of dried fish. The beans must be fully cooked if they start out dried.
whyItTastes: A charred fish, a soft plantain, and a bean relish give three textures. Palm oil adds fruit and color. Onion and a little chili keep the beans savory. The Atlantic catch and the weekend table are why the plate is large. Leaving the cassava out avoids a food this recipe is not equipped to process safely.
authenticTouch: Grill the fish whole and simmer the beans until they are completely soft. If you use dried kidney beans, boil them hard. Do not hold them warm from raw.
method: Grill a whole fish, and serve it with fully cooked beans and ripe plantain.
served: The fish beside the beans and plantain, with onion. It is a shared plate.
funFacts: Mufete is an Angolan plate of grilled fish with beans and plantain.
Luanda weekends are closely associated with the dish.
variations: Whatever firm local fish is fresh, named as that fish.
Sweet potato in place of plantain if plantain is not ripe.
ingredients: 1 whole firm fish, about 3 lb, gutted and scaled
2 cups dried beans, or 4 cups beans already boiled until tender
2 tablespoons palm oil or another oil
steps: If the beans are dried, boil them in plenty of water until completely tender. Kidney beans must be boiled hard, not held warm from raw. Drain them.
Simmer the plantains in salted water until soft, or grill them beside the fish. Rub the fish with salt and oil.
Grill the fish until the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh flakes.
Toss the beans with onion, chili, and palm oil. Serve with the fish and plantain. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Congolese Liboke
culture: Congo Basin cooks wrapping fish in leaves and cooking the packets
flavor: Fish steamed in a leaf with tomato, onion, and chili, finished over the grill.
history: Liboke is fish cooked in a leaf packet in the Congo Basin, grilled or set in the coals so the parcel steams. The local leaf is part of the aroma. If that leaf is hard to buy, spinach or chard will wrap the fish, and the substitute should be named. Kinshasa tables know the dish from river fish. The fish is cooked until it flakes. This is not a fried fillet.
background: Cooks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo wrap fish with aromatics and cook the packet. Spinach or chard is a stand-in, not the forest leaf. The method is a packet, whether the heat is a grill or steam.
whyItTastes: The leaf holds moisture, so the fish steams in tomato and onion while the outside of the packet picks up smoke if it sits on a grill. Chili perfumes the juice. A substitute green will not taste identical to the local leaf, which is why it has to be named. The packet is the technique that makes liboke different from a bare grilled fish.
authenticTouch: Wrap the packet tightly so the juice does not run into the fire. If you use chard or spinach, say so at the table.
method: Season fish, wrap it in leaves with tomato and onion, and cook the packets on a grill until the fish flakes.
served: Open the packet at the table, with the juices, and eat the fish with a starch cooked separately.
funFacts: Liboke is fish cooked in a leaf packet in the Congo Basin.
Spinach or chard can wrap the fish when the local leaf is hard to buy, and that substitute should be named.
variations: Steamed on a rack over boiling water if you cannot grill the packets.
A whole small fish in each packet instead of a fillet.
ingredients: 4 firm fish fillets, about 6 oz each
1 large bunch chard or spinach, as the stand-in leaf
steps: Salt the fish. Oil the leaves. This packet uses chard or spinach because the local leaf may be hard to buy, and it should be called that.
Wrap each fillet with tomato, onion, and chili in several leaves so the juice stays in. Tie with kitchen string.
Grill the packets over medium coals, turning once, until the fish inside reaches 145°F (63°C) and flakes. Open one packet to check.
Serve in the leaves. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Malagasy Zebu Brochettes
culture: Malagasy street and home cooks grilling zebu beef skewers
flavor: Beef cubes with ginger, garlic, and a charred edge.
history: Zebu cattle are the common beef of Madagascar, and brochettes of that meat are street and home food in Antananarivo and in smaller towns. The cubes are marinated simply with ginger, garlic, and oil, then grilled. Zebu is a breed of cattle, not a different species of dinner, and the cut is whole muscle. The skewers are everyday food rather than a ceremony invented for visitors.
background: Malagasy grillers cook zebu brochettes at markets and at home. The meat is beef from zebu. It is not a seafood brochette from the coast, which would be a different catch.
whyItTastes: Zebu beef is leaner than many feedlot steaks, so ginger, garlic, and oil help the surface brown without drying the center if the cubes are not tiny. Charcoal adds smoke. The highland city habit of a quick skewer is practical food, sold by the stick. Salt is the rest of the seasoning.
authenticTouch: Do not cut the cubes paper-thin. A slightly larger piece of lean zebu stays juicier. Rest the skewers before you bite through one.
method: Season zebu or other beef cubes, skewer them, and grill them to a safe temperature.
served: With a small salad or rice. They are eaten from the skewer.
funFacts: Zebu cattle are the common beef of Madagascar.
Brochettes of that beef are ordinary street and home food, not a staged ceremony.
variations: Ordinary beef if zebu is not sold where you live, named as beef, not as zebu.
A pinch of chili in the oil.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb zebu beef or other beef steak, cut in 1 inch cubes
steps: Toss the beef with ginger, garlic, salt, and oil. If the meat is not zebu, say so. Thread onto skewers.
Grill over hot coals, turning.
Cook whole beef to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve from the skewer. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Namibian Braai Lamb
culture: Namibian cooks grilling lamb on a braai
flavor: Lamb chops with salt, pepper, and braai smoke.
history: A Namibian braai draws on German settlement in what is now Namibia and on South African braai practice. Lamb chops are a straightforward grill in Windhoek and on farms. Game is also braaied in Namibia. This page does not invent an oryx recipe or any other game formula. The lamb is salted and cooked as a whole cut. The cookout is a shared fire, not a costume.
background: Namibian households braai lamb as ordinary meat. The German and South African influences are part of how the cookout arrived and changed. Game exists on other fires and is not faked here.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat, salt, and hardwood or charcoal smoke are the whole flavor. Dry air and a hot grid brown the fat edge quickly. The braai form, a social fire with several meats possible, is shared with South Africa and also sits in a country where German-speaking farmers left sausage and baking habits beside the grid. This plate stays with lamb so it does not pretend to be a game dish.
authenticTouch: Salt the chops and grill them hot. If someone at the table talks about game, do not substitute an invented oryx method.
method: Season lamb chops and grill them on a braai, then rest them.
served: With a salad and potatoes. It is a straightforward chop plate.
funFacts: Namibian braai practice has German and South African influences.
Game is also braaied in Namibia, and this page does not invent an oryx recipe.
variations: A lamb shoulder roasted longer, still checked with a thermometer.
A coil of sausage beside the chops only if the sausage reaches 160°F (71°C).
ingredients: 8 lamb chops or 2 lb lamb steaks
steps: Oil the lamb and season it with salt and pepper.
Grill over a hot braai, turning once.
Cook whole lamb to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve with salad. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Zimbabwean Braai Chicken
culture: Zimbabwean cooks grilling chicken over charcoal
flavor: Chicken with garlic, paprika, and charcoal.
history: Grilled chicken is an ordinary Zimbabwean braai, cooked in Harare yards and at weekend gatherings. The seasoning is often garlic, salt, and a little paprika or chili. This page does not add a ceremony the cookout does not need. Sadza, the maize porridge, is a usual side and is kin to other regional porridges without being the same plate. The bird is poultry and is cooked through.
background: Zimbabwean households braai chicken as normal food. It is not a ritual dish on this page. It is not peri-peri by another name unless you add that chile on purpose.
whyItTastes: Chicken skin over charcoal is smoky and salty, and garlic browns in the fat. A mild paprika colors it without turning the meal into a chile contest. The braai is social in the way many southern African cookouts are social: people, fire, and time. The taste is that plain fire, which is enough.
authenticTouch: Cut the chicken into pieces so the thighs finish. Check the thick meat, not the wing tip.
method: Season chicken pieces and grill them over charcoal until the thigh is cooked.
served: With sadza or a salad. The maize side is separate.
funFacts: Grilled chicken is an ordinary Zimbabwean braai.
This page does not add a ceremony the cookout does not need.
variations: A hotter chili rub if that is how your household likes it.
A whole bird spatchcocked, still checked at the thigh.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 4 lb, cut into pieces
steps: Rub the chicken with garlic, paprika, salt, pepper, and oil.
Grill over medium charcoal, turning so the skin browns without burning.
Cook until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest 5 minutes. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Zambian Charcoal Chicken
culture: Zambian cooks grilling a plain charcoal chicken
flavor: Chicken with salt, a little garlic, and charcoal smoke.
history: Charcoal chicken in Zambia is a plain cookout bird, sold and cooked in Lusaka and at home. Nshima, a maize porridge, is the starch people often eat with it, and that porridge is its own food. No ritual is invented here to make the chicken sound older than a weeknight fire. The seasoning is salt, garlic, and maybe a mild chili. The meat is poultry and is cooked through.
background: Zambian households and roadside grills cook this as ordinary food. It is not a ceremony and not a copy of a restaurant chain. The fire is charcoal.
whyItTastes: Salt and charcoal are the flavor. Garlic helps the skin taste finished. A mild chili is optional heat, not a brand sauce. Nshima on the side is mild and filling, which is why a simply grilled bird makes sense next to it. The honesty of a plain recipe is the point.
authenticTouch: Do not add a story the cookout does not have. Salt the skin and keep the coals medium so the outside does not carbonize before the thigh is done.
method: Season chicken and grill it over charcoal until the thigh reaches a safe temperature.
served: With nshima or a salad. The porridge is a side.
funFacts: Charcoal chicken in Zambia is a plain cookout bird.
No ceremony is invented here to explain it.
variations: A pinch of chili in the salt.
Pieces rather than a whole bird.
steps: Rub the chicken with salt, garlic, oil, and chili.
Grill over medium charcoal, turning now and then.
Cook until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), not touching bone.
Rest 5 minutes. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Mali Lamb Brochettes
culture: Sahel street cooks grilling lamb skewers in Bamako
flavor: Lamb with cumin, paprika, and chili, without a groundnut crust.
history: Lamb brochettes are Sahel street food in Mali, grilled in Bamako and in other towns. They are related to suya and to dibi in the broad sense of West African lamb over coals, and the spice here is not the same as either. This mix is cumin, paprika, and chili, and it leaves out groundnut. The lamb is a whole-muscle cube. It is a stick from a street fire, not a staged ceremony.
background: Malian street grillers cook these skewers for people passing. The kinship with suya and dibi is named so the dishes are not collapsed into one. The spice is this one.
whyItTastes: Cumin and paprika toast on lamb fat and taste warmer than a plain salted chop, while the missing groundnut keeps it away from yaji. Chili is present and not the entire story. Charcoal in a dry-season street adds a clean smoke. Related fires across the Sahel share a skewer and still season it differently, which is what this page is trying to keep straight.
authenticTouch: Use lamb cubes, not a mince, and do not dust them with groundnut. Turn them until the fat edge browns.
method: Season lamb with cumin and paprika, skewer it, and grill it, then rest.
served: With onion and tomato. It is street food.
funFacts: Lamb brochettes are Sahel street food in Mali.
They are related to suya and to dibi, and the spice is not the same as either.
variations: Beef cubes with the same dry spice.
A hotter chili if the pepper you have is mild.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless lamb, cut in 1 inch cubes
steps: Toss the lamb with cumin, paprika, chili, salt, and oil. There is no groundnut in this mix. Thread onto skewers.
Grill over hot coals, turning.
Cook whole lamb to at least 145°F (63°C) and give it a 3-minute rest.
Serve with onion. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: Moroccan Kefta Brochettes
culture: Moroccan grill cooks pressing spiced minced lamb onto skewers
flavor: Minced lamb with cumin, paprika, and parsley, grilled on a stick.
history: Moroccan kefta brochettes are spiced minced lamb grilled on skewers in Fez, Marrakesh, and at home. They stay distinct from Egyptian kofta: this mix leads with cumin and paprika, and it is served as a brochette. The Egyptian plate on its own page leans on parsley, coriander, and a beef-and-lamb mix. Both are grilled mince. This one is ground and cooked through. It is not mechoui, the celebration roast.
background: Moroccan street and home grillers make kefta as a quick skewer. North Africa is the region. It is not a lamb shoulder and not the Egyptian kofta recipe copied under another name.
whyItTastes: Paprika and cumin toast on the outside of a small mince skewer, and parsley keeps it from tasting only of spice. Charcoal dries the surface. The brochette shape means more crust than a thick patty. That crust, plus the spice balance, is what separates it from the Egyptian mix even though both are called by related names.
authenticTouch: Keep the mince cold and the onion squeezed dry so the brochettes do not slip off the skewers.
method: Mix minced lamb with cumin and paprika, mold it onto skewers, and grill until the center is cooked.
served: With salad and cumin on the side. It is a skewer, not the whole roast.
funFacts: Moroccan kefta brochettes are spiced minced lamb on skewers.
They are distinct from Egyptian kofta in the spice and in the brochette habit.
variations: A little beef in the mince, still ground.
Patties on the grill if you have no skewers, cooked to the same temperature.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry
steps: Mix the lamb, onion, cumin, paprika, parsley, and salt. Chill 15 minutes.
Mold onto skewers. Heat the grill to medium-hot.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C). Ground lamb is cooked through.
Serve with salad. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.

name: South African Pap
culture: South African cooks stirring maize porridge for a braai
flavor: Stiff white maize porridge, mild and ready for a relish or a grill.
history: Pap is the South African name, from Afrikaans, for a maize porridge served beside a braai. Stiff pap is firm enough to eat with the fingers or to set under a relish. Neighboring staples such as sadza, nshima, and ugali are related and are not the same plate. This recipe is maize meal, water, and salt, with a little oil. It is a side, not the chop.
background: South African households make pap for the braai and for ordinary meals. It is vegetarian food as written. It is not a sweet breakfast porridge unless you change it on purpose.
whyItTastes: Maize meal swells in salted water into a mild, toasty starch that carries chakalaka, gravy, or juices from the grill. The stiffness is a choice: loose pap is a different texture. The grain is a southern African staple with a long history in the region, and the braai made the stiff version a cookout side. Oil at the end keeps it from drying into crumbs.
authenticTouch: Add the meal in a stream while stirring so it does not lump, then let it steam covered. Stir stiff pap with a strong spoon.
method: Boil salted water, stir in maize meal, and cook until the porridge is thick and the raw taste is gone.
served: Beside the grill or with chakalaka. It is a side.
funFacts: Pap is a maize porridge and a standard braai side in South Africa.
Sadza, nshima, and ugali are related neighboring staples and are not the same plate.
variations: A softer porridge with more water, for a different texture.
A spoon of pan juices on top, which would change the pot and is not in this recipe.
steps: Boil the water with the salt. Pour in the maize meal in a stream, stirring.
Lower the heat, cover, and cook, stirring often, until the porridge is thick and no longer tastes raw. This can take about 30 minutes.
Stir in the oil. There is no animal-protein thermometer target. The side is done when it is thick and cooked through.
Serve hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a canning recipe.

name: South African Chakalaka
culture: South African cooks simmering a vegetable relish for the braai
flavor: Tomato, pepper, onion, and beans with chili and a little curry-style spice.
history: Chakalaka is a vegetable relish served with pap at a South African braai. A single inventor is not established, so this page does not name one. Township kitchens and later canned versions spread it. This pot uses onion, pepper, tomato, chili, and beans that are already boiled if they began dried. It is a side. The spice is cumin, paprika, and chili.
background: South African cooks make chakalaka to sit next to pap. It is vegetables and beans. It is not a lamb curry. The history does not need a fake founder.
whyItTastes: Tomato and onion cook down into a relish, beans make it filling, and chili keeps it lively next to mild pap. The spices are warm rather than a long list of secret blends. It was built as food that stretches a meal, which is why it belongs at a braai where the grill is the center and the relish feeds the table.
authenticTouch: Cook the vegetables until the tomato breaks down. If you start with dried beans, boil them until they are completely tender before they join the pot.
method: Soften onion and pepper, add tomato, spice, and cooked beans, and simmer into a relish.
served: Warm or at room temperature, beside pap. The relish itself is the recipe.
funFacts: Chakalaka is a vegetable relish served with pap at a South African braai.
A single inventor is not established, so this page does not name one.
variations: Grated carrot in the pot, which many cooks add.
A hotter chili for a sharper relish.
ingredients: 2 cups cooked beans, boiled until tender if they started dried
steps: If the beans are dried, boil them until completely tender before using them. Kidney beans must be boiled hard, not held warm from raw.
Soften the onion and peppers in oil. Add paprika, cumin, chili, tomatoes, and salt.
Stir in the cooked beans and simmer until the relish is thick. There is no animal-protein thermometer target.
Taste for salt. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Roosterkoek
