culture: South African braai cooks grilling rounds of bread dough
flavor: Grilled bread dough with a browned crust and a soft interior.
history: Roosterkoek is bread dough cooked on a braai grid in South Africa. The Afrikaans name means grill cake. It is a side at cookouts, torn and eaten beside the fire. The dough is wheat, yeast, water, salt, and oil. It is vegetarian. It is not a vetkoek fried in deep fat, which is a different bread.
background: South African braai cooks bake these on the grid while the coals are still useful. The food is bread. It is not the chop and not a sweet cake, despite the word koek.
whyItTastes: Dough on a grid browns where it touches the metal and stays soft inside if the coals are moderate. A little smoke clings to the crust. Wheat and salt are the taste, which is why it works next to a salty grill and a sharp relish. It is camp bread: made because the fire is already going.
authenticTouch: Cook over coals, not flames, and turn the cakes when they have a proper crust. Split one to be sure the center is not doughy.
method: Make a simple yeast dough, shape rounds, and grill them on a braai grid until they are cooked through.
served: Hot, torn open, beside the braai. A dairy spread is not in this dough.
funFacts: Roosterkoek is bread dough cooked on a South African braai grid.
The Afrikaans name means grill cake, and the bread is not the same as deep-fried vetkoek.
variations: A little crushed garlic on the hot bread after grilling.
Smaller rounds if the grid is crowded.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, salt, sugar, oil, and water into a dough. Knead until smooth. Cover and let it rise until puffy, about an hour.
Divide into eight rounds. Let them rest 15 minutes. Heat a braai to moderate coals.
Grill the rounds, turning, until both sides are browned and the center is cooked through, not raw dough. There is no animal-protein thermometer target.
Serve hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Punjabi Tandoori Chicken
culture: Punjabi tandoor cooks, and the Delhi restaurant kitchens that made the red chicken a standard plate
flavor: Yogurt-marinated chicken with Kashmiri chili, lemon, and a charred skin.
history: Tandoor bread and meat are older in the northwest of the subcontinent than any one restaurant plate. The usual restaurant history of the bright red tandoori chicken places it in twentieth-century Delhi, at Moti Mahal, with the cook Kundan Lal Gujral. A home oven can take the same yogurt marinade, and it should be named as a home oven when there is no clay tandoor.
background: This is a whole chicken opened flat, cooked by Punjabi tandoor practice and by Delhi restaurant habit. Yogurt in the marinade means dairy. It is not a vegan dish, and it is not boneless chicken tikka.
whyItTastes: A charcoal tandoor gives dry, fierce heat, so the yogurt and Kashmiri chili brown instead of steaming. Lemon and ginger cut the fat under the skin. In Delhi the restaurant bird became redder and more vivid than older northwest tandoor meat. A home oven still browns the marinade, without the clay draft.
authenticTouch: Loosen the skin and rub some marinade under it. Open the bird so the thigh is not buried against another piece of raw chicken.
method: Marinate a butterflied chicken in yogurt, Kashmiri chili, ginger, and lemon, then cook it in a tandoor or a very hot home oven.
served: Cut it into pieces and eat it with sliced onion, lemon, and a cucumber salad.
funFacts: Tandoor bread and meat are older in the northwest than the bright restaurant chicken.
The usual restaurant history names Moti Mahal in Delhi and the cook Kundan Lal Gujral.
variations: A home oven at high heat is the honest substitute when you have no clay tandoor.
Kashmiri chili is used here for color. A hotter chili powder makes a different dish.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 3.5 pounds, backbone removed and opened flat
steps: Stir the yogurt, chili, ginger, garlic, lemon juice, oil, salt, and cumin. Coat the chicken, including under the skin. Refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

If you have a tandoor, heat it until the wall is very hot. If you do not, heat a home oven to 450°F (230°C) and call that oven what it is. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Cook the chicken until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve it below that temperature. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest the chicken 5 minutes, then cut it into pieces. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Chicken Tikka
culture: Punjabi grill cooks who cube boneless chicken for the tandoor or a hot grate
flavor: Boneless chicken, tangy from yogurt and warm with cumin and chili.
history: Chicken tikka is boneless chicken in pieces, cooked on skewers in a tandoor or over a hot grill. It is a different plate from tandoori chicken, which is the whole bird. The marinade is the same family of yogurt, chili, and ginger used across Punjabi tandoor cooking. A home grill is a fair stand-in if you say it is a grill.
background: These are cubes of thigh, not a butterflied chicken and not a creamy malai tikka. Yogurt means dairy, so the dish is not vegan. It belongs to Punjabi and North Indian grill practice.
whyItTastes: Small pieces brown fast, so the yogurt marinade chars at the edge while the thigh stays juicy. Cumin and chili sit on the surface instead of hiding inside a whole bird. The taste is the high heat of a tandoor or a hot grate, which is why a crowded, cool pan will not taste the same.
authenticTouch: Use thigh meat. Breast cubes dry out before the marinade has a chance to color.
method: Marinate boneless chicken thighs in yogurt and spices, thread them on skewers, and cook them in a tandoor or on a hot grill.
served: Slide the pieces off the skewers and eat them with onion, lemon, and a spoon of the yogurt you held back from the raw marinade.
funFacts: Chicken tikka is boneless pieces. It is a different dish from whole tandoori chicken.
Thigh meat stays moister on a hot skewer than lean breast meat does.
variations: A hot grill replaces a tandoor if you name it as a grill.
A little extra chili makes the edge hotter. This batch stays medium.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless chicken thighs, cut in 1.5-inch cubes
steps: Mix the yogurt, chili, ginger, garlic, cumin, salt, oil, and lemon. Coat the chicken and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The meat is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Thread the cubes on skewers, leaving a little space between pieces. Heat a tandoor, or heat a grill until the grate is very hot and say so if it is a grill. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Cook, turning, until the center of the thickest cube reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve the chicken rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest the skewers a few minutes and serve them hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Seekh Kebab
culture: North Indian Muslim grill cooks who press minced lamb onto skewers
flavor: Minced lamb with onion, green chili, cilantro, and warm spice, browned on a skewer.
history: Seekh means skewer. The kebab is minced lamb pressed along that skewer and cooked over charcoal or in a tandoor. It is a North Indian Muslim grill dish, kin to other minced kebabs and different from boti, which is cut in chunks. Awadhi cooks in Lucknow made very fine versions; this one is a home seekh, spiced and grilled, not a claim about one inventor.
background: The meat is ground lamb, so it has to be cooked through. There is no yogurt and no wheat in the mix. It is not a chunk kebab and not a cream-based kakori paste.
whyItTastes: Fat in the lamb bastes the mince as it turns, and onion and green chili keep it from tasting like a plain sausage. Charcoal browns the outside while the center comes up to a ground-meat temperature. Cilantro and cumin are the green, bright note against that browned lamb.
authenticTouch: Wet your hands and press the mince on firmly. Loose meat falls into the fire before it sets.
method: Knead ground lamb with onion, chili, and spice, press it onto skewers, and grill it until the center is fully cooked.
served: Slide the kebabs onto a plate and eat them with onion, mint, and lemon.
funFacts: Seekh refers to the skewer the minced lamb is cooked on.
Ground lamb has to reach a higher temperature than a whole lamb chop.
variations: A flat metal skewer holds the mince better than a thin round stick.
A hotter green chili is a common change. This amount is medium.
ingredients: 1 small onion, very finely chopped and squeezed dry
steps: Knead the lamb with the onion, cilantro, chili, ginger, garlic, cumin, coriander, and salt until the mince is sticky. Keep it cold. It is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Press the mince into long shapes around flat skewers. Refrigerate them if they wait. Do not leave garlic sitting in a warm kitchen. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Grill over a hot fire, turning gently, until the center of each kebab reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest them 3 minutes off the fire. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Boti Kebab
culture: North Indian kebab cooks who grill cubes of lamb rather than mince
flavor: Lamb chunks with yogurt, chili, and ginger, charred at the edges.
history: Boti kebab is lamb cut in chunks and threaded on skewers, not minced. It sits in the same North Indian kebab tradition as seekh, and the difference is the cut of meat. Yogurt, ginger, and chili are the usual marinade in restaurant and home grills. The chunks are whole muscle, so they are cooked and rested like other whole lamb, not like ground meat.
background: This is cubed lamb from a leg or shoulder, grilled by North Indian kebab cooks. Yogurt makes it a dairy dish. It is not seekh, which is mince, and it is not a whole roasted leg.
whyItTastes: A chunk of lamb keeps a juicy center while the yogurt marinade spots and browns. Ginger and chili season the surface. On charcoal the fat at the edge crisps. That is a different bite from minced seekh, where the spice is mixed all the way through.
authenticTouch: Cut the cubes the same size so they finish together. A thick cube next to a thin one will leave one of them overcooked.
method: Marinate lamb chunks in yogurt and spice, skewer them, and grill them to a whole-muscle temperature with a rest.
served: Eat the chunks with onion, a green herb chutney if you have one made fresh, and lemon.
funFacts: Boti is cut lamb on a skewer. Seekh is the minced kebab in the same grill tradition.
Whole lamb chunks are rested after they leave the fire.
variations: Shoulder cubes have more fat. Leg cubes are leaner and still work if they are not overcooked.
A hotter chili powder is common in some kitchens. This marinade is medium.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless lamb leg, cut in 1.5-inch chunks
steps: Mix the yogurt, ginger, garlic, chili, cumin, salt, and oil. Coat the lamb and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the chunks on skewers. Heat a grill or a tandoor until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the lamb 3 minutes before serving. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Paneer Tikka
culture: North Indian restaurant and home cooks who grill fresh cheese for people who do not eat meat
flavor: Firm paneer and peppers, stained with yogurt and Kashmiri chili, browned at the edges.
history: Paneer tikka is a vegetarian tandoor plate: cubes of fresh cheese with peppers and onion, in a yogurt marinade like chicken tikka. It is a restaurant and home dish of the tandoor menu, not an old whole-animal roast. The cheese is dairy, so the plate is vegetarian and not vegan. A hot grill works if you do not have a tandoor.
background: There is no meat, fish, or egg. Yogurt and paneer are dairy. It is the cheese version of a tikka skewer, cooked by North Indian kitchens that already run a tandoor for bread and meat.
whyItTastes: Paneer does not melt the way aged cheese does, so it can sit on a skewer and take a browned edge. Yogurt and chili cling to the cubes, and pepper and onion soften and char. The flavor is the same tandoor family as chicken tikka, with milk instead of meat.
authenticTouch: Dry the paneer cubes before they go into the marinade. Wet cubes steam and fall apart.
method: Marinate paneer, pepper, and onion in yogurt and chili, then cook them on skewers in a tandoor or on a hot grill until browned.
served: Eat the hot cubes with onion and lemon. There is no meat on the plate.
funFacts: Paneer is fresh milk cheese, so the skewer is vegetarian and not vegan.
A hot grill can stand in for a tandoor if the cubes are kept moving.
variations: A home grill is honest to name as a grill when you have no tandoor.
A pinch more chili heat is easy to add. This batch is medium.
ingredients: 14 ounces paneer, cut in 1-inch cubes and patted dry
1 red bell pepper, cut in chunks
steps: Stir the yogurt, chili, cumin, salt, oil, and lemon. Fold in the paneer, pepper, and onion. Refrigerate for 20 minutes. Do not leave the mixture warm on the counter.
Thread the cheese and vegetables on skewers. Heat a tandoor or a hot grill.
Cook, turning, until the paneer is hot through and the edges are browned, about 12 to 15 minutes. There is no meat temperature for cheese.
Serve hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Tandoori Fish
culture: North Indian tandoor cooks who marinate firm fish in yogurt and chili
flavor: Firm fish with a tangy yogurt crust, chili color, and a short, hot cook.
history: Tandoori fish is firm fish in a yogurt and chili marinade, cooked in a tandoor or a very hot oven. It is part of the same North Indian tandoor menu as the chicken, using fish instead of poultry. It is not fried Amritsari fish, which is a batter fry from Amritsar and a different technique. Yogurt keeps dairy in the dish.
background: The cook is a tandoor or a labeled home oven, not a frying pan. There is fish and dairy. It is not the chickpea-batter fish of Amritsar, and it is not a vegan plate.
whyItTastes: Fish cooks quickly, so the yogurt marinade browns before the flesh dries. Chili and ajwain, a sharp seed used with fish in North Indian cooking, sit on that crust. The tandoor taste is dry heat and char, which a fryer full of oil does not give.
authenticTouch: Choose a steak that is at least an inch thick. Thin fillets fall apart and overcook before the marinade colors.
method: Marinate thick fish steaks in yogurt, chili, and ajwain, then cook them in a tandoor or a very hot home oven until the center flakes.
served: Eat it with onion, lemon, and a plain salad. Do not batter or fry it.
funFacts: This is tandoor-cooked fish. It is not fried Amritsari fish.
Yogurt in the marinade means the plate contains dairy.
variations: Kingfish, salmon, or another firm steak can be used if the local fish is the same thickness.
A home oven at high heat should be called an oven, not a tandoor.
ingredients: 4 firm fish steaks, about 6 ounces each
steps: Mix the yogurt, chili, ginger, garlic, ajwain, salt, lemon, and oil. Coat the fish and refrigerate it for 20 minutes. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a tandoor, or heat a home oven to 450°F (230°C) and name it as an oven. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Cook the steaks until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Do not fry them. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve hot with lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Mughal-Style Raan
culture: Cooks working in the Mughal spice tradition who roast a whole lamb leg
flavor: A lamb leg with yogurt, ginger, and warm Mughal spice, sliced after a rest.
history: Raan is a roasted leg of lamb seasoned in the Mughal style: yogurt, ginger, garlic, and warm spices such as cardamom and cumin. It was a feast cut in imperial and later restaurant kitchens of North India, cooked in a tandoor when the oven was large enough and in a covered oven when it was not. This page uses a home oven if you have no tandoor, and it says so. The leg is whole muscle, cooked and rested, not minced.
background: This is one lamb leg, not a skewer kebab. Yogurt in the paste means dairy. The spice list is the Mughal pantry of ginger, garlic, and cardamom, used by North Indian feast cooks.
whyItTastes: A whole leg keeps its juices if it is not rushed, and the yogurt paste browns into a crust. Cardamom and cumin perfume the fat. In a tandoor the crust dries faster. A home oven is gentler and still gives you the spiced lamb, which is the part that makes raan itself.
authenticTouch: Score the leg and push the paste into the cuts. A paste that sits only on the surface seasons the crust and leaves the center plain.
method: Coat a lamb leg with a yogurt and spice paste and roast it in a tandoor or, labeled as such, a home oven, then rest it.
served: Slice it and eat it with onion, lemon, and rice.
funFacts: Raan is a whole lamb leg, not a minced kebab.
A home oven is a substitute here and should be called an oven, not a tandoor.
variations: A bone-in leg takes longer than a boneless one. Use the thermometer either way.
Saffron is a festive addition and is not required for the spice to read as Mughal.
steps: Score the leg. Mix the yogurt, ginger, garlic, salt, chili, cumin, cardamom, and oil, and rub it into the cuts. Refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

If you have a tandoor large enough, heat it for roasting. Otherwise heat a home oven to 350°F (175°C) and call the cook an oven roast. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Roast until the center of the thickest muscle, away from the bone, reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the leg 3 minutes, then slice it. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Hyderabad Pathar ka Gosht
culture: Hyderabadi cooks who sear mutton on a flat stone griddle
flavor: Thin mutton steaks, spiced and seared on a very hot flat stone or a cast-iron griddle.
history: Pathar ka gosht is a Hyderabad dish of mutton cooked on a pathar, a thick flat stone used as a griddle. The meat is usually a thin steak, marinated with yogurt and spice, and it cooks fast on that hot surface. This home recipe uses a cast-iron griddle. It does not ask you to heat a found rock; a restaurant pathar is a purpose-made cooking stone, not a river stone from outside.
background: Hyderabadi cooks sear whole-muscle mutton this way. It is not a minced kebab and not a tandoor chicken. Yogurt in the marinade means dairy. The home pan is a griddle, named as a griddle.
whyItTastes: A screaming-hot flat surface browns thin mutton before the inside dries, which is why the steaks are cut thin. Yogurt, chili, and coriander make a savory crust. The stone in a Hyderabad shop holds heat the way a thick cast-iron griddle does at home.
authenticTouch: Pound or slice the mutton thin. A thick chop will steam on the griddle and miss the point of the dish.
method: Marinate thin mutton steaks, then sear them on a cast-iron griddle standing in for the Hyderabad stone.
served: Eat it at once with onion, lemon, and a piece of bread only if you want wheat on the side. The meat itself has none.
funFacts: Pathar means stone. In Hyderabad the meat is cooked on a flat cooking stone.
This recipe uses a cast-iron griddle and does not heat a found rock.
variations: Lamb leg steaks are the right cut if mutton is not sold.
A hotter chili is used in some Hyderabadi kitchens. This batch is medium.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless mutton or lamb leg, sliced 1/3 inch thick
steps: Mix the yogurt, ginger, garlic, coriander, chili, salt, and oil. Coat the meat and refrigerate it for 30 minutes. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The meat is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Heat a cast-iron griddle until it is very hot. This griddle stands in for a Hyderabad pathar. Do not heat a found rock. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Sear the steaks until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Work in batches so the pan stays hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the meat 3 minutes. Serve it hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Kakori Kebab
culture: Awadhi cooks in Kakori and Lucknow who mince lamb until it is very fine
flavor: Very finely minced lamb, pale and soft, with cream, white pepper, and warm spice.
history: Kakori kebab is named for Kakori, near Lucknow, and it belongs to Awadhi cooking. The lamb is minced very fine, finer than a standard seekh, and it is seasoned with warm spice rather than a harsh chili heat. Cream is part of many kitchen versions, which makes the kebab dairy. It can be cooked on a skewer or on a flat griddle; this is the home version of that Lucknow kebab, not a single undisputed origin tale.
background: Awadhi cooks in Kakori and Lucknow are the people tied to this kebab. It is ground lamb, cooked through, with cream. It is not a chunky boti and not a coarse seekh.
whyItTastes: Fine mincing changes the texture: the kebab stays soft instead of coarse. Cream and lamb fat keep it tender, and cardamom and white pepper perfume it without a red-chili crust. On a skewer or a hot griddle the outside browns just enough to smell like a grill.
authenticTouch: Mince twice, or chop by hand until the meat is almost a paste. Coarse mince is a seekh, not a kakori.
method: Work lamb and cream into a fine paste, shape it on skewers or as small cakes, and cook it on a grill or a griddle until the center is done.
served: Serve it with onion and a little mint. The chili heat is mild on purpose.
funFacts: The kebab is associated with Kakori, a town near Lucknow, and with Awadhi cooking.
The meat is minced finer than a typical seekh kebab.
variations: Skewers are traditional. A hot griddle is a fair home method for the same paste.
Cashew is used in some kitchens and would add a tree nut. This paste uses cream instead.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds lamb, minced twice until very fine
1 small onion, boiled and mashed, water pressed out
steps: Mix the fine lamb, cream, onion, cardamom, white pepper, salt, ginger, and garlic into a smooth paste. Keep it cold. It is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Shape the paste on flat skewers, or form small cakes for a griddle. Refrigerate them until the pan or grill is hot. Do not leave the paste at room temperature. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Cook on a hot grill or griddle, turning carefully, until the center reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest 3 minutes and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Bihari Kebab
culture: Cooks from Bihar, and the North Indian grill shops that serve this mustard-spiced beef
flavor: Thin beef with mustard, mustard oil, ginger, and chili, grilled on skewers.
history: Bihari kebab is beef, often cut thin, marinated with mustard and mustard oil and grilled on skewers. The name points to Bihar, and the kebab is also cooked in North Indian cities by cooks who carried that seasoning with them. Mustard is the marker, more than a yogurt sauce. The meat is whole muscle, so it is rested after it reaches temperature; it is not a minced seekh.
background: This is skewered beef in a Bihari mustard marinade. Mustard and mustard oil are in the paste. There is no yogurt and no wheat. It is a grill kebab, not a stew.
whyItTastes: Mustard oil is sharp and aromatic, and ground mustard clings to thin beef. Chili heat sits on top of that. A hot skewer browns the oil instead of boiling it. The result is pungent in a way a yogurt boti is not, which is why the two kebabs can share a street and still be different.
authenticTouch: Slice the beef thin across the grain. Thick pieces hide the mustard in the middle and take too long on the skewer.
method: Marinate thin beef in mustard, mustard oil, ginger, and chili, then grill it on skewers and rest it.
served: Eat it with onion and lemon. The heat is meant to be hot.
funFacts: Mustard and mustard oil are the seasoning that marks Bihari kebab.
The beef is kept in pieces on skewers, not minced.
variations: A little raw papaya is sometimes used to soften the meat. It is left out of this batch.
Green chili can replace some of the red chili. Keep the mustard either way.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds beef sirloin, sliced thin across the grain
steps: Mix the mustard oil, ground mustard, ginger, garlic, chili, salt, and lemon. Coat the beef and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The beef is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the slices on skewers without folding them into thick bundles. Heat the grill. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill until the center of the thickest slice reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the beef 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Balochistan Sajji
culture: Baloch cooks in Balochistan who roast a whole chicken beside the coals
flavor: Whole chicken, mostly salt, with dry heat from coals set beside the bird.
history: Sajji is a Balochistan roast, especially associated with Baloch cooks. A whole chicken is salted and cooked slowly beside coals, not over a bed of flame and not in a yogurt tandoor marinade. The seasoning is salt, which is the point. It is a Pakistani dish from Balochistan; a covered grill with the coals pushed to one side is the home version of that beside-the-fire cook.
background: Baloch cooks salt a whole chicken and give it time next to the coals. There is no chili paste and no yogurt. It is a different bird from Delhi tandoori chicken.
whyItTastes: Salt and slow side heat leave the chicken tasting like chicken, with a little smoke from the coals and a drier skin than a steamed bird. Balochistan's cooking here is spare on purpose. Spice would hide the thing sajji is known for.
authenticTouch: Keep the coals to the side. If the skin burns while the thigh is still raw, the fire is under the bird instead of beside it.
method: Salt a whole chicken and cook it on a spit or a rack beside coals until the thigh is done.
served: Break it into pieces and eat it with lemon and flatbread only if you want wheat beside it. The chicken itself is only salt and fire.
funFacts: Sajji from Balochistan is a salted whole chicken cooked slowly beside coals.
The seasoning is salt. A yogurt chili marinade is a different dish.
variations: Lamb sajji is also cooked in Balochistan. This page is the chicken.
A covered kettle grill with the coals banked to one side is the home setup.
steps: Pat the chicken dry. Rub it with oil, salt, and pepper, including a little salt in the cavity. Refrigerate it until the fire is ready. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Bank a charcoal fire to one side of a covered grill, or set the bird on a spit with the coals beside it, not piled under the breast. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Cook with the lid on, turning as needed, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve it rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest it 10 minutes, then cut it up. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Peshawar Chapli Kebab
culture: Pashtun cooks in Peshawar who pan-fry wide cakes of minced beef
flavor: A wide, thin beef cake with tomato, cilantro, green chili, and cumin, fried on a griddle.
history: Chapli kebab is a Peshawar dish of Pashtun cooks: minced beef, shaped wide and flat, and pan-fried on a griddle. Tomato, cilantro, and green chili are mixed into the meat. Cornmeal is the binder in this recipe so the cakes hold without wheat. It is ground beef and has to be cooked through; it is a Pakistani kebab from Peshawar, cooked on a plancha, not on a tandoor skewer.
background: Peshawar grill shops and home kitchens fry these cakes in shallow oil on a wide pan. There is no yogurt and no wheat in this written recipe. It is not a seekh and not a Balochistan sajji.
whyItTastes: A wide, thin cake gets crust on both sides, and the beef fat fries the edges. Tomato and cilantro stay bright inside. Green chili is the heat. That griddle fry is why chapli tastes different from a charcoal skewer of the same mince.
authenticTouch: Shape them wide and thin. A thick cake browns outside and stays undercooked in the middle unless you cook it much longer.
method: Mix ground beef with tomato, chili, and cornmeal, shape thin cakes, and fry them on a griddle until the center is done.
served: Eat them hot with onion, lemon, and a sliced tomato.
funFacts: Chapli kebab is associated with Peshawar and with Pashtun cooking there.
The cakes are wide and pan-fried, not molded onto a skewer.
variations: Wheat flour is a common binder and would add gluten. This recipe uses cornmeal.
An egg is sometimes mixed in and would add egg. This batch has none.
ingredients: 3 tablespoons neutral oil, for the griddle
steps: Mix the beef, tomato, cilantro, chili, onion, cornmeal, cumin, coriander, and salt. Do not add wheat flour. The meat is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Shape eight wide, thin cakes. Heat a griddle with the oil over medium heat. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Fry until both sides are browned and the center of each cake reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest them 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Nepali Sekuwa
culture: Nepali grill cooks who thread meat on skewers and cook it over charcoal
flavor: Goat chunks with ginger, turmeric, and chili, grilled over a hot fire.
history: Sekuwa is a Nepali grilled skewer, sold in shops and cooked at home, with meat cut in pieces rather than minced. Goat is a usual meat. Ginger, turmeric, and chili are worked into the marinade, and the skewers go over charcoal. It is Nepali cooking; a yogurt-heavy North Indian boti is a different marinade even when both use a skewer.
background: Nepali cooks grill these skewers in cities such as Pokhara and Kathmandu and in smaller shops along the roads. This recipe uses goat, in whole chunks. There is no wheat and no dairy in the marinade.
whyItTastes: Goat has a deeper flavor than young chicken, and turmeric and chili stain the surface before the fire browns it. A hot charcoal grate gives a dry edge. Lemon at the table brightens the fat. The taste sits with Nepali grill shops, where the skewer is the everyday plate.
authenticTouch: Do not crowd the skewers. Goat chunks that touch each other steam instead of grilling.
method: Marinate goat chunks with ginger, turmeric, and chili, then grill them on skewers and rest them.
served: Eat the meat with onion, lemon, and a dusting of chili if you want it hotter.
funFacts: Sekuwa is Nepali grilled meat on skewers, cut in pieces rather than minced.
Goat is a usual meat for the skewer.
variations: Chicken sekuwa is common and would be cooked to a poultry temperature. This page is goat.
A hotter chili oil on the side is how many shops let you raise the heat.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless goat, cut in 1.5-inch chunks
steps: Mix the ginger, garlic, turmeric, chili, cumin, salt, oil, and lemon. Coat the goat and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The meat is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the chunks on skewers with a little space between them. Heat a charcoal or gas grill. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the meat 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Sri Lankan Grilled Prawns
culture: Coastal Sri Lankan cooks who grill prawns with chili, lime, and curry leaf
flavor: Prawns with chili, garlic, lime, and curry leaf, cooked just until they turn opaque.
history: Grilled prawns are a coastal Sri Lankan plate, seasoned with chili, garlic, lime, and curry leaf and cooked quickly over a hot fire. Negombo and other west-coast towns land the prawns that make this a local grill. The heat is from chili, and the cook is short because shellfish toughen when they stay on the grate. This is Sri Lankan coastal cooking, with its own spice and its own shore.
background: Coastal cooks grill whole prawns in the shell or peeled, with a chili paste. There is shellfish in the dish. There is no wheat batter and no dairy. It is a grill, not a fry.
whyItTastes: Prawns are sweet, and lime and chili cut that sweetness. Curry leaf, torn into the oil, adds the herbal note associated with Sri Lankan cooking. A hot grate chars the spice paste in a few minutes, which is all the time the prawns need.
authenticTouch: Pull them when they turn opaque. Another five minutes on a hot grate makes them rubbery even if the chili paste smells good.
method: Toss prawns with chili, garlic, lime, and curry leaf, then grill them until the flesh is opaque.
served: Eat them with lime and a little extra chili on the side if you want more heat.
funFacts: Curry leaf, chili, and lime are the coastal seasoning on these prawns.
Shellfish are ready when the flesh is opaque, not when the shells have blackened.
variations: Leave the shells on if you want more protection from the fire. Peel them to eat.
A milder chili powder lowers the heat. This batch is hot.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds large prawns, peeled and deveined
steps: Toss the prawns with oil, garlic, chili, curry leaves, salt, lime juice, and pepper. Refrigerate them for 15 minutes. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The prawns are still raw. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Heat a grill until the grate is hot. Oil the grate lightly. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Grill the prawns, turning once, until the flesh is opaque and the center reaches 145°F (63°C). Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Serve at once with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).

name: Goan Recheado Mackerel
culture: Goan Catholic and coastal home cooks who stuff mackerel with a red chili paste
flavor: Grilled mackerel stuffed with a hot red paste of chili, garlic, and vinegar.
history: Recheado is a Goan word from Portuguese recheado, meaning stuffed. In Goa the stuffing for mackerel is a red paste of dried chili, garlic, ginger, spice, and vinegar, packed into a slit in the fish and then grilled or pan-cooked. Vinegar and chili reflect Goa's coastal and Catholic kitchen, shaped in part by Portuguese colonial trade. This version is grilled; it is a Goan fish, from India, and the paste is hot.
background: Goan home cooks stuff fresh mackerel with this paste. There is fish and vinegar, and no dairy and no wheat. It is a grill, not a tandoor yogurt fish.
whyItTastes: Mackerel is oily, so it stands up to vinegar and a heavy chili paste. The paste steams inside the slit while the skin crisps on the grill. That contrast, sharp inside and charred outside, is why a plain salted mackerel is a different dinner.
authenticTouch: Cut the slit deep enough to hold the paste, and do not leave a mound of paste on the skin where it will burn.
method: Grind a chili and vinegar paste, stuff it into mackerel, and grill the fish until it flakes.
served: Eat the fish with lime and a little rice. The heat is hot.
funFacts: Recheado comes from the Portuguese word for stuffed, used in Goa for this chili paste.
The fish is grilled with the paste inside, not fried in a batter.
variations: Pomfret is also stuffed this way in Goa. Mackerel is the fish on this page.
A milder dried chili lowers the heat. Kashmiri chili alone will not taste like a hot recheado.
ingredients: 4 small whole mackerel, cleaned, heads on or off
8 dried hot red chilies, stemmed and soaked in warm water
2 tablespoons palm vinegar or white vinegar
steps: Blend the soaked chilies, garlic, ginger, cumin, pepper, vinegar, salt, and oil into a thick paste. Slit each mackerel and fill the slit with paste. Refrigerate the fish. The fish is still raw. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill to a steady medium-hot fire. Oil the grate. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Grill the fish, turning once, until the center of the thickest fish reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Kolkata Kathi Kebab
culture: Kolkata kebab cooks who grill spiced meat on skewers for the street
flavor: Skewered lamb with yogurt, ginger, and chili, browned over a hot fire.
history: Kathi kebab is the skewered meat of a Kolkata street plate. In the city it is often rolled into a paratha and eaten as a kathi roll. This recipe cooks only the meat. The paratha stays a pairing, not an ingredient, so the kebab has no wheat if the marinade has none; yogurt, ginger, and chili are the marinade; the lamb is whole muscle on a skewer, from an Indian kitchen in Kolkata.
background: Kolkata street cooks grill this meat and, when you ask, wrap it. The written dish is the skewer. Yogurt means dairy. There is no flour in the bowl, which is deliberate so the meat can be gluten-free.
whyItTastes: A hot skewer browns the yogurt marinade on small pieces of lamb, and ginger and chili stay bright. The Kolkata roll adds a toasted paratha around that meat. Leaving the paratha on the side lets you taste the kebab itself, which is the grilled part of the street plate.
authenticTouch: Cut the lamb small enough to cook through on a street-style skewer. Huge chunks are a different roast.
method: Marinate lamb in yogurt and spice with no wheat, grill it on skewers, and rest it. Offer a paratha beside it if you want the roll.
served: Eat the meat with onion and lemon. A paratha can sit on the side as a pairing and is not part of the marinade.
funFacts: In Kolkata the kebab is often eaten in a paratha roll. The bread is a pairing on this page.
The marinade has no wheat, so the meat itself can be gluten-free.
variations: Chicken pieces are also sold on Kolkata skewers and would need a poultry temperature. This is lamb.
Wrapping the meat in a paratha makes the street roll and adds wheat.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless lamb, cut in 1-inch chunks
steps: Mix the yogurt, ginger, garlic, chili, cumin, salt, lemon, and oil. Do not add wheat flour. Coat the lamb and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the lamb on skewers. Heat a grill until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Rest the meat 3 minutes. Serve the kebab with onion and lemon. If you add a paratha, keep it as a side. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Malai Chicken Tikka
culture: North Indian tandoor cooks who marinate boneless chicken in cream
flavor: Boneless chicken in a mild cream marinade, with cardamom and white pepper.
history: Malai means cream. Malai chicken tikka is boneless chicken in a cream marinade, cooked in a tandoor or on a hot grill, and it is a milder plate than chili-red chicken tikka. It is a North Indian restaurant and home dish in the tandoor family. Cream is dairy, so the dish is not vegan; the pieces are not a whole tandoori chicken.
background: Tandoor cooks in Delhi and other North Indian cities sell this pale, mild tikka beside the red one. There is chicken and cream. There is no wheat. The heat is mild on purpose.
whyItTastes: Cream browns into a soft crust instead of a sharp chili crust, and cardamom perfumes the fat. White pepper gives aroma without painting the meat red. High heat still matters: the cream should spot and color, not boil in a cool pan.
authenticTouch: Do not add a heavy hand of red chili. If the marinade looks like the red tikka, it is no longer malai.
method: Marinate boneless chicken in cream, cardamom, and white pepper, then cook it in a tandoor or on a hot grill.
served: Eat the pieces with onion and lemon. The plate is mild.
funFacts: Malai means cream, and the marinade is a cream marinade.
The chicken is boneless. It is not the whole tandoori bird.
variations: A hot grill replaces a tandoor if you say it is a grill.
A green chili on the side can add heat without stirring it into the cream.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless chicken thighs, cut in cubes
steps: Mix the cream, ginger, garlic, cardamom, white pepper, salt, oil, and lemon. Coat the chicken and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Thread the cubes on skewers. Heat a tandoor, or heat a grill and call it a grill. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Cook until the center of the thickest cube reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve the chicken rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest a few minutes and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Afghan Lamb Tikka
culture: Afghan grill cooks who salt lamb and cook it in chunks on skewers
flavor: Lamb chunks with salt, cumin, and a little chili, grilled over charcoal.
history: Afghan tikka is lamb in chunks on skewers, seasoned with salt, fat, cumin, and often a little chili, and cooked over charcoal. It is a Central Asian grill from Afghanistan, cooked in Kabul and in other cities by Afghan grill cooks. The seasoning is spare next to a yogurt-heavy North Indian marinade. The meat is whole muscle and is rested after it reaches temperature.
background: Afghan cooks grill this lamb over charcoal, often with naan nearby in the market. This recipe does not put bread or yogurt into the meat. It is a Kabul-style skewer of lamb, from Afghanistan.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat, salt, and cumin are enough when the charcoal is hot. A little chili warms the crust without covering the meat. The dry climate of the plateau is not a flavor by itself. The flavor is the lamb and the fire, which is why the marinade stays short.
authenticTouch: Salt the lamb early enough for the salt to dissolve on the meat, and keep the chunks similar in size.
method: Season lamb chunks with salt, cumin, and chili, skewer them, and grill them over a hot fire, then rest them.
served: Eat the lamb with onion, a squeeze of lemon, and cilantro if you want a green bite.
funFacts: Afghan tikka is lamb on skewers, seasoned simply and cooked over charcoal.
The meat is whole chunks, rested after grilling.
variations: Some cooks add a spoon of oil and crushed coriander. The salt and cumin stay.
Chicken tikka in Afghan shops would need a poultry temperature. This is lamb.
ingredients: 2 pounds boneless lamb leg, cut in 1.5-inch chunks
steps: Toss the lamb with salt, cumin, chili flakes, and oil. Refrigerate it for 20 minutes. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the chunks on skewers. Heat a charcoal grill until the coals are hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the lamb 3 minutes. Serve with onion and lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Thai Gai Yang
culture: Isan cooks in northeastern Thailand who grill chicken with garlic and coriander root
flavor: Grilled chicken with garlic, coriander root, white pepper, and fish sauce.
history: Gai yang is grilled chicken from Isan, in northeastern Thailand, usually a bird opened flat and cooked over charcoal. Coriander root, garlic, and white pepper are pounded into the marinade, and fish sauce provides the salt. The chicken is often eaten with a chili dipping sauce. Across the Mekong, Lao ping kai is a related grill; this page is the Thai bird.
background: Isan cooks and Bangkok shops that learned from them grill this chicken. Fish sauce means the dish contains fish as well as chicken. There is no dairy and no wheat in the marinade. The chili sauce can sit beside it.
whyItTastes: Coriander root is earthier than the leaf, and with garlic and white pepper it makes a fragrant paste that chars on the skin. Charcoal dries the surface while the thigh cooks through. Fish sauce salts the meat more deeply than a sprinkle of salt at the end. The sour chili dip, if you serve one, is there to cut the fat.
authenticTouch: Pound the coriander root and garlic. Chopped leaf coriander is a different flavor and will burn.
method: Marinate a butterflied chicken with a coriander-root paste and grill it over charcoal until the thigh is done.
served: Chop it into pieces and eat it with sticky rice and a chili dip such as nam jim jaew.
funFacts: Gai yang is the grilled chicken of Isan, in northeastern Thailand.
Coriander root, garlic, and white pepper are the usual pounded marinade.
variations: A hotter dipping sauce is how the table raises the heat. The chicken marinade here is mild.
Thigh pieces cook faster than a whole bird and still need the same poultry temperature.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 3.5 pounds, backbone removed
4 cilantro roots, or 1/2 cup cilantro stems, chopped
steps: Pound the cilantro roots or stems, garlic, and white pepper to a paste. Stir in fish sauce, oil, sugar, and salt. Rub the chicken and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Heat a charcoal grill for medium heat, with a cooler side if the skin starts to darken too fast. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Grill, turning, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve it rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest 5 minutes, then chop it. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Thai Moo Ping
culture: Bangkok street cooks who grill sweet pork on small skewers
flavor: Sweet, salty pork skewers with garlic, white pepper, and a little coconut milk.
history: Moo ping is a Thai street skewer of pork, sold from small grills in Bangkok and other cities. The marinade is sweet and salty, with garlic, white pepper, fish sauce or salt, sugar, and often a spoon of coconut milk so the edges brown. The pork is cut in thin pieces, which makes it a whole-muscle skewer rather than a sausage. It is everyday street food, cooked to order.
background: Street cooks thread the pork and grill it in front of you. Coconut milk is not a dairy milk. Fish sauce, if used, contains fish. This recipe uses fish sauce. There is no wheat and no peanut in the marinade.
whyItTastes: Sugar and coconut milk caramelize on a hot grate, and fish sauce salts the pork. White pepper and garlic stay sharp under that sweetness. Thin slices cook before the sugar turns black, which is why the skewers are small.
authenticTouch: Keep the pieces thin and do not let the sugar flame up. A black skewer tastes bitter.
method: Marinate thin pork in coconut milk, sugar, garlic, and fish sauce, then grill it on skewers.
served: Eat the skewers hot, with sticky rice or a sour chili dip.
funFacts: Moo ping is a sweet pork skewer sold from small street grills in Thailand.
Coconut milk helps the edges brown. It is not dairy.
variations: Palm sugar and white sugar are both used. This recipe uses palm sugar.
A chili dip on the side adds heat. The skewer itself is mild.
steps: Mix the coconut milk, palm sugar, fish sauce, garlic, white pepper, and oil. Coat the pork and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the slices on small skewers. Heat a grill until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning often, until the center of the thickest slice reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Thai Kor Moo Yang
culture: Thai grill cooks who cook pork neck over charcoal and slice it for the table
flavor: Pork neck with garlic, fish sauce, and white pepper, sliced after a rest.
history: Kor moo yang is grilled pork neck, a cut with fat and lean in the same slice. Thai cooks marinate it with garlic, white pepper, and fish sauce, grill it over charcoal, and slice it against the grain. It is a common plate in Chiang Mai and across the country, often with a spicy dip. The neck is whole muscle, not ground pork.
background: Grill shops cook the neck in a larger piece than moo ping and slice it at the board. Fish sauce means fish is an allergen along with pork. There is no wheat and no dairy.
whyItTastes: Pork neck stays moist because of the fat running through it, and a hot grill browns that fat. Garlic and white pepper are the aroma, and fish sauce is the salt. Slicing it thin lets the dip season each piece. A lean loin would dry out on the same fire.
authenticTouch: Rest the neck before you slice it. Cutting it on the grill dumps the juice onto the coals.
method: Marinate a pork neck in garlic, fish sauce, and white pepper, grill it, rest it, and slice it.
served: Slice it and eat it with sticky rice, herbs, and a chili dip.
funFacts: Kor moo is pork neck, a cut with fat through the lean meat.
The neck is grilled in a piece and sliced, not cubed onto small skewers.
variations: A shoulder steak can stand in if neck is not sold. Keep it a whole cut.
The dipping sauce can be very hot while the meat stays mild.
steps: Rub the pork with garlic, fish sauce, white pepper, oil, sugar, and salt. Refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a charcoal grill to medium-high, with room to move the meat if the fat flares. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes, then slice it. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Thai Pla Pao
culture: Thai riverside cooks who pack a whole fish in salt and grill it
flavor: A whole fish steamed inside a salt crust, with moist flesh and a clean taste.
history: Pla pao is a Thai way of grilling a whole fish inside a jacket of salt, often set near an open fire. The salt crust keeps the flesh moist and seasons it. River fish and tilapia are both used. The crust is cracked open at the table; it is not a chili curry and not a fried fish; the only heat is the fire, not chili.
background: Riverside and home cooks in Thailand pack the fish in salt and give it time by the fire. There is fish and salt, and no chili in the crust. Egg white is sometimes used to bind a salt dough. This recipe uses egg white, so it contains egg.
whyItTastes: The salt crust blocks direct flame, so the fish steams in its own moisture instead of drying. A little salt reaches the flesh. Herbs in the cavity perfume it without a sauce. When the crust is cracked, the fish tastes clean, which is the point of the method.
authenticTouch: Make the crust thick enough that you cannot see the skin. Thin salt burns and does not protect the fish.
method: Stuff a whole fish, pack it in a salt and egg-white crust, and cook it beside a fire or in a hot oven until the flesh flakes.
served: Crack off the salt crust and eat the fish with lime and a chili sauce on the side if you want heat.
funFacts: Pla pao cooks the fish inside a salt crust so the flesh steams.
The crust is broken away. It is not a sauce you eat by the spoon.
variations: A hot oven can finish the crust if you do not have an open fire. Say that it is an oven.
Lemongrass in the cavity is a common herb. Chili is for the table, not the crust.
ingredients: 1 whole fish, about 2 pounds, cleaned and scaled
steps: Fill the cavity with lemongrass and lime leaves. Stir the salt, egg whites, and water into a packable crust. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

Pack the crust all over the fish in a thick layer. Heat an open fire with a grill rack to the side, or heat an oven to 400°F (200°C) and call it an oven. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

Cook until the center of the thickest part reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Crack a little crust to check, then close it if it needs more time. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Rest it briefly, crack away the crust, and serve the fish. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Nam Jim Jaew
culture: Isan cooks who pound a chili and toasted-rice dip for grilled meat
flavor: Hot, sour, and salty, with toasted rice, chili, lime, and fish sauce.
history: Nam jim jaew is the Isan dipping sauce served with grilled chicken and grilled pork. Toasted sticky-rice powder thickens it, dried chili provides the heat, and lime and fish sauce make it sour and salty. Shallot is usual. It is a table sauce, not a cooked glaze; fish sauce means it contains fish, so it is not a vegetarian condiment even though there is no piece of meat in the bowl.
background: Isan cooks set this bowl beside gai yang and pork. The rice is toasted, not boiled into porridge. There is no dairy and no wheat if you toast rice, not barley. Keep it cold, and do not treat it as a preserve.
whyItTastes: Toasted rice smells nutty and gives the sauce body so it clings to grilled meat. Lime cuts fat, dried chili brings heat, and fish sauce is the salt of the Mekong table. Shallot adds a sharp fresh bite. Without the toasted rice, the same liquids would be a thinner nam jim.
authenticTouch: Toast the rice until it smells popped, then grind it. Raw rice flour will taste raw and dusty.
method: Toast rice and grind it, then stir it with chili, lime, fish sauce, and shallot.
served: Spoon it over grilled chicken or pork, or leave it in a bowl for dipping.
funFacts: Toasted rice powder is what makes jaew different from a thin chili fish sauce.
Fish sauce is in the bowl, so the sauce is not vegetarian.
variations: More dried chili makes it extra-hot. This cup is hot.
A little extra lime is the right fix if the fish sauce is very salty.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons uncooked sticky rice or jasmine rice
steps: Toast the rice in a dry pan until it is golden and smells nutty. Grind it to a coarse powder. There is no meat to cook in this sauce.
Stir the rice powder with fish sauce, lime juice, chili, shallot, and sugar.
Taste for salt and sour. Add cilantro.
Serve the same day. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. This is not a canning recipe. Do not leave it at room temperature.

name: Hanoi Bun Cha
culture: Hanoi cooks who grill pork and serve it with rice noodles and a sweet-sour bowl
flavor: Grilled pork patties and pork belly with rice noodles, herbs, and a lime-fish sauce bowl.
history: Bun cha is a Hanoi lunch: grilled pork, rice noodles, herbs, and a sweet-sour bowl of fish sauce, lime, and sugar. The pork is often both a minced patty and a slice of belly. Rice noodles do not contain wheat, so the written dish is gluten-free if you do not add a wheat sauce. It is street and shop food in Hanoi, eaten at midday more than as a court recipe.
background: Hanoi cooks grill the pork over charcoal and set noodles and herbs on the table. The patties are ground pork. The belly is a whole cut. Fish sauce contains fish. There is no wheat in the noodles or the marinade.
whyItTastes: Charcoal sweetens the edges of the pork, and the dipping bowl is sour, salty, and a little sweet, which cuts the fat of the belly. Rice noodles stay mild so the grill and the lime show. Herbs add freshness. Wheat noodles would make a different bowl.
authenticTouch: Grill the patties over real heat so they brown. If they only poach in a pan of sauce, they are not bun cha.
method: Season ground pork and pork belly, grill both to their own temperatures, and serve them with rice noodles and a lime-fish sauce bowl.
served: Put noodles in a bowl, add herbs and the warm pork, and spoon on the dipping sauce.
funFacts: Bun cha is a Hanoi plate of grilled pork and rice noodles.
Rice noodles contain no wheat when they are made only from rice.
variations: Some shops serve only the patties. This page includes belly as well.
Extra chili in the bowl raises the heat. The written bowl is mild.
ingredients: 1 pound pork belly, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 small head of lettuce, leaves separated
steps: Mix the ground pork with 1 tablespoon fish sauce, half the garlic, and the pepper. Shape thin patties. Rub the belly with the remaining garlic and 1 tablespoon fish sauce. Refrigerate both. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook the ground pork to 160°F (71°C). Cook the pork belly, a whole cut, to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes.

Stir the remaining fish sauce with lime juice, sugar, and 1/4 cup water for the bowl. Boil the rice noodles, drain them, and rinse them cool. Cook the ground pork to 160°F (71°C). Cook the pork belly, a whole cut, to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes.

Grill the patties and the belly over a hot fire. The center of each patty must reach 160°F (71°C). The belly must reach at least 145°F (63°C). Cook the ground pork to 160°F (71°C). Cook the pork belly, a whole cut, to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes.

Rest the belly 3 minutes. Serve pork, noodles, and lettuce with the sauce. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook the ground pork to 160°F (71°C). Cook the pork belly, a whole cut, to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes.

name: Vietnamese Nem Nuong
culture: Southern and south-central Vietnamese cooks who grill sweet ground pork on skewers
flavor: Sweet grilled pork mince on skewers, with garlic and a little sugar.
history: Nem nướng is grilled ground pork, shaped on skewers or as small logs, and it is especially associated with south-central cities such as Nha Trang. The mince is slightly sweet, with garlic and fish sauce, and it is wrapped at the table with herbs and rice paper. It is street and feast food, not a dried cured sausage. Ground pork has to be cooked through.
background: Cooks in Nha Trang and other southern kitchens grill this mince to order. Fish sauce contains fish. There is no wheat in the meat. Rice paper at the table is a wrapper, not a wheat tortilla, when it is made from rice.
whyItTastes: Sugar browns on the skewer and keeps the pork from tasting plain. Fish sauce and garlic season the mince all the way through, unlike a sauce poured on at the end. Herbs and rice paper make each bite fresh against that sweet grill.
authenticTouch: Keep the logs small. A thick roll of ground pork browns outside and stays under temperature in the center.
method: Season ground pork, shape it on skewers, and grill it until the center reaches the temperature for ground meat.
served: Wrap pieces in rice paper with herbs and lettuce, and dip them in a fish-sauce dip.
funFacts: Nem nướng is grilled ground pork, strongly associated with Nha Trang.
It is cooked fresh. It is not a cured sausage.
variations: A spoon of toasted rice powder in the dip adds the same nutty note used in other Vietnamese grills.
Honey would sweeten it and would add honey. This recipe uses sugar.
steps: Mix the pork, fish sauce, sugar, garlic, pepper, oil, and salt. Refrigerate the mince. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. It is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Shape the mince around flat skewers in small logs. Heat a grill. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Grill, turning, until the center of each log reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Vietnamese Suon Nuong
culture: Vietnamese home cooks who grill pork chops with lemongrass and fish sauce
flavor: Pork chops with lemongrass, garlic, sugar, and fish sauce, charred at the edge.
history: Sườn nướng is Vietnamese grilled pork chop or pork rib meat, marinated with lemongrass, garlic, sugar, and fish sauce. It is a home and cơm tấm plate, the broken-rice meal of southern Vietnam, and it is also grilled in home kitchens farther north. The chop is a whole cut, cooked and rested. It is not the ground pork of nem nướng.
background: Home cooks and rice-plate shops grill these chops over charcoal. Fish sauce contains fish. Lemongrass and sugar are the aroma. There is no wheat and no dairy in the marinade.
whyItTastes: Lemongrass oil chars lightly and perfumes the fat, while sugar helps the surface brown. Fish sauce salts the meat. A hot grill does this faster than a covered bake, which is why the chop tastes like a grill and not like a braise.
authenticTouch: Pound the lemongrass before it goes into the marinade. Whole stalks on the side will not season the pork.
method: Marinate pork chops with lemongrass, garlic, sugar, and fish sauce, then grill them and rest them.
served: Slice the chops and eat them with rice, cucumber, and a fish-sauce dip.
funFacts: Sườn nướng is a grilled pork chop, a usual part of a southern Vietnamese rice plate.
Lemongrass, sugar, and fish sauce are the marinade.
variations: Thin rib pieces are used in some kitchens. This page uses chops, which are a whole cut.
A spoon of honey would add honey. Sugar is the sweetener here.
ingredients: 4 bone-in pork chops, about 3/4 inch thick
steps: Stir the lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, sugar, oil, and pepper. Coat the chops and refrigerate them. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill until it is hot. Oil the grate lightly. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning once, until the center of each chop reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the chops 3 minutes. Slice and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Lao Sai Oua
culture: Lao cooks who season ground pork with lemongrass and grill it as a fresh sausage
flavor: Grilled pork sausage heavy with lemongrass, galangal, lime leaf, and chili.
history: Sai oua is a Lao sausage of ground pork mixed with lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaf, shallot, and chili, then grilled. It is a fresh sausage, cooked the day it is mixed, not a cured or dried link. Luang Prabang and other Lao towns sell it beside sticky rice. Ground pork has to reach a ground-meat temperature; this recipe forms the meat into logs without a curing salt.
background: Lao cooks grill sai oua for markets and family meals. The herbs are in the meat, not only in a dip. Fish sauce contains fish. There is no wheat and no dairy. Do not cure it or hang it to dry.
whyItTastes: Lemongrass, galangal, and lime leaf are strong enough to stand up to pork fat, and chili makes the link hot. Grilling browns the outside so the herbs smell toasted. Sticky rice cools the heat. A plain garlic sausage would miss the herb pile that defines sai oua.
authenticTouch: Mince the lemongrass very fine. Long fibers stay tough inside the sausage.
method: Mix ground pork with lemongrass, galangal, lime leaf, and chili, shape logs, and grill them until the center is done.
served: Slice the sausage and eat it with sticky rice and herbs.
funFacts: Sai oua is a fresh Lao pork sausage seasoned with lemongrass and lime leaf.
It is cooked the day it is mixed. This recipe does not cure the meat.
variations: A natural casing makes a tighter link. A log shape without casing is the home method here.
Fewer chilies make it milder. The written sausage is hot.
ingredients: 2 stalks lemongrass, tender parts minced fine
steps: Mix the pork with lemongrass, galangal, lime leaf, shallot, chili, fish sauce, and salt. Keep it cold. Do not add curing salt. The meat is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Shape four logs. Refrigerate them while the grill heats. Cook them the same day. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Grill, turning, until the center of each log reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest 3 minutes, then slice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Lao Ping Kai
culture: Lao cooks along the Mekong who grill chicken the way their side of the river does it
flavor: Grilled chicken with lemongrass, garlic, and fish sauce, chopped for sticky rice.
history: Ping kai is Lao grilled chicken. On the Thai side of the same border, gai yang is the cousin: both are charcoal chickens eaten with sticky rice and a chili dip, from shared border cooking along the Mekong. They are not one recipe. This marinade uses lemongrass with the garlic and fish sauce; the bird is cooked through, then chopped.
background: Lao cooks grill ping kai for markets and home meals in Vientiane and in towns down the river. Fish sauce contains fish. There is no dairy and no wheat. It is the Lao chicken, related to Isan gai yang and seasoned on this page with lemongrass.
whyItTastes: Lemongrass and garlic char on the skin and perfume the fat, and fish sauce salts the meat. Sticky rice and a sour dip are the rest of the plate, because the chicken itself is rich from the skin. Shared ingredients along the border explain the family resemblance. The lemongrass here is the Lao tilt.
authenticTouch: Open the chicken flat so the thighs meet the heat. A whole closed bird burns at the wing before the joint is done.
method: Marinate a butterflied chicken with lemongrass, garlic, and fish sauce, and grill it until the thigh is done.
served: Chop it and eat it with sticky rice and a chili dip.
funFacts: Ping kai is Lao grilled chicken, a cousin of Thai gai yang from shared Mekong cooking.
The two chickens are related and they are not the same recipe.
variations: A hotter dip is served on the side. The marinade here is mild.
Thighs alone can be grilled when a whole bird is too much. They still need 165°F (74°C).
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 3.5 pounds, backbone removed
steps: Mix the lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, oil, pepper, sugar, and salt. Rub the chicken and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Heat a charcoal grill for medium heat. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Grill, turning, until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve it rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Malaysian Chicken Satay
culture: Malay grill cooks, including the satay shops of Kajang, who serve chicken with peanut sauce
flavor: Turmeric chicken skewers with a warm peanut sauce.
history: Malaysian satay ayam is chicken on small skewers, marinated with turmeric, lemongrass, and coriander, and served with a peanut sauce. Kajang, in Selangor, is one of the towns known for satay shops. Peanuts reached Southeast Asian sauces through later trade. The sauce contains peanut, so the dish is not nut-free; a Singapore hawker satay is a related city plate and not this Kajang shop.
background: Malay cooks grill the skewers over charcoal and pound or simmer the peanut sauce beside them. There is chicken and peanut. There is no dairy. This recipe does not use soy sauce, so there is no wheat in the written dish.
whyItTastes: Turmeric and lemongrass scent the chicken, and charcoal dries the edges of small pieces. The peanut sauce is rich, slightly sweet, and hot from chili, which is why the meat itself can stay mild. Peanut, not a cream gravy, is the sauce that makes Malaysian chicken satay what it is.
authenticTouch: Cut the chicken small. Large cubes do not cook like satay and they shed the sauce.
method: Marinate chicken with turmeric and lemongrass, grill it on skewers to a poultry temperature, and serve it with a peanut sauce.
served: Eat the skewers with the peanut sauce, cucumber, and rice.
funFacts: Kajang is a Selangor town known for Malay satay shops.
The sauce is peanut, so this satay is not nut-free.
variations: Beef or goat satay uses the same sauce family and a different meat temperature.
A Singapore hawker satay is a different stall, even when the sauce is also peanut.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless chicken thighs, cut in small pieces
steps: Toss the chicken with lemongrass, turmeric, coriander, salt, and oil. Refrigerate it. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Serve with the peanut sauce. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Indonesian Sate Kambing
culture: Madurese and East Javanese grill cooks who sell goat satay with sweet soy
flavor: Goat skewers glazed with sweet soy, with a little chili heat at the edge.
history: Sate kambing is goat satay, strongly associated with Madura and East Java, where it is grilled on small skewers and brushed with sweet soy. Surabaya is a city where that Madurese grill is easy to find. Kecap manis, the sweet soy, usually contains wheat as well as soy. The goat is cut in small whole pieces, not minced; it is a different satay from a peanut-heavy chicken satay.
background: Madurese cooks and East Javanese stalls grill goat this way. Sweet soy is the glaze. There is no peanut in this recipe, and there is no dairy. The wheat is in the kecap manis.
whyItTastes: Goat is sharper than chicken, and sweet soy caramelizes on the edges so the sharpness has a glossy counterweight. Chili in the glaze warms it without hiding the meat. A peanut sauce would pull it toward a different satay. Here the soy glaze is the point.
authenticTouch: Brush the glaze near the end. If it goes on at the start, the sugar burns before the goat is cooked.
method: Season goat chunks, grill them on skewers, and brush them with kecap manis once the meat is nearly done.
served: Eat the skewers with rice, cucumber, and a little extra chili if you want it hotter.
funFacts: Sate kambing from Madura and East Java is goat, often finished with sweet soy.

variations: A peanut sauce is served with some Javanese satay and would add peanut. This glaze does not.

name: Balinese Sate Lilit
culture: Balinese cooks who press minced seafood onto lemongrass stalks
flavor: Minced fish and shrimp with coconut, lime leaf, and chili, grilled on lemongrass.
history: Sate lilit is a Balinese skewer of minced seafood pressed around a stalk, often lemongrass, and grilled. Coconut, chili, lime leaf, and shallot are mixed into the mince. It is temple-offering food and also everyday food in Balinese homes and warungs. The fish and shrimp are cooked until opaque; this is a seafood satay, not the pork spit of babi guling.
background: Balinese cooks shape this mince by hand around the stalk. There is fish and shrimp. Coconut milk is not dairy. There is no peanut and no wheat in the mix. It is a different Balinese fire from the spit-roasted pig.
whyItTastes: Coconut fat keeps the mince moist, and lime leaf and chili perfume it. Lemongrass used as the skewer shares a little of its oil with the paste as it grills. The result is aromatic and richer than a plain fish cake, which is why the stalk is part of the dish and not only a stick.
authenticTouch: Press the mince on firmly and oil your hands. A loose coating falls into the grate.
method: Mix fish and shrimp with coconut and spice, press the paste onto lemongrass stalks, and grill until the seafood is opaque.
served: Eat the skewers hot, with rice and a little extra lime.
funFacts: Sate lilit is minced seafood pressed onto a stalk, a Balinese grill.

name: Balinese Babi Guling
culture: Hindu Balinese cooks who season a pig for feast days and for the shops that sell it afterward
flavor: Pork with turmeric, lemongrass, garlic, and chili, cooked until it can be sliced or pulled.
history: Babi guling is spit-roasted pig in Hindu Balinese cooking, prepared for temple ceremonies and family rites and also sold in shops, especially around Gianyar. The spice paste is turmeric, lemongrass, chili, garlic, and other aromatics rubbed into the meat. A whole pig on a spit is the ceremony and the shop version. This page uses a pork shoulder at home and says so; it is not a ceremony, and it is not a joke about the feast.
background: Hindu Balinese cooks tend this pork for important days, and specialist shops roast it for people who are not holding a rite that week. The home shoulder is a substitute. Candlenut in the paste is a tree nut. There is no dairy and no wheat.
whyItTastes: Turmeric and lemongrass perfume the fat, and chili warms the paste that steams inside the meat. A long cook softens the shoulder after it is already safe to eat. On a real spit the skin crackles over coals. A home oven can still give you the spice and the tender pork, which is the part a cook can reach without the ceremony.
authenticTouch: Rub the paste into deep cuts. A paint of spice on the outside leaves the center plain.

funFacts: Babi guling is spit-roasted pig in Hindu Balinese feast cooking.

name: Lombok Ayam Taliwang
culture: Sasak cooks on Lombok who grill chicken under a very hot chili paste
flavor: Grilled chicken covered in a very hot chili paste with garlic and candlenut.
history: Ayam taliwang is grilled chicken from Taliwang, in West Lombok, now cooked across the island and in Mataram. The paste is built on a large amount of hot chili, with garlic, shrimp paste, and candlenut. It is meant to be extra-hot. Sasak cooks grill the chicken and often fry or grill it again with more paste; this is a home grill of that Lombok chicken.
background: Lombok cooks, Sasak kitchens in particular, make this chili paste for chicken. Shrimp paste is shellfish. Candlenut is a tree nut. The chicken has to be cooked through. It is not a mild coconut curry.
whyItTastes: The chili is the dish. Garlic and shrimp paste make the paste savory under the heat, and candlenut thickens it. Grilling dries the paste onto the skin so it tastes toasted, not like a boiled sauce. A mild marinade would miss why Taliwang is famous.
authenticTouch: Seed some of the chilies only if you must. Putting the chilies in and then sweetening the paste turns it into a different chicken.

served: Eat it with rice and extra paste on the side for people who want still more heat.
funFacts: Ayam taliwang is named for Taliwang in West Lombok and is known for its heat.

variations: A second brush of paste near the end is how some cooks deepen the crust.

name: Malaysian Ikan Bakar
culture: Malaysian coastal cooks who grill fish and serve it with sambal
flavor: Charcoal-grilled fish with a hot sambal of chili, lime, and shrimp paste.
history: Ikan bakar means grilled fish, and in Malaysia it is a coastal meal: a whole fish or a large piece, cooked over charcoal and eaten with sambal. The east coast, including Terengganu, grills a great deal of fish this way. The sambal here uses chili, lime, and shrimp paste. It is not a fried fish and not a coconut curry; the flesh is cooked until it flakes.
background: Coastal Malay cooks and grill stalls sell ikan bakar wrapped in banana leaf or set straight on the grate. Shrimp paste in the sambal is shellfish, and the fish is fish. There is no wheat and no peanut in this sambal.
whyItTastes: Oily or firm coastal fish can take a hot sambal and a smoky grate. Shrimp paste adds a savory depth that chili alone does not have, and lime keeps the sauce sharp. The banana leaf, when you have one, steams the spice onto the skin. Without it, the grill still chars the fish, which is the bakar part.
authenticTouch: Oil the grate and do not flip a delicate fish more than once. The sambal can go on after the first side has set.
