served: Eat the fish with rice and the sambal spooned on at the table.
funFacts: Ikan bakar is grilled fish, a coastal Malaysian meal rather than a curry.
Shrimp paste in the sambal is a shellfish ingredient.
variations: Banana leaf around the fish is common when the leaf is sold. Parchment is only a wrapper, not a leaf.
A milder chili makes a gentler sambal. This one is hot.

name: Kelantan Ayam Percik
culture: Kelantanese cooks who grill chicken and baste it with a coconut-chili sauce
flavor: Grilled chicken basted with a coconut sauce of lemongrass, chili, and turmeric.
history: Ayam percik is a Kelantan grilled chicken, basted with a coconut-milk sauce while it cooks. Lemongrass, chili, garlic, and turmeric flavor that sauce. Kota Bharu and the villages around it are the place the dish is tied to. The chicken is grilled, not boiled in the sauce; coconut milk is not dairy, and this recipe leaves out shrimp paste and nuts.
background: Kelantanese cooks grill the chicken and brush the sauce on so it clings and browns. There is chicken in the dish, and no peanut, candlenut, dairy, or wheat in this written sauce. The heat is medium.
whyItTastes: Coconut milk, reduced on the skin, tastes toasted and slightly sweet, and lemongrass and turmeric keep it fragrant. Chili warms the baste. If the sauce only sits in a bowl, you miss the grilled crust that makes percik different from a coconut stew.
authenticTouch: Baste in thin layers. A thick flood of sauce puts the fire out and peels off.

served: Eat it with rice and a little of the remaining sauce.
funFacts: Ayam percik is Kelantan grilled chicken with a coconut baste.

variations: Shrimp paste is used by some cooks and would add shellfish. It is not in this pot.

name: Cebu Lechon
culture: Cebu cooks who turn a whole pig on a spit for feasts, and home cooks who roast a shoulder instead
flavor: Slow-roasted pork with salt, garlic, lemongrass, and a crackled skin if the heat allows it.
history: Cebu lechon is a whole pig cooked on a spit, seasoned with salt and stuffed with aromatics such as lemongrass, garlic, and spring onion. It is feast food in Cebu, at family events and in specialist shops. A home kitchen that cannot turn a whole pig can roast a pork shoulder with the same seasoning. That shoulder is a home substitute, and it should be labeled as one; it is not the whole Cebu spit.
background: Cebu cooks are known for a simply seasoned lechon, with the herbs inside the pig rather than a heavy glaze. This page uses a shoulder. There is no dairy and no wheat in the seasoning. The liver sauce is a separate dish.
whyItTastes: Salt and a long cook make the pork taste like pork, and lemongrass and garlic inside the meat perfume the drippings. On a spit the skin blisters over coals. A home oven can still brown a shoulder and keep the Cebu seasoning, which is the part you can do without a whole animal and a pit crew.
authenticTouch: Salt the meat, not only the skin. A salty crust over bland pork is not the Cebu seasoning.

name: Filipino Inihaw Liempo
culture: Filipino backyard cooks who grill pork belly over charcoal
flavor: Grilled pork belly with soy, calamansi, garlic, and a sour dip.
history: Inihaw na liempo is Filipino grilled pork belly. Inihaw means grilled, and liempo is the belly. Home cooks and roadside grills in Manila marinate it with soy sauce, calamansi or vinegar, and garlic, then cook it over charcoal. Soy sauce brings soy and, in ordinary brands, wheat; the belly is a whole cut, rested after it reaches temperature; it is not a whole lechon.
background: Filipino cooks grill belly for family meals and small stands. The marinade has soy and wheat. There is no dairy. A vinegar dip is served at the table so each person can sour the slice.
whyItTastes: Belly is fat and meat in layers, so a hot grill crisps the fat while the lean stays juicy. Soy and calamansi season that fat with salt and acid. Garlic chars at the edge. The dip is sharp on purpose, because the meat is rich.
authenticTouch: Score the skin side lightly and watch for flare-ups. Burning the fat black makes the belly bitter.

name: Bacolod Chicken Inasal
culture: Bacolod cooks in Negros who grill chicken with vinegar, annatto, and lemongrass
flavor: Tangy grilled chicken with annatto oil, garlic, lemongrass, and cane vinegar.
history: Chicken inasal is grilled chicken from Bacolod, on the island of Negros. The marinade uses vinegar, garlic, lemongrass, pepper, and annatto oil, which stains the meat a warm color. It is a city dish of Bacolod, cooked on open grills and in homes. The chicken is cooked through; this recipe does not add soy sauce, so the written marinade has no wheat.

name: Filipino Inihaw Bangus
culture: Filipino cooks, especially in Pangasinan, who grill stuffed milkfish
flavor: Grilled milkfish stuffed with tomato, onion, and calamansi.
history: Inihaw na bangus is grilled milkfish, a Filipino fish often stuffed with tomato, onion, and calamansi before it meets the charcoal. Dagupan, in Pangasinan, is a city tied to bangus farming and to this fish on the grill. The flesh is cooked until it flakes. This stuffing has no soy sauce, so the written fish has no wheat; it is a grill, not a fried bangus.
background: Pangasinan cooks and home grills across the Philippines stuff and grill milkfish. There is fish, and no dairy and no wheat in this recipe. Tomato and onion go inside the cavity. The skin needs a hot grate and a careful turn.
whyItTastes: Milkfish is rich, and tomato, onion, and calamansi steam inside the cavity and cut that richness. The grill chars the skin. A stuffing that is only salt would miss the fresh contrast Filipino cooks put in the fish.
authenticTouch: Dry the skin well before it hits the grate. Wet skin sticks and tears, and the stuffing falls out.
method: Stuff a cleaned milkfish with tomato, onion, and calamansi, then grill it until the center flakes.
served: Eat it with rice and a vinegar dip. Watch for bones. Milkfish has many.
funFacts: Bangus is milkfish. Dagupan in Pangasinan is closely tied to the fish.
The usual grill stuffing is tomato, onion, and a sour citrus.
variations: A spoon of soy sauce in the stuffing is common and would add soy and wheat. This stuffing has none.
Fillets work if a whole fish is not sold. Cook them to the same fish temperature.
ingredients: 1 whole milkfish, about 2 pounds, cleaned and scaled
3 tablespoons calamansi juice, or lime juice
steps: Dry the fish. Fill the cavity with tomato, onion, calamansi juice, salt, and pepper. Rub the skin with oil. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill and oil the grate. Tie the cavity closed with a skewer or kitchen string if it gapes. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve hot, and mind the bones. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Filipino Isaw
culture: Filipino street cooks who clean and grill chicken intestines on skewers
flavor: Grilled chicken intestine, salted, with a sour vinegar dip.
history: Isaw is chicken intestine, cleaned and grilled on skewers, sold at Filipino street grills and night markets. It is ordinary offal cooking, the same family of thrift as other organ meats on those carts. The intestines have to be fresh, cleaned, and cooked to a poultry-offal temperature. A vinegar dip is the usual partner; this page treats the work as cooking, with a thermometer, and without a joke.
background: Street cooks in Manila and other cities grill isaw beside pork and chicken parts. Buy the intestines fresh from a butcher, preferably already turned and cleaned. There is no wheat and no dairy in this seasoning. Cook them the day you buy them.
whyItTastes: Chicken intestine is rich and slightly chewy when it is cooked through and not burned. Salt and a little garlic season it, and the vinegar dip cuts the fat the way it does for grilled pork. Charcoal adds a light bitterness at the edge. The point is a clean, hot skewer, not a dare.
authenticTouch: Rinse the intestines in cold water until the water runs clean, and discard any that smell sour. Do not try to rescue a spoiled tray with extra garlic.
method: Clean fresh chicken intestines, simmer them until they reach a safe temperature, then grill them on skewers to brown.
served: Eat them hot with a vinegar dip and rice.
funFacts: Isaw is chicken intestine grilled on a skewer, a regular item at Filipino street grills.
Poultry offal is cooked to 165°F (74°C), the same floor as other chicken.
variations: Pork intestine is a different skewer and is not this recipe.
A chili in the vinegar dip adds heat. The skewers here are mild.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds fresh chicken intestines, from a butcher, cleaned
water to cover, for the simmer
steps: Rinse the intestines in several changes of cold water. If the butcher has not cleaned them, turn them and rinse until the water is clear. Discard any that smell spoiled. The offal is still raw. Cook poultry offal to 165°F (74°C).
Put them in a pot with salt, garlic, and water to cover. Simmer until a skewer through the thickest part reads 165°F (74°C). Drain. Cook poultry offal to 165°F (74°C).

Thread them on skewers, brush very lightly with vinegar and pepper, and grill over a hot fire only until browned. Check that they are still at 165°F (74°C) before serving. Cook poultry offal to 165°F (74°C).
Serve hot with a vinegar dip. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry offal to 165°F (74°C).

name: Singapore Hawker Satay
culture: Malay and other hawker cooks in Singapore who grill satay in a cooked-food center
flavor: Chicken skewers with turmeric and a peanut sauce, from a hawker stall rather than a roadside shed.
history: Singapore hawker satay is grilled meat on skewers sold in hawker centers, often by Malay cooks, with a peanut sauce, cucumber, and rice cakes on the side. It shares a family with Malaysian satay and it is not the same stall: a hawker-center satay in Singapore is a city cooked-food-center plate, not a Kajang shop. Peanut in the sauce means the dish is not nut-free. The chicken is cooked through.
background: Hawker cooks work in public cooked-food centers with many stalls side by side. This recipe is the chicken satay and its peanut sauce. There is no dairy. The peanut is the allergen that keeps it off a nut-free table.
whyItTastes: Turmeric, cumin, and lemongrass season small pieces of chicken, and a hot grate browns them quickly. The peanut sauce is sweet, spicy, and rich, which is the spoonful that defines the plate. Eating it at a hawker table, with the sauce in a small bowl, is the Singapore setting. The spice is close to Malay satay because the cooks who built those stalls cooked in that tradition.
authenticTouch: Serve the sauce beside the skewers, not cooked onto them from the start. Early peanut sauce burns.
method: Marinate chicken, grill it on skewers to a poultry temperature, and serve a separate peanut sauce.
served: Eat the skewers with the sauce, cucumber, and onion.
funFacts: Singapore hawker satay is a cooked-food-center plate. It is not a Kajang satay shop.
Peanut sauce means the dish is not nut-free.
variations: Beef and mutton satay are sold at the same stalls and need their own temperatures.
Ketupat, a rice cake, is a common side when you can get it.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless chicken thighs, cut in small pieces
steps: Toss the chicken with lemongrass, turmeric, cumin, salt, and oil. Refrigerate it. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Simmer the peanuts, sugar, chili, and coconut milk with a pinch of salt until thick. This is a hawker-style sauce, served on the side. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Skewer the chicken and grill until the center reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve it rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Serve with the peanut sauce. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Cambodian Sach Ko Ang
culture: Cambodian grill cooks who skewer beef and serve it with lime and a dipping sauce
flavor: Beef skewers with lemongrass, fish sauce, and sugar, served with lime.
history: Sach ko ang is Cambodian grilled beef, often cut small and cooked on skewers over charcoal. Lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, and a little sugar are a usual marinade in Phnom Penh grill stands. The beef is whole muscle, rested after it reaches temperature. It is street and restaurant food, eaten with rice or as a snack with a sour dip.
background: Cambodian cooks grill this beef at street fires and in open-front shops. Fish sauce contains fish. There is no wheat and no dairy in the marinade. The pieces stay in chunks, not a mince.
whyItTastes: Lemongrass and a little sugar brown on a hot skewer, and fish sauce salts the beef. Lime at the table brightens the crust. The grill is quick because the pieces are small, so the outside chars before the center dries out.
authenticTouch: Cut the beef across the grain and keep the pieces even. Mixed sizes finish at different times.
method: Marinate beef with lemongrass, garlic, and fish sauce, grill it on skewers, and rest it.
served: Eat it with lime, rice, and a small dish of fish sauce with chili if you want heat.
funFacts: Sach ko ang is Cambodian grilled beef, often sold on skewers.
Lemongrass and fish sauce are a usual marinade at Phnom Penh grills.
variations: A prahok dip is served by some cooks and would add more fermented fish. It is not in this marinade.
Short ribs can be used if they are cut small enough to grill as a whole cut.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds beef sirloin, cut in 1-inch chunks
steps: Toss the beef with lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, sugar, oil, and pepper. Refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The beef is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread it on skewers. Heat a grill until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the beef 3 minutes. Serve with lime. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Yangon Pork Skewers
culture: Street cooks in Yangon who grill small pork skewers with turmeric, garlic, and chili
flavor: Pork skewers stained with turmeric, garlic, and chili, grilled over a street fire.
history: In Yangon, street grills sell small pork skewers seasoned with turmeric, garlic, and chili and cooked over charcoal. This page uses that plain description. It does not invent a classical or royal name for a street skewer. The pork is cut in pieces, grilled, and rested like other whole pork; it is everyday food from a city sidewalk, seasoned the way those stalls season it.
background: Yangon street cooks thread the pork and grill it to order. Turmeric colors the meat. There is no wheat, dairy, or peanut in this mix. The name on this page is a description of the food and the city, not a fake classical title.
whyItTastes: Turmeric, garlic, and chili make a direct, savory crust, and pork fat browns over a small charcoal fire. The skewers are small, so the seasoning stays on the surface where you taste it. A long sauce would turn them into a different dish. The street version is the spice and the grill.
authenticTouch: Use a light hand with the oil. Too much oil drips, flares, and coats the pork in soot.
method: Toss pork chunks with turmeric, garlic, and chili, grill them on skewers, and rest them.
served: Eat them hot, with rice and a lime wedge.
funFacts: These are Yangon street pork skewers seasoned with turmeric, garlic, and chili.
The page uses a plain name for a street food and does not invent a classical title.
variations: A hotter chili is easy to add. This batch is medium.
Chicken pieces would need a poultry temperature. This skewer is pork.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds pork shoulder, cut in 1-inch chunks
steps: Toss the pork with turmeric, garlic, chili, salt, oil, and lime juice. Refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Thread the chunks on skewers. Heat a charcoal grill. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Cantonese Char Siu
culture: Cantonese roast-shop cooks who lacquer pork and hang it in a hot oven
flavor: Sweet-salty pork with a lacquered edge, five spice, and a little char.
history: Char siu means fork-roast. Cantonese cooks hung strips of pork from forks in a roast oven so the fat dripped away and the glaze lacquered the meat. Roast shops in Guangzhou and other Cantonese cities still sell it that way. This recipe uses a rack in a home oven and says so; it is not a restaurant fork oven; soy sauce and hoisin bring soy and wheat.
background: Cantonese roast shops are the home of this pork. A home oven on a rack borrows the glaze and not the oven. There is pork, soy, wheat, and sesame oil. There is no dairy. The meat is a whole cut, rested, not a pulled shoulder.
whyItTastes: Sugar and maltose brown into a lacquer, and five spice and fermented seasoning sit in that sweetness. Hanging the meat in a shop oven dries the surface. A home rack still lets heat reach all sides, which is closer to a fork roast than a pork sitting in a puddle of sauce. The wheat in the soy sauce is part of that Cantonese seasoning, not an accident.
authenticTouch: Put the pork on a rack over a pan. If it braises in the glaze, the lacquer never forms.
method: Coat pork strips with a soy, hoisin, and five-spice glaze and roast them on a rack in a home oven until the center is done, then rest them.
served: Slice it and eat it with rice and a few greens.
funFacts: Char siu means fork-roast, from the forks that held the pork in a Cantonese oven.
A home oven on a rack is a substitute and should be called a home oven.
variations: Fermented red bean curd deepens the color and still counts as soy.
Honey in the glaze would add honey. This glaze uses sugar and maltose.
ingredients: 2.5 pounds boneless pork shoulder, cut into long strips
steps: Stir the soy sauce, hoisin, maltose or sugar, five spice, sesame oil, garlic, and neutral oil. Coat the pork and refrigerate it. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Heat a home oven to 425°F (220°C). Set the pork on a rack over a pan. This is a home oven, not a Cantonese fork oven. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Roast, turning once, until the center of the thickest strip reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes, then slice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Cantonese Siu Yuk
culture: Cantonese roast-shop cooks who blister pork skin over a fierce oven
flavor: Roast pork belly with blistered skin, salt, and five spice under the crackling.
history: Siu yuk is Cantonese roast pork with a blistered skin, sold in the same roast shops as char siu. The skin is dried, salted, and hit with high heat so it bubbles, while five spice seasons the meat underneath. A restaurant oven runs hotter and drier than most homes. This is a home-oven version, labeled as such; the belly is a whole cut and is rested; there is no soy sauce in this rub, so the written recipe has no wheat.
background: Cantonese roast shops hang or rack the belly until the skin crackles. Home cooks can dry the skin and use a hot oven. There is pork, salt, and five spice. There is no dairy and no wheat in this rub.
whyItTastes: Dry skin plus high heat makes the crackling, and the fat underneath bastes the meat. Five spice stays under the skin so it does not burn. Salt is the main seasoning, which is why siu yuk tastes less sweet than char siu from the same shop. A covered braise would soften the skin and miss the dish.
authenticTouch: Dry the skin, uncovered, in the refrigerator before you roast it. Wet skin steams and stays leathery.
method: Salt and dry a pork belly, rub five spice on the meat side, and roast it in a home oven until the center is done and the skin has blistered.
served: Chop it into pieces and eat it with rice and mustard greens.
funFacts: Siu yuk is Cantonese roast pork bought for the crackling skin.
This rub has no soy sauce, so the written recipe has no wheat.
variations: A final few minutes of very high heat helps the bubbles if the skin is already dry.
A spoon of vinegar rubbed on the skin is used by some cooks to help it dry.
ingredients: 2.5 pounds skin-on pork belly, in one slab
1/2 teaspoon salt, extra, for the skin
steps: Score the skin in a tight crosshatch, cutting into the skin and not deep into the meat. Rub vinegar and the extra salt on the skin. Rub five spice and the remaining salt on the meat side only. Refrigerate the slab uncovered for at least 4 hours so the skin dries. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Heat a home oven to 450°F (230°C). Set the belly on a rack, skin side up. This is a home oven, not a roast-shop oven. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Roast until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C) and the skin has blistered. If the meat is ready and the skin is pale, give it a short hotter blast and check the temperature again. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes, then chop it. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Home-Roast Peking Duck
culture: Beijing restaurant kitchens that lacquer duck, and home cooks who roast a simpler bird
flavor: Roast duck with lacquered skin, eaten with scallion, cucumber, and wheat pancakes.
history: Peking duck is a Beijing restaurant duck, lacquered and roasted so the skin crisps, then carved and eaten with scallion, cucumber, and a sweet sauce in thin wheat pancakes. Restaurant ovens and a long drying step are part of that service. This is a simplified home roast. It is not a restaurant ticket, and it does not reproduce a hung duck oven; the duck still has to reach a poultry temperature; the pancakes and hoisin contain wheat, and hoisin contains soy.
background: Beijing restaurants built the dish guests travel for. A home oven can roast a duck and serve the same accompaniments if you say it is the home roast. There is duck, wheat, soy, and sesame in the sauce. There is no dairy.
whyItTastes: Duck skin renders and crisps when the bird is dried and roasted in open heat, and the fat underneath keeps the meat rich. Scallion and cucumber are cool against that fat. A sweet wheat-and-soy sauce ties the pancake to the skin. A restaurant oven does this more evenly. The home bird can still taste of rendered duck, which is the center of the plate.
authenticTouch: Dry the skin. A wet duck steams, and the pancake then wraps soft skin, which is a different meal.
method: Dry a duck, roast it in a home oven until the thigh is done, and serve the carved meat with scallion, cucumber, hoisin, and wheat pancakes.
served: Slice skin and meat and eat them in small wheat pancakes with scallion, cucumber, and hoisin.
funFacts: Peking duck is a Beijing restaurant roast. This page is a simplified home roast, not a restaurant ticket.
Duck is poultry and is cooked to 165°F (74°C).
variations: A day of uncovered drying in the refrigerator improves the skin.
Store-bought wheat pancakes are the wrapper. Rice wrappers would be a different dish.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons maltose or brown sugar, dissolved in 1/2 cup hot water
steps: Pat the duck dry. Rub the cavity with salt and five spice. Paint the skin with the maltose or sugar water. Refrigerate the duck uncovered so the skin dries. The duck is still raw. Do not leave it on the counter to dry. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Heat a home oven to 375°F (190°C). Set the duck on a rack. This is a home roast, not a restaurant ticket and not a hung oven. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Roast until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve the duck rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Rest it 10 minutes, carve it, and serve with pancakes, scallion, cucumber, and hoisin stirred with the sesame oil. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Xinjiang Lamb Skewers
culture: Uyghur street-grill cooks in Xinjiang who season lamb with cumin and chili
flavor: Lamb skewers with salt, cumin, and dried chili, grilled over a street fire.
history: In Xinjiang, Uyghur street grills cook small lamb skewers over charcoal and dust them with cumin and dried chili. The seasoning is salt, cumin, and chili, put on as the meat cooks. This page is about that street food. It is not a political essay, and it does not treat the cooks as a symbol of anything except the grill they run; the lamb is whole muscle and is rested.
background: Uyghur grill cooks in cities such as Ürümqi sell these skewers from small fires. There is no yogurt marinade and no wheat on the meat. The fat, the cumin, and the chili are the dish.
whyItTastes: Cumin and dried chili bloom in lamb fat over a hot fire, which is why the spices are added to the cooking meat and not only stirred into a raw paste. Salt keeps the lamb direct. Small pieces char at the edge and stay juicy inside. A sweet glaze would hide the cumin that marks this street grill.
authenticTouch: Sprinkle the cumin and chili in more than one pass while the skewers turn. One heavy dump falls off into the coals.
method: Skewer small pieces of lamb, grill them hot, and season them with salt, cumin, and chili as they cook, then rest them.
served: Eat the skewers as soon as they have rested, while the cumin is still fragrant.
funFacts: Uyghur street grills in Xinjiang season lamb skewers with cumin and chili.
The spices go on the meat over the fire, not only in a marinade bowl.
variations: A hotter chili flake is a personal shake at the stall. The written amount is medium.
Fat from the lamb tail is sometimes interleaved. A fatty shoulder chunk is the home stand-in.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless lamb, cut in small chunks with a little fat
steps: Toss the lamb with oil and half the salt. Thread it on flat skewers. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a charcoal grill until it is very hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Grill, turning, and dust with the remaining salt, cumin, and chili as the fat starts to render. Cook until the center of the thickest chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the lamb 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Cantonese Roast Goose
culture: Cantonese roast-shop cooks in Hong Kong who hang goose until the skin lacquered
flavor: Roast goose with a seasoned skin, five spice, and a savory gravy from the pan.
history: Cantonese roast goose is a roast-shop bird, especially associated with Hong Kong shops that also sell char siu and siu yuk. The goose is seasoned, lacquered, and roasted until the skin is glossy and the meat is cooked through. A shop oven is not a home oven. This page roasts a goose, or a large goose leg if a whole bird will not fit, in a home oven and says so; goose is poultry and is cooked to 165°F (74°C); soy sauce in the seasoning brings soy and wheat.
background: Hong Kong roast shops are the reference for this goose. The home oven is a substitute. There is goose, soy, and wheat. There is no dairy. It is not a festival story this page cannot source. It is a roast-shop technique brought into a kitchen.
whyItTastes: Goose is fattier than a chicken, so a hot oven renders the skin and leaves the meat rich. Five spice and soy season that fat. In a shop the bird hangs and the skin dries evenly. At home a rack over a pan collects the fat and still browns the skin, which is the taste you can reach without the shop.
authenticTouch: Prick the skin, not the meat, so fat can escape and the skin can crisp. Deep holes dry the flesh.
method: Season a goose with five spice and soy, roast it on a rack in a home oven, and cook it until the thigh reaches a poultry temperature.
served: Chop it into pieces and eat it with rice and a spoon of the defatted pan juices.
funFacts: Cantonese roast goose is a roast-shop bird strongly associated with Hong Kong.
Goose is cooked to 165°F (74°C), like other poultry.
variations: A whole goose leg is the right size when a whole bird will not fit the oven. Check the temperature at the bone line without touching bone.
Maltose in the glaze is traditional in some shops. This recipe uses a soy and five-spice rub.
ingredients: 1 whole goose, about 8 pounds, or 2 large goose legs
steps: Prick the skin all over. Rub the goose with soy sauce, five spice, salt, and oil, and put the garlic in the cavity. Refrigerate it uncovered if you have time to dry the skin. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The goose is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Heat a home oven to 375°F (190°C). Set the goose on a rack. This is a home oven, not a Hong Kong roast shop. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Roast until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone. Do not serve it rare. Pour off fat as it collects so the pan does not scorch. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest 10 minutes, then chop. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Korean Samgyeopsal
culture: Korean cooks who grill pork belly at the table and wrap it in lettuce
flavor: Plain grilled pork belly, salty at the table, wrapped with lettuce and a dab of sauce.
history: Samgyeopsal is Korean grilled pork belly, cut in strips and cooked at the table or on a restaurant grill. The meat is often unmarinated, so the fat and the grill do the work, and people wrap the slices in lettuce with garlic, chili, and ssamjang. It is a widespread Korean meal, not a single-restaurant invention this page will pretend to date. The belly is a whole cut and is rested; this recipe does not put wheat or sesame into the meat.
background: Korean homes and barbecue restaurants grill belly this way, often on a round grill in the middle of the table. The written meat is only pork, salt, and pepper. Sauce and sesame live in the ssamjang, which is a separate bowl. There is no dairy.
whyItTastes: Belly browns in its own fat on a hot grill, and an unmarinated slice tastes like pork and fire rather than like a soy glaze. Lettuce, raw garlic, and a fermented chili paste then season each bite differently. That is why the meat is left plain: the table does the seasoning after the grill.
authenticTouch: Cut the strips so they can be turned with chopsticks or tongs, and pour off fat if the grill floods. A pool of fat boils the meat.
method: Salt pork belly lightly, grill it until it is cooked and rested, and serve it for lettuce wraps.
served: Wrap slices in lettuce with garlic and ssamjang. Put rice on the table.
funFacts: Samgyeopsal is pork belly grilled in strips, often with no marinade.
The seasoning at the table is lettuce, garlic, and a paste, not a glaze on the raw meat.
variations: A quick dip in sesame oil and salt is common and would add sesame. The meat here is only salt and pepper.
Pork neck, moksal, is the leaner neighbor of this belly.
ingredients: 2 pounds pork belly, sliced into grillable strips
1 head green lettuce, leaves separated and washed
4 garlic cloves, sliced, for the table
steps: Pat the belly dry and season it with salt and pepper. The pork is still raw. Keep the lettuce and garlic separate. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill or a table grill pan until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center of each strip reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes. Serve it with lettuce and garlic. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Korean Beef Galbi
culture: Korean cooks who marinate beef short ribs and grill them over charcoal
flavor: Beef short ribs in a sweet soy marinade with pear, garlic, and sesame.
history: Galbi is Korean grilled beef short rib. The meat is often cut thin across the bone, marinated with soy sauce, sugar, garlic, sesame, and grated pear or apple, then grilled. It is a restaurant and home barbecue dish. Ordinary soy sauce contains wheat, and sesame oil contains sesame; the rib meat is a whole cut, cooked and rested; it is not pork belly, and it is not the thinly sliced bulgogi from a different cut.
background: Korean barbecue tables grill galbi over charcoal or on a gas grill set into the table. The marinade has soy, wheat, and sesame. There is no dairy. Pear tenderizes and sweetens the surface.
whyItTastes: Soy, sugar, and pear brown quickly on a thin rib, and sesame oil perfumes the fat. Garlic stays sharp. The bone and the thin cut mean a short grill, so the marinade becomes a crust instead of a boiled sauce. A thick uncut roast would not taste like galbi even with the same bowl.
authenticTouch: If the ribs are thick, ask the butcher to cut them flanken-style, across the bones. Thick English-cut ribs are a different grill.
method: Marinate thin beef short ribs in soy, pear, garlic, and sesame, then grill them and rest them.
served: Cut the meat off the bone if you like and eat it with rice, lettuce, and ssamjang.
funFacts: Galbi is beef short rib, often cut thin across the bone for the grill.
Ordinary soy sauce in the marinade contains wheat.
variations: Pork galbi uses the same marinade family on pork ribs and still needs a whole-pork temperature and rest.
A gluten-free soy sauce would change the wheat allergen. This uses ordinary soy sauce.

Heat a grill until it is hot. Drain extra marinade off the meat so it does not steam. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the ribs 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Korean Bulgogi
culture: Korean home cooks who slice beef thin, marinate it, and grill it quickly
flavor: Very thin beef, sweet and savory with soy, pear, and sesame, seared in a minute.
history: Bulgogi is thinly sliced Korean beef, marinated with soy, sugar, garlic, sesame, and often grated pear or onion, then grilled or seared. The name means fire meat. Home cooks and restaurants both make it, and the thin cut is the modern everyday form. It is not galbi, which is a short rib, and it is not an ancient court menu this page will invent a date for; ordinary soy sauce contains wheat; the beef is a whole muscle, sliced thin, and it is still rested after it reaches temperature.
background: Korean households keep this marinade for celebrations and ordinary dinners. There is beef, soy, wheat, and sesame. There is no dairy. The slices are thin enough to cook in a very short time on a hot pan or grill.
whyItTastes: A thin slice takes the marinade on almost all of its surface, so the soy and pear taste are in every bite. Sesame oil aromatically browns in the fat. High heat sears it before the juice floods the pan. That wide seasoned surface is why bulgogi tastes sweeter and softer than a thick grilled steak with the same soy.
authenticTouch: Freeze the beef for 30 minutes so you can slice it thin. Thick slices are a steak, not bulgogi.
method: Slice beef thin, marinate it in soy, pear, garlic, and sesame, and grill or sear it quickly, then rest it.
served: Eat it with rice, lettuce, and a little ssamjang.
funFacts: Bulgogi is thinly sliced beef. Galbi is the short-rib grill.
The sweet soy marinade covers almost the whole surface because the slices are thin.
variations: A grill pan on the stove is a fair home method. A charcoal grill is the outdoor one.
Onion in the marinade is as common as pear. This recipe uses both.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds beef sirloin, sliced very thin
steps: Mix the soy sauce, pear, onion, sugar, garlic, sesame oil, and sesame seeds. Coat the beef and refrigerate it for 20 minutes. The beef is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill or a heavy pan until it is very hot. Cook in batches so the meat sears. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Cook until the slices reach at least 145°F (63°C). Thin meat moves fast. Check it. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the beef 3 minutes. Serve with rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Korean Grilled Mackerel
culture: Korean coastal cooks who salt mackerel and grill it
flavor: Oily mackerel, salted and grilled until the skin blisters and the flesh flakes.
history: Godeungeo-gui is Korean grilled mackerel, a common fish on coastal tables and in homes. Busan, a port city, lands a great deal of it. The fish is salted and grilled, sometimes after a short cure in salt, and it is eaten with rice and a sharp banchan. This recipe salts it the same day and grills it; it is not a dried fish and not a curry; the flesh is cooked until it flakes.
background: Korean cooks grill mackerel because the fish is oily enough to stand up to high heat. There is fish, salt, and a little oil. There is no wheat, dairy, or sesame in this written fish. Serve kimchi beside it if you want the sour contrast.
whyItTastes: Mackerel fat crisps under the skin on a hot grate, and salt is enough to season an oily fish. A light char adds bitterness that keeps the richness in check. Rice and a fermented vegetable on the side do the rest. A heavy sauce would cover the point of a simple salt grill.
authenticTouch: Score the skin so the thick part cooks before the tail burns. Oil the grate. Mackerel sticks.
method: Salt mackerel and grill it until the center is opaque and flakes.
served: Eat it with rice, a lemon or a grill lemon is less usual than a Korean table of kimchi, so put kimchi beside it.
funFacts: Godeungeo-gui is salted grilled mackerel, a regular Korean fish.
Busan is a port city where this fish is part of the local catch.
variations: A light sprinkle of sesame oil after grilling would add sesame. It is not in this recipe.
Fillets cook faster than a butterflied whole fish. Use the thermometer either way.
ingredients: 4 mackerel fillets, or 2 small whole mackerel, split open
steps: Pat the fish dry, rub it with salt and oil, and let it stand in the refrigerator for 15 minutes. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill and oil the grate well. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve hot with rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Korean Gopchang
culture: Korean grill cooks who clean beef intestine and cook it on a hot plate
flavor: Grilled beef intestine with salt, garlic, and sesame oil, chewy and rich.
history: Gopchang is beef small intestine, grilled at Korean barbecue restaurants that specialize in offal. The pieces are cleaned, often briefly boiled, and then grilled with salt, garlic, and sesame oil. It is a regular part of Korean meat grilling, cooked for the texture and the fat, not as a stunt. Beef offal is cooked and rested; sesame oil means sesame is in the dish.
background: Specialist restaurants and some home cooks grill gopchang on a hot plate. Buy it fresh and cleaned from a butcher you trust. There is beef and sesame. There is no wheat and no dairy in this seasoning. Cook it the day you buy it.
whyItTastes: Intestine is mostly texture and fat. A hot grill browns the fat, salt and garlic season it, and sesame oil adds a toasted smell. A short boil before the grill renders some of the richness and makes the pieces easier to cook evenly. Dipping sauces at a Korean table then cut that fat with salt and chili.
authenticTouch: Trim and rinse carefully, and skip any piece that smells sour. Strong spice will not fix a bad piece of offal.
method: Rinse cleaned beef intestine, simmer it until it is safe, then grill it with garlic and sesame oil and rest it.
served: Eat it hot with a salt-and-pepper dip, lettuce, and rice.
funFacts: Gopchang is beef small intestine grilled at Korean offal barbecue restaurants.
Beef offal is cooked to at least 145°F (63°C) and rested.
variations: Pork intestine is a different dish. This page is beef.
A chili paste on the side raises the heat. The grill seasoning here is mild.
ingredients: water to cover, for the simmer
steps: Rinse the intestine in cold water and trim anything discolored. If it smells spoiled, discard it. The offal is still raw. Cook beef offal to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Simmer it in water until the thickest part reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Drain and cool it enough to handle. Cook beef offal to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Toss it with sesame oil, garlic, salt, and pepper. Grill over high heat until browned, and confirm the center is still at least 145°F (63°C). Cook beef offal to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest it 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook beef offal to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Korean Moksal
culture: Korean grill cooks who cook pork neck at the table, a different cut from the belly
flavor: Grilled pork neck, meatier than belly, with salt and a lettuce wrap.
history: Moksal is Korean grilled pork neck, cooked at the same kind of table grill as samgyeopsal and often left unmarinated. The neck is leaner than the belly and still has enough fat to grill well. It is a cut choice, not a different cuisine. People wrap the slices in lettuce with garlic and ssamjang; the pork is a whole cut and is rested; this seasoning is salt and pepper only.
background: Korean barbecue restaurants list moksal beside belly so a table can choose a meatier slice. There is no soy, wheat, sesame, or dairy on the meat in this recipe. The paste, if you use it, is the separate ssamjang.
whyItTastes: Neck has more chew and a porkier taste than a fatty belly strip, and a hot grill browns it without a sweet marinade. Salt is enough because the wrap brings garlic and fermented chili afterward. Treating it as belly with a new name would miss why people order the neck.
authenticTouch: Slice it against the grain after it rests. The neck is tougher than belly if you cut it with the grain.
method: Salt pork neck and grill it to a whole-pork temperature, rest it, and slice it for wraps.
served: Wrap the slices in lettuce with garlic and ssamjang, and eat them with rice.
funFacts: Moksal is pork neck. Samgyeopsal is pork belly. They share a grill and they are different cuts.
The neck is often grilled without a marinade.
variations: A sesame-oil dip would add sesame. It is not on the meat here.
A thin marinade of apple and onion is used by some cooks. This page keeps the cut plain.
ingredients: 4 garlic cloves, sliced, for the table
steps: Pat the pork dry and season it with salt and pepper. The pork is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill or a table grill until it is hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning, until the center reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the pork 3 minutes, then slice it against the grain. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Japanese Yakitori
culture: Tokyo yakitori cooks who grill small chicken skewers over charcoal
flavor: Chicken thigh on small skewers, salted, with a clean charcoal taste.
history: Yakitori is chicken grilled on small skewers over charcoal, a specialty of Japanese shops and of alley stands in Tokyo. Salt and a sweet soy tare are the two usual finishes. This page is the salted chicken, shio, so the meat itself has no soy sauce. The tare is a separate sauce; the chicken is cooked through; thigh is the usual piece because it stays juicy on a small skewer.
background: Yakitori cooks tend a narrow charcoal grill and turn the skewers constantly. There is chicken, salt, and a little oil. There is no wheat and no dairy on this salted version. It is not the ground chicken tsukune and not a whole roast bird.
whyItTastes: Small pieces of thigh pick up charcoal bitterness at the skin and stay juicy inside. Salt lets that chicken taste show. A tare would add sweetness and soy. Serving the salt skewers plain is how a shop shows the fire. The tare can still sit on the counter for people who want it.
authenticTouch: Use flat or thin skewers and leave a little space between pieces. Packed meat steams.
method: Salt chicken thigh pieces, skewer them, and grill them over charcoal until the center is done.
served: Eat the skewers hot. A tare can be offered from the separate recipe if you want the sweet glaze.
funFacts: Yakitori shops usually offer both salt and a sweet soy tare.
This page is the salted skewer, so the chicken itself has no soy sauce.
variations: Scallion between the chicken pieces is a common skewer called negima.
Brushing on tare makes the other classic finish and adds soy and wheat.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless chicken thighs, cut in bite-size pieces
steps: Toss the chicken with salt and oil. Thread it on skewers with a piece of scallion here and there. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Heat a charcoal grill until the coals are hot and the grate is close to them. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Grill, turning often, until the center of the thickest piece reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve it rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest a minute and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Japanese Yakiniku
culture: Restaurant cooks in Japan, including Zainichi Korean grill restaurants, who cook meat at the table
flavor: Thin beef and onion grilled at the table, with a soy dip.
history: Yakiniku is the Japanese restaurant practice of grilling meat at the table. It grew in the twentieth century in the hands of Korean cooks in Japan, including Zainichi Korean communities, and it became a widespread night out in cities such as Osaka and Tokyo. It is not an ancient Japanese court dish. The meat is often beef, grilled in small pieces and dipped; ordinary soy sauce in the dip contains wheat; the beef is a whole cut, cooked and rested.
background: Yakiniku restaurants set a grill in the table and bring raw plates the guests cook. That restaurant form is twentieth-century and tied to Korean cooks in Japan. This home version grills beef and onion and serves a soy dip. There is beef, soy, wheat, and sesame. There is no dairy.
whyItTastes: Small pieces of beef brown fast, and a sweet-salty dip seasons them after the grill, so you taste both the meat and the sauce. Onion sweetens on the same grate. The style traveled through Korean restaurants in Japanese cities, which is why the dip resembles Korean barbecue sauces and the setting is a Japanese restaurant grill. Calling it a court recipe would erase that history.
authenticTouch: Cook a few pieces at a time. A crowded table grill steams the beef and misses the char.
method: Grill thin beef and onion over high heat, rest the beef, and dip it in a soy and sesame sauce.
served: Eat it with rice and the dip, straight from the grill.
funFacts: Yakiniku restaurants in Japan grew in the twentieth century among Korean cooks, including Zainichi Korean communities.
It is a restaurant grill. It is not an ancient Japanese court dish.
variations: Tongue, liver, and other cuts are on a full restaurant menu. This page is beef and onion.
Beef offal, if you add it, needs its own temperature and a careful source.
steps: Stir the soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, garlic, and sesame seeds for the dip. Keep it separate from the raw beef. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill or a table grill. The beef is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill the beef and onion until the center of the beef reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
