name: Japanese Unagi Kabayaki
culture: Japanese eel shops that split eel and grill it with a sweet soy glaze
flavor: Grilled eel with a sweet soy glaze, rich and lacquered.
history: Unagi no kabayaki is eel split open, grilled, and brushed with a sweet sauce of soy, mirin, and sugar. Eel shops in cities such as Hamamatsu specialize in it. The eel is fully cooked, not raw. Ordinary soy sauce contains wheat; this is a home grill of fillets, not a claim that a kitchen can copy a specialist shop's long-reduced sauce pot; the fish reaches 145°F (63°C).
background: Japanese eel restaurants grill kabayaki to order and serve it over rice. There is fish, soy, and wheat. There is no dairy. Buy eel from a fishmonger who has already filleted it if you do not have the skill to do that safely.
whyItTastes: Eel is fatty, so a sweet soy glaze clings and caramelizes instead of soaking in and disappearing. Mirin adds aroma and shine. The grill browns the sauce in a second pass, which is the kabayaki smell. Plain salted eel is a different dish. The sweetness is the point of this one.
authenticTouch: Glaze in thin coats and grill between coats. One thick layer slides off and burns in the coals.
method: Grill eel fillets, brush them with a soy, mirin, and sugar sauce, and cook them until the flesh is opaque.
served: Serve the eel over rice, with the extra sauce spooned on.
funFacts: Kabayaki is eel opened flat and grilled with a sweet soy sauce.
Hamamatsu is one of the Japanese cities known for eel shops.
variations: A shop sauce reduced for years is their pot. This sauce is made the day you cook.
Sansho pepper on the side is a usual fragrance and is not in the glaze.
steps: Simmer the soy sauce, mirin, sugar, and sake for 3 minutes. The eel is still raw. Keep the sauce separate. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill and oil it lightly. Grill the eel, skin side first if the skin is on. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Brush with sauce and continue until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Brush once more at the end. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve over rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Japanese Sanma Shioyaki
culture: Japanese home and izakaya cooks who salt-grill Pacific saury in autumn
flavor: Salt-grilled Pacific saury, oily and direct, with grated daikon and lemon.
history: Sanma no shioyaki is Pacific saury grilled with salt. In Japan it is an autumn fish, grilled at home and in small restaurants when the catch is in. Kesennuma and other ports land it. The method is salt and a hot grill, not a soy glaze; the flesh is cooked until it flakes; grated daikon and a citrus wedge are the usual plate, to cut the oil.
background: Home cooks salt the fish and grill it under a broiler or over a grate. There is fish and salt, and no wheat, dairy, or sesame in this recipe. It is a seasonal salt grill, not kabayaki.
whyItTastes: Saury is very oily, so salt and char are enough. The skin crisps and the oil bastes the flesh. Grated daikon is sharp and watery, which cuts that oil the way a heavy sauce would not. Out of season the fish is simply harder to find. The recipe does not change.
authenticTouch: Salt it shortly before grilling and dry the skin. A long salty soak makes a different, firmer fish.
method: Salt Pacific saury and grill it until the center is opaque, then serve it with grated daikon.
served: Eat it with rice, grated daikon, and a lemon or sudachi wedge.
funFacts: Sanma shioyaki is Pacific saury grilled with salt, an autumn fish in Japan.
Grated daikon is served beside it to cut the oil.
variations: A broiler can stand in for a grill if you watch the skin. Name it as a broiler.
Mackerel can be salted the same way when saury is not in the market. It is a different fish.
ingredients: 4 whole Pacific saury, cleaned, or 4 saury fillets
1 cup grated daikon radish, for serving
steps: Pat the fish dry and salt both sides. Refrigerate it for 15 minutes. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill and oil the grate lightly. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve with grated daikon and lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Hokkaido Jingisukan
culture: Hokkaido restaurant and home cooks who grill lamb and vegetables on a domed pan
flavor: Lamb and onion seared on a hot domed pan, salted, with a little cabbage.
history: Jingisukan takes its name from Genghis Khan. In Japan that name is twentieth-century marketing, tied to lamb grilling in Hokkaido, not a recipe from the Mongol court. Sapporo restaurants cook lamb and vegetables on a domed metal pan at the table. Sheep farming on Hokkaido is the local supply; the lamb is a whole cut, cooked and rested; this recipe salts the meat and does not use soy sauce.
background: Hokkaido cooks grill lamb this way in specialty rooms and at home on the same style of pan. A heavy skillet is the honest substitute if you do not own the dome. There is lamb and vegetables. There is no wheat and no dairy in this version. It is not a Mongol khorkhog.
whyItTastes: Lamb fat seasons the onion and cabbage on the same pan, and salt keeps the meat direct. The dome, when you have one, lets fat run to the rim where the vegetables sit. The name is a sales name from the twentieth century. The taste is Hokkaido lamb and a hot pan, which does not require a story about a medieval army.
authenticTouch: Cook the lamb in batches on a very hot pan. If you fill the pan, the meat boils in onion water.
method: Sear lamb and vegetables on a domed pan or a heavy skillet, and rest the lamb.
served: Eat the lamb and vegetables together, with rice.
funFacts: The name Jingisukan, from Genghis Khan, is twentieth-century marketing in Japan.
It is a Hokkaido lamb grill. It is not a recipe from the Mongol court.
variations: A soy dip is served in some Sapporo shops and would add soy and wheat. This pan is salted.
A heavy skillet stands in for the domed pan.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds boneless lamb, sliced 1/4 inch thick
steps: Season the lamb with salt and pepper. The lamb is still raw. Have the vegetables ready beside the pan. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a domed jingisukan pan or a heavy skillet until it is very hot. Oil it lightly. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Sear the lamb and vegetables until the center of the lamb reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the lamb 3 minutes. Serve with the vegetables and rice. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Japanese Tsukune
culture: Yakitori cooks who grind chicken, bind it, and grill it on skewers
flavor: Grilled chicken meatballs on skewers, seasoned with soy, ginger, and scallion.
history: Tsukune is ground chicken shaped on a skewer and grilled at a yakitori shop. It sits beside the salted thigh skewers, and it is often finished with tare. Ground chicken has to be cooked through, to a higher temperature than a chop. This recipe puts a little soy sauce and egg in the mix, so it contains soy, wheat, and egg; it is a Tokyo yakitori-shop meatball, cooked the day it is mixed.
background: Yakitori cooks grill tsukune over the same charcoal as the other skewers. There is chicken, egg, soy, and wheat. There is no dairy. It is not a beef kebab and not a cured sausage.
whyItTastes: Grinding the chicken spreads soy, ginger, and scallion through the bite, and the grill browns the outside. Egg helps the mince hold. A tare, if you brush it on, adds sweetness at the end. The charcoal bitterness on the crust is the shop flavor, which a boiled meatball does not have.
authenticTouch: Keep the ovals small and press out air pockets. A thick ball burns outside and stays under temperature inside.
method: Mix ground chicken with egg, soy, and ginger, shape it on skewers, and grill it until the center reaches the temperature for ground poultry.
served: Eat the skewers hot, with rice. A tare from the separate recipe can be brushed on if you want it glossy.
funFacts: Tsukune is the ground-chicken skewer at a yakitori shop.
Ground poultry is cooked to 165°F (74°C).
variations: Cartilage is mixed into some shop tsukune for crunch. It is left out here.
A brush of tare at the end adds more soy and wheat, which are already in the mix.
steps: Mix the chicken, egg, soy sauce, ginger, scallions, salt, and oil. The chicken is still raw. Keep it cold. Cook ground poultry to 165°F (74°C).
Shape small ovals on skewers. Heat a grill. Cook ground poultry to 165°F (74°C).
Grill, turning, until the center of each oval reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve ground chicken rare. Cook ground poultry to 165°F (74°C).
Rest a minute and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground poultry to 165°F (74°C).

name: Taiwanese Grilled Sausage
culture: Night-market cooks in Taiwan who grill a sweet fresh pork sausage
flavor: A slightly sweet pork sausage, grilled, with garlic and five spice.
history: Taiwanese grilled sausage is a night-market pork sausage, a little sweet, cooked over charcoal and often served on a stick. Taipei night markets made it a standard snack. This recipe mixes fresh pork and cooks it the same day. It uses no curing salt and it is not hung to dry; soy sauce in the mix contains soy and wheat; it is a Taiwanese sausage; it does not need a China label to be itself.
background: Night-market grills in Taiwan cook these links to order. The written mix is fresh ground pork, sugar, soy sauce, and five spice. There is no dairy. Do not cure it. Cook it through as ground meat.
whyItTastes: Sugar and a little soy caramelize on the casing, and five spice perfumes the fat. Grilling beats boiling because the skin browns and the sweetness concentrates. Sticky rice is sometimes tucked into a split sausage. The sausage itself is the sweet pork and the fire.
authenticTouch: Form small, even logs if you are not using casings. A huge log will brown before the center is safe.
method: Mix fresh pork with sugar, soy sauce, and five spice, shape links or logs, and grill them the same day until the center is done.
served: Eat them hot, with garlic and a little raw cabbage if you want a sharp bite beside the sweetness.
funFacts: The sweet grilled pork sausage is a Taiwanese night-market food.
This mix is cooked the day it is made. It is not a cured sausage.
variations: A purchased fresh Taiwanese sausage can be grilled if you still check the center temperature.
Gluten-free soy sauce would remove the wheat. This recipe uses ordinary soy sauce.
steps: Mix the pork, soy sauce, sugar, rice wine, garlic, five spice, salt, and oil. Do not add curing salt. Refrigerate the mix and cook it the same day. The pork is still raw. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Shape eight small logs. Heat a grill to medium. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Grill, turning, until the center of each log reaches 160°F (71°C). Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).
Rest 3 minutes. Serve hot and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook ground meat to 160°F (71°C).

name: Mongolian Khorkhog
culture: Mongolian cooks who stew lamb with vegetables in a heavy closed pot
flavor: Lamb cooked in a closed pot with onion, carrot, and potato, salty and rich.
history: Khorkhog is a Mongolian lamb dish cooked in a closed container with vegetables. The traditional method heats stones and puts those stones in the pot with the meat. This recipe does not do that. It uses a heavy covered pot on the stove; do not heat found river rocks for this dish; rocks from a river can hold water and can crack or explode when they are put in a fire; stones are mentioned here only as the traditional method you are not reproducing with found rocks; the lamb is a whole cut and is cooked at least to a safe temperature.
background: Mongolian cooks make khorkhog for gatherings, in a large metal churn or a heavy pot in the older method. The home version on this page is the covered pot, without stones. There is lamb, onion, carrot, and potato. There is no wheat and no dairy in the pot.
whyItTastes: A closed pot keeps lamb fat with the vegetables, so the potato and carrot taste of the meat and the lamb stays moist. Salt is the seasoning. The traditional stones were a way to carry heat inside the pot. A heavy lid on a stove holds that steam without the risk of a wet rock exploding. The dish is the lamb and the vegetables, not the hazard.
authenticTouch: Use a heavy pot with a tight lid and do not lift it every few minutes. The steam is the cook.
method: Salt lamb and vegetables in a heavy covered pot and cook them until the lamb is at least at a safe temperature and tender. Do not add rocks.
served: Eat the lamb, potato, carrot, and onion together, with the juices in the pot.
funFacts: Traditional khorkhog uses heated stones in the pot. This recipe uses a heavy covered pot and no stones.
Do not heat found river rocks. They can hold water and can crack or explode.
variations: A covered pot set beside a controlled outdoor fire is still a pot, not a bag of hot rocks.
Mutton is used where it is the local sheep. Treat it as a whole cut and check the temperature.
ingredients: 3 pounds boneless lamb shoulder, in large chunks
steps: Put the lamb, salt, pepper, onion, carrot, potato, and water in a heavy pot with a tight lid. The lamb is still raw. Do not add stones of any kind. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Cover the pot and set it over medium heat on a stove. This is the home method. The traditional stone method is not what you are doing, and found river rocks can explode. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Cook until the center of the thickest lamb chunk reaches at least 145°F (63°C). You may continue until the lamb is tender if the temperature stays at or above that mark. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

Rest the lamb 3 minutes in the pot with the lid off the heat. Serve the meat and vegetables. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Korean Ssamjang
culture: Korean cooks who stir a fermented paste for lettuce wraps
flavor: Salty, hot, and savory, from soybean paste, chili paste, garlic, and sesame.
history: Ssamjang is the Korean paste set on the table for ssam, the lettuce wraps that hold grilled pork or beef. It is stirred from doenjang, a fermented soybean paste, and gochujang, a fermented chili paste, with garlic, sesame oil, and a little onion. Many commercial gochujang brands contain wheat. The paste is not cooked; it is a condiment for the grill, not the meat itself.
background: Korean homes mix ssamjang by the spoon for a barbecue meal. There is soy, wheat, and sesame. There is no meat, dairy, egg, or honey in this bowl, so it is vegetarian. Keep it cold. It is not a canned preserve.
whyItTastes: Doenjang is salty and deeply savory, and gochujang adds chili and a little sweetness. Sesame oil rounds the ferments, and raw garlic keeps the paste sharp against grilled fat. On a Korean table it seasons a plain slice of belly or neck after the fire, which is why those meats can be cooked with only salt.
authenticTouch: Stir it thick enough to sit on a lettuce leaf. A watery mix runs off the meat and seasons the table instead.
method: Stir doenjang, gochujang, garlic, onion, and sesame oil into a thick paste.
served: Put a little on a lettuce leaf with grilled meat and rice.
funFacts: Ssamjang is the wrap paste for Korean grilled meat, made from doenjang and gochujang.
Many gochujang brands contain wheat, so this paste is not assumed gluten-free.
variations: A spoon of honey is common and would add honey and remove the vegan label. This paste uses no honey.
More gochujang makes it hotter. This balance is medium.
ingredients: 2 tablespoons gochujang (chili paste; many brands contain wheat)
steps: Stir the doenjang, gochujang, garlic, onion, sesame oil, sesame seeds, and water into a thick paste. There is no meat in the bowl.
Taste for salt. Doenjang is already salty, so do not add salt first.
Cover it and refrigerate it until the meat is ready. Do not leave garlic sitting in oil at room temperature.
Serve cold or cool with lettuce wraps. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Yakitori Tare
culture: Yakitori cooks who keep a sweet soy glaze for the skewers
flavor: A sweet, salty soy glaze with mirin, reduced until it clings to a skewer.
history: Tare is the sweet soy glaze brushed on yakitori. Shop pots are sometimes reduced again and again in the same pan. This recipe makes a fresh tare from soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar, with no chicken bones in the pot, so the written sauce has no meat. Some restaurant tare is simmered with chicken, and that would be a different bowl; ordinary soy sauce contains wheat; it is a glaze, not a table salsa.
background: Tokyo yakitori shops brush tare on in the last moments so the sugar does not burn. This pan has soy and wheat, and no meat, dairy, egg, or sesame. It is vegetarian. Cool it and keep it cold. It is not a canned sauce.
whyItTastes: Soy, mirin, and sugar reduce into a lacquer that tastes sweet and salty at once, and a little bitterness from the grill sticks to it. Brushed on late, it glazes the chicken instead of boiling it. A shop pot that has held years of drippings is deeper. A fresh pot is still the same idea: soy and sugar meeting charcoal.
authenticTouch: Reduce it until it coats a spoon. A thin soy splash runs off the skewer and flares in the coals.
method: Simmer soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar until the glaze clings, then cool it.
served: Brush it on grilled chicken in the last minute, or serve a spoon of it beside salted yakitori.
funFacts: Yakitori tare is a sweet soy glaze. Salt is the other usual finish.
This pot has no chicken in it. Some shop sauces are reduced with meat and would not be vegetarian.
variations: A strip of ginger in the pot is a common aroma. It is left out here.
Brushing the tare on earlier burns the sugar. Add it at the end.
steps: Stir the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and water in a small pan. There is no meat in this tare.
Simmer it over medium heat until it thickens enough to coat a spoon, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Cool it. Do not brush a boiling glaze onto food you are about to serve without letting the chicken finish at a safe temperature first.
Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a week. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Filipino Lechon Sarsa
culture: Filipino feast cooks who grind a liver sauce for roast pork
flavor: A savory brown sauce of chicken liver, vinegar, garlic, and bread crumbs.
history: Lechon sarsa is the liver sauce served with Filipino roast pig, including Cebu lechon. Liver is simmered with vinegar, garlic, sugar, and bread crumbs, then blended. The liver has to reach 165°F (74°C) because this recipe uses chicken liver, which is poultry offal. Bread crumbs contain wheat; it is a sauce for the pork, not the pork itself, and it is cooked and refrigerated, not canned.
background: Feast cooks in the Philippines make a pot of sarsa while the pig or the shoulder roasts. There is chicken liver and wheat. There is no dairy and no peanut. Cook the liver through. Do not serve it pink.
whyItTastes: Liver gives the sauce a deep savory taste, and vinegar keeps it from feeling heavy on fatty pork. Sugar rounds the vinegar, and bread crumbs thicken the pot so it sits on the meat. Garlic is the aroma. Without the vinegar it would taste muddy. The acid is why it belongs with lechon.
authenticTouch: Brown the liver first so the sauce tastes roasted, then add the vinegar. Boiling raw liver in vinegar from the start tastes harsh.
method: Cook chicken liver to 165°F (74°C) with garlic and vinegar, then blend it with bread crumbs into a sauce.
served: Spoon it over chopped roast pork, or serve it in a bowl beside the meat.
funFacts: Lechon sarsa is a liver sauce for Filipino roast pork.
Chicken liver in this pot is cooked to 165°F (74°C).
variations: Pork liver is used in some pots. This page uses chicken liver so the temperature is the poultry-offal one.
A gluten-free crumb would change the wheat allergen. These are wheat bread crumbs.
steps: Trim the livers. They are still raw. Heat the oil and cook the onion and garlic for a minute. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. Cook the liver to 165°F (74°C).
Add the livers and cook them until the center of the thickest piece reaches 165°F (74°C). Do not serve the liver pink. Cook the liver to 165°F (74°C).

Add vinegar, sugar, salt, bread crumbs, and water. Simmer 5 minutes. Blend until mostly smooth, and check that the sauce is hot and the liver was already at 165°F (74°C). Cook the liver to 165°F (74°C).
Serve warm with pork. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. This is not a canning recipe. Cook the liver to 165°F (74°C).

name: Toyomansi Dip
culture: Filipino cooks who mix soy sauce and calamansi as a dip for grilled food
flavor: Salty soy cut with sour calamansi, with garlic and black pepper.
history: Toyomansi is a Filipino dipping sauce of toyo, soy sauce, and kalamansi, the small citrus squeezed over grilled pork, chicken, and fish. It is a table mix, stirred when the grill is going, not a cooked glaze. Ordinary soy sauce contains soy and wheat. This bowl has no meat and no chili, so the heat stays at none; chili can be added by the person eating.
background: Filipino tables set this dip beside inihaw. There is soy and wheat, and no meat, dairy, egg, or peanut. It is vegetarian. Use it the day you mix it, and refrigerate it. It is not a preserve.
whyItTastes: Soy is salty and dark, and calamansi is sharply sour, so together they cut grilled fat the way a heavy gravy would not. Garlic and black pepper make it more than salted citrus. On a Manila grill table it is the spoonful that finishes liempo, chicken, or fish without covering the charcoal taste.
authenticTouch: Squeeze the calamansi at the last hour. The juice dulls if the dip sits all day in a warm kitchen.
method: Stir soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, and black pepper.
served: Put it in a small bowl and let people spoon it over grilled meat or fish.
funFacts: Toyomansi is soy sauce and calamansi, a standard Filipino grill dip.
Ordinary soy sauce contains wheat.
variations: Sliced chili makes it hot. The written dip has none.
Lime juice can stand in when calamansi is not sold. The dip will be a little less fragrant.
ingredients: 1/4 cup calamansi juice, or lime juice
steps: Stir the soy sauce, calamansi or lime juice, garlic, pepper, and water. There is no meat in the dip.
Taste it. If the soy is very salty, add another spoon of citrus, not more salt.
Refrigerate it until the grill is ready. Do not leave garlic sitting out in the sauce for hours.
Serve cool, the same day. Refrigerate leftovers and use them within a few days. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Australian Lamb Chops
culture: Australian home cooks who grill lamb chops over a hot fire
flavor: Lamb chops with salt, garlic, and lemon, seared over a hot grill.
history: Lamb chops are a standard Australian grill, cooked at home and at club barbecues in towns such as Albury and across the sheep country inland. The chop is a whole muscle from a loin or a leg steak, salted, grilled, and rested. Australia raises a large share of the world's sheep, and the chop is one ordinary way that meat is cooked. There is no chili in this recipe; the seasoning is salt, garlic, and lemon.
background: Australian home cooks grill these chops on a gas or charcoal grate. There is lamb, and no wheat, dairy, or peanut in the seasoning. It is a weeknight grill, not a ceremonial roast and not a minced kebab.
whyItTastes: A hot grate browns the fat cap on a chop, and salt is enough for lamb that already tastes like lamb. Garlic and lemon sit on that crust. Inland sheep country produces the meat. The fire is what turns a raw chop into dinner, without a long marinade to hide it.
authenticTouch: Take the chops out of the refrigerator before they hit a ripping-hot grate, and do not press them flat. Pressing squeezes out the juice you rested them to keep.
method: Salt lamb chops, grill them over high heat, and rest them.
served: Eat them with lemon, a green salad, and potatoes.
funFacts: Lamb chops are an ordinary Australian home grill.
The chop is a whole cut and is rested after it leaves the fire.
variations: Rosemary on the side is common. It is not required for the salt and fire to work.
A thicker leg steak needs more time than a thin loin chop. Use the thermometer.
steps: Rub the chops with salt, pepper, garlic, and oil. Refrigerate them until the grill is hot. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The lamb is still raw. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Heat a grill until the grate is very hot. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Grill, turning once, until the center of the thickest chop reaches at least 145°F (63°C). Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.
Rest the chops 3 minutes. Serve with lemon. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb, or goat to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes.

name: Australian Grilled Prawns
culture: Australian coastal cooks who grill prawns quickly over a hot fire
flavor: Prawns with garlic, lemon, and parsley, grilled until the flesh turns opaque.
history: Grilled prawns are a coastal Australian meal, especially along the tropical north and the Queensland shore around Cairns, where prawns are landed and cooked the same day when the catch allows. The method is a hot grate, garlic, lemon, and a short cook. Shellfish are done when they are opaque. This is a plain coastal grill, seasoned and taken off the heat before the prawns toughen.
background: Coastal home cooks and fish shops grill large prawns in the shell or peeled. There is shellfish, and no wheat, dairy, or chili in this recipe. Parsley and lemon finish the plate. Cook them the day you buy them.
whyItTastes: Prawns are sweet, and a short blast of heat sets that sweetness before it turns rubbery. Garlic browns in the oil, and lemon cuts the richness. The tropical coast supplies the prawns. The recipe does not need a slogan. It needs a hot grate and a thermometer or a clear look at opaque flesh.
authenticTouch: Pull them as soon as they turn opaque. Extra time on a hot grate is how sweet prawns become dry.
method: Toss prawns with garlic, oil, and lemon, and grill them until the flesh is opaque.
served: Eat them with lemon, parsley, and bread only if you want wheat on the side. The prawns themselves have none.
funFacts: Large prawns are a coastal Australian grill, cooked briefly over high heat.
They are ready when the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
variations: Leaving the shells on protects the meat and makes them messier to eat.
A pinch of chili is a personal addition. This batch has none.
ingredients: 1.5 pounds large prawns, peeled and deveined
steps: Toss the prawns with oil, garlic, salt, and lemon juice. Refrigerate them for 15 minutes. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. The prawns are still raw. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Heat a grill until the grate is hot. Oil it lightly. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Grill, turning once, until the flesh is opaque and the center reaches 145°F (63°C). Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Toss with parsley and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook shellfish until the flesh is opaque and reaches 145°F (63°C).

name: Grilled Australian Barramundi
culture: Northern Australian cooks who grill barramundi, a coastal and river fish
flavor: Barramundi fillets with salt, lemon, and a little oil, grilled until they flake.
history: Barramundi is a well-known Australian fish, Lates calcarifer, caught and farmed in the north, including waters around Darwin. Fillets are grilled with salt and lemon and served the day they are cooked. The flesh is mild and is ready when it reaches 145°F (63°C) and flakes. This is a northern Australian fish grill, not a chili curry and not a smoked whole fish.
background: Cooks in Darwin and other northern towns grill barramundi at home and in small restaurants. There is fish, salt, and lemon. There is no wheat, dairy, or peanut. The skin can stay on if you like it crisp.
whyItTastes: Barramundi is mild and a little sweet, so salt, lemon, and a hot grate are enough. The skin, if you leave it on, crisps and protects the flesh. Overcooking dries it, which is why the temperature matters more than a heavy sauce. The northern coast and the rivers are where the fish lives. The plate is that fish and the fire.
authenticTouch: Oil the grate and start skin-side down if the skin is on. Turning too soon tears the fillet.
method: Salt barramundi fillets and grill them until the center is opaque and flakes.
served: Eat the fish with lemon, a salad, and potatoes or rice.
funFacts: Barramundi is an Australian coastal and river fish, often grilled as a fillet.
The flesh is cooked to 145°F (63°C), until it flakes.
variations: A whole small fish can be grilled if it fits the grate. Check the temperature at the thickest point.
Dill or parsley on top is a fresh finish and does not change the cook.
steps: Pat the fillets dry and rub them with salt, pepper, and oil. The fish is still raw. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Heat a grill and oil the grate. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Grill, turning once, until the center reaches 145°F (63°C) and the flesh is opaque and flakes. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.
Serve with lemon and parsley. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) until it is opaque and flakes.

name: Australian Damper
culture: Settler camp cooks and stockmen who baked a simple wheat bread in the coals
flavor: A plain wheat loaf, crusty outside and dense inside, with salt and the smell of the fire.
history: Damper is a settler campfire bread of wheat flour, water, and salt, baked in the coals or in a camp oven by stockmen and colonial travelers. Aboriginal Australians milled native seeds and cooked their own breads long before wheat arrived. This recipe is the settler loaf. It is not an Aboriginal ceremony, and it is not a native-seed bread; Ballarat and other inland camps are one historical setting for flour-and-water bread on a journey; the loaf contains wheat.
background: Settler cooks mixed this dough when yeast and an oven were not at hand. There is wheat, salt, and water. There is no dairy, egg, or meat, so the written loaf is vegan. It is camp bread, not a ritual. Do not present it as Aboriginal food.
whyItTastes: Wheat flour and salt, cooked against heat, make a dense crumb and a hard crust. A campfire dries the outside faster than a kitchen oven and can leave a little ash and smoke. That plainness is the point of a ration bread. Native-seed breads have their own flavors and their own makers. This one tastes of wheat and fire because that is what the settlers carried.
authenticTouch: Cook it through. A handsome crust can hide a wet center of raw dough. Break one open and look.
method: Mix flour, salt, and water, shape a round, and bake it in a camp oven or a home oven until the center is cooked.
served: Tear it and eat it warm with grilled meat or with nothing but salt.
funFacts: Damper is a settler campfire bread of wheat flour, water, and salt.
It is not an Aboriginal ceremony. Aboriginal Australians have their own breads from native seeds.
variations: A camp oven in the coals is the older method. A home oven is the kitchen method and should be named as an oven.
A spoon of dairy fat would change the loaf. This one uses water.
ingredients: 3 cups wheat flour, plus more for the bench
1 cup water, plus more if the dough is dry
steps: Stir the flour, salt, and baking powder. Add the water and mix a soft dough. There is no meat in this bread.
Shape a round loaf and dust it with flour. Heat a camp oven by a fire, or heat a home oven to 400°F (200°C) and call it an oven.
Bake until the crust is firm and the center is no longer wet dough, about 30 minutes. If you used a camp oven, keep the coals around it, not only under it, so the bottom does not burn.
Cool it a few minutes, then break it open. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours if the weather is hot. This is not a canning recipe.

name: Torres Strait Kup Murri
culture: Torres Strait Islander cooks who steam food in an earth oven for community gatherings
flavor: Chicken and sweet potato steamed with chili, garlic, and leaf, in a covered pot.
history: Kup murri is a Torres Strait earth oven: food layered with hot stones and leaves and covered so it steams. Torres Strait Islander cooks prepare it for community gatherings. A backyard pot is not that oven, and it is not a ceremony. This page uses a heavy covered pot with chicken, sweet potato, and chili, and it says so; the chicken is cooked to a poultry temperature; there is no raw cassava in the pot.
background: Torres Strait Islander families on islands such as Thursday Island have their own earth-oven practice. The written recipe is a home covered cook for people who are not holding that ceremony. There is chicken, and no wheat, dairy, or peanut. Treat the pot as dinner, not as the community oven.
whyItTastes: A closed pot steams chicken and sweet potato together, so the tuber takes on the meat juices and the chili and garlic perfume the steam. An earth oven does this against hot stones and leaves. The home pot can echo the steam and the seasoning. It cannot stand in for the gathering, and it should not be described as if it did.
authenticTouch: Keep the lid on. If you stir it often, you are boiling a stew, not steaming a closed cook.
method: Season chicken and sweet potato, seal them in a heavy covered pot, and cook until the chicken is done. Call this a home pot, not a ceremony.
served: Serve the chicken and sweet potato together, with the juices.
funFacts: Kup murri is a Torres Strait earth oven used for community gatherings.
A home covered pot is not that oven and is not a ceremony.
variations: Banana leaves can line the pot when they are sold. Parchment is only a liner.
Fish can replace chicken in some cooks and would need a fish temperature. This pot is chicken.
ingredients: 2 pounds sweet potato, peeled and cut in chunks
steps: Toss the chicken with onion, garlic, chili, salt, and oil. The chicken is still raw. Do not leave garlic in oil at room temperature. Put the chicken and sweet potato in a heavy pot with the water. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Cover the pot tightly. This is a home pot. It is not a Torres Strait ceremony and it is not an earth oven. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Cook over medium heat, lid on, until the thickest chicken piece reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone, and the sweet potato is tender. Do not serve the chicken rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest a few minutes and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Maori Hangi
culture: Maori cooks who steam food in a hangi, an earth oven, for gatherings on the marae
flavor: Chicken, sweet potato, and cabbage steamed in a covered pot, salty and soft.
history: A hangi is a Maori earth oven. Heated stones, baskets of meat and vegetables, and wet coverings steam the food in the ground, including at gatherings on the marae. Rotorua is one place visitors see public hangi. A backyard imitation is not a marae hangi; this page uses a heavy covered pot with chicken, kumara, and cabbage, and it names that limit; the chicken is cooked to a poultry temperature; do not dig a pit in a lawn and call it the ceremony.
background: Maori cooks run a hangi for hui and for manuhiri, the guests. The foods often include chicken, pork, kumara, potato, and cabbage. This pot uses chicken and vegetables only, so one temperature rules the meat. There is no wheat and no dairy. It is a home steam, not a marae hangi.
whyItTastes: Steam from a closed oven makes the chicken and the kumara taste of each other, without a hard crust. Cabbage sweetens in that steam. Stones and wet sacks in the ground hold the heat for hours at a real hangi. A covered pot on a stove can borrow the softness and cannot borrow the marae. The honesty is part of cooking it at home.
authenticTouch: Season the food before it goes in the pot. A hangi seasons the baskets, not the table afterward only.
method: Pack chicken, kumara, and cabbage in a heavy covered pot and cook until the chicken is done. Say plainly that this is not a marae hangi.
served: Serve the chicken, kumara, and cabbage together.
funFacts: A hangi is a Maori earth oven, including the one used for gatherings on the marae.
A backyard covered pot is not a marae hangi.
variations: Pork is common in a hangi and would need its own temperature if you add it. This pot is chicken.
Potato can sit beside the kumara. Keep the lid on either way.
ingredients: 2 pounds kumara or sweet potato, peeled and chunked
steps: Toss the chicken with onion, salt, and oil. Layer it with kumara and cabbage in a heavy pot. Add the water. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Cover the pot. A backyard imitation is not a marae hangi. Do not present this pot as one. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Cook over medium heat, lid on, until the thickest chicken piece reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone, and the kumara is tender. Do not serve the chicken rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest a few minutes and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Fijian Lovo
culture: Fijian cooks who steam meat and root vegetables in a lovo, an earth oven
flavor: Chicken steamed with coconut, garlic, and sweet potato, mild and rich.
history: A lovo is a Fijian earth oven, a pit of heated stones used for feasts, with meat, root vegetables, and sometimes a coconut parcel in leaves. This page is a home covered pot, not a full lovo and not a ceremony. Chicken, canned coconut milk, spinach in place of leaves that may not be sold, and sweet potato are the foods. There is no raw cassava; the chicken is cooked to a poultry temperature.
background: Fijian cooks prepare a lovo for community meals. The home pot borrows the coconut and the closed steam. There is chicken and coconut. Coconut milk is not dairy. There is no wheat and no peanut. Name the pot as a pot.
whyItTastes: Coconut milk and closed steam make the chicken rich, and sweet potato soaks up the juice. Garlic and a little chili perfume the pot. In a lovo the leaves and the stones add their own smell. At home the coconut and the chicken are the tastes you can actually make, without pretending the kitchen floor is a pit.
authenticTouch: Use canned coconut milk, shaken, and do not try to process raw cassava for this meal.
method: Cook chicken, sweet potato, spinach, and canned coconut milk in a covered pot until the chicken is done.
served: Serve the chicken, greens, and sweet potato with the coconut juices.
funFacts: A lovo is a Fijian earth oven. This page is a covered home pot, not a pit.
The recipe uses sweet potato and canned coconut milk, not raw cassava.
variations: Taro leaves can replace the spinach when a shop sells them as a food leaf, not a random garden leaf.
A little more chili makes the pot hotter. This one is mild.
ingredients: 1 pound sweet potato, peeled and chunked
steps: Put the chicken, coconut milk, sweet potato, spinach, garlic, chili, and salt in a heavy pot. Do not add cassava. The chicken is still raw. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Cover the pot. This is a home cook, not a Fijian lovo pit and not a ceremony. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

Cook over medium heat until the thickest chicken piece reaches 165°F (74°C), away from the bone, and the sweet potato is tender. Do not serve the chicken rare. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest a few minutes and serve. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Cook poultry to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, not touching bone.

name: Samoan Umu
culture: Samoan cooks who steam pork and coconut parcels in an umu, an earth oven
flavor: Pork shoulder steamed with canned coconut milk and spinach, rich and salty.
history: An umu is a Samoan earth oven, used for Sundays and family gatherings, with pork and parcels of coconut and leaves. This home pot uses canned coconut milk and spinach when taro leaves are not sold, and it does not use raw cassava. A covered pot is not an umu pit. The pork is a shoulder, cooked until it is safe and tender enough to slice.
background: Samoan cooks run an umu for household gatherings. This recipe is the home covered cook: pork, canned coconut, and spinach. There is no wheat and no dairy. Coconut is not a tree nut in this allergen list. Do not grate raw cassava into the pot.
whyItTastes: Pork fat and coconut milk are both rich, and a closed pot keeps them together so the greens taste savory. Taro leaves have a mineral taste. Spinach is the shop substitute and is milder, which is an honest swap when the leaf is not sold. The umu pit adds smoke and leaf. The pot still gives you the coconut pork that is the edible idea of the parcel.
authenticTouch: Shake the can of coconut milk so the fat is mixed through. A separated can makes a watery pot and a lump of coconut fat.
method: Cook a pork shoulder with canned coconut milk and spinach in a covered pot until it is safe and tender. Do not use raw cassava.
served: Slice the pork and serve it with the greens and the coconut juice.
funFacts: A Samoan umu is an earth oven. This recipe is a covered pot with canned coconut milk.
Spinach stands in for taro leaves when the leaves are not sold. Raw cassava is not used.
variations: Taro leaves can replace the spinach when you can buy them as food. Do not use an unknown garden leaf.
A Tongan umu uses different foods. It is a different page.
steps: Rub the pork with oil and salt. Put it in a heavy pot with onion, spinach, coconut milk, and water. Do not add cassava. The pork is still raw. Cook the pork to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).
Cover the pot. This is a home cook, not a Samoan umu pit. Cook the pork to at least 145°F (63°C) and rest 3 minutes. For meat you want to pull, continue to about 195–205°F (90–96°C).

history: A Tongan umu is an earth oven, used for Sunday meals and gatherings, and the foods are not the same as a Samoan umu. One Tongan parcel, lu sipi, cooks lamb with coconut and onion in leaves. name: Papua New Guinea Mumu
culture: Cooks in Papua New Guinea who steam food in a mumu, knowing the practice is not the same in every place
flavor: Chicken and sweet potato steamed with ginger and greens in a covered pot.
history: Mumu, in Papua New Guinea, is an earth-oven cook, and the practice differs by community. One village's leaves, meats, and stones are not a national recipe. This page does not pretend they are. It is a home covered cook of chicken, sweet potato, ginger, and greens, for a kitchen in Port Moresby or anywhere else; it is not a ceremony; there is no raw cassava; the chicken is cooked to a poultry temperature.
background: People across Papua New Guinea cook with earth ovens in ways that are local. A single written pot cannot represent them. This pot is chicken and sweet potato, with ginger. There is no wheat, dairy, or peanut. Call it a home covered cook.
whyItTastes: Ginger and closed steam scent the chicken, and sweet potato takes the juices. Greens wilt into the pot and keep it from tasting only of meat. A community mumu can include foods and timings this page will not universalize. The home pot tastes of the ingredients you actually put in it, which is the honest limit.
authenticTouch: Say that practices differ. Do not add a leaf you cannot name, and do not add raw cassava.
method: Cook chicken, sweet potato, ginger, and greens in a covered pot until the chicken is done. Treat it as a home cook, not as every mumu.

name: Vanuatu Laplap Packet
culture: Ni-Vanuatu cooks who grate a root, mix it with coconut, and bake it in leaves
flavor: Grated sweet potato and canned coconut milk, steamed in a packet until thick.
history: Laplap is a Vanuatu dish of grated starchy root mixed with coconut and cooked in leaves, often in an earth oven. This packet uses sweet potato and canned coconut milk.
